questions.stem: SLAKING of lime is the process in which:
options: Quicklime (calcium oxide) reacts with water to form hydrated lime (calcium hydroxide)
Hydrated lime absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and hardens
Limestone is heated in a kiln to drive off carbon dioxide
Lime putty is ground with sand to make mortar
questions.solution:
**QUICKLIME reacting with WATER to form hydrated lime** — evolving considerable heat and expanding in volume.

**The lime cycle, of which slaking is one stage:**

| Stage | Reaction | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **CALCINATION (burning)** ← | **CaCO₃ + heat → CaO + CO₂** ← | **Limestone burnt at about 900 °C to give QUICKLIME** ← (option c) |
| **SLAKING (hydration)** ← | **CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + HEAT** ← | **This question — quicklime plus water gives HYDRATED lime** ← |
| **CARBONATION (setting)** ← | **Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O** ← | **The lime mortar hardens by reabsorbing carbon dioxide from the AIR** ← (option b) |

> **THE CYCLE RETURNS TO ITS STARTING POINT, WHICH IS WHY IT IS CALLED A CYCLE: the calcium carbonate driven out of the limestone in the kiln is reabsorbed from the atmosphere as the mortar sets.**

> **The final hardened material is chemically the same as the limestone it came from, and the whole process is a way of turning rock into a workable paste and back into rock again.**

**The slaking reaction and its hazards:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is strongly EXOTHERMIC** ← | **The mixture can reach boiling point; quicklime and water spatter violently** ← |
| **The volume INCREASES by two to three times** ← | **The material swells and breaks up into a fine powder or paste** ← |
| **Quicklime is CAUSTIC and dangerous to handle** ← | **It burns skin and eyes, and it slakes with the moisture in the eye or the lung** ← |
| **It must be slaked in a controlled manner** | **Adding quicklime to water, not water to quicklime** ← |

> **THE EXPANSION IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE REASON LIME MUST BE FULLY SLAKED BEFORE USE, AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT: an unslaked particle of quicklime built into a mortar or a plaster will slake LATER, when moisture reaches it.**

> **It then expands two or three times within the hardened material, and blows a conical pit out of the surface — the defect known as "BLOWING" or "popping" in lime plaster.**

> **This is why lime putty is traditionally MATURED — stored under water for weeks or months before use — to ensure every particle has slaked, and why hydrated lime is sold as a bagged powder already slaked at the works.**

> **It is also the same expansion mechanism as the UNSOUNDNESS of cement caused by free lime, which the Le Chatelier test detects — one phenomenon, appearing in two materials.**

**The forms of lime and their uses:**

| Form | Note |
|---|---|
| **QUICKLIME (CaO)** | **The kiln product; must be slaked before use; caustic** ← |
| **HYDRATED lime (Ca(OH)₂), bagged as a dry powder** ← | **Slaked at the works and ready to use — the common commercial form** ← |
| **LIME PUTTY** | **Slaked with excess water and matured; used for fine plaster and conservation work** ← |
| **FAT (high calcium) lime** ← | **Sets ONLY by carbonation, in air; NOT under water; slow but very workable** ← |
| **HYDRAULIC lime** ← | **Contains clay impurities, so it sets by HYDRATION as well and can harden UNDER WATER** ← |

> **THE CARBONATION SET OF FAT LIME IN THE FOURTH ROW HAS A CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING AND IT IS OFTEN SURPRISING: a lime mortar sets from the OUTSIDE INWARDS, as carbon dioxide penetrates from the surface.**

> **A thick lime wall can take years to carbonate fully through its depth, and the core of a very thick old wall may still contain uncarbonated lime centuries later.**

> **That slowness is a defect for construction speed and a virtue for the building: lime mortar remains slightly plastic for a long time, so it accommodates settlement and thermal movement without cracking, and it is SOFTER than the masonry units — so any cracking occurs in the joint, where it can be repointed, rather than through the stones.**

> **That is the essential argument for using lime rather than cement mortar in the repair of historic masonry, and it is why cement pointing on an old stone building does real damage: the hard cement forces the movement and the decay into the stone instead.**

examTip.trick: **Calcination (rock → quicklime) → SLAKING (quicklime + water → hydrated lime, with heat) → carbonation (hardening by absorbing CO₂).** Option (c) is calcination, (b) carbonation.
examTip.trap: **Unslaked particles slake LATER inside the hardened plaster and expand 2-3 times, blowing pits in the surface** — hence maturing lime putty, and the same mechanism as cement unsoundness.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fat lime sets from the OUTSIDE INWARDS by carbonation, and stays slightly plastic for years** — which is why lime mortar accommodates movement and why cement pointing damages historic masonry.

questions.stem: CATHODIC PROTECTION of steel reinforcement or of a buried steel pipeline works by:
options: Coating the steel with an impermeable barrier
Removing all oxygen from the surrounding medium
Making the steel to be protected the cathode of an electrochemical cell
Raising the pH of the surrounding concrete or soil
questions.solution:
**By making the steel the CATHODE of an electrochemical cell** — either by connecting it to a more reactive sacrificial anode, or by applying an impressed current — so that the corrosion reaction cannot proceed on it.

**The principle:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Corrosion is an ELECTROCHEMICAL process** ← | **Iron dissolves at ANODIC areas and oxygen is reduced at CATHODIC areas** ← |
| **Metal is lost only at the ANODE** ← | **The cathode is protected** ← |
| **So if the whole steel surface is made CATHODIC, no part of it can dissolve** ← | **Which is the entire idea** ← |
| **The anodic reaction is forced to occur SOMEWHERE ELSE** ← | **On a sacrificial anode, or at an inert impressed-current anode** ← |

> **CORROSION IS NOT PREVENTED — IT IS RELOCATED, and that is the honest description of the technique.**

> **Something must corrode; cathodic protection simply ensures that it is a cheap, replaceable piece of zinc or magnesium rather than the structure.**

**The two systems:**

| System | How | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **SACRIFICIAL (galvanic) anode** ← | **A block of ZINC, MAGNESIUM or ALUMINIUM connected to the steel; being more reactive, it corrodes preferentially** ← | **Small or moderate structures; no power needed; simple; the anodes must be REPLACED periodically** ← |
| **IMPRESSED CURRENT** ← | **A DC power supply drives current from an INERT anode through the electrolyte to the steel** ← | **Large structures, high-resistivity soil; adjustable; needs power and monitoring** ← |

> **THE GALVANIC SERIES IS WHAT MAKES THE FIRST SYSTEM WORK: magnesium, zinc and aluminium are ANODIC to iron, so when connected they corrode and the iron does not.**

> **Copper and stainless steel are CATHODIC to iron — so connecting steel to copper does the opposite, accelerating the steel's corrosion.**

> **That is the mechanism of BIMETALLIC (galvanic) CORROSION, and it is why a copper water pipe connected directly to a galvanised steel one corrodes the steel rapidly at the joint, and why dissimilar metals in contact must be electrically isolated.**

**GALVANISING, which is the same principle applied as a coating:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A zinc coating protects steel in TWO ways at once** ← | ← |
| **1. As a BARRIER, excluding water and oxygen** | **Like any coating** ← |
| **2. SACRIFICIALLY, if the coating is scratched** ← | **The exposed steel becomes cathodic to the surrounding zinc, so it does NOT rust even where bare** ← |
| **Contrast with a PAINT coating** ← | **Scratch paint and the exposed steel rusts immediately, and the rust then lifts the paint from beneath** ← |

> **THE SECOND MECHANISM IS WHAT MAKES GALVANISING SO MUCH BETTER THAN PAINT FOR EXPOSED STEELWORK, and it is the property most worth knowing about it: a galvanised surface TOLERATES DAMAGE.**

> **A scratch, a drilled hole, a cut end — the steel exposed at any of these is protected by the zinc around it, for a distance of several millimetres.**

> **A painted surface does not tolerate damage at all: a single scratch initiates rust that spreads underneath the paint film, and the coating fails progressively from that one point.**

> **On site, where steelwork is handled, dropped, drilled and cut, tolerance of damage is worth a great deal more than a superior initial barrier — which is why galvanising is specified for elements that will be handled and painting for those that will not.**

**And the reinforcement case, which is where this matters most in civil engineering:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Steel in sound alkaline concrete is PASSIVE and does not corrode** ← | **The natural protection, and the best one** ← |
| **CARBONATION or CHLORIDE ingress destroys that passivity** ← | **And corrosion begins** ← |
| **Cathodic protection can then be applied to an existing structure** ← | **Anodes fixed to the surface or embedded, driving the steel cathodic** ← |
| **It is used for repairing chloride-contaminated structures** ← | **Bridges, marine structures, car parks — where removing all the contaminated concrete is impracticable** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESCRIBES ONE OF THE FEW REPAIR TECHNIQUES THAT ADDRESSES THE CAUSE RATHER THAN THE SYMPTOM: patching spalled concrete on a chloride-contaminated structure often makes matters worse, because the new alkaline patch becomes cathodic and accelerates corrosion in the contaminated concrete around it — the well-known "incipient anode" or halo effect.**

> **Cathodic protection makes the whole reinforcement cathodic and stops the process everywhere at once, which patch repair cannot do.**

> **It is expensive and it requires permanent monitoring and a power supply for the life of the structure — so it is a commitment rather than a repair, and that is the trade being made.**

examTip.trick: **Make the whole steel surface the CATHODE** — metal dissolves only at the anode. Corrosion is not prevented, it is RELOCATED onto a cheap replaceable anode.
examTip.trap: **Copper and stainless steel are CATHODIC to iron** — connecting them accelerates the steel's corrosion. That is bimetallic corrosion, and why dissimilar metals must be isolated.
examTip.mnemonic: **Galvanising TOLERATES DAMAGE — a scratch is still protected by the zinc around it; scratched paint rusts and lifts.** Which is why handled steelwork is galvanised and undisturbed steelwork is painted.

questions.stem: For the same concrete, the compressive strength measured on a standard CYLINDER (150 mm diameter × 300 mm high) compared with that on a standard CUBE (150 mm) is approximately:
options: 0.8 times the cube strength
Equal to the cube strength
1.25 times the cube strength
Half the cube strength
questions.solution:
**About 0.8 times the cube strength** — the cylinder gives the LOWER value.

**Why the two differ:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **The ASPECT RATIO differs** ← | **The cylinder is 2:1 (height to diameter); the cube is 1:1** ← |
| **PLATEN RESTRAINT: friction between the machine's platens and the specimen's ends restrains the lateral expansion** ← | **Producing a triaxial confinement near the ends, which INCREASES the apparent strength** ← |
| **In a CUBE, that restraint reaches through the WHOLE specimen** ← | **The cone of restrained material from each face meets in the middle, so the whole cube is confined** ← |
| **In a CYLINDER, the MIDDLE THIRD is free of the restraint** ← | **It is twice as tall, so the central region fails in genuinely uniaxial compression** ← |
| **Hence the cylinder gives a LOWER and more REALISTIC value** ← | ← |

> **THE CYLINDER IS THEREFORE THE BETTER TEST OF THE MATERIAL AND THE CUBE THE MORE CONVENIENT ONE, and that is the honest summary.**

> **The cube's platen restraint inflates the result, and it also produces the characteristic double-cone (hourglass) failure — the corners survive because they are confined, and the sides spall away.**

> **A cylinder fails through a single diagonal shear plane or by vertical splitting, which is closer to how concrete actually fails in a structure.**

**Which is used where, and why:**

| Region | Standard specimen | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **India, Nepal, the United Kingdom and much of Europe** | **CUBE, 150 mm** ← | **Simpler to make and to handle; no capping needed; self-supporting in the mould** ← |
| **United States, and most international research** | **CYLINDER, 150 × 300 mm** ← | **More representative; but it must be CAPPED to give plane parallel ends** ← |
| **Eurocode notation** | **Quotes BOTH, as f_ck,cyl / f_ck,cube** ← | **For example C25/30 means 25 MPa cylinder and 30 MPa cube — and 25/30 = 0.83** ← |

> **THE EUROCODE DESIGNATION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL MEMORY AID FOR THE RATIO: C25/30, C30/37, C40/50 — every pair is a cylinder strength and a cube strength for the same concrete, and every ratio is close to 0.8.**

> **So a grade quoted without saying which specimen was used is ambiguous by 20 per cent, and confusing the two in a design is a serious error — an M30 cube-strength concrete is NOT a 30 MPa cylinder-strength one.**

**The other factors that affect a measured strength, which are worth knowing because they are all in the same direction:**

| Factor | Effect on the measured strength |
|---|---|
| **Larger SPECIMEN** | **LOWER strength — a larger volume contains a larger flaw** ← |
| **Faster RATE of loading** ← | **HIGHER apparent strength — concrete is rate-sensitive** ← |
| **Ends not PLANE or not PARALLEL** | **LOWER — the load concentrates on high spots** ← |
| **Specimen tested WET (as cured)** ← | **LOWER — about 10 to 15 per cent below the same specimen tested dry** ← |
| **Poor compaction of the specimen** | **LOWER, and it does not reflect the concrete in the structure** ← |

> **THE WET-VERSUS-DRY EFFECT IN THE FOURTH ROW IS SUBSTANTIAL AND IT IS THE REASON THE TESTING CONDITION IS SPECIFIED: cubes are tested in the condition in which they were cured, and drying a specimen before testing would raise the result by more than 10 per cent.**

> **Since the standard requires testing wet, a laboratory that lets its cubes dry on the bench for a day before testing is systematically over-reporting the strength — and doing so in the direction that conceals a problem.**

> **The SIZE effect in the first row has the same character: it is a real property of a brittle material, in which failure begins at the largest flaw present, and a larger specimen is more likely to contain a large one.**

> **This is also why a 100 mm cube gives a slightly higher result than a 150 mm one, and why the specimen size must be stated with any strength result.**

examTip.trick: **Cylinder ≈ 0.8 × cube.** The cube's platen restraint reaches right through it and inflates the result; a cylinder's middle third fails in genuinely uniaxial compression.
examTip.trap: **A grade is ambiguous by 20 % without the specimen type** — M30 cube strength is NOT 30 MPa cylinder strength. Eurocode C25/30 states both, and 25/30 = 0.83.
examTip.mnemonic: **Test WET as cured** — letting cubes dry on the bench raises the result by 10-15 %, in the direction that conceals a problem. And larger specimens read LOWER, because they contain larger flaws.

questions.stem: The REBOUND (Schmidt) HAMMER used for the non-destructive testing of concrete measures:
options: The depth of carbonation of the cover concrete
The velocity of an ultrasonic pulse through the member
The surface hardness of the concrete
The electrical resistivity of the concrete
questions.solution:
**The SURFACE HARDNESS of the concrete**, from which the compressive strength is INFERRED by a calibrated correlation.

**How it works, and its essential limitation:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A spring-loaded mass strikes the surface and REBOUNDS** ← | **The rebound distance is read on a scale as the rebound number** ← |
| **A harder surface absorbs less energy, so the rebound is greater** ← | ← |
| **The rebound number is correlated with compressive strength by a chart** ← | **Supplied by the manufacturer, or better, established for the actual concrete** ← |
| **It measures only the OUTER 30 mm or so** ← | **The surface layer, which may not represent the body of the member at all** ← |

> **THE DEPTH LIMITATION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE FUNDAMENTAL OBJECTION AND IT MUST BE UNDERSTOOD: the rebound hammer tests the SKIN of the concrete.**

> **A member with excellent surface concrete and honeycombed, poorly compacted concrete behind it will give an excellent rebound number.**

> **Conversely, a sound member whose surface has been carbonated, wetted, or worn will read low despite being perfectly adequate inside.**

> **So the correlation between rebound number and strength is genuinely weak, and the manufacturer's generic chart may be wrong by ±25 per cent or more.**

**What affects the reading, other than the strength:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **SURFACE MOISTURE** ← | **A wet surface reads LOWER — by up to 20 per cent** ← |
| **CARBONATION** ← | **Carbonated concrete is HARDER at the surface, so an old member reads HIGH — sometimes by 50 per cent** ← |
| **The AGGREGATE immediately beneath the point struck** ← | **Hitting a hard aggregate particle gives a high reading, a void or mortar a low one** ← |
| **The direction of the hammer** | **Horizontal, upward or downward — each needs its own correction** ← |
| **The member's MASS and rigidity** ← | **A thin or unrestrained member absorbs energy by moving, and reads LOW — so slabs must be propped** ← |
| **Surface texture and finish** | ← |

> **THE CARBONATION EFFECT IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST MISLEADING BECAUSE IT ACTS IN THE UNSAFE DIRECTION: an old structure being assessed for its residual strength has a carbonated surface, which reads HIGH.**

> **So the rebound hammer flatters exactly the structures whose strength is most in doubt, and an unwary assessment can conclude that a deteriorating member is sound.**

> **The remedy is to grind away the carbonated layer before testing, and better still to CALIBRATE the hammer against cores taken from the actual structure.**

**How it should properly be used:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Take at least 10 to 12 readings at each location and use the MEDIAN** ← | **Discarding outliers — individual readings are highly scattered** ← |
| **Use it for COMPARISON and UNIFORMITY, not for absolute strength** ← | **Its real strength: it identifies which parts of a structure are weaker than others, quickly and cheaply** ← |
| **CALIBRATE against cores from the same structure if a strength value is needed** ← | **Which converts it from a rough indicator into a useful survey tool** ← |
| **Combine with other methods** | **The SONREB approach uses rebound number AND ultrasonic pulse velocity together, which is considerably more reliable than either** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE HONEST DESCRIPTION OF THE INSTRUMENT'S VALUE AND IT IS A REAL ONE: as a way of surveying a large structure quickly to find the weak areas, the rebound hammer is excellent — cheap, fast, portable, and requiring no power.**

> **A hundred readings across a bridge deck in a morning will reliably identify which spans are different from the others, and the cores can then be taken where they matter.**

> **Used that way it is a screening tool that directs expensive testing, which is exactly the right role for a cheap and imprecise measurement.**

**The other non-destructive methods, for comparison:**

| Method | Measures |
|---|---|
| **REBOUND hammer** | **Surface hardness → strength (weakly)** ← |
| **ULTRASONIC PULSE VELOCITY (UPV)** ← | **The velocity of a pulse through the member — indicating density, uniformity, VOIDS and cracks throughout the DEPTH** ← (option b) |
| **COVER METER** | **The depth of cover and the bar diameter and spacing** ← |
| **HALF-CELL POTENTIAL** | **The PROBABILITY of active reinforcement corrosion** ← |
| **CARBONATION depth (phenolphthalein)** | **A partly destructive test on a broken face** ← (option a) |
| **CORE testing** | **The only DIRECT measure of in-situ strength — partly destructive** ← |

> **THE UPV IN THE SECOND ROW COMPLEMENTS THE REBOUND HAMMER PRECISELY BECAUSE IT LOOKS THROUGH THE MEMBER RATHER THAN AT ITS SKIN: a low pulse velocity indicates a void, a crack or poor compaction anywhere along the path.**

> **Together, a high rebound number with a low pulse velocity is a clear signature of good surface concrete over poor interior — exactly the case that either instrument alone would miss.**

From which its compressive strength is INFERRED by a calibrated correlation.

examTip.trick: **Surface HARDNESS, correlated to strength.** Option (b) is UPV, (a) the carbonation test. It reads only the outer 30 mm or so.
examTip.trap: **CARBONATION makes an old surface harder, so it reads HIGH** — flattering exactly the structures whose strength is most in doubt. Grind the surface, and calibrate against cores.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use it for UNIFORMITY, not absolute strength** — a hundred readings find the weak spans in a morning, and the cores then go where they matter. High rebound plus LOW pulse velocity means good skin over bad interior.

questions.stem: In the terminology of a masonry ARCH, the VOUSSOIRS are:
options: The vertical supports from which the arch springs
The WEDGE-SHAPED units of stone or brick of which the arch ring is built
The horizontal courses above the arch's crown
The temporary timber framework on which the arch is built
questions.solution:
**The WEDGE-SHAPED units of stone or brick of which the arch ring is built.**

**The terminology of an arch:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **VOUSSOIR** ← | **Each wedge-shaped unit forming the arch ring** ← |
| **KEYSTONE** | **The central, topmost voussoir — placed last, and it locks the arch** ← |
| **SPRINGING** | **The level and the point at which the arch begins to curve from its support** ← |
| **SPRINGER** | **The lowest voussoir, at the springing** ← |
| **ABUTMENT / PIER** ← | **The support that carries the arch and resists its outward THRUST** ← (option a) |
| **INTRADOS (soffit)** | **The INNER curved surface of the arch** ← |
| **EXTRADOS** | **The OUTER curved surface** ← |
| **CROWN** | **The highest point of the extrados** |
| **HAUNCH** | **The part of the arch between the crown and the springing** ← |
| **SPANDREL** | **The roughly triangular area between the extrados and the horizontal above** ← |
| **RISE** | **The height from the springing line to the intrados at the crown** ← |
| **SKEWBACK** | **The inclined surface on the abutment from which the arch springs** ← |
| **CENTERING** | **The temporary TIMBER or steel framework supporting the arch during construction** ← (option d) |

> **THE CENTERING IN THE LAST ROW IS WORTH SINGLING OUT BECAUSE IT EXPLAINS THE KEYSTONE'S SIGNIFICANCE: an arch is not self-supporting until it is COMPLETE.**

> **Until the keystone is in place, the arch ring is simply a row of blocks that would fall inward, so it must be built on centering.**

> **The moment the keystone is driven home, the ring becomes continuous, the thrust line can develop, and the arch supports itself — and the centering can be struck.**

> **That is why the keystone acquired its symbolic meaning, and it is a genuine structural fact rather than a metaphor: remove any one voussoir and the arch falls, but the keystone is the one whose insertion completes it.**

**How an arch actually works:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **An arch carries load entirely in COMPRESSION** ← | **Which is why it can be built of stone and brick, materials with no tensile strength** ← |
| **The load is transmitted from voussoir to voussoir along a LINE OF THRUST** ← | **A compressive path curving down to the abutments** ← |
| **The arch is STABLE so long as the line of thrust stays WITHIN the middle third of the arch ring** ← | **The middle-third rule again — no tension can develop in the joints** ← |
| **The thrust at the abutment has a large HORIZONTAL component** ← | **Which the abutment must resist — and which is the arch's characteristic demand** ← |

> **THE HORIZONTAL THRUST IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ARCH'S DEFINING STRUCTURAL FEATURE AND THE SOURCE OF MOST ARCH FAILURES: a beam pushes DOWN on its supports; an arch pushes down AND OUTWARD.**

> **If the abutment spreads even slightly, the arch's geometry changes, the line of thrust shifts, and hinges form.**

> **This is why arch bridges have massive abutments, why the outermost arch of a multi-span viaduct needs a much larger abutment than the internal piers (which are balanced by the arch on either side), and why the collapse of one span of an arch viaduct can unbalance and bring down its neighbours.**

> **THE MIDDLE-THIRD CONDITION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE SAME RULE MET WITH ECCENTRIC LOADING AND WITH GRAVITY DAMS, and it appears here for the same reason: masonry cannot take tension.**

> **A masonry arch does not fail by CRUSHING — the stresses are usually far below the stone's strength. It fails by the line of thrust wandering outside the ring, opening a joint on one face, forming a hinge, and turning the arch into a mechanism once four hinges have formed.**

> **Which means that an arch's safety is a question of GEOMETRY rather than of material strength — a remarkable result, and the basis of the whole modern analysis of masonry structures.**

examTip.trick: **Voussoirs are the wedge-shaped ring units; the keystone is the central one.** Option (a) is the abutment, (d) the centering.
examTip.trap: **An arch is not self-supporting until the KEYSTONE is in** — until then it stands on centering. A genuine structural fact behind the metaphor.
examTip.mnemonic: **A masonry arch fails by GEOMETRY, not strength** — the line of thrust leaves the middle third, a joint opens, hinges form, and four hinges make a mechanism. And the outward THRUST is what abutments are for.

questions.stem: Among the traditional timber roof trusses, the KING POST truss and the QUEEN POST truss differ in that the queen post truss:
options: Has a single central vertical member
Is used only for spans below 5 m
Has no tie beam
Has TWO vertical posts with a horizontal straining beam between them
questions.solution:
**The queen post truss has TWO vertical posts with a horizontal straining beam between them**, and it suits larger spans than the king post truss.

**The two trusses compared:**

| Feature | KING POST | QUEEN POST |
|---|---|---|
| **Vertical posts** | **ONE, central** ← (option a) | **TWO, symmetrically placed** ← |
| **Between the posts** | — | **A horizontal STRAINING BEAM, with a straining sill on the tie beam below** ← |
| **Suitable span** | **5 to 8 m** ← | **8 to 12 m** ← |
| **Roof shape** | **A simple gable, with the ridge at the king post's head** | **The same, or with a flat central portion** ← |
| **The central space** | **Obstructed by the king post** | **CLEAR between the queen posts — usable as a room** ← |

> **THE CLEAR CENTRAL SPACE IN THE LAST ROW WAS A REAL ARCHITECTURAL ADVANTAGE HISTORICALLY: a queen post truss leaves the middle of the roof space open, so an attic room can be formed between the posts.**

> **A king post truss has a member down the middle of the space and cannot.**

**The members of a king post truss and what each does:**

| Member | Action | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **TIE BEAM (the bottom chord)** | **TENSION** ← | **Resists the outward spread of the rafter feet — the member that makes it a truss rather than a pair of leaning rafters** ← |
| **PRINCIPAL RAFTERS** | **COMPRESSION** ← | **Carry the roof load down to the supports** ← |
| **KING POST** | **TENSION** ← | **It HANGS from the rafters' apex and HOLDS UP the middle of the tie beam** ← |
| **STRUTS** | **COMPRESSION** ← | **Support the principal rafters at their midpoints, halving their effective span** ← |
| **Purlins, common rafters, battens** | ← | **Carrying the covering** ← |

> **THE KING POST'S ACTION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST COMMONLY MISUNDERSTOOD FEATURE OF THE WHOLE TRUSS AND IT IS WORTH STATING CLEARLY: the king post is in TENSION, not compression.**

> **It looks like a column standing on the tie beam, and it does the opposite — it HANGS from the apex and SUSPENDS the tie beam's midpoint, preventing it sagging under its own weight and any ceiling load.**

> **That is why the joint at the top of the king post is a tension connection, why it is strapped with iron in traditional carpentry, and why cutting or notching a king post is so damaging.**

> **A member in compression can tolerate a notch; a member in tension cannot, because the tension must pass through the reduced section and through the joint.**

**THE TIE BEAM IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE DEFINING MEMBER OF A TRUSS AND ITS IMPORTANCE IS EASILY UNDERESTIMATED:**

> **Two rafters leaning against each other push OUTWARD at their feet, and that outward thrust must be resisted by the walls — which is why an unrestrained roof spreads the walls of an old building outward at eaves level, a very common defect.**

> **A tie beam converts the thrust into an internal tension within the truss, so the truss delivers only a VERTICAL load to the walls.**

> **That is the entire difference between a TRUSS and a simple couple roof, and it is why removing or cutting a tie beam — to make headroom, to fit a staircase, to run a duct — is one of the most dangerous alterations that can be made to an existing roof.**

> **It converts a truss back into a pair of rafters, the walls begin to spread, and the roof sags progressively. The damage appears over months as cracking at the wall heads, and by the time it is noticed the geometry has changed permanently.**

**And the modern successor, for context:**

> **Traditional king and queen post trusses have largely been replaced by lightweight TRUSSED RAFTERS — factory-made, closely spaced at 600 mm, using thin timbers joined with punched metal plates.**

> **They are cheaper, faster and use far less timber, and they carry the same caution in a sharper form: a trussed rafter is designed as a complete triangulated unit, and cutting ANY member — for a water tank, a hatch, a duct — destroys it.**

> **Unlike a traditional truss, which has some redundancy in its heavy members, a trussed rafter has none at all.**

And so suits LARGER spans than the king post truss.

examTip.trick: **King post: ONE central post, 5-8 m span. Queen post: TWO posts with a straining beam, 8-12 m, and a clear central space.**
examTip.trap: **The KING POST is in TENSION** — it hangs from the apex and suspends the tie beam's midpoint. It looks like a column and does the opposite.
examTip.mnemonic: **The TIE BEAM is what makes it a truss** — it converts the rafters' outward thrust into internal tension, so the walls get only vertical load. Cutting it is among the most dangerous alterations possible.

questions.stem: A symmetrical I-section has overall dimensions of 200 mm width and 400 mm depth, with flanges 20 mm thick and a web 20 mm thick. Its moment of inertia about the centroidal axis parallel to the flanges is:
options: 267 × 10⁶ mm⁴
320 × 10⁶ mm⁴
367 × 10⁶ mm⁴
questions.solution:
**About 367 × 10⁶ mm⁴.**

**The computation, by SUBTRACTION — the quickest route for a symmetrical I-section:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Treat the section as a full rectangle 200 × 400 MINUS the two rectangular voids** ← | **Which is valid because the section is symmetric about both axes, so all three rectangles share the same centroid** ← |
| **Each void is (200 − 20)/2 = 90 mm wide and 400 − 2(20) = 360 mm deep** | **Two of them, so a combined width of 180 mm** ← |
| **I = (B D³ − b d³) / 12** | **= (200 × 400³ − 180 × 360³) / 12** ← |
| **200 × 64 × 10⁶** | **= 12,800 × 10⁶** |
| **180 × 46.656 × 10⁶** | **= 8,398 × 10⁶** |
| **Difference ÷ 12** | **= 4,402 × 10⁶ / 12 = 366.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |

> **Option (d) 1,067 × 10⁶ is the SOLID 200 × 400 rectangle — a useful upper bound, and the answer must be well below it.**

> **THE SUBTRACTION METHOD WORKS ONLY BECAUSE ALL THREE RECTANGLES SHARE A CENTROID, which is worth stating as a condition: for a symmetric I-section it is exact and takes one line.**

> **For an UNSYMMETRIC section — unequal flanges, or a channel — the centroid must first be located and the parallel axis theorem applied to each part, and the subtraction shortcut is not available.**

**A CHECK by addition, which should give the same answer:**

| Part | I about its own centroid | A h² | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Web, 20 × 360** | **20 × 360³/12 = 77.8 × 10⁶** | **h = 0, so nothing** ← | **77.8 × 10⁶** |
| **Each flange, 200 × 20** | **200 × 20³/12 = 0.13 × 10⁶** ← | **A h² = 4,000 × 190² = 144.4 × 10⁶** ← | **144.5 × 10⁶ each** |
| **Two flanges** | ← | ← | **289.0 × 10⁶** |
| **TOTAL** | ← | ← | **77.8 + 289.0 = 366.8 × 10⁶ ✓** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE LINE IN THE WHOLE CALCULATION AND IT DEMONSTRATES THE POINT MADE ABOUT THE PARALLEL AXIS THEOREM: each flange's OWN moment of inertia is 0.13 × 10⁶, and its TRANSFER term is 144.4 × 10⁶.**

> **The transfer term is over a THOUSAND times the flange's own contribution.**

> **So essentially the whole of the flanges' effectiveness comes from WHERE they are, not from their own bending stiffness — which is why they are put at the extremes and why the section is shaped as it is.**

**And the efficiency of the section, which is the reason for using it:**

| Comparison | Value |
|---|---|
| **This I-section's area** | **2(200 × 20) + 20 × 360 = 8,000 + 7,200 = 15,200 mm²** ← |
| **Its moment of inertia** | **366.8 × 10⁶ mm⁴** |
| **A SOLID rectangle of the SAME area, 200 wide** | **76 mm deep, giving I = 200 × 76³/12 = 7.3 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **Ratio** | **The I-section is FIFTY TIMES stiffer for the same material** ← |

> **A FACTOR OF FIFTY FOR THE SAME QUANTITY OF STEEL IS THE WHOLE JUSTIFICATION FOR THE SHAPE, and it is worth computing once to appreciate the magnitude.**

> **The material has not changed and its quantity has not changed. Only its DISTRIBUTION has, and the section has become fifty times stiffer in bending.**

> **That is the most dramatic illustration available of the principle that in bending, geometry matters more than quantity — and it is why a rolled steel section costs more per tonne than a plate and is still far cheaper per unit of capacity.**

examTip.trick: **I = (BD³ − bd³)/12 = (200×400³ − 180×360³)/12 = 367 × 10⁶ mm⁴.** Option (d) is the solid rectangle — a useful upper bound.
examTip.trap: **Subtraction works only because all three rectangles share a CENTROID** — valid for a symmetric I-section, and not for a channel or unequal flanges.
examTip.mnemonic: **Each flange's own I is 0.13 × 10⁶ and its TRANSFER term is 144 × 10⁶ — a thousandfold.** And the section is FIFTY times stiffer than a solid rectangle of the same area. Distribution, not quantity.

questions.stem: For the same cross-sectional AREA of material, a HOLLOW circular section compared with a SOLID circular one has:
options: A larger moment of inertia and a larger radius of gyration
The same moment of inertia, since the area is the same
A smaller moment of inertia
A larger area but a smaller perimeter
questions.solution:
**A LARGER moment of inertia and a larger radius of gyration**, because the same material is distributed further from the neutral axis.

**A worked comparison, since the magnitude is the point:**

| Section | Dimensions | Area | I |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SOLID circle** | **100 mm diameter** | **7,854 mm²** | **π(100)⁴/64 = 4.91 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **HOLLOW circle of the SAME area** | **150 mm outside, 111.8 mm inside** ← | **7,854 mm²** | **π(150⁴ − 111.8⁴)/64 = 16.2 × 10⁶ mm⁴** ← |
| **Ratio** | ← | **1.0** | **3.3 times** ← |

> **THE SAME STEEL, ARRANGED AS A TUBE INSTEAD OF A BAR, IS MORE THAN THREE TIMES AS STIFF — and the improvement grows as the tube is made thinner and larger in diameter.**

**Why, in one sentence:**

> **I depends on the SQUARE of each element's distance from the axis, so material near the centre contributes almost nothing while material at the perimeter contributes a great deal.**

> **Removing the material from the middle costs almost no moment of inertia, and putting that same material at a larger radius adds a great deal.**

> **A solid section is therefore an inefficient use of material in bending, because its central core is nearly idle.**

**Where this matters, and where it does not:**

| Loading | Does a hollow section help? |
|---|---|
| **BENDING** | **YES, greatly — I is what matters** ← |
| **TORSION** ← | **YES, greatly — and the polar moment behaves the same way** ← |
| **BUCKLING as a column** ← | **YES, greatly — the radius of gyration r = √(I/A) increases, so the slenderness ratio FALLS for the same length** ← |
| **DIRECT TENSION** ← | **NO DIFFERENCE AT ALL — capacity depends only on the AREA, and the shape is irrelevant** ← |
| **Direct compression, short column** | **No difference — again governed by area** ← |

> **THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THE FIRST THREE ROWS AND THE LAST TWO IS THE PRINCIPLE WORTH CARRYING: shape matters where the STRESS DISTRIBUTION varies across the section, and it does not where the stress is uniform.**

> **In bending, torsion and buckling the stress varies with distance from the axis, so where the material sits is decisive.**

> **In direct tension the stress is uniform, every square millimetre carries the same load, and a tube and a bar of equal area are exactly equivalent.**

> **This is why tension members are made of flats, rods and angles — cheap solid shapes — while compression members and beams are tubes and I-sections.**

**The limits, since a tube cannot be made indefinitely thin:**

| Limit | Note |
|---|---|
| **LOCAL BUCKLING of the thin wall** ← | **Beyond a diameter-to-thickness ratio of about 50 to 90 for steel, the wall buckles locally before the section can develop its strength** ← |
| **This is why section CLASSIFICATION exists** | **Plastic, compact, semi-compact and slender, by the width-to-thickness ratios** ← |
| **Manufacturing and handling** | **Very thin tubes are easily dented, and a dent destroys the local stability** ← |
| **Corrosion of the inside surface** ← | **A closed tube's interior cannot be inspected or painted — so it is SEALED, and the trapped air's oxygen is soon exhausted** ← |
| **Connections are harder** | **Bolting to a tube requires access to only one side, or welded end plates** ← |

> **THE SEALING SOLUTION IN THE FOURTH ROW IS ELEGANT AND WORTH KNOWING: a completely sealed hollow section needs no internal protection at all.**

> **The small quantity of air trapped inside contains a finite amount of oxygen; a negligible amount of corrosion consumes it, and the process then stops for want of a reactant.**

> **So a sealed tube is protected by the corrosion of its own first few micrometres, permanently and at no cost — provided the seal is genuinely complete.**

> **The failure case is a tube that is NOT properly sealed: water enters through a small gap, cannot drain, is replenished with oxygen, and the tube corrodes from the inside where nobody can see it. Which is why drainage holes are specified where sealing cannot be guaranteed — the opposite strategy, and both work; what does not work is a half-sealed tube.**

Its material is distributed further from the neutral axis.

examTip.trick: **I depends on the SQUARE of the distance from the axis, so central material is nearly idle.** The same area as a tube can be three times stiffer or more.
examTip.trap: **Shape matters for bending, torsion and BUCKLING; it makes NO difference in direct tension**, where the stress is uniform and only the area counts. Hence flats for ties, tubes for struts.
examTip.mnemonic: **A properly SEALED tube needs no internal protection** — the trapped oxygen is quickly consumed and corrosion stops. A HALF-sealed tube is the failure case: water in, no drainage, rusting invisibly.

questions.stem: In PLANE TABLE surveying, the method of RESECTION is used to:
options: Locate a detail point by drawing rays from two known stations
Determine the plotted position of the table itself
Measure the distance between two inaccessible points
Draw the traverse legs between successive stations
questions.solution:
**To determine the PLOTTED POSITION OF THE TABLE ITSELF**, by sighting BACK to points already plotted on the sheet.

**The four methods of plane tabling:**

| Method | What is being found | How |
|---|---|---|
| **RADIATION** | **DETAIL points around one station** ← | **Rays drawn from the single station to each point; distances measured and scaled off** ← |
| **INTERSECTION** | **DETAIL points, especially inaccessible ones** ← (option a) | **Rays drawn from TWO known stations; the point lies where they cross — NO distance measurement needed** ← |
| **TRAVERSING** | **The successive STATIONS of a survey line** ← (option d) | **Ray drawn forward, distance measured, table moved and re-oriented** ← |
| **RESECTION** ← | **The POSITION OF THE TABLE ITSELF** ← | **Sighting BACK to at least two or three plotted points** ← |

> **THE DIRECTION OF WORKING IS WHAT DISTINGUISHES RESECTION FROM THE OTHERS AND IT IS THE KEY TO REMEMBERING IT: in radiation, intersection and traversing, the surveyor stands at a KNOWN place and locates UNKNOWN points.**

> **In RESECTION the reverse holds: the surveyor stands at an UNKNOWN place and locates HIMSELF from known points.**

> **That is what makes it so useful — the table can be set up wherever the ground is convenient and the view is good, and its position determined afterwards.**

**The methods of performing a resection:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **By the two-point problem** | **Using two plotted points and an auxiliary station — laborious** ← |
| **By the THREE-POINT problem** ← | **Using three plotted points — the standard case, solved by the trial-and-error, mechanical (tracing paper), or graphical (Bessel's) method** ← |
| **By a BACK RAY, having traversed from a plotted station** | **The simplest case** ← |
| **By the INTERSECTION OF TWO BACK RAYS** | ← |

> **THE TRACING PAPER METHOD IS THE MOST INGENIOUS OF THESE AND IS WORTH KNOWING: a sheet of tracing paper is fixed over the table, an arbitrary point marked on it, and rays drawn to the three known points from there.**

> **The tracing paper is then moved over the plan until each of the three rays passes through its corresponding plotted point — and when all three do, the arbitrary point coincides with the true position of the station.**

> **It requires no calculation, no construction and no trial orientation of the table, and it works because the ANGLES between the three rays are fixed by the observation while their absolute position is not.**

**THE TRIANGLE OF ERROR AND THE DANGER CIRCLE, which are the two things always asked:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **If the table's orientation is slightly wrong, the three back rays do not meet at a point** ← | **They form a small TRIANGLE OF ERROR** ← |
| **The true position is found by adjusting the orientation until the triangle closes** ← | **By the trial method, or by Lehmann's rules** ← |
| **The DANGER (great) CIRCLE is the circle passing through the THREE known points** ← | **If the station lies ON or NEAR it, the solution is INDETERMINATE — the rays meet at a point for any orientation** ← |
| **So the three points must be chosen so the station is well AWAY from that circle** ← | ← |

> **THE DANGER CIRCLE IS A GENUINE GEOMETRIC INDETERMINACY RATHER THAN A PRACTICAL DIFFICULTY, and its cause is worth understanding: angles subtended at the circumference of a circle by a fixed chord are all EQUAL.**

> **So if the observer stands on the circle through the three points, the observed angles between them are the same as they would be from any other point on that circle — and the observation therefore contains no information about which point it was.**

> **The remedy is entirely in the CHOICE of the three known points: they should be well distributed around the observer, and the observer should be inside the triangle they form or well clear of the circle through them.**

> **That is a decision made before any observation, and it is why the selection of control points is the part of a resection that actually determines whether it will work.**

By sighting BACK to at least two or three points that are already plotted on the sheet.

examTip.trick: **Resection locates the TABLE ITSELF from plotted points; the other three methods locate unknown points from a known station.** Option (a) is intersection, (d) traversing.
examTip.trap: **The TRIANGLE OF ERROR means the orientation is slightly wrong** — adjust until it closes. And the DANGER CIRCLE through the three known points makes the solution indeterminate.
examTip.mnemonic: **Equal angles are subtended from anywhere on a circle** — which is exactly why standing on the danger circle gives no information about where you are. Choose control points well distributed around you.

questions.stem: In measuring BRICKWORK for a bill of quantities under the standard mode of measurement, openings such as doors and windows are:
options: Never deducted, since the labour of forming them compensates
Deducted only if they exceed 5 m² in area
Deducted at their full size, with small openings below a stated area (commonly 0.1 m²) NOT deducted
Deducted at half their area
questions.solution:
**Deducted at their full size, with SMALL openings below a stated area — commonly 0.1 m² — NOT deducted**, because the small saving is offset by the extra labour of forming them.

**The principle behind the deduction rules:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A large opening saves a substantial quantity of material and labour** ← | **So it must be deducted, or the contractor is paid for work not done** ← |
| **A SMALL opening saves very little material** ← | **And it ADDS labour: cutting bricks, forming the reveal, and the interruption to the bricklayer's rhythm** ← |
| **Deducting it would therefore UNDER-pay the contractor** ← | **The work is more troublesome per square metre, not less** ← |
| **So a threshold is set, below which no deduction is made** ← | **A pragmatic rule that saves both measurement effort and argument** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE REAL JUSTIFICATION AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: the rule is not a convenience or a rounding — it reflects the fact that a small hole in a wall costs MORE per square metre of wall, not less.**

> **A measurement convention that ignored this would systematically underpay for fiddly work and overpay for plain work, and contractors would price accordingly — inflating the rate for all brickwork to cover it.**

> **A rule that matches the measurement to the actual effort produces more honest rates, and that is what a mode of measurement is FOR.**

**The general principles of a standard mode of measurement:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **Measurement must be UNAMBIGUOUS** ← | **So that the contractor's quantity and the engineer's agree, and the tender is comparable between bidders** ← |
| **It must reflect the WORK ACTUALLY DONE, as nearly as is practical** ← | ← |
| **It must be ECONOMICAL to apply** ← | **A rule requiring every brick to be counted would be exact and useless** ← |
| **The unit must suit the work** | **m³ for excavation and concrete, m² for plaster and formwork, m for skirting and kerbs, number for doors and fittings** ← |
| **What is INCLUDED in a rate must be stated** ← | **Otherwise the same item is priced differently by different bidders and the tenders are not comparable** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW EXPLAINS THE WHOLE FAMILY OF THRESHOLD RULES IN THE STANDARD: measurement is not free, and a rule must be worth applying.**

> **Deducting a 0.05 m² ventilation hole from a wall of 200 m² alters the quantity by a fortieth of one per cent and takes as long to measure and check as a large opening — so the standard says do not bother, and both parties save the effort.**

**Other common threshold and convention rules, which follow the same logic:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Openings below about 0.1 m² are not deducted from masonry, plaster and painting** ← | **This question** ← |
| **Voids below a stated size are not deducted from excavation** | ← |
| **Measurement is to the NEAREST specified unit** | **Commonly 0.01 m for dimensions and 0.01 m² or m³ for quantities** ← |
| **Work is measured NET AS FIXED IN PLACE** ← | **No allowance for waste, laps or bulking — those are in the RATE, not the quantity** ← |
| **Excavation is measured on the NET dimensions of the structure** ← | **Working space and side slopes are the contractor's problem and are priced into the rate** ← |

> **THE "NET AS FIXED" PRINCIPLE IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SINGLE CONVENTION AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MOST OFTEN CAUSES DISPUTES WITH INEXPERIENCED CONTRACTORS: the quantity measured is what appears in the finished work, and nothing else.**

> **Reinforcement is measured at its net length, not including the wastage from cutting; concrete at its net volume, not including what is spilled; excavation at the net dimensions, not including the extra dug for working space or to make the sides stand.**

> **All of that additional material and effort is real and must be paid for — and it is paid for through the RATE, which the contractor builds up knowing the convention.**

> **A contractor who prices the net quantity at a rate covering only the net material will lose money on every item, and it is one of the commonest reasons an inexperienced tenderer is the lowest bidder and then fails.**

The labour and material saved is offset by the extra work of forming them.

examTip.trick: **Full deduction for openings, with none below about 0.1 m²** — because a small opening saves little material and ADDS labour, so deducting it would underpay.
examTip.trap: **The rule reflects real cost, not convenience** — a fiddly wall costs more per m², and a convention that ignored that would inflate every brickwork rate to compensate.
examTip.mnemonic: **Work is measured NET AS FIXED IN PLACE** — no waste, laps, bulking or working space in the QUANTITY; all of it in the RATE. Pricing the net quantity at a net-material rate is how inexperienced tenderers lose money.

questions.stem: The SEDIMENTATION (hydrometer) analysis of fine-grained soil rests on STOKES' LAW, which states that a spherical particle settling in a fluid reaches a terminal velocity proportional to:
options: The particle's diameter
The square of the particle's diameter
The cube of the particle's diameter
The square root of the particle's diameter
questions.solution:
**The SQUARE of the particle's diameter.**

**Stokes' law:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **v = (γ_s − γ_w) D² / (18 μ)** ← | **v the terminal velocity, D the diameter, μ the dynamic viscosity** ← |
| **So v ∝ D²** ← | **A particle twice the diameter settles FOUR times as fast** ← |
| **Rearranged for the analysis** | **D = √[18 μ v / (γ_s − γ_w)] — the diameter is found from the settling velocity** ← |
| **And v is simply the depth ÷ the elapsed time** ← | **Which is what the hydrometer reading and the stopwatch give** ← |

> **THE SQUARE RELATION IS WHAT MAKES THE METHOD PRACTICAL AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: because the velocity goes as D², particles of different size separate very rapidly in the suspension.**

> **A 0.05 mm particle settles a hundred times faster than a 0.005 mm one, so by taking readings at increasing times, progressively finer fractions are measured.**

> **The hydrometer measures the DENSITY of the suspension at a known depth, which tells you how much solid is still in suspension above that level — and everything coarser than the size corresponding to that time has already settled past it.**

**The assumptions, and where they fail:**

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| **The particles are SPHERICAL** ← | **Clay particles are FLAT PLATES, which settle much more slowly than a sphere of the same mass** ← |
| **They settle INDEPENDENTLY, without interference** ← | **Requires a dilute suspension — typically 50 g of soil in a litre** ← |
| **The flow around each particle is LAMINAR** ← | **Which fails for particles above about 0.2 mm, where the settling becomes turbulent** ← |
| **The particles are fully DISPERSED, not flocculated** ← | **Which is why a DEFLOCCULATING agent (sodium hexametaphosphate) is added** ← |
| **The temperature is constant** | **Viscosity changes with temperature, so a correction is applied** ← |

> **THE SHAPE ASSUMPTION IN THE FIRST ROW MEANS THE RESULT IS NOT A TRUE PARTICLE SIZE AT ALL, and this is worth being clear about: what the analysis reports is an EQUIVALENT SETTLING DIAMETER — the diameter of the sphere that would settle at the observed rate.**

> **A plate-shaped clay particle settles slowly, so it is reported as being smaller than its actual largest dimension.**

> **That is not an error in the method; it is the definition of what is being measured, and it happens to be the property that matters for most soil behaviour — how the particle moves in water.**

> **THE DEFLOCCULATION IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE STEP WHOSE OMISSION RUINS THE TEST: clay particles in ordinary water attract one another and clump into flocs.**

> **A floc of a hundred clay particles settles as a single large particle, so the analysis reports the soil as being far coarser than it is — and the result can be wrong by an order of magnitude in the clay fraction, which is the fraction the test exists to measure.**

> **The soil is therefore soaked with a dispersing agent and stirred mechanically before the test, and a sample that was allowed to flocculate must be redone rather than corrected.**

**The two halves of a particle size distribution, and where they join:**

| Method | Range | Principle |
|---|---|---|
| **SIEVE analysis** | **Above 75 μm** ← | **Mechanical separation by physical size** ← |
| **SEDIMENTATION (hydrometer or pipette)** | **Below 75 μm** ← | **Settling velocity, by Stokes' law** ← |
| **The two are COMBINED into one curve** ← | **The sieve result gives the coarse end and the hydrometer the fine end, joined at the 75 μm sieve** ← |

> **THE JOIN AT 75 μm IS WHERE THE TWO METHODS MUST AGREE, and a discontinuity in the combined curve at that point is the standard indicator that something went wrong — usually incomplete washing of the fines through the sieve, or flocculation in the sedimentation cylinder.**

> **Checking that the curve is smooth across the join is therefore the first thing to do with a combined grading, and it costs nothing.**

examTip.trick: **v = (γ_s − γ_w)D²/(18μ), so v ∝ D²** — a particle twice the diameter settles FOUR times as fast, which is what makes the separation practical.
examTip.trap: **The result is an EQUIVALENT SETTLING DIAMETER, not a true size** — clay particles are flat plates and settle slower than spheres, so they report as finer than their largest dimension.
examTip.mnemonic: **Omit the DEFLOCCULATING agent and flocs settle as single large particles** — the clay fraction can read an order of magnitude too coarse. And check the sieve/hydrometer curve joins smoothly at 75 μm.

questions.stem: In earthwork specification, RELATIVE COMPACTION differs from RELATIVE DENSITY (density index) in that relative compaction is:
options: The ratio of the void ratio to the maximum void ratio
Applicable only to clays
The same quantity expressed as a percentage
The ratio of the field dry density achieved to the maximum dry density from a standard laboratory compaction test
questions.solution:
**The ratio of the FIELD dry density achieved to the MAXIMUM dry density from a standard laboratory compaction test**, expressed as a percentage.

**The two quantities compared:**

| Quantity | Definition | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| **RELATIVE COMPACTION, R** ← | **γ_d(field) / γ_d(max, Proctor) × 100** ← | **A LABORATORY COMPACTION test — Standard or Modified Proctor** ← |
| **RELATIVE DENSITY (density index), I_D** ← | **(e_max − e) / (e_max − e_min) × 100** ← (option a is close but incomplete) | **The soil's own MAXIMUM and MINIMUM void ratios** ← |

> **THEY ARE DIFFERENT MEASURES AGAINST DIFFERENT REFERENCES, AND THEY DO NOT CONVERT SIMPLY, which is what the question tests:**

| Aspect | Relative compaction | Relative density |
|---|---|---|
| **Used for** | **ALL soils — the general specification measure** ← | **COHESIONLESS soils only (sands and gravels)** ← |
| **Reference** | **A laboratory compaction curve** | **The loosest and densest states achievable** ← |
| **Typical specified value** | **95 to 98 per cent for structural fill; 90 to 95 for general fill** ← | **70 per cent or more for a dense state** ← |
| **Can it exceed 100 per cent?** | **YES — field compaction can beat the laboratory result** ← | **NO, by definition it is capped at 100** ← |
| **At relative density zero** | **Relative compaction is about 80 per cent, NOT zero** ← | **Zero** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE COMPARISON AND IT SHOWS WHY THE TWO CANNOT BE USED INTERCHANGEABLY: a sand at its LOOSEST possible state has a relative density of ZERO, and a relative compaction of roughly 80 per cent.**

> **A specification demanding "80 per cent relative compaction" for a sand therefore demands nothing at all — the material meets it when simply tipped.**

> **This is why relative DENSITY is the proper measure for granular fill: it is scaled between the soil's own achievable extremes, so it measures how far the compaction has actually progressed.**

> **Relative compaction compresses that whole range into the band from 80 to 100 per cent, where a few percentage points make an enormous difference to the soil's behaviour and are easily lost in testing scatter.**

**THE "OVER 100 PER CENT" RESULT IN THE FOURTH ROW SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IS PERFECTLY LEGITIMATE:**

> **The laboratory maximum is the maximum for THAT COMPACTIVE EFFORT — the standard Proctor's 592 kJ/m³, or the modified Proctor's 2,700 kJ/m³.**

> **A heavy field roller making many passes can apply more energy than a standard Proctor test, and the field density then exceeds the laboratory maximum.**

> **A field result of 103 per cent of standard Proctor is therefore not an error and not a cause for suspicion — though a result of 115 per cent probably indicates the wrong laboratory curve is being used, most often because the fill material has changed and nobody has run a new Proctor test on it.**

**And the practical business of measuring the field density:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **SAND REPLACEMENT (sand cone)** ← | **A hole is dug, the soil weighed, and the hole's volume measured by filling it with calibrated sand — the traditional reference method** ← |
| **CORE CUTTER** | **A cylinder driven into the soil — quick, but only for cohesive soils free of stones** ← |
| **NUCLEAR density gauge** ← | **Fast, non-destructive, and gives moisture content too — but requires licensing and radiation handling** ← |
| **Water/sand balloon** | ← |

> **THE SAND REPLACEMENT METHOD'S RELIABILITY DEPENDS ENTIRELY ON ITS CALIBRATION, and the commonest field error is using sand whose bulk density has not been checked recently: damp sand, contaminated sand, or sand from a different source all pour to a different density, and the computed hole volume is then wrong.**

> **Since the volume is in the denominator of the density, a 5 per cent error in the calibration is a 5 per cent error in the reported compaction — which is the whole width of the acceptance band.**

examTip.trick: **Relative compaction = field γ_d / laboratory maximum γ_d, for ALL soils. Relative density = (e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min), for COHESIONLESS soils only.**
examTip.trap: **A sand at its loosest has relative density ZERO and relative compaction about 80 %** — so specifying 80 % relative compaction for a sand demands nothing at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Field results above 100 % are legitimate** — a heavy roller can beat the Proctor's compactive effort. But above about 115 % suspect the wrong laboratory curve for a changed material.

questions.stem: The SEEPAGE VELOCITY of water through a soil differs from the DISCHARGE (Darcy) velocity in that the seepage velocity:
options: Is the actual average velocity of water in the voids
Is smaller than the discharge velocity
Is the velocity measured at the soil's surface
Is the same quantity under a different name
questions.solution:
**It is the ACTUAL average velocity of the water in the VOIDS**, obtained by dividing the discharge velocity by the POROSITY — and it is therefore always GREATER.

**The relation:**

| Quantity | Definition | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **DISCHARGE (superficial, Darcy) velocity, v** | **The discharge divided by the TOTAL cross-sectional area, solids included** ← | **v = k i** ← |
| **SEEPAGE (actual) velocity, v_s** | **The discharge divided by the area of the VOIDS only** ← | **v_s = v / n, with n the porosity** ← |

> **THE DISCHARGE VELOCITY IS A FICTION AND THE SEEPAGE VELOCITY IS REAL, and that is the cleanest way to hold the distinction:**

> **Water does not flow through the solid grains. It flows only through the voids, which occupy perhaps 30 to 40 per cent of the cross-section.**

> **So the same discharge passing through a smaller actual area must move faster — by the factor 1/n, which for n = 0.35 is about 2.9 times.**

> **The discharge velocity is nevertheless the more useful quantity for computing FLOW, because multiplying it by the gross area gives the discharge directly, with no need to know the porosity — which is precisely why Darcy's law is written in terms of it.**

**When each is needed:**

| Use | Which velocity |
|---|---|
| **Computing the QUANTITY of seepage** ← | **DISCHARGE velocity — Q = k i A, with A the gross area** ← |
| **Computing the TIME for water, or a contaminant, to travel a distance** ← | **SEEPAGE velocity — because that is the speed at which the water actually moves** ← |
| **Checking whether the flow is LAMINAR (Reynolds number)** | **Seepage velocity, in principle** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHERE USING THE WRONG ONE HAS REAL CONSEQUENCES, AND IT MATTERS MOST IN CONTAMINANT TRANSPORT: if a leachate plume is moving from a landfill toward a well, the time it takes is the distance divided by the SEEPAGE velocity.**

> **Using the discharge velocity instead overestimates the travel time by a factor of about three, which is exactly the wrong direction for a public health assessment — it suggests there is three times as long to act as there really is.**

> **The same applies to estimating how long a reservoir's seepage takes to emerge downstream, and to designing any groundwater protection zone.**

**And DARCY'S LAW itself, since this is its natural home:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **v = k i, where i is the HYDRAULIC GRADIENT = head loss ÷ path length** ← | **A LINEAR relation between velocity and gradient** ← |
| **Valid only for LAMINAR flow** ← | **Reynolds number below about 1 — which covers essentially all soils finer than coarse gravel** ← |
| **It FAILS in coarse gravel and rockfill** ← | **Where the flow is turbulent and v ∝ √i rather than i** ← |
| **And it becomes doubtful at very LOW gradients in clay** | **Where a threshold gradient may have to be exceeded before flow begins at all** ← |

> **THE LINEARITY IN THE FIRST ROW IS WHAT MAKES SEEPAGE ANALYSIS TRACTABLE, and it is worth recognising as the reason flow nets work at all: a linear relation between velocity and gradient leads directly to the LAPLACE equation, whose solutions are the orthogonal flow net.**

> **Turbulent flow through rockfill obeys no such equation, which is why seepage through a rockfill dam shell or a gabion cannot be analysed with a flow net and needs an entirely different treatment.**

> **This is the same point met in the fluid mechanics chapter from the other side — Darcy's law is linear because the flow is laminar, and pipe flow's head loss goes as V² because it is turbulent. One distinction, two chapters.**

And it is therefore always GREATER than the discharge velocity.

examTip.trick: **v_s = v/n, so the seepage velocity is always GREATER** — water flows only through the voids, perhaps a third of the area, so it must move about three times faster.
examTip.trap: **Use the DISCHARGE velocity for quantities (Q = kiA) and the SEEPAGE velocity for travel TIMES.** Getting it wrong overestimates a contaminant's travel time threefold.
examTip.mnemonic: **Darcy's law is LINEAR because the flow is laminar** — which is what gives the Laplace equation and the flow net. It fails in rockfill, where flow is turbulent and v ∝ √i.

questions.stem: NEWMARK'S INFLUENCE CHART is used in soil mechanics to determine:
options: The bearing capacity factors for a given angle of internal friction
The time factor for a given degree of consolidation
The vertical stress increase at a point beneath a loaded area of any shape
The permeability of a stratified deposit
questions.solution:
**The vertical stress increase beneath a loaded area of ANY SHAPE** — by drawing the area to a scale set by the depth of the point and COUNTING the influence units it covers.

**How it is used:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The chart is a set of concentric circles divided by radial lines** ← | **Forming a large number of small "influence units", each contributing the SAME stress** ← |
| **Each chart carries an INFLUENCE VALUE — commonly 0.005** ← | **Meaning each unit contributes 0.005 of the applied pressure** ← |
| **The loaded area is drawn on tracing paper to a scale such that the chart's SCALE LINE equals the DEPTH z of the point** ← | **This is the crucial step — the scale CHANGES with the depth** ← |
| **The plan is placed with the POINT of interest over the chart's CENTRE** ← | ← |
| **The influence units covered by the loaded area are COUNTED** | **Including partial units, estimated** ← |
| **Δσ = (influence value) × (number of units) × (applied pressure)** ← | ← |

> **THE SCALING RULE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE HEART OF THE METHOD AND THE PART ALWAYS EXAMINED: the drawing scale is set so that the chart's marked line length represents the DEPTH at which the stress is wanted.**

> **A point deep down means the depth is large, so the area is drawn SMALL, covers fewer units, and the stress is less.**

> **A point near the surface means the area is drawn LARGE, covers many units, and the stress is high.**

> **So the depth enters the calculation entirely through the drawing scale, and a separate diagram must be prepared for every depth — which is the method's principal labour.**

**Why it exists, when closed-form solutions are available:**

| Method | Applies to |
|---|---|
| **BOUSSINESQ point load formula** | **A single concentrated load** ← |
| **Closed-form integrations** | **Circular and RECTANGULAR uniformly loaded areas — the standard cases** ← |
| **The 2:1 approximate method** | **Rectangular footings, roughly** ← |
| **NEWMARK's chart** ← | **ANY shape whatever — an L-shaped raft, an irregular tank base, an embankment cross-section, a group of scattered footings** ← |
| **And it handles the point being OUTSIDE the loaded area** ← | **Which the simple superposition of rectangles handles awkwardly** ← |

> **THE IRREGULAR SHAPE CAPABILITY IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE WHOLE JUSTIFICATION: real foundations are frequently not rectangles, and a raft with re-entrant corners, an irregular tank, or the combined effect of several separate footings cannot be handled by the standard formulae without laborious superposition.**

> **Newmark's chart handles any of them with the same effort — draw the shape and count.**

> **It also handles the point OUTSIDE the loaded area naturally, simply by placing the centre where the point is; the standard rectangular solution requires the area to be built up as a sum and difference of rectangles all having a corner at the point, which is error-prone.**

**Its place today, stated honestly:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It has been largely superseded by numerical integration and finite element analysis** ← | **A computer can integrate over any shape in milliseconds** ← |
| **But it remains valuable as a CHECK and as a teaching device** ← | **Because it makes the superposition principle physically visible** ← |
| **And it is usable with no computer at all** | **Which still matters** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE REASON IT IS STILL TAUGHT AND IT IS A GOOD ONE: the chart makes it VISIBLE that the stress at a point is the sum of contributions from every element of the load, that near elements contribute more than distant ones, and that the influence spreads and weakens with depth.**

> **A student who has counted squares on a Newmark chart understands the Boussinesq stress distribution in a way that running a program does not provide — and the underlying assumptions of the whole approach, which are worth remembering, come with it.**

> **Those assumptions are the ones common to all Boussinesq-based methods: the soil is treated as a HOMOGENEOUS, ISOTROPIC, LINEARLY ELASTIC HALF-SPACE of infinite extent, and the stress distribution is INDEPENDENT of the soil's modulus.**

> **The last of those is a remarkable and useful result — the stress does not depend on how stiff the soil is — but the homogeneity assumption is violated in every layered deposit, and where a stiff layer overlies a soft one the real stress distribution differs substantially from the Boussinesq prediction.**

examTip.trick: **Draw the loaded area so the chart's SCALE LINE equals the DEPTH z, put the point over the centre, and count units: Δσ = (influence value) × (units) × (pressure).**
examTip.trap: **The depth enters only through the DRAWING SCALE** — a new diagram is needed for every depth. Deeper means drawn smaller, fewer units, less stress.
examTip.mnemonic: **Its value is handling ANY shape and points OUTSIDE the loaded area** — an L-shaped raft or scattered footings that the rectangular formulae handle only by awkward superposition.

questions.stem: For an INFINITE SLOPE in a cohesionless soil with STEADY SEEPAGE parallel to the slope surface and the water table AT the surface, the factor of safety compared with the same slope when DRY is:
options: Unchanged, since the soil's friction angle is the same
Roughly halved
Doubled
Increased slightly
questions.solution:
**Roughly HALVED** — the effective normal stress is reduced to that from the SUBMERGED unit weight, while the driving component still comes from the TOTAL unit weight.

**The two cases:**

| Case | Factor of safety |
|---|---|
| **DRY cohesionless infinite slope** | **F = tan φ′ / tan β** ← |
| **With SEEPAGE parallel to the surface, water table at the surface** ← | **F = (γ′/γ_sat) × (tan φ′ / tan β)** ← |

> **THE RATIO γ′/γ_sat IS THE ENTIRE EFFECT, and its value is close to one half for almost every soil:**

| Quantity | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **γ_sat** | **About 20 kN/m³** ← |
| **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w** | **20 − 9.81 = 10.2 kN/m³** ← |
| **γ′/γ_sat** | **10.2 / 20 = 0.51** ← |

> **SO SEEPAGE PARALLEL TO THE SLOPE ROUGHLY HALVES THE FACTOR OF SAFETY, and that single result is the most important quantitative fact in slope stability.**

**Why it happens — the asymmetry is the point:**

| Component | Which unit weight applies |
|---|---|
| **The DRIVING force down the slope** ← | **The TOTAL (saturated) weight — the whole mass of soil AND water is being pulled down the slope** ← |
| **The RESISTING force** ← | **Depends on the EFFECTIVE normal stress, which uses the SUBMERGED weight, because pore pressure reduces it** ← |
| **So the numerator is halved and the denominator is not** ← | **And the factor of safety halves with it** ← |

> **THAT ASYMMETRY IS THE WHOLE MECHANISM AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: the water adds its weight to the driving force and subtracts its pressure from the resisting force.**

> **It works against stability at both ends, which is why the effect is so large.**

**What this explains, which is a great deal:**

| Observation | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **A slope stands for decades and fails in the monsoon** ← | **Nothing about the soil changed; the water table rose and the factor of safety halved** ← |
| **Failures occur DURING or shortly after prolonged rain** ← | **When the water table has risen to the surface and seepage is parallel to the slope** ← |
| **A slope stable at 30° when dry needs about 17° when saturated for the same margin** ← | **For φ′ = 35°: dry F = 1 at β = 35°; with seepage, F = 1 at β ≈ 19.6°** ← |
| **DRAINAGE is the most effective stabilisation measure** ← | **It is the only measure that restores the factor of safety by a factor of two** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION AND IT IS WHY DRAINAGE COMES BEFORE STRUCTURE IN EVERY SLOPE STABILISATION DECISION: no retaining wall, anchor or reinforcement doubles a slope's factor of safety for the cost of a drain.**

> **Lowering the water table below the failure surface removes the pore pressure entirely and restores the dry-slope factor of safety — and it does so passively, permanently and cheaply, provided the drains keep working.**

> **That proviso is the weak point: a horizontal drain that silts up, or a counterfort drain whose outlet is blocked, quietly returns the slope to its saturated condition, and the stabilisation that was paid for is no longer there.**

> **Drain outlets should therefore be visible, accessible and inspected, and a slope stabilised by drainage carries a permanent maintenance obligation exactly as an embanked river does.**

**And the general form, for a c-φ soil:**

> **F = [c′ + (γ_sat − γ_w) z cos²β tan φ′] / (γ_sat z sin β cos β)**

> **The cohesion term is INDEPENDENT of depth z while the friction terms are proportional to it — so as the potential failure surface is taken deeper, the cohesion's contribution becomes proportionately smaller.**

> **In a purely cohesive soil the critical surface is therefore as SHALLOW as possible, and in a c-φ soil the critical depth is found by trial — which is why an infinite slope analysis must be repeated at several depths rather than assumed.**

The effective stress is reduced to the submerged unit weight while the driving weight remains the total unit weight.

examTip.trick: **F drops by the factor γ′/γ_sat ≈ 10.2/20 ≈ 0.5** — roughly halved. Dry: F = tan φ′/tan β. With seepage: multiply by γ′/γ_sat.
examTip.trap: **The asymmetry is the mechanism** — the water ADDS to the driving weight and SUBTRACTS from the effective normal stress. It works against stability at both ends.
examTip.mnemonic: **This is why slopes fail in the monsoon having stood for decades** — and why DRAINAGE is the only measure that doubles the factor of safety for the price of a drain. But the drains must keep working.

questions.stem: Among methods of stabilising an unstable natural slope, the measure that generally gives the greatest improvement for the least cost is:
options: A reinforced concrete retaining wall at the toe
Soil nailing over the whole face
Grouting the slope with cement
Drainage
questions.solution:
**DRAINAGE** — surface interception and subsurface drains, lowering the water table and keeping rainfall out of the slope.

**Why drainage is so effective:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Pore water pressure is usually the TRIGGER of failure, not the cause of the slope's existence** ← | **The slope stood for years; the water made it fail** ← |
| **Lowering the water table can DOUBLE the factor of safety** ← | **The γ′/γ_sat effect — no structural measure comes close for the money** ← |
| **It is PASSIVE — no structure, no maintenance of a load-bearing element** ← | ← |
| **It is cheap and can be built with local labour and materials** | ← |
| **It addresses the CAUSE rather than resisting the effect** ← | ← |

> **THE COMPARISON IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE THAT SETTLES THE PRIORITY, and it is worth being concrete about: a retaining wall at the toe of a large slope resists a small fraction of the driving force, at high cost, and does nothing about the water.**

> **A drainage system removes the water and restores the strength throughout the whole mass.**

> **On a large slide, a wall of any affordable size is simply too small to matter — the mass moving may be tens of thousands of tonnes — while drainage acts on all of it.**

**The drainage measures, in order of priority:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURFACE water interception ABOVE the slope** ← | **A catch drain at the crest, preventing runoff from entering the slope at all — the cheapest and most effective single item** ← |
| **SEALING tension cracks** ← | **Clay fill or polythene, stopping direct rainfall entry — an immediate emergency measure** ← |
| **Surface regrading to shed water, and VEGETATION** | **Grass and shrubs intercept rain, bind the surface and transpire water** ← |
| **HORIZONTAL (sub-horizontal) drains bored into the slope** ← | **Perforated pipes draining the mass by gravity — highly effective and requiring no power** ← |
| **Counterfort or trench drains** | **Deep drainage trenches filled with granular material, running down the slope** ← |
| **Deep wells with pumps** | **A last resort — effective but requiring permanent power and maintenance** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MEASURE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT IS THE BEST VALUE OF ALL: a large share of the water entering an unstable slope comes as RUNOFF FROM THE GROUND ABOVE IT rather than as rain falling on the slope itself.**

> **A single catch drain along the crest, properly lined and with a secure outfall, diverts all of that before it arrives.**

> **It costs a fraction of any works on the slope itself, it can be built quickly, and on many Nepali hillside slides it is the intervention that stops the movement.**

> **The outfall matters as much as the drain: a catch drain that discharges onto the slope a hundred metres to the side has simply moved the problem, and an unlined one leaks its collected water straight into the ground it was built to protect.**

**The other measures and where they belong:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **REGRADING — unload the head, load the toe** ← | **Reduces the driving moment and increases the resisting one; often the most effective structural measure and it uses only earthmoving plant** ← |
| **Toe RETAINING structures — walls, gabions, crib walls** | **Suitable for SMALL slides; too small to matter on large ones** ← |
| **SOIL NAILING and anchors** ← | **Effective and expensive; suits steep cuttings and where space is constrained** ← |
| **Piles and dowels through the failure surface** | **For a shallow, well-defined slip surface** ← |
| **VEGETATION and bio-engineering** ← | **Roots bind the surface soil and transpire water; slow to establish but cheap, self-maintaining and well suited to Nepali hill slopes** ← |
| **Grouting** | **Rarely effective in soil slopes — the grout takes the easy paths and leaves the weak ones** ← |

> **THE REGRADING IN THE FIRST ROW DESERVES ITS PLACE JUST BEHIND DRAINAGE AND IS OFTEN FORGOTTEN: taking weight off the HEAD of a slide and placing it at the TOE improves both sides of the factor of safety at once, uses no materials, and needs only an excavator.**

> **The material removed from the head is exactly what is needed at the toe, so the haul is short and there is no spoil to dispose of.**
