> **THE BIO-ENGINEERING IN THE FIFTH ROW IS PARTICULARLY WELL DEVELOPED IN NEPAL AND IS WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: planting grasses, shrubs and trees in engineered arrangements — brush layers, palisades, fascines, live check dams — stabilises shallow slope failures at a small fraction of the cost of structures.**

> **It is slow, it works only for shallow surface instability rather than deep-seated slides, and it improves with time rather than deteriorating — which is the reverse of every structural measure, and a considerable advantage over a fifty-year horizon.**

examTip.trick: **Drainage attacks the CAUSE and can double the factor of safety** — no structural measure comes close per rupee. Water is usually the trigger, not the reason the slope exists.
examTip.trap: **A toe wall on a large slide is too small to matter** — the moving mass may be tens of thousands of tonnes, while drainage acts on all of it.
examTip.mnemonic: **A CATCH DRAIN at the crest is the best value of all** — much of the water arrives as runoff from above, not as rain on the slope. And REGRADING (unload the head, load the toe) improves both sides at once.

questions.stem: For advancing a borehole through a deposit of dense gravel and boulders below the water table, the most suitable boring method is:
options: Percussion (cable tool) boring
Hand auger boring
Wash boring
Trial pitting
questions.solution:
**PERCUSSION (cable tool) boring** — a heavy chisel repeatedly dropped to break up the material, the debris removed by bailer.

**The boring methods and what each suits:**

| Method | How | Suits | Fails in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TRIAL PIT / trench** ← | **Excavated by hand or machine; the soil is SEEN in place** ← | **Shallow depths (up to 3-4 m); the best possible information where practicable** ← | **Below the water table; and depth is limited by safety** ← |
| **HAND AUGER** | **A screw auger turned by hand** | **Soft to firm cohesive soils and sands above the water table, to about 6 m** ← | **Gravel, stiff clay, below the water table** ← (option b) |
| **WASH boring** | **A chopping bit with water jetted down the rods; cuttings wash up the annulus** ← | **Advancing quickly through soft soils; sampling at intervals** ← | **Gravel and boulders; and the cuttings give POOR identification** ← (option c) |
| **PERCUSSION (cable tool)** ← | **A heavy chisel dropped repeatedly; a bailer removes the debris** ← | **GRAVEL, cobbles, BOULDERS, and hard strata; works below the water table** ← | **It DISTURBS the soil heavily, so samples are poor** ← |
| **ROTARY drilling** | **A rotating bit with flushing fluid** | **ROCK, and deep holes; gives continuous CORE in rock** ← | **Expensive; needs a rig and water** ← |
| **Rotary AUGER (mechanical)** | **A power-driven flight or bucket auger** | **Cohesive soils to considerable depth; large diameter possible** ← | **Boulders** ← |

> **THE GRAVEL-AND-BOULDER CASE ELIMINATES ALMOST EVERY OTHER METHOD, which is what makes the question's answer clear: an auger cannot turn through a boulder, a wash boring's jet cannot cut one, and a trial pit cannot be sunk safely below the water table into gravel.**

> **Percussion boring works precisely because it BREAKS the obstruction rather than trying to cut or displace it.**

> **Its cost is the sample quality: the chiselling shatters and remoulds everything, so a percussion hole tells you what strata are present and at what depth, and very little about their properties.**

> **In practice a percussion hole is therefore used to advance THROUGH the difficult material, with undisturbed samples or in-situ tests taken in the softer strata between.**

**THE TRIAL PIT IN THE FIRST ROW DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS UNDERVALUED: where the depth and the water table allow it, a trial pit gives information no borehole can.**

> **The soil is seen IN PLACE, in section, with its fabric, fissures, roots, layering and any old fill or buried services visible and photographable.**

> **A borehole returns a 100 mm cylinder and a description; a pit shows the ground.**

> **For shallow foundations, for road subgrades and for investigating a slope's near-surface materials, a few pits are worth more than several boreholes and cost far less — and the standard practice of specifying boreholes by default, without any pits, loses a great deal for no reason.**

> **The limitation is absolute though: a pit deeper than about 1.2 m must be supported or battered, and entering an unsupported pit is among the most reliable ways to be killed on a construction site.**

**And the requirements common to all boring, which determine whether the investigation is any use:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The hole must be STABLE** ← | **Casing, or drilling mud, below the water table or in granular soils — otherwise it collapses and the samples are meaningless** ← |
| **Keep the borehole FULL of water or mud below the water table** ← | **Or the base heaves and the soil beneath is disturbed before it is sampled or tested — the same point as with SPT** ← |
| **Log the strata as they are encountered, by a competent person** ← | **The log is the product; the hole is only the means** ← |
| **Seal the hole on completion** ← | **An abandoned open borehole is a direct path for surface contamination into an aquifer, and a hazard** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH STATING AS A PRINCIPLE: a site investigation's value lies in the LOG and the samples, not in the metres drilled.**

> **A deep hole logged carelessly by someone who cannot identify the strata is worth less than a shallow one logged well, and it costs more — which is why the qualification of the person supervising the boring matters more than the specification of the rig.**

Then removed by bailer.

A heavy chisel is repeatedly dropped to break up the material.

examTip.trick: **Percussion BREAKS the obstruction** — an auger cannot turn through a boulder and a wash jet cannot cut one. The cost is heavily disturbed samples.
examTip.trap: **Trial pits give information no borehole can** — the soil is seen in place with its fabric, fissures and layering. But never enter one deeper than about 1.2 m unsupported.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep the hole FULL of water below the water table** — or the base heaves and the soil is disturbed before it is sampled. And the LOG is the product; the hole is only the means.

questions.stem: In the design of an ANCHORED sheet pile bulkhead, the FREE EARTH SUPPORT method differs from the FIXED EARTH SUPPORT method in that free earth support assumes:
options: The wall is not anchored at all
The soil below the dredge line offers no resistance
The pile is driven so deep that its toe is effectively fixed against rotation
The pile is embedded just enough for the toe to be free to rotate
questions.solution:
**The pile is embedded just enough for its toe to be FREE TO ROTATE** — so the wall behaves as a simply supported beam spanning between the anchor and the passive resistance.

**The two methods compared:**

| Aspect | FREE earth support | FIXED earth support |
|---|---|---|
| **Assumed toe condition** | **FREE to rotate — the embedment is the minimum for stability** ← | **FIXED against rotation — the pile is driven deeper, into firmer ground** ← |
| **Structural analogy** | **A simply supported beam: anchor at one end, passive resistance at the other** ← | **A propped cantilever, or a beam fixed at one end** ← |
| **Deflected shape** | **The toe MOVES outward** ← | **The toe is held, and there is a point of CONTRAFLEXURE below the dredge line** ← |
| **Depth of embedment required** | **LESS** ← | **MORE — typically 20 to 40 per cent deeper** ← |
| **Maximum BENDING MOMENT in the pile** | **HIGHER** ← | **LOWER — the fixity relieves the span moment** ← |
| **Anchor force** | **HIGHER** | **Lower** ← |
| **Analysis** | **SIMPLE — statically determinate, solved by taking moments about the anchor** ← | **More complex; indeterminate, needing the equivalent beam method** ← |

> **THE TRADE-OFF IN ROWS FOUR AND FIVE IS THE WHOLE DESIGN DECISION AND IT IS A CLEAN ONE: free earth support gives a SHORTER pile with a BIGGER section; fixed earth support gives a LONGER pile with a SMALLER section.**

> **Which is cheaper depends on the relative cost of length and of section modulus, and on whether the ground below the dredge line is firm enough to provide the fixity at all.**

> **In soft soil the toe cannot be fixed however deep the pile is driven, so free earth support is the only valid assumption — the method is not a free choice but a consequence of the ground.**

**How free earth support is analysed, since its simplicity is its merit:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Draw the ACTIVE pressure diagram on the retained side and the PASSIVE on the dredged side** ← | ← |
| **The unknowns are the embedment depth d and the anchor force T** | **Two unknowns** ← |
| **Take MOMENTS about the ANCHOR point** ← | **This eliminates T, leaving one equation in d — which is solved (usually a cubic, by trial)** ← |
| **Then resolve HORIZONTALLY to find T** ← | ← |
| **Apply a factor of safety** | **Either on the passive resistance (commonly 1.5 to 2) or by increasing the embedment by 20 to 40 per cent** ← |

> **TAKING MOMENTS ABOUT THE ANCHOR IS THE KEY STEP AND IT IS WHY THE METHOD IS DETERMINATE: it removes the anchor force from the equation, so the embedment can be found independently.**

> **That single choice of moment centre turns a two-unknown problem into two successive one-unknown problems, and it is worth recognising as a general technique — take moments about the point through which the unknown you do not want passes.**

**The practical points that decide whether such a wall performs:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The ANCHOR must be placed OUTSIDE the active wedge** ← | **Beyond the failure plane rising at 45° + φ/2 from the pile's toe — otherwise the anchor moves with the soil it is anchoring** ← |
| **DRAINAGE behind the wall is essential** ← | **Water pressure acts with K = 1 and can exceed the soil pressure — weep holes or a granular drain** ← |
| **The dredge level may be LOWERED later** ← | **By scour, by future dredging, or by an excavation — and the passive resistance vanishes with it** ← |
| **Corrosion of the sheet piles and the tie rods** | **Particularly at the splash zone and at the tie rod's connections** ← |
| **The tie rod must tolerate SETTLEMENT of the fill above it** ← | **Which drags it down and can bend or break it — hence supporting it on small piers or wrapping it** ← |

> **THE ANCHOR POSITION IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST COMMON AND MOST SERIOUS DESIGN ERROR IN ANCHORED WALLS AND IT IS COMPLETELY AVOIDABLE: an anchor block placed within the active wedge is founded in soil that is itself trying to move outward.**

> **As the wall deflects, the wedge moves, the anchor moves with it, and the wall deflects further — the anchor provides no restraint whatever, though it looks substantial.**

> **The rule is geometric and easy to check on a section: draw the failure plane from the pile's toe at 45° + φ/2 to the horizontal, and the anchor must be entirely beyond it.**

> **THE TIE ROD SETTLEMENT IN THE LAST ROW IS A REAL AND SOMEWHAT SURPRISING FAILURE MODE: the fill placed over the tie rod settles, and the rod — anchored at both ends — is dragged into a sag.**

> **Being a slender tension member with no bending capacity, it can be permanently deformed or broken by the settlement alone, without any load from the wall.**

> **Supporting the rods on small brick or concrete piers at intervals, and placing the fill around them carefully, prevents it — and it is a detail that costs almost nothing and is regularly omitted.**

examTip.trick: **Free earth support: toe FREE to rotate, shorter pile, HIGHER moment. Fixed earth support: toe FIXED, longer pile, LOWER moment.** A clean trade between length and section.
examTip.trap: **In soft soil the toe cannot be fixed however deep you drive** — so free earth support is forced by the ground, not chosen. And take moments about the ANCHOR to eliminate T.
examTip.mnemonic: **The anchor must lie OUTSIDE the active wedge** — beyond the plane at 45° + φ/2 from the toe, or it moves with the soil it is restraining. Check it geometrically on the section.

questions.stem: A COMPACTION pile, as distinct from an end-bearing or a friction pile, is one that is:
options: Driven to refusal on hard rock
Driven into a loose granular deposit primarily to densify the surrounding soil rather than to carry load through the pile itself
Used to resist uplift or tension
Installed at an inclination to resist horizontal forces
questions.solution:
**Driven into a LOOSE granular deposit primarily to DENSIFY the surrounding soil**, rather than to carry load through the pile itself.

**The classification of piles by FUNCTION:**

| Type | Function |
|---|---|
| **END-BEARING pile** | **Transmits its load to a firm stratum at its base — rock or dense sand** ← (option a) |
| **FRICTION (floating) pile** | **Carries its load by SKIN FRICTION along its shaft, where no firm stratum is within reach** ← |
| **COMPACTION pile** ← | **DENSIFIES a loose granular deposit; the pile itself may carry little load, and is sometimes made of sand or gravel rather than concrete** ← |
| **TENSION (uplift, anchor) pile** | **Resists upward force — from buoyancy, from overturning, or from an anchored structure** ← (option c) |
| **BATTER (raking) pile** | **Driven at an inclination to resist HORIZONTAL loads** ← (option d) |
| **SHEET pile** | **Retains soil or water; a wall rather than a load-carrying pile** ← |
| **FENDER and dolphin piles** | **Absorb impact from vessels** ← |

> **THE COMPACTION PILE IS THE ODD ONE OUT AND THAT IS WHAT THE QUESTION TURNS ON: every other type in the table carries load THROUGH the pile.**

> **A compaction pile improves the GROUND, and the improved ground then carries the load — sometimes by a shallow foundation, with the piles' own capacity ignored entirely.**

> **It is a ground improvement technique that happens to use a pile as its tool, rather than a foundation element.**

**How compaction piles work:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **DISPLACEMENT — the pile's volume pushes the surrounding soil outward** ← | **Reducing its void ratio directly** ← |
| **VIBRATION from driving rearranges loose granular particles into a denser packing** ← | **Which is why they suit sands and not clays** ← |
| **The effect extends several diameters around each pile** | **So a grid of piles densifies the whole mass** ← |
| **They are ineffective, and can be harmful, in CLAY** ← | **Clay is not densified by vibration; it is remoulded, loses strength, and generates pore pressure** ← |

> **THE CLAY EXCLUSION IN THE LAST ROW IS ABSOLUTE AND IS THE MOST IMPORTANT LIMITATION: displacement piles driven into soft clay do not improve it.**

> **They remould it, destroy whatever structure gave it its strength, and generate excess pore pressures that reduce the effective stress temporarily.**

> **The ground is worse immediately after driving than before, and it recovers over weeks as the pore pressures dissipate — which is the SET-UP effect noted with pile load testing, seen here from the other side.**

**The related ground improvement techniques, which the compaction pile sits among:**

| Technique | Note |
|---|---|
| **COMPACTION piles** | **This question** ← |
| **STONE COLUMNS (granular piles)** ← | **Columns of compacted stone formed by vibro-replacement — they densify the soil AND provide a stiff, free-draining inclusion; effective in soft clays too, where compaction piles are not** ← |
| **VIBROFLOTATION** ← | **A vibrating probe lowered into loose sand, densifying it with water jetting; no pile is left behind** ← |
| **DYNAMIC COMPACTION** ← | **A heavy weight dropped repeatedly from a height onto the ground surface — crude, cheap, effective to several metres, and very noisy** ← |
| **PRELOADING with vertical drains** | **For soft clays — consolidating the ground in advance under a temporary surcharge** ← |
| **Grouting and deep soil mixing** | ← |

> **THE STONE COLUMN IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE TECHNIQUE THAT HAS LARGELY DISPLACED THE COMPACTION PILE, and its advantage is that it works in soils where a displacement pile does not.**

> **In a soft clay a stone column does three things at once: it carries load as a stiff inclusion, it drains the clay so consolidation is accelerated, and it reinforces the mass against shear.**

> **It is also cheaper than a concrete pile, uses only stone, and is installed by a rig that does not need to lift heavy precast units.**

> **The trade-off is that a stone column relies on the surrounding soil to CONFINE it — a stone column in a very soft clay bulges outward under load and loses capacity — so there is a lower limit to the clay strength for which it is suitable, typically around 15 to 20 kPa undrained shear strength.**

> **Below that, the column is not confined and the technique fails, which is why the site investigation must establish the soft clay's strength before the ground improvement method can be chosen.**

examTip.trick: **A compaction pile improves the GROUND; every other pile type carries load THROUGH the pile.** Option (a) end bearing, (c) tension, (d) batter.
examTip.trap: **They work only in granular soils** — driven into soft clay they remould it, generate pore pressure and leave the ground WORSE than before, recovering only as the pressures dissipate.
examTip.mnemonic: **STONE COLUMNS have largely displaced them** — they carry load, drain the clay and reinforce it at once. But they need the surrounding soil to CONFINE them, so below about 15-20 kPa they bulge and fail.

questions.stem: A long STRIP footing rests at shallow depth on a saturated clay of undrained shear strength 60 kPa (φ = 0). Taking Terzaghi's bearing capacity factor N_c as 5.7 and a factor of safety of 3, the NET SAFE bearing capacity is:
options: 57 kPa
76 kPa
100 kPa
114 kPa
questions.solution:
**114 kPa.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **For φ = 0, the N_q and N_γ terms VANISH** ← | **N_q = 1 and N_γ = 0, so only the cohesion term survives in NET terms** ← |
| **Net ultimate bearing capacity** | **q_nu = c N_c = 60 × 5.7** ← |
| **= 342 kPa** | ← |
| **Net SAFE bearing capacity = q_nu / FoS** | **= 342 / 3** |
| **q_ns** | **= 114 kPa** ← |

> **Option (c) 100 kPa comes from using N_c = 5.14 — the exact plasticity solution for a strip footing — instead of Terzaghi's 5.7, and it is a legitimate value under a different theory, which makes it the best distractor.**

> **The question specifies 5.7, so Terzaghi's value must be used; but it is worth knowing that the two coexist in the literature and differ by about 11 per cent.**

**Why the φ = 0 case is so much simpler:**

| Term | For φ = 0 |
|---|---|
| **c N_c** | **The only term that contributes to the NET capacity** ← |
| **q N_q** | **N_q = 1, so this term equals the overburden q itself — it cancels when the NET capacity is taken** ← |
| **0.5 γ B N_γ** | **N_γ = 0, so this term VANISHES entirely** ← |

> **THE VANISHING OF THE N_γ TERM HAS A CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING AND IT IS FREQUENTLY EXAMINED: for a footing on SATURATED CLAY in the undrained condition, the bearing capacity is INDEPENDENT OF THE FOOTING'S WIDTH.**

> **Making the footing wider does not increase its bearing PRESSURE capacity at all — it increases only the total load, in proportion to the area.**

> **In SAND the opposite holds: the N_γ term is proportional to B, so a wider footing has a higher permissible pressure as well as a larger area, and widening improves matters twice over.**

> **That single difference — width matters in sand, not in clay — explains a great deal about how foundations on the two materials are proportioned.**

**The distinction between GROSS and NET, which the question depends on:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS ultimate, q_u** | **The TOTAL pressure at the base at failure, including the overburden** ← |
| **NET ultimate, q_nu** | **q_u − q, the INCREASE over what was already there before excavation** ← |
| **Net SAFE, q_ns** | **q_nu / FoS** ← |
| **Gross safe** | **q_ns + q — the net safe value PLUS the overburden added back** ← |
| **SAFE BEARING PRESSURE** ← | **The lesser of the net safe bearing capacity and the pressure limited by permissible SETTLEMENT** ← |

> **THE FACTOR OF SAFETY IS APPLIED TO THE NET VALUE AND NOT THE GROSS, and the reason is worth understanding: the overburden pressure q was ALREADY acting on the soil before the footing was built.**

> **The soil has carried it indefinitely without failing, so there is no need to apply a factor of safety to it.**

> **Only the ADDITIONAL pressure imposed by the structure is new, and it is that increase which the factor of safety must cover.**

> **Applying the factor to the gross value is a common error and it is unnecessarily conservative — the deeper the footing, the greater the penalty it imposes for no reason.**

> **THE LAST ROW OF THE TABLE IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL POINT AND IT IS WHY THIS CALCULATION IS RARELY THE END OF THE MATTER: the safe bearing PRESSURE is the LESSER of the strength-based value and the settlement-based one.**

> **For a footing on stiff clay or dense sand, the strength calculation usually gives a generous figure and SETTLEMENT governs.**

> **Computing 114 kPa and adopting it without checking the settlement is therefore only half the design — and on a compressible clay the permissible pressure may be a third of the strength-based value.**

examTip.trick: **q_nu = c N_c = 60 × 5.7 = 342 kPa; net safe = 342/3 = 114 kPa.** Option (c) uses N_c = 5.14, the exact plasticity value — legitimate under a different theory.
examTip.trap: **For φ = 0 the N_γ term VANISHES, so bearing capacity in clay is INDEPENDENT of footing width.** In sand it is proportional to B, so widening helps twice over.
examTip.mnemonic: **Apply the FoS to the NET value** — the overburden was already there and needs no factor. And the safe bearing PRESSURE is the lesser of strength and SETTLEMENT, which usually governs.

questions.stem: The property that distinguishes a FLUID from a SOLID is that a fluid:
options: Deforms continuously under an applied shear stress
Cannot resist any compressive stress
Has no definite mass
Always takes the shape of a sphere
questions.solution:
**A fluid DEFORMS CONTINUOUSLY under an applied shear stress, however small that stress may be.**

**The distinction, set out:**

| Material | Response to a small SHEAR stress |
|---|---|
| **SOLID** | **Deforms by a FINITE amount and then STOPS, in equilibrium with the stress; it recovers when the stress is removed if the deformation was elastic** ← |
| **FLUID** | **Deforms CONTINUOUSLY and does not stop, for as long as the stress is applied — that is, it FLOWS** ← |

> **THE WORDS "HOWEVER SMALL" ARE THE ESSENTIAL PART OF THE DEFINITION AND ARE OFTEN OMITTED, and without them the statement is not a definition at all:**

> **A solid subjected to a large enough shear stress also deforms continuously — that is what yielding is.**

> **What distinguishes a fluid is that there is NO THRESHOLD. Any shear stress, however tiny, produces continuous deformation, so a fluid at rest can sustain no shear stress whatever.**

> **That single consequence — a fluid at rest has no shear stress — is what makes hydrostatics work: pressure at a point in a static fluid is the same in every direction, precisely because there is no shear to make it otherwise.**

**Option (b) is worth rejecting explicitly:**

> **A fluid resists COMPRESSION very well. Water is nearly incompressible, and its bulk modulus of about 2.2 GPa is a real and substantial resistance.**

> **What a fluid cannot resist is SHEAR — and it cannot generally resist TENSION either, which is why cavitation occurs when the pressure falls to the vapour pressure rather than the water being pulled apart.**

**The borderline cases, which the definition handles interestingly:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **A BINGHAM PLASTIC — toothpaste, fresh concrete, sewage sludge** ← | **It requires a YIELD stress before flowing, so strictly it is NOT a fluid by this definition — it behaves as a solid below the yield stress** ← |
| **PITCH or glacier ice** ← | **Deforms continuously under its own weight, but over YEARS — so it is a fluid on a geological timescale and a solid on a human one** ← |
| **Sand and other granular materials** | **Flow, but by particle rearrangement rather than as a continuum** ← |

> **THE PITCH CASE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE FAMOUS ONE AND IT MAKES A REAL POINT: whether a material is a fluid depends on the TIMESCALE of observation.**

> **The University of Queensland's pitch drop experiment, running since 1927, has produced about nine drops — pitch is unambiguously a fluid, with a viscosity some 200 billion times that of water.**

> **Glacier ice is the engineering case: it deforms continuously under its own weight and flows down valleys at metres per year, which is why glaciers are analysed as very viscous fluids and not as solids.**

**And the consequences of the definition, which run through the whole subject:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A fluid at rest sustains NO shear stress** ← | **Hence pressure is equal in all directions at a point — Pascal's law** ← |
| **A fluid takes the shape of its container** | **Because it cannot resist the shear needed to hold any other shape** ← |
| **Shear stress in a moving fluid depends on the RATE of deformation, not the amount** ← | **τ = μ (du/dy) — velocity GRADIENT, not displacement — which is the fundamental difference from Hooke's law for a solid** ← |
| **The NO-SLIP condition holds at a boundary** | **The fluid in contact with a surface moves with it** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCE BETWEEN FLUID AND SOLID MECHANICS AND IT IS WORTH STATING AS A PAIR: for a SOLID, stress is proportional to STRAIN (τ = G γ). For a FLUID, stress is proportional to the RATE OF STRAIN (τ = μ dγ/dt).**

> **A solid remembers its original shape and resists departure from it; a fluid has no memory of shape at all and resists only the SPEED of the change.**

> **Every difference between the two subjects follows from that one substitution of a rate for a displacement.**

examTip.trick: **Continuous deformation under ANY shear stress, however small.** The words "however small" are the definition — a solid also flows above its yield stress.
examTip.trap: **A fluid resists COMPRESSION well** (water's bulk modulus is 2.2 GPa). It cannot resist SHEAR, and generally not TENSION either — hence cavitation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Solid: stress ∝ STRAIN (τ = Gγ). Fluid: stress ∝ RATE of strain (τ = μ du/dy).** A solid remembers its shape; a fluid resists only the speed of change. Every difference follows from that.

questions.stem: A simple PIEZOMETER tube cannot be used to measure:
options: The pressure of water in a pipe flowing full
The pressure at the base of an open tank
Negative (vacuum) pressures, or the pressure of a gas
The pressure at any point below the free surface
questions.solution:
**Negative (vacuum) pressures, or the pressure of a GAS** — and it is impractical for large pressures, which would need an excessively tall tube.

**Why each of those fails:**

| Limitation | Reason |
|---|---|
| **NEGATIVE pressure** ← | **The liquid would be SUCKED DOWN the tube and air drawn into the pipe — the piezometer would admit air rather than measure the pressure** ← |
| **GAS pressure** ← | **There is no liquid column to rise; the gas would simply escape from the open top of the tube** ← |
| **LARGE pressures** ← | **A pressure of 3 bar needs a tube over 30 m tall — absurd** ← |
| **Very SMALL pressures** | **The rise is too small to read accurately, and capillarity in a fine tube distorts it** ← |

> **THE PIEZOMETER'S SIMPLICITY IS BOTH ITS VIRTUE AND ITS LIMITATION: it is nothing but a vertical open tube tapped into the pipe, and the height the liquid rises IS the pressure head directly, with no calculation at all.**

> **For a modest positive pressure of a liquid, nothing is more accurate or more reliable — there is no instrument to calibrate and nothing to go wrong.**

> **It fails in exactly the cases where its open top and its reliance on the flowing liquid itself become problems.**

**The instruments and what each overcomes:**

| Instrument | Overcomes |
|---|---|
| **PIEZOMETER** | **Nothing — the baseline; simple, accurate, limited** ← |
| **U-TUBE MANOMETER with mercury** ← | **Measures LARGE pressures in a short tube, because mercury is 13.6 times denser — and it measures NEGATIVE pressures and GASES too, since the measured fluid is separated from the atmosphere by the gauge liquid** ← |
| **DIFFERENTIAL manometer** ← | **Measures the DIFFERENCE in pressure between two points directly — as across a venturimeter or an orifice plate** ← |
| **INVERTED U-tube manometer, with air or a lighter liquid** ← | **For SMALL differences in liquid pressure — it magnifies the reading** ← |
| **MICROMANOMETER / inclined tube** ← | **Very small pressures — an inclined tube converts a small vertical rise into a long, readable movement along the tube** ← |
| **BOURDON gauge** | **Rugged, direct-reading, portable; but it needs calibration and is less accurate** ← |
| **Pressure TRANSDUCER** | **Electrical output for recording and telemetry** ← |

> **THE MERCURY U-TUBE IN THE SECOND ROW SOLVES THREE OF THE PIEZOMETER'S FOUR PROBLEMS AT ONCE, and the reason is worth seeing: introducing a second, DENSER liquid means a given pressure produces a much shorter column.**

> **A pressure requiring 30 m of water needs only 2.2 m of mercury.**

> **And because the gauge liquid separates the measured fluid from the atmosphere, the instrument no longer depends on the measured fluid reaching the open end — so gases and vacuums can be measured.**

> **THE INCLINED TUBE IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ELEGANT SOLUTION TO THE OPPOSITE PROBLEM and it is worth knowing the principle: if the tube is inclined at angle θ to the horizontal, a vertical rise h produces a movement of h/sin θ ALONG the tube.**

> **At θ = 10°, sin θ = 0.174, so the reading is magnified about six times.**

> **The magnification is free — no mechanism, no electronics, just geometry — and it is why inclined manometers are still used for measuring small air pressures in ventilation work.**

**And the practical point about tapping a piezometer into a pipe, which decides whether the reading is right:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The tapping must be FLUSH with the inside wall and free of burrs** ← | **A protruding or burred tapping disturbs the flow and reads the local dynamic effect rather than the static pressure** ← |
| **It must be perpendicular to the flow** ← | **A tapping facing upstream reads the STAGNATION pressure — static plus dynamic — which is a different quantity** ← |
| **Small diameter, and free of air bubbles** | **Air in the tube gives a false reading** ← |

> **The second row is the distinction between a piezometer and a PITOT tube stated as a construction detail: the same hole, facing sideways, measures STATIC pressure; facing upstream, it measures STAGNATION pressure.**

> **The difference between the two is the dynamic head — which is precisely how a pitot-static tube measures velocity, and why the orientation of a tapping is not a matter of convenience.**

examTip.trick: **A piezometer is an open tube, so it fails for negative pressures (air is drawn in), for gases (nothing rises), and for large pressures (an absurd tube height).**
examTip.trap: **A mercury U-tube solves three of those at once** — 13.6 times denser gives a short column, and the gauge liquid separates the measured fluid from the atmosphere.
examTip.mnemonic: **An INCLINED tube magnifies a small reading by 1/sin θ — about six times at 10°** — free magnification from geometry alone. And a tapping facing UPSTREAM reads stagnation, not static.

questions.stem: For a body FULLY SUBMERGED in a liquid, the condition for STABLE equilibrium is that:
options: The centre of buoyancy lies above the centre of gravity
The centre of gravity lies above the centre of buoyancy
The metacentre lies above the centre of gravity
The two centres coincide
questions.solution:
**The CENTRE OF BUOYANCY must lie ABOVE the centre of gravity.**

**Why the condition differs from that for a FLOATING body — which is the point of the question:**

| Body | Condition for stability | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **FULLY SUBMERGED** ← | **B ABOVE G** ← | **The displaced volume is FIXED, so B does not move when the body tilts — the only restoring possibility is B being above G** ← |
| **FLOATING (partly submerged)** ← | **The METACENTRE M above G** ← (option c) | **The displaced volume CHANGES SHAPE as the body tilts, so B MOVES sideways — and that movement can create a righting moment even with G above B** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE LIES ENTIRELY IN WHETHER B CAN MOVE, and once that is grasped both conditions are obvious:**

> **In a SUBMERGED body — a submarine, a buried pipeline, a diving bell — the whole body is under water, so the displaced volume is the body's own volume and it does not change when the body rotates.**

> **B therefore stays at the centroid of the body's volume, fixed relative to the body. If B is above G, tilting creates a couple that rights the body. If B is below G, tilting creates a couple that overturns it. There is no third possibility.**

> **In a FLOATING body, tilting changes the SHAPE of the immersed volume — more on one side, less on the other — so B shifts toward the immersed side.**

> **That sideways shift can put the buoyant force's line of action outboard of G, creating a righting moment even though G is above B, which is how a ship with a high centre of gravity floats stably.**

**The three states, for both cases:**

| State | Submerged body | Floating body |
|---|---|---|
| **STABLE** | **B above G** ← | **M above G (positive GM)** ← |
| **NEUTRAL** | **B and G coincide** ← | **M and G coincide (GM = 0)** ← |
| **UNSTABLE** | **B below G** ← | **M below G (negative GM)** ← |

> **A SUBMARINE IS THE CLEAREST ILLUSTRATION OF THE SUBMERGED CASE, and its design reflects it directly: the heavy machinery, batteries and ballast are placed LOW in the hull and the buoyancy tanks HIGH, deliberately putting G below B.**

> **A submarine is therefore stable in roll by construction, and it cannot capsize while fully submerged.**

> **When it surfaces, however, it becomes a FLOATING body and the metacentric criterion takes over — and a surfaced submarine, with its narrow round hull, has notoriously poor stability and rolls badly.**

> **The same vessel, two different criteria, depending only on whether it is fully immersed.**

**THE METACENTRIC HEIGHT for a floating body, since the comparison invites it:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **GM = BM − BG** ← | **With BM = I/V, where I is the second moment of the WATERPLANE area and V the displaced volume** ← |
| **A WIDER vessel has a much larger I** ← | **I goes as the beam CUBED, so beam is what gives stability** ← |
| **A large GM gives a STIFF vessel** | **Strong righting moment, but a short, violent rolling period — uncomfortable and hard on the cargo** ← |
| **A small positive GM gives a TENDER vessel** ← | **Gentle, slow roll — comfortable, but less margin against capsize** ← |

> **THE TRADE IN THE LAST TWO ROWS IS A REAL NAVAL ARCHITECTURE DECISION AND IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE: more stability is not simply better.**

> **A vessel with a very large GM snaps upright violently after each wave, and the accelerations can injure the crew, shift the cargo and damage the structure.**

> **A comfortable ship has a modest positive GM — enough for safety, not so much as to make it jerk — which is why loading a ship is a matter of achieving a target GM rather than maximising it.**

examTip.trick: **SUBMERGED: B above G. FLOATING: M above G.** The difference is that a submerged body's displaced volume cannot change shape, so B cannot move.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is the FLOATING condition** — a well-made distractor, since the metacentric criterion is the one usually taught first.
examTip.mnemonic: **A submarine is stable submerged by construction (heavy gear low, tanks high) and rolls badly on the surface** — same vessel, two criteria. And BM = I/V, with I going as the BEAM CUBED.

questions.stem: Compared with an ORIFICE METER, a VENTURIMETER measuring the same discharge in the same pipe has:
options: A higher permanent head loss and a lower cost
The same head loss but a lower coefficient of discharge
A much lower permanent head loss and a higher coefficient of discharge
A lower coefficient of discharge and a shorter length
questions.solution:
**A much LOWER permanent head loss and a HIGHER coefficient of discharge** — at the cost of being longer, bulkier and considerably more expensive.

**The comparison:**

| Property | VENTURIMETER | ORIFICE METER |
|---|---|---|
| **Coefficient of discharge C_d** | **0.95 to 0.99** ← | **0.60 to 0.65** ← |
| **PERMANENT head loss** | **LOW — only 10 to 20 per cent of the differential** ← | **HIGH — 50 to 80 per cent of the differential** ← |
| **Length and space needed** | **LONG — a converging cone, throat and a long diverging cone** ← | **A thin PLATE between two flanges** ← |
| **Cost** | **HIGH** ← | **VERY LOW** ← |
| **Wear and silting** | **Less affected; smooth passages** ← | **The sharp edge WEARS and rounds, and the C_d drifts** ← |
| **Suits** | **Large pipes, permanent installations, and where PUMPING COST matters** ← | **Temporary measurement, small pipes, and where cheapness matters** ← |

> **THE HEAD LOSS DIFFERENCE IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES BETWEEN THEM IN PRACTICE, AND THE REASON IS ENTIRELY IN THE DIVERGING CONE:**

> **Both meters accelerate the flow to create a pressure difference, and both must then decelerate it again.**

> **The venturimeter does so through a LONG, GENTLE diverging cone — typically 5° to 7° included angle — so the flow follows the wall without separating, and most of the kinetic energy is recovered as pressure.**

> **An orifice plate has no diverging section at all. The jet emerges, separates, and dissipates its energy in violent turbulence downstream — exactly like a sudden enlargement.**

> **So the venturimeter's expense buys back most of the head, permanently, on every cubic metre that passes for the whole life of the installation.**

**THE ECONOMIC ARGUMENT IS WORTH MAKING CONCRETE, because it is how the choice is actually justified:**

> **A meter on a pumped main causing a permanent loss of 1 m of head, on a flow of 100 litres per second, wastes about 1 kW continuously — some 8,800 kWh a year, every year.**

> **Over twenty years the pumping energy wasted by an orifice plate can far exceed the cost of a venturimeter, and the calculation usually favours the venturi wherever the flow is large and continuous and the water is pumped.**

> **Where the flow is by GRAVITY and there is surplus head available, the head loss costs nothing and the orifice plate's cheapness wins — which is why the same measurement is made two different ways in two different installations.**

**Why the coefficients differ so much, which is the other half of the comparison:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **C_d = C_c × C_v — the contraction and velocity coefficients** ← | ← |
| **In a VENTURI, the flow is GUIDED by the converging cone right to the throat** ← | **So there is essentially no vena contracta: C_c ≈ 1, and C_d is limited only by friction** ← |
| **In an ORIFICE, the jet CONTRACTS beyond the plate to a vena contracta** ← | **Of about 0.62 of the orifice area — which is where nearly all of the low C_d comes from** ← |

> **THE VENA CONTRACTA IS THEREFORE THE SINGLE EXPLANATION FOR BOTH DIFFERENCES: it reduces the effective area (lowering C_d) and it produces the separated, turbulent flow downstream (raising the head loss).**

> **The venturi's converging cone exists precisely to prevent it, and everything else about the comparison follows.**

> **The intermediate device, worth knowing, is the FLOW NOZZLE: a shaped convergent inlet with no diverging cone. It has the venturi's high C_d, because the flow is guided, and much of the orifice's head loss, because there is no recovery — so it is a genuine middle option, shorter than a venturi and more accurate than an orifice.**

But it is longer, bulkier and considerably more expensive.

examTip.trick: **Venturi C_d 0.95-0.99 and 10-20 % head loss; orifice C_d 0.60-0.65 and 50-80 % loss.** The venturi is long and expensive, the orifice a plate between flanges.
examTip.trap: **Both differences come from the VENA CONTRACTA** — the orifice's jet contracts to 0.62 of the area (low C_d) and then dissipates in turbulence (high loss). The converging cone prevents both.
examTip.mnemonic: **On a PUMPED main the head loss is a permanent energy bill** — 1 m at 100 l/s wastes ~8,800 kWh a year. On a GRAVITY main with spare head, the orifice's cheapness wins.

questions.stem: In a FORCED vortex, as distinct from a FREE vortex:
options: The velocity varies inversely with the radius, and no external energy is supplied
The fluid rotates as a solid body with the tangential velocity proportional to the radius, and external energy must be continuously supplied
The free surface is horizontal
The flow is always irrotational
questions.solution:
**The fluid rotates as a SOLID BODY, with the tangential velocity PROPORTIONAL to the radius — and external energy must be supplied continuously to maintain it.**

**The two vortices compared:**

| Property | FREE (potential) vortex | FORCED (rotational) vortex |
|---|---|---|
| **Velocity distribution** | **v × r = constant, so v ∝ 1/r — FASTEST at the centre** ← (option a) | **v = ω r, so v ∝ r — SLOWEST at the centre, zero on the axis** ← |
| **External energy** | **NONE required — the motion persists from the fluid's own momentum** ← | **Must be supplied CONTINUOUSLY, by an impeller, a rotating vessel or a stirrer** ← |
| **Rotationality** | **IRROTATIONAL everywhere except at the singular centre** ← (so option d belongs to the free vortex) | **ROTATIONAL throughout — every particle spins about its own axis** ← |
| **Free surface profile** | **A hyperbolic funnel, z ∝ −1/r²** ← | **A PARABOLOID of revolution, z ∝ r²** ← |
| **Bernoulli's equation** | **APPLIES between any two points, since the flow is irrotational** ← | **Applies only ALONG a streamline, not between different radii** ← |
| **Examples** | **Water draining from a bath; flow in a spiral casing; a tornado's outer region; flow through a turbine's guide vanes** ← | **Water in a rotated bucket; a centrifugal pump's impeller passages; a tornado's core** ← |

> **THE ENERGY ROW IS THE PHYSICAL DISTINCTION AND THE OTHERS FOLLOW FROM IT: a free vortex is a fluid coasting on its own angular momentum, which is conserved — hence v r = constant.**

> **A forced vortex is a fluid being DRIVEN, so its angular momentum is continually supplied and it settles into rigid-body rotation.**

> **Stop driving a forced vortex and it decays; a free vortex needs nothing to sustain it but the absence of friction.**

**THE FREE SURFACE PROFILES ARE THE MOST VISIBLE DIFFERENCE AND ARE WORTH BEING ABLE TO PICTURE:**

| Vortex | Surface | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **FORCED** | **A shallow PARABOLIC dish, rising toward the rim** ← | **z = ω²r²/2g — the surface rises as r², and the whole body rotates together** ← |
| **FREE** | **A deep, narrow FUNNEL plunging at the centre** ← | **z falls as 1/r², so it drops steeply and asymptotically near the axis** ← |

> **THE BATHTUB DRAIN IS A FREE VORTEX AND ITS NARROW PLUNGING FUNNEL IS THE SIGNATURE — the velocity rises without limit toward the centre, which is why the surface falls so steeply there.**

> **A bucket of water spun on a turntable is a forced vortex, and its surface is a gentle dish — which is the principle behind the spinning-liquid mirror telescopes, whose mercury surface is an exact paraboloid.**

**And the case that combines both — the RANKINE VORTEX — which is what actually occurs in nature:**

| Region | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **The CORE, near the axis** | **FORCED — viscosity makes the fluid rotate as a solid body, so v ∝ r and the velocity is finite at the centre** ← |
| **OUTSIDE the core** | **FREE — v ∝ 1/r** ← |
| **The maximum velocity** | **At the boundary between the two** ← |

> **THE RANKINE VORTEX EXISTS BECAUSE THE PURE FREE VORTEX IS PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE AT ITS CENTRE: v ∝ 1/r predicts an INFINITE velocity on the axis, which no real fluid can achieve.**

> **Viscosity intervenes near the axis and forces that small core into rigid-body rotation, capping the velocity at a finite value.**

> **A tornado, a hurricane, a drain vortex and the vortex shed from an aircraft wing are all Rankine vortices — forced in the core, free outside — and the maximum wind speed of a tornado occurs at the edge of its core rather than at its centre, which is a direct consequence.**

> **The engineering relevance is at INTAKES: a free vortex forming over a pump or turbine intake draws air down its funnel into the machine, causing loss of efficiency, vibration and cavitation — which is why a minimum SUBMERGENCE is specified and why anti-vortex devices are fitted.**

examTip.trick: **FORCED: v = ωr (solid body, energy supplied, paraboloid surface, rotational). FREE: v ∝ 1/r (no energy needed, funnel surface, irrotational).** Options (a) and (d) describe the free vortex.
examTip.trap: **Bernoulli applies between ANY two points in a free vortex (irrotational) but only ALONG a streamline in a forced one.**
examTip.mnemonic: **A real vortex is a RANKINE vortex — forced core, free outside** — because v ∝ 1/r would give infinite velocity on the axis. Hence a tornado's peak wind is at the core edge, not the centre.

questions.stem: The EQUIVALENT PIPE of a compound pipeline is defined as a single pipe which, for the same total discharge, has:
options: The same total length as the compound pipeline
The same average diameter as the pipes it replaces
The same total volume of water
The same total head loss as the compound pipeline
questions.solution:
**The same TOTAL HEAD LOSS for the same discharge** — so that the single pipe can be substituted for the compound one in any calculation.

**DUPUIT'S EQUATION, which follows for pipes in SERIES:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **For pipes in series, the head losses ADD and the discharge is COMMON** ← | **h_f = h_1 + h_2 + h_3 + …** ← |
| **Each loss is h = f L Q² / (12.1 D⁵)** ← | **For the Darcy formula written in terms of discharge** ← |
| **Equating the equivalent pipe's loss to the sum, with f and Q common** | ← |
| **L/D⁵ = L₁/D₁⁵ + L₂/D₂⁵ + L₃/D₃⁵** ← | **DUPUIT'S equation** ← |

> **THE FIFTH POWER OF THE DIAMETER IS THE STRIKING FEATURE OF THIS RELATION AND IT IS THE REASON THE CONCEPT IS USEFUL RATHER THAN MERELY TIDY:**

> **Because D appears to the fifth power, a SMALL reduction in diameter produces an enormous increase in head loss.**

> **Halving the diameter multiplies the loss by 2⁵ = 32 for the same discharge.**

> **So in a compound pipeline the SMALLEST pipe dominates the total loss almost completely, and the equivalent diameter comes out close to the smallest one rather than to any average — which is why option (b) is so far wrong.**

**A worked illustration, since the magnitude is the point:**

| Pipe | Length | Diameter | L/D⁵ (D in m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **500 m** | **0.30 m** | **500/0.00243 = 205,800** ← |
| **2** | **500 m** | **0.20 m** | **500/0.00032 = 1,562,500** ← |
| **Sum** | **1,000 m** | ← | **1,768,300** |
| **Equivalent pipe, 1,000 m long** | ← | **D = (1,000/1,768,300)^0.2 = 0.226 m** ← | ← |

> **THE 200 mm PIPE, THOUGH ONLY HALF THE PIPELINE'S LENGTH, CONTRIBUTES NEARLY 90 PER CENT OF THE HEAD LOSS — and the equivalent diameter of 226 mm is far closer to 200 than to the arithmetic mean of 250.**

> **That is the practical lesson: in a pipeline of mixed diameters, the short narrow section is where the head is being lost, and replacing it is where the improvement lies.**

> **A utility trying to increase the delivery of an old main should look for the narrowest reach rather than uprating the whole line — and the D⁵ law means the gain from fixing it can be dramatic.**

**For pipes in PARALLEL, the equivalent is found differently:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **In parallel, the HEAD LOSS is COMMON and the DISCHARGES add** ← | **The reverse of the series case** ← |
| **So the relation is on √(D⁵/L) rather than L/D⁵** ← | **√(D⁵/L) = √(D₁⁵/L₁) + √(D₂⁵/L₂) + …** ← |
| **The equivalent pipe is LARGER than any of them** | **As it must be, since it carries the sum of their discharges** ← |

> **THE PATTERN IS THE SAME AS FOR ELECTRICAL RESISTANCES AND IS WORTH RECOGNISING: in SERIES the resistances (here, the L/D⁵ terms) add directly; in PARALLEL the conductances add.**

> **A pipe network is an electrical network with head in place of voltage and discharge in place of current — and the only difference is that the pipe's "resistance" depends on the flow itself, since the loss goes as Q² rather than Q.**

> **That non-linearity is precisely why pipe networks must be solved ITERATIVELY, by Hardy Cross or by a matrix solver, while an electrical network can be solved directly.**

It may be substituted for it in calculations.

examTip.trick: **Same head loss for the same discharge.** In series, Dupuit: L/D⁵ = ΣLᵢ/Dᵢ⁵. In parallel, √(D⁵/L) = Σ√(Dᵢ⁵/Lᵢ).
examTip.trap: **D to the FIFTH power** — halving the diameter multiplies the loss by 32. So the SMALLEST pipe dominates the total, and the equivalent diameter is near it, not near any average.
examTip.mnemonic: **A pipe network is an electrical one with head for voltage and discharge for current** — except the resistance depends on the flow (Q², not Q), which is why it must be solved iteratively.

questions.stem: The ECONOMIC DIAMETER of a pumping main is the diameter at which:
options: The sum of the annual capital charge on the pipe and the annual pumping cost is a minimum
The velocity is exactly 1 m/s
The pipe cost is least
The head loss is zero
questions.solution:
**The diameter at which the sum of the annual CAPITAL charge on the pipe and the annual PUMPING cost is a MINIMUM.**

**The two opposing costs:**

| Cost | Behaviour as the diameter increases |
|---|---|
| **CAPITAL cost of the pipe (annualised)** ← | **RISES — a larger pipe costs more to buy, to lay and to bed** ← |
| **PUMPING (energy) cost** ← | **FALLS steeply — the head loss varies roughly as 1/D⁵, so a modest increase in diameter cuts the energy sharply** ← |
| **The TOTAL** | **Falls, reaches a MINIMUM, and then rises** ← |
| **That minimum is the ECONOMIC diameter** ← | ← |

> **THE SHAPE OF THE CURVE IS THE SAME AS THAT FOR THE ECONOMIC LIFE OF PLANT, AND SO IS THE LOGIC: one cost rises, another falls, and the optimum is where their sum is least.**

> **Option (c) is the trap — the CHEAPEST PIPE is not the economic one, because it condemns the scheme to a high pumping bill for its whole life.**

> **And option (d) is unattainable: zero head loss requires infinite diameter.**

**Why the curve is FLAT near its minimum, which is the practically useful property:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The total cost curve is SHALLOW around the optimum** ← | **A diameter 10 per cent away from the ideal typically costs only 1 or 2 per cent more in total** ← |
| **So the nearest COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE size is almost always acceptable** ← | **Pipes come in standard diameters, and there is no need to agonise between them** ← |
| **But the penalty grows quickly further out** | **A pipe half the economic diameter is very expensive to run** ← |

> **THE FLATNESS IN THE FIRST ROW IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT SAVES EFFORT: the economic diameter calculation does not need to be precise.**

> **Its purpose is to establish which of two or three standard sizes to adopt, and a rough calculation settles that as reliably as a refined one.**

> **What it must NOT be used for is to justify going well below the optimum on the grounds of capital shortage — the penalty there is real, permanent, and paid every year in electricity.**

**What the answer depends on, and why it changes:**

| Factor | Effect on the economic diameter |
|---|---|
| **The cost of ENERGY** ← | **Dearer power pushes the economic diameter UP** ← |
| **The number of HOURS pumped per day** ← | **Continuous pumping justifies a much larger pipe than intermittent pumping** ← |
| **The DISCOUNT RATE** | **A high rate weights the present capital cost more heavily and shrinks the diameter** ← |
| **Pipe cost per metre** | ← |
| **The design LIFE** | **A longer life justifies more capital for lower running cost** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW HAS A CONSEQUENCE THAT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED IN WATER SUPPLY DESIGN AND IT WORKS AGAINST THE INTUITIVE CHOICE: designing a pumping main for a short daily pumping period — say 8 hours — requires a HIGHER discharge to deliver the same daily volume, which means a higher velocity and much higher losses in a given pipe.**

> **Pumping for 20 hours a day at a lower rate uses a smaller pipe AND less energy for the same daily volume, because the loss goes as Q².**

> **So the pumping hours and the pipe diameter must be optimised TOGETHER rather than the hours being fixed first — and the common practice of assuming a convenient pumping period and then sizing the main can produce a scheme that is expensive in both capital and energy.**

**And the rules of thumb, which are what actually get used:**

| Guide | Note |
|---|---|
| **A velocity of 0.9 to 2.4 m/s in a pumping main** ← | **Below that, silt deposits; above it, the losses and surge become excessive** ← |
| **Around 1.0 to 1.5 m/s is typical of an economic design** ← | **Which is where option (b)'s figure comes from — it is a symptom of the answer, not the definition** ← |
| **Lea's formula, D = 0.97 to 1.22 √Q** | **A quick first estimate in SI units** ← |

> **Option (b) is therefore not absurd — economic diameters do commonly give velocities near 1 m/s — but it mistakes a typical RESULT for the CRITERION, and it would give the wrong answer wherever energy is unusually cheap or unusually dear.**

examTip.trick: **Minimum of (annualised pipe capital + annual pumping energy).** Capital rises with D, energy falls as roughly 1/D⁵, and the sum has a minimum.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) mistakes a typical RESULT (about 1 m/s) for the criterion** — the economic velocity shifts with the price of energy and the hours pumped.
examTip.mnemonic: **The curve is FLAT near the optimum** — 10 % off costs 1-2 % more, so just take the nearest standard size. And optimise the PUMPING HOURS with the diameter: longer hours mean a smaller pipe AND less energy.

questions.stem: In the classification of gradually varied flow profiles, the letters M, S, C, H and A denote the:
options: Direction in which the depth is changing
Number of control sections present
Type of channel bed slope — Mild, Steep, Critical, Horizontal and Adverse
Magnitude of the Froude number
questions.solution:
**The type of channel BED SLOPE — Mild, Steep, Critical, Horizontal and Adverse.**

**The five slope categories:**

| Letter | Slope | Defined by |
|---|---|---|
| **M — MILD** | **Normal depth y_n GREATER than critical depth y_c** ← | **The bed slope is less than the critical slope** ← |
| **S — STEEP** | **y_n LESS than y_c** ← | **The slope exceeds the critical slope** ← |
| **C — CRITICAL** | **y_n EQUALS y_c** ← | **A special case** |
| **H — HORIZONTAL** | **Zero bed slope, so y_n is INFINITE** ← | **Uniform flow is impossible** ← |
| **A — ADVERSE** | **The bed rises in the direction of flow, so y_n does not exist** ← | **Uniform flow is impossible** ← |

> **THE CLASSIFICATION IS BY THE RELATION BETWEEN y_n AND y_c, NOT BY THE SLOPE'S NUMERICAL VALUE, and that is the point most often missed:**

> **A slope of 1 in 1,000 is MILD for one discharge and could be STEEP for another, because y_n and y_c both depend on the discharge.**

> **"Mild" and "steep" are therefore properties of the slope AND the flow together, not of the channel alone — and a single channel can change category as its discharge varies through the year.**

**The zones and the numbering:**

| Zone | Position of the actual depth y |
|---|---|
| **Zone 1** | **ABOVE both y_n and y_c** ← |
| **Zone 2** | **BETWEEN y_n and y_c** ← |
| **Zone 3** | **BELOW both** ← |

> **So an M1 profile is a mild slope with the depth above both — the classic BACKWATER curve upstream of a dam or a weir.**

> **An M2 is a mild slope with the depth between the two — a DRAWDOWN curve, as at a free overfall.**

> **An M3 is a mild slope below both — supercritical flow on a mild slope, as beneath a sluice gate, running toward a hydraulic jump.**

**The profiles that matter most in practice:**

| Profile | Where it occurs | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| **M1** ← | **Upstream of a dam, weir, or any obstruction on a mild slope** ← | **The BACKWATER curve — rising, and extending a long way upstream** ← |
| **M2** | **Approaching a free overfall or a sudden steepening** ← | **DRAWDOWN — the depth falls toward critical at the brink** ← |
| **M3** | **Downstream of a sluice gate on a mild slope** ← | **Rising toward the jump that must occur** ← |
| **S2** | **Just downstream of a steepening, or a reservoir outlet onto a steep slope** | **Falling toward normal depth** ← |
| **S1** | **Upstream of an obstruction on a steep slope** ← | **Following a hydraulic jump** ← |

> **THE M1 BACKWATER CURVE IS THE MOST IMPORTANT OF ALL FOR ENGINEERING PURPOSES AND ITS LENGTH IS ROUTINELY UNDERESTIMATED: a weir raising the water by 2 m on a channel of slope 1 in 2,000 influences the level for KILOMETRES upstream.**

> **The profile approaches the normal depth ASYMPTOTICALLY, so there is no definite end to it — by convention the extent is taken to where the depth is within 1 per cent of normal.**

> **This is what determines the land affected by a barrage's afflux, the extent of a reservoir's true influence, and how far upstream a bridge's constriction raises flood levels — and computing it is one of the commoner practical tasks in river engineering.**

**And the two rules that let any profile be sketched without computation:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **The profile approaches the NORMAL depth line ASYMPTOTICALLY** ← | **It never crosses it, and flattens as it nears it** ← |
| **It crosses the CRITICAL depth line VERTICALLY** ← | **Which is physically impossible to sustain, so a hydraulic JUMP or a free fall occurs there instead** ← |
| **Computation proceeds from a CONTROL section** | **Upstream for subcritical, downstream for supercritical** ← |

> **THE SECOND RULE IS WHY HYDRAULIC JUMPS EXIST AT ALL, and it is worth seeing the connection: the gradually varied flow equation has dy/dx tending to infinity as the depth approaches critical.**

> **A vertical water surface is not physically possible, so the flow cannot pass smoothly through the critical depth — it must do so abruptly, through a jump when going from supercritical to subcritical.**

> **The mathematics announces the jump before any experiment does, which is a satisfying instance of an equation's breakdown pointing directly to a real phenomenon.**

examTip.trick: **M mild, S steep, C critical, H horizontal, A adverse — classified by whether y_n is greater or less than y_c**, not by the slope's numerical value.
examTip.trap: **The same channel can be MILD at one discharge and STEEP at another**, since both y_n and y_c depend on Q. The category belongs to the slope AND the flow.
examTip.mnemonic: **Profiles approach NORMAL depth asymptotically and cross CRITICAL vertically** — and since a vertical water surface is impossible, a hydraulic JUMP occurs instead. The equation predicts the jump.

questions.stem: For the MOST ECONOMICAL (best hydraulic) TRIANGULAR open channel section, the side slopes must make an angle with the vertical of:
options: 45°, so that the two sides are at right angles to one another and the hydraulic radius equals y/(2√2)
Any angle — a triangular section's efficiency does not depend on the side slope
questions.solution:
**45° to the vertical** — so the two sides are at right angles to each other, and the hydraulic radius is y/(2√2).

**The result and its derivation in outline:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **For a triangular section with side slope angle θ to the vertical, A = y² tan θ and P = 2y sec θ** ← | ← |
| **The most economical section is the one with the MINIMUM WETTED PERIMETER for a given area** ← | **Which is equivalent to the maximum hydraulic radius** ← |
| **Express P in terms of A and θ and minimise with respect to θ** | ← |
| **The minimum occurs at θ = 45°** ← | **A half-square, standing on its apex — the two sides meeting at a right angle** ← |
| **At that condition, R = y / (2√2) = 0.354 y** ← | ← |

> **THE HALF-SQUARE RESULT HAS THE SAME CHARACTER AS THE OTHER ECONOMICAL SECTIONS AND IS WORTH SEEING AS PART OF THE FAMILY:**

| Section | Most economical proportion | Hydraulic radius |
|---|---|---|
| **RECTANGULAR** | **b = 2y — width twice the depth, a half-square lying down** ← | **R = y/2** ← |
| **TRIANGULAR** | **Side slopes at 45° to the vertical — a half-square standing on its apex** ← | **R = y/(2√2)** ← |
| **TRAPEZOIDAL** | **A HALF-HEXAGON, with side slopes at 60° to the horizontal (1 : 1/√3)** ← | **R = y/2** ← |
| **CIRCULAR, for maximum DISCHARGE** | **Flowing at about 0.95 of its full depth** ← | ← |
| **The absolute best of all shapes** | **A SEMICIRCLE** ← | **R = y/2** ← |

> **THE PATTERN RUNNING THROUGH THE TABLE IS THE MOST USEFUL THING TO CARRY: in every case the most economical section is the one that comes CLOSEST TO A SEMICIRCLE within the constraints of its shape.**

> **A semicircle has the minimum perimeter for a given area of any open shape, so it is the ideal — and the best rectangle, the best triangle and the best trapezium are each the closest approach to it that their geometry allows.**

> **The half-hexagon trapezium is closest, which is why it is the standard for a lined canal; the rectangle and the triangle are progressively further away.**

> **Note also that the best rectangle and the best trapezium both give R = y/2, exactly as a semicircle does — a satisfying result, and a useful check.**

**Why the semicircle is not simply used, since it is optimal:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is difficult and expensive to EXCAVATE a curved section in soil** ← | **Straight-sided sections are cut by ordinary plant and checked with a straight edge** ← |
| **Its sides are near-vertical at the top, which is unstable in soil** ← | **The side slopes of an earth channel are governed by the SOIL, not by hydraulics** ← |
| **It is used where the section is PRECAST or formed** ← | **Small concrete channels, half-round drains, and pipes flowing part full** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONSTRAINT THAT USUALLY DECIDES AN EARTH CHANNEL'S SHAPE, AND IT OVERRIDES THE HYDRAULIC OPTIMUM: the most economical trapezium requires side slopes of 60° to the horizontal, which is about 1 horizontal to 1.7 vertical.**

> **Very few soils will stand at that slope under water, saturated and subject to drawdown.**

> **So the side slopes are fixed first by the soil — commonly 1.5:1 or 2:1 in ordinary soils — and the most economical section is then found for THAT fixed side slope, which gives a different and flatter optimum.**

> **That is the form the problem usually takes in practice: not "what is the best trapezium?" but "given side slopes of 1.5:1, what is the best bed width to depth ratio?" — and the answer is the section whose bed width plus the two slopes give the minimum perimeter for the area.**

> **THE TRIANGULAR SECTION ITSELF IS USED WHERE THE DISCHARGE IS SMALL AND VARIABLE — roadside drains, small field channels and V-notch measuring flumes — because its width shrinks with the depth, so it maintains a reasonable velocity at low flows where a rectangular channel would spread out and silt.**

examTip.trick: **45° to the vertical — a half-square on its apex, with the sides at a right angle. R = y/(2√2).**
examTip.trap: **Rectangle b = 2y (R = y/2), triangle 45° (R = y/2√2), trapezium a HALF-HEXAGON (R = y/2)** — each is the closest approach to a SEMICIRCLE its shape allows.
examTip.mnemonic: **Side slopes are fixed by the SOIL, not by hydraulics** — few soils stand at the half-hexagon's 60°. So the real problem is the best bed-width ratio for a GIVEN slope.

questions.stem: The S-CURVE (S-hydrograph) is constructed in hydrology in order to:
options: Separate base flow from a recorded hydrograph
Determine the time of concentration of a catchment
Plot the cumulative rainfall of a storm
Derive a unit hydrograph of a different duration from one that is already available
questions.solution:
**To DERIVE a unit hydrograph of a different duration** from one that is already available.

**How it works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Take the known D-hour unit hydrograph** | **Say a 4-hour UH** ← |
| **Add together an INFINITE SERIES of such unit hydrographs, each lagged by D hours** ← | **In practice, enough of them to reach a steady state** ← |
| **The sum rises and then levels off at a CONSTANT value** ← | **This is the S-CURVE — the response to a continuous rainfall excess of 1/D cm per hour applied indefinitely** ← |
| **To obtain a D′-hour UH: take the S-curve, lag a COPY of it by D′ hours, and SUBTRACT** ← | ← |
| **Multiply the difference by D/D′** ← | **To rescale it back to ONE unit of rainfall excess** ← |

> **THE FINAL MULTIPLICATION IN THE LAST ROW IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN, and omitting it gives a hydrograph of the right shape and the wrong magnitude.**

> **The reason for it is straightforward: the difference between the two S-curves represents rainfall excess falling at the rate 1/D cm per hour for D′ hours — which is a total of D′/D cm, not 1 cm.**

> **Multiplying by D/D′ scales it back to the one unit that a unit hydrograph is defined by.**

**What the S-curve physically represents:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is the catchment's response to a CONTINUOUS, indefinitely long rainfall excess** ← | **At the constant rate 1/D cm per hour** ← |
| **It rises, at first steeply, then more gently** ← | **As progressively more of the catchment begins contributing** ← |
| **It reaches EQUILIBRIUM when the whole catchment is contributing simultaneously** ← | **Which occurs at the TIME OF CONCENTRATION** ← |
| **The equilibrium discharge is Q_e = 2.78 A / D** ← | **In m³/s, with A in km² and D in hours — a useful CHECK on the curve** ← |

> **THE EQUILIBRIUM CHECK IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST VALUABLE PRACTICAL POINT AND IT SHOULD ALWAYS BE APPLIED: the S-curve must level off at exactly 2.78 A/D, because at equilibrium the outflow equals the inflow over the whole catchment.**

> **If the computed curve does not settle at that value, the underlying unit hydrograph is inconsistent — its ordinates do not sum to the correct volume.**

> **And if the curve OSCILLATES about the equilibrium value rather than settling smoothly, which is very common, the unit hydrograph's ordinates contain errors that the summation has amplified.**

**THE OSCILLATION PROBLEM DESERVES ITS OWN NOTE, since it always arises in practice:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **The derived unit hydrograph's ordinates are never perfectly consistent** ← | **They come from real, imperfect data** ← |
| **The S-curve summation ACCUMULATES those small errors** ← | **And they appear as a hunting oscillation about the equilibrium line** ← |
| **The oscillation grows if the assumed duration D is WRONG** ← | **Which is the most useful diagnostic: severe hunting usually means the storm duration was mis-estimated** ← |
| **The remedy is to SMOOTH the S-curve by eye before using it** ← | **Which is legitimate, because the true response is known to be smooth** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW MAKES THE OSCILLATION USEFUL RATHER THAN MERELY ANNOYING: if the S-curve hunts badly, the duration attributed to the original unit hydrograph is probably incorrect.**

> **Adjusting D and recomputing until the curve settles smoothly is a genuine way of establishing the effective duration of the storm that produced it — which is often uncertain, since real rainfall does not fall at a uniform rate for a neat number of hours.**

**And the simpler alternative, worth knowing because it is quicker when it applies:**

> **The SUPERPOSITION method derives a unit hydrograph whose duration is an INTEGER MULTIPLE of the known one — a 12-hour UH from a 4-hour UH, say — simply by adding three 4-hour unit hydrographs each lagged by 4 hours and dividing by 3.**

> **It requires no S-curve at all and involves no scaling subtleties.**

> **The S-curve method is needed only when the required duration is NOT a multiple — obtaining a 3-hour UH from a 4-hour one, for instance — and that is precisely when it earns its complexity.**

examTip.trick: **Sum lagged unit hydrographs to get the S-curve, lag a copy by D′, subtract, then MULTIPLY BY D/D′.** The final scaling is the step most often forgotten.
examTip.trap: **The S-curve must level off at Q_e = 2.78 A/D** (A in km², D in hours) — always check it. Failure to settle there means the unit hydrograph's volume is wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **Severe hunting about the equilibrium usually means the assumed DURATION is wrong** — adjust D until it settles. And for an INTEGER multiple, plain superposition is quicker and needs no S-curve.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 10 kN/m over the LEFT HALF of its span only. The maximum bending moment in the beam is:
options: 40 kNm
45 kNm
60 kNm
80 kNm
questions.solution:
**45 kNm.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Total load** | **W = 10 × 4 = 40 kN, acting at its centroid 2 m from A** ← |
| **Reactions, by moments about B** | **R_A × 8 = 40 × 6, so R_A = 30 kN** ← |
| **And R_B** | **= 40 − 30 = 10 kN** |
| **Maximum BM occurs where the SHEAR is ZERO** ← | **In the loaded region, V = 30 − 10x = 0, giving x = 3 m from A** ← |
| **M at that section** | **= 30 × 3 − 10 × 3²/2 = 90 − 45** |
| **M_max** | **= 45 kNm** ← |

> **Option (d) 80 kNm is wL²/8, the answer for a UDL over the WHOLE span — the value most likely to be quoted from memory without noticing that the load covers only half.**

> **Option (c) 60 kNm is R_A × 2, the moment at the load's centroid, which is not where the maximum occurs.**

**Why the maximum is at 3 m and not at 2 m or 4 m:**

| Location | Shear | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **At A** | **+30 kN** | ← |
| **At 3 m** | **30 − 30 = ZERO** ← | **The maximum bending moment** ← |
| **At 4 m (the end of the load)** | **30 − 40 = −10 kN** ← | **The shear has already changed sign, so the moment is past its peak** ← |
| **From 4 m to B** | **Constant at −10 kN** | **So the moment falls linearly to zero at B** ← |

> **THE RULE THAT MAXIMUM MOMENT OCCURS AT ZERO SHEAR IS THE ONLY THING NEEDED TO LOCATE IT, and it is worth using rather than guessing: setting V = 0 gives the position directly, in one line, for any loading.**

> **The common error is to assume the maximum is at midspan. It is at midspan only when the loading is SYMMETRIC — and here the load is not, so the maximum has shifted toward the loaded end.**

**A useful sanity check on the answer:**

| Comparison | Note |
|---|---|
| **Full-span UDL of 10 kN/m: M_max = wL²/8 = 80 kNm** ← | **The upper bound — the same intensity over twice the length** ← |
| **Half the total load (40 kN) as a single point load at midspan: WL/4 = 80 kNm** ← | **Also 80** ← |
| **This case: 45 kNm** | **Comfortably below both, as it must be** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW GIVES THE MOST USEFUL BRACKET IN BEAM PROBLEMS AND IS WORTH REMEMBERING AS A HABIT: for a given total load W on a span L, the maximum moment lies between WL/8 (spread uniformly over the whole span) and WL/4 (concentrated at midspan).**

> **Here W = 40 kN and L = 8 m, so the bracket is 40 to 80 kNm — and 45 falls within it, near the lower end, which is right for a load spread over half the span and offset from midspan.**

> **Any answer outside that bracket for a downward load on a simply supported span is wrong, and the check takes five seconds.**

**And the shape of the diagrams, which confirms the reasoning:**

| Region | Shear | Moment |
|---|---|---|
| **0 to 4 m (loaded)** | **Falls LINEARLY from +30 to −10** ← | **PARABOLIC — rising to 45 kNm at 3 m, then falling** ← |
| **4 to 8 m (unloaded)** | **CONSTANT at −10 kN** ← | **LINEAR — falling from 40 kNm at 4 m to zero at B** ← |

> **Note that the moment at the end of the load (4 m) is R_B × 4 = 40 kNm, which is LESS than the 45 kNm peak — confirming that the maximum lies inside the loaded region, and providing an independent check on the whole calculation.**

examTip.trick: **R_A = 30 kN; shear zero at x = 3 m; M = 30(3) − 10(3²)/2 = 45 kNm.** Option (d) is wL²/8 for a FULL-span UDL.
examTip.trap: **Maximum moment is at midspan only for SYMMETRIC loading** — here it shifts toward the loaded end. Always locate it by setting the shear to zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **For a total load W on span L, M_max lies between WL/8 (spread) and WL/4 (concentrated at midspan)** — a five-second bracket that catches most errors.

questions.stem: When a beam carries an INCLINED concentrated load, the analysis must include, in addition to the shear force and bending moment diagrams:
options: A torsion diagram
A deflection diagram
A twisting moment diagram
An axial thrust (normal force) diagram
questions.solution:
**An AXIAL THRUST (normal force) diagram** — because the load's component along the beam's axis produces a direct axial force in the member.

**The resolution of an inclined load:**

| Component | Effect |
|---|---|
| **PERPENDICULAR to the beam's axis** ← | **Produces SHEAR and BENDING, exactly as an ordinary transverse load does** ← |
| **ALONG the beam's axis** ← | **Produces AXIAL THRUST or PULL — a direct force, which the shear and moment diagrams do not represent at all** ← |

> **THE POINT IS THAT THREE DIAGRAMS ARE NEEDED RATHER THAN TWO, and the third is easily forgotten because most beam problems have purely vertical loads on a horizontal beam, where the axial component is zero.**

> **The moment the load is inclined — or the beam itself is inclined — an axial force appears, and it must be combined with the bending stress rather than ignored.**

**How the axial thrust is distributed, which is the distinctive part:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The axial force is CONSTANT between the points of application of axial loads** ← | **It is a step function, changing only where an axial component is applied** ← |
| **Which support resists it depends on the SUPPORT CONDITIONS** ← | **A HINGED support can take axial force; a ROLLER cannot** ← |
| **With one hinge and one roller, the ENTIRE axial force goes to the hinge** ← | **And the thrust diagram is constant from the hinge to the load and zero beyond it** ← |

> **THE SUPPORT CONDITION IN THE SECOND ROW DETERMINES THE WHOLE THRUST DIAGRAM AND IS THE PART EXAMINATIONS TEST: a simply supported beam has a hinge at one end and a roller at the other precisely so that it is statically determinate, and the roller cannot resist any horizontal force.**

> **So all of the axial component is carried by the hinged end, and the axial force exists only in the portion of the beam between that hinge and the point where the inclined load acts.**

> **On the other side of the load, toward the roller, the axial force is ZERO — which surprises people, and follows directly from the roller's inability to resist it.**

**Combining the axial force with the bending stress:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The stresses ADD algebraically** ← | **σ = P/A ± M/Z** ← |
| **A COMPRESSIVE thrust adds to the compressive bending stress on one face and RELIEVES the tension on the other** ← | ← |
| **Which can be beneficial or harmful, depending on which face governs** ← | **In a masonry or concrete member, a compressive thrust that suppresses the tension is HELPFUL — which is the principle of prestressing** ← |
| **And if the thrust is COMPRESSIVE and the member slender, BUCKLING must be checked** ← | **A beam-column, with the P-delta interaction** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONNECTS THIS DIRECTLY TO PRESTRESSING AND TO THE ARCH, and the connection is worth making: an axial compression superimposed on bending reduces the tensile stress.**

> **A prestressed beam is exactly that arrangement, deliberately created; an arch achieves it by geometry; and an inclined load on a beam produces it incidentally.**

> **In each case the same expression σ = P/A ± M/Z governs, and the middle-third and kern conditions met earlier are simply the statement of when the compressive term is large enough to keep the whole section in compression.**

**Where inclined loads and axial thrust in beams actually arise:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **INCLINED members — rafters, staircase waist slabs, ramps** ← | **A vertical load on an inclined member always has a component along it** ← |
| **Cable and stay forces on a beam or a tower** ← | **A stay pulling at an angle applies both a transverse and an axial component** ← |
| **Wind or earthquake loads on a frame** | **Introducing axial forces into beams that carry only bending under gravity** ← |
| **Braced frames and portal frames generally** | **Where every member carries axial force and moment together** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE COMMONEST CASE AND IT CONNECTS TO THE STAIRCASE QUESTION: an inclined waist slab carrying a vertical load has a component along its slope, so it acts as a beam AND a compression member.**

> **For an ordinary staircase the axial force is small and is conventionally neglected — but for a steeply inclined ramp or a long rafter it is not, and neglecting it in a slender member is how a design misses a buckling check entirely.**

examTip.trick: **Resolve the load: the perpendicular component gives shear and moment; the AXIAL component gives a thrust diagram.** Three diagrams, not two.
examTip.trap: **A ROLLER cannot resist axial force**, so the whole thrust goes to the hinged end — and the axial force is ZERO between the load and the roller.
examTip.mnemonic: **σ = P/A ± M/Z, and a compressive thrust SUPPRESSES the tension** — which is prestressing, the arch, and the middle-third rule all in one expression. Check buckling if the member is slender.

questions.stem: For a DUCTILE material such as mild steel, the theory of failure that agrees best with experiment and is generally adopted in design is:
options: The maximum shear stress theory (Tresca) or the maximum distortion energy theory (von Mises)
The maximum principal stress theory (Rankine)
The maximum principal strain theory (Saint-Venant)
The total strain energy theory (Haigh)
questions.solution:
**The MAXIMUM SHEAR STRESS theory (Tresca), or the maximum DISTORTION ENERGY theory (von Mises)** — both agree well with experiment for ductile materials, and von Mises is the closer.

**The five classical theories and where each applies:**

| Theory | Failure criterion | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **MAXIMUM PRINCIPAL STRESS (Rankine)** | **The largest principal stress reaches the uniaxial strength** ← | **BRITTLE materials — cast iron, concrete, masonry** ← (option b) |
