| **MAXIMUM PRINCIPAL STRAIN (Saint-Venant)** | **The largest principal strain reaches the uniaxial yield strain** ← | **Little used; unsatisfactory for both classes** ← (option c) |
| **MAXIMUM SHEAR STRESS (Tresca / Guest)** ← | **The maximum shear stress reaches half the uniaxial yield stress** ← | **DUCTILE materials — safe and simple** ← |
| **TOTAL STRAIN ENERGY (Haigh)** | **The total strain energy per unit volume reaches its uniaxial value** ← | **Superseded** ← (option d) |
| **DISTORTION (shear) STRAIN ENERGY (von Mises / Hencky)** ← | **The energy of DISTORTION alone reaches its uniaxial value** ← | **DUCTILE materials — the BEST agreement with experiment** ← |

> **THE DIVISION IS BETWEEN BRITTLE AND DUCTILE MATERIALS AND IT IS THE ORGANISING IDEA OF THE WHOLE TOPIC:**

> **A BRITTLE material fails by CLEAVAGE — it pulls apart on a plane normal to the greatest tensile stress — so a criterion based on the maximum principal STRESS describes it.**

> **A DUCTILE material fails by YIELDING, which is a SHEARING process: dislocations slide on planes of maximum shear.**

> **So a criterion based on SHEAR describes it, and the maximum principal stress is largely irrelevant — which is why a ductile material subjected to HYDROSTATIC pressure, with no shear at all, does not yield however great the pressure.**

> **That last observation is the decisive experimental fact, and it is what condemns the maximum principal stress and total strain energy theories for ductile materials: both predict failure under hydrostatic pressure, and it does not occur.**

**Why von Mises beats Tresca, and why Tresca is nevertheless used:**

| Aspect | TRESCA | VON MISES |
|---|---|---|
| **Agreement with experiment** | **Good, and CONSERVATIVE** ← | **BETTER — closest of all to observed yielding** ← |
| **In pure shear, yield occurs at** | **0.5 σ_y** ← | **0.577 σ_y** ← |
| **Mathematical form** | **Simple — the largest of three differences** ← | **A quadratic expression, smooth and differentiable** ← |
| **Used in** | **Some codes, and hand calculation** ← | **Finite element analysis universally — the "von Mises stress" plotted by every program** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST QUOTED DIFFERENCE AND IT IS WHERE THE TWO PART COMPANY MOST WIDELY: in PURE SHEAR, Tresca predicts yielding at 0.5 of the tensile yield stress and von Mises at 0.577.**

> **Experiment gives values close to 0.577, so von Mises is right and Tresca is about 15 per cent conservative.**

> **That conservatism is why Tresca survives: it is simpler, it never over-estimates the strength, and 15 per cent is an acceptable price for a hand calculation.**

> **The THIRD row explains von Mises' dominance in computation: being smooth and differentiable, it suits numerical solution, whereas Tresca's criterion has corners that cause difficulties in an iterative plasticity algorithm.**

**And the practical point about mixed materials:**

| Material | Theory |
|---|---|
| **Structural STEEL** | **von Mises (or Tresca)** ← |
| **CAST IRON, CONCRETE, MASONRY, ROCK, glass** ← | **Maximum principal stress — or better, a modified criterion recognising that their COMPRESSIVE strength greatly exceeds their tensile** ← |
| **Soils** | **Mohr-Coulomb, which is Tresca generalised to include a friction term** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WORTH NOTICING BECAUSE IT UNIFIES TWO SUBJECTS: the MOHR-COULOMB criterion used throughout soil mechanics is the maximum shear stress theory with the shear strength made dependent on the normal stress, through the friction angle.**

> **Set φ = 0 and Mohr-Coulomb reduces exactly to Tresca — which is why the undrained analysis of clay, with φ_u = 0, uses a criterion identical in form to the one used for mild steel.**

> **One failure theory, appearing in structural mechanics and in geotechnics with different names.**

examTip.trick: **Ductile → SHEAR-based (Tresca or von Mises); brittle → maximum principal STRESS (Rankine).** Ductile yielding is a shearing process; brittle failure is cleavage.
examTip.trap: **A ductile material under HYDROSTATIC pressure does not yield** — no shear. That single fact condemns the principal-stress and total-strain-energy theories for ductile materials.
examTip.mnemonic: **In pure shear: Tresca 0.5σ_y, von Mises 0.577σ_y** — experiment favours von Mises, so Tresca is about 15 % conservative. And MOHR-COULOMB with φ = 0 IS Tresca.

questions.stem: For high-strength steels and cold-worked reinforcement, which show NO distinct yield point, the strength used in design is the PROOF STRESS, defined as the stress at which:
options: The specimen fractures
The stress-strain curve first departs from a straight line
A specified permanent (plastic) strain remains after the load is removed — commonly 0.2 per cent for steel
The elongation reaches 20 per cent
questions.solution:
**The stress at which a specified PERMANENT strain remains after unloading** — conventionally 0.2 per cent for steel.

**Why a convention is needed at all:**

| Material | Stress-strain behaviour |
|---|---|
| **MILD STEEL** | **A distinct YIELD PLATEAU — an unmistakable point at which the strain increases at constant stress** ← |
| **HIGH-STRENGTH and COLD-WORKED steels** ← | **The curve bends over GRADUALLY, with no plateau and no identifiable yield point at all** ← |
| **So "the yield stress" has no meaning for them** ← | **And a conventional substitute must be defined** ← |

> **THE PROOF STRESS IS THEREFORE A DEFINITION RATHER THAN A MEASUREMENT OF A PHYSICAL EVENT, and that is the point worth grasping: nothing particular happens to the steel at its 0.2 per cent proof stress.**

> **The value is chosen because 0.2 per cent permanent strain is small enough to be structurally harmless and large enough to be measured reliably.**

> **It is a working convention agreed so that different steels can be compared and specified, and a different offset — 0.1 or 0.5 per cent — would give a different number for the same steel.**

**How it is determined graphically:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Plot the stress-strain curve** | ← |
| **Mark the specified offset on the STRAIN axis — 0.002 for 0.2 per cent** ← | ← |
| **From that point, draw a line PARALLEL to the initial ELASTIC portion of the curve** ← | **Parallel, because unloading follows the elastic slope** ← |
| **Where that line CUTS the curve is the proof stress** ← | ← |

> **THE PARALLEL LINE IN THE THIRD STEP IS THE ESSENTIAL CONSTRUCTION AND ITS LOGIC IS PHYSICAL: when a specimen loaded beyond its elastic limit is UNLOADED, it recovers elastically — along a line parallel to the original elastic slope.**

> **So the point where the offset line meets the curve is precisely the stress from which unloading would leave 0.2 per cent permanent strain behind.**

> **The construction is not arbitrary; it traces what would actually happen if the specimen were unloaded from that stress.**

**The proof stress in the reinforcement grades:**

| Grade | Characteristic strength f_y | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250 (mild steel)** | **250 MPa** | **A genuine YIELD POINT** ← |
| **Fe 415, Fe 500, Fe 550** ← | **415, 500, 550 MPa** | **0.2 per cent PROOF stress — these are cold-worked or TMT bars with no yield plateau** ← |
| **Prestressing wire and strand** | **1,570 to 1,860 MPa** | **Proof stress, and design is on a specified percentage of it** ← |

> **THE ABSENCE OF A YIELD PLATEAU IN THE HIGHER GRADES HAS A CONSEQUENCE THAT MATTERS FOR DUCTILITY AND CONNECTS TO EARLIER MATERIAL: mild steel's plateau is what gives it its enormous warning deformation and its capacity to redistribute load.**

> **A cold-worked bar has a higher strength and a SHORTER, less pronounced yielding range — so it is stronger and LESS ductile.**

> **This is why the codes tighten the neutral-axis depth limit as the steel grade rises (0.53, 0.48, 0.46 for Fe 250, 415, 500), and why seismic codes specify a minimum elongation and a minimum ratio of ultimate to yield strength for reinforcement in ductile detailing.**

> **Strength alone is not sufficient; the steel must also be able to yield and hold on while the section rotates, and the higher grades give less of that margin.**

**And the related definitions, which the distractors reach for:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **LIMIT OF PROPORTIONALITY** | **Where the curve first DEPARTS from a straight line** ← (option b) |
| **ELASTIC LIMIT** | **The greatest stress from which the specimen recovers fully — slightly above the proportional limit** ← |
| **PROOF stress** | **A specified permanent set — this question** ← |
| **ULTIMATE tensile strength** | **The maximum nominal stress reached** ← |
| **BREAKING stress** | **At fracture** ← (option a) |

> **The limit of proportionality in the first row is not used for design, and the reason is practical: it is very difficult to determine reliably, because it depends on how precisely the departure from linearity can be detected — which depends on the instrument.**

> **The proof stress, by contrast, is defined by a construction that any laboratory can repeat identically, which is exactly the property a specification value must have.**

examTip.trick: **Draw a line from 0.002 strain PARALLEL to the elastic slope; where it cuts the curve is the 0.2 % proof stress.** Option (b) is the limit of proportionality.
examTip.trap: **It is a CONVENTION, not a physical event** — nothing happens to the steel at that stress. A different offset gives a different number for the same steel.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fe 250 has a real yield point; Fe 415/500/550 use PROOF stress** — cold-worked bars are stronger and LESS ductile, which is why x_u,max/d tightens as the grade rises.

questions.stem: UNSYMMETRICAL BENDING of a beam occurs when:
options: The beam's cross-section has no axis of symmetry
The plane of the applied loading does NOT contain a principal axis of the cross-section
The beam is loaded beyond its elastic limit
The supports are at different levels
questions.solution:
**When the PLANE of the loading does not contain a PRINCIPAL AXIS** of the cross-section — so the beam bends about both principal axes and deflects out of the plane of the load.

**Why the plane of loading matters:**

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **The load acts in a plane containing a PRINCIPAL axis** ← | **SIMPLE bending — the beam deflects IN the plane of the load, and the neutral axis is the other principal axis** ← |
| **The load acts in any OTHER plane** ← | **UNSYMMETRICAL bending — the load is RESOLVED into components along the two principal axes, the beam bends about both, and the resultant deflection is NOT in the load's plane** ← |

> **OPTION (A) IS THE COMMON MISCONCEPTION AND IT IS WORTH CORRECTING DIRECTLY: unsymmetrical bending is NOT a property of the SECTION but of the LOADING'S ORIENTATION relative to it.**

> **A perfectly symmetrical rectangular section loaded on its diagonal undergoes unsymmetrical bending.**

> **And a thoroughly unsymmetrical section — an angle, a channel — loaded in a plane containing one of its principal axes undergoes SIMPLE bending.**

> **The name is misleading, which is why it is sometimes called BIAXIAL bending or skew bending instead, and those terms describe it better.**

**How it is analysed:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Locate the PRINCIPAL AXES of the section** ← | **The perpendicular pair about which the PRODUCT OF INERTIA is zero — and about which I is maximum and minimum** ← |
| **2. Resolve the load into components along those two axes** | ← |
| **3. Compute the bending moment about each principal axis** | ← |
| **4. Superpose the stresses: σ = M_u v / I_u + M_v u / I_v** ← | **Two simple bending problems added** ← |
| **5. Locate the NEUTRAL AXIS from the condition σ = 0** ← | **It is INCLINED, and generally NOT perpendicular to the plane of loading** ← |

> **THE FIRST STEP IS THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY, AND FOR A SYMMETRIC SECTION IT IS TRIVIAL: any axis of symmetry IS a principal axis, and so is the axis perpendicular to it.**

> **So a rectangle, an I-section and a channel all have their principal axes along the obvious horizontal and vertical directions, and no calculation is needed.**

> **An ANGLE section has no axis of symmetry (unless equal-legged, where the diagonal is one), so its principal axes are INCLINED — and finding them requires computing the product of inertia and rotating to the angle at which it vanishes.**

> **That is why an angle used as a beam is the classic unsymmetrical bending problem, and why an unequal angle purlin bends in a direction nobody expects.**

**THE INCLINED NEUTRAL AXIS IN THE LAST STEP IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE and it is worth stating plainly:**

> **In simple bending, the neutral axis is perpendicular to the plane of loading, and the beam deflects straight down under a vertical load.**

> **In unsymmetrical bending the neutral axis is INCLINED at some other angle, and the beam deflects PERPENDICULAR to that neutral axis — which is NOT the direction of the load.**

> **So a vertical load on an angle purlin produces a deflection with a sizeable SIDEWAYS component, and the maximum stress occurs at the corner FURTHEST from the inclined neutral axis rather than at the extreme top or bottom fibre.**

> **A designer who computes M/Z about the horizontal axis alone will substantially underestimate the stress, and the error is not small — it can exceed 50 per cent for a slender angle.**

**Where it arises in practice:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **PURLINS on a sloping roof** ← | **The classic case: gravity load is vertical, and the purlin's axes are inclined with the roof slope, so neither component is along a principal axis** ← |
| **ANGLE and channel sections used as beams** ← | **Their principal axes are inclined or their shear centre is offset** ← |
| **Any beam with a load applied at an angle** | ← |
| **Members in a three-dimensional frame** | ← |

> **THE PURLIN CASE IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE ONE ALWAYS SET AS A PROBLEM AND IT HAS A NEAT PRACTICAL REMEDY: SAG RODS.**

> **Tie rods run between the purlins at midspan, restraining the deflection in the weak direction — the component parallel to the roof slope.**

> **With sag rods at midspan, the purlin spans its full length for the strong-axis bending and only half its length for the weak-axis bending, and since the weak-axis moment falls to a quarter, the problem largely disappears.**

> **A few cheap rods therefore transform the design, which is why they are standard on any roof of significant span — and why omitting them produces purlins that sag visibly along the slope.**

examTip.trick: **It depends on the LOAD'S ORIENTATION, not on the section's symmetry** — a rectangle loaded on its diagonal bends unsymmetrically; an angle loaded along a principal axis does not.
examTip.trap: **The neutral axis is INCLINED and the deflection is perpendicular to IT, not to the load** — so the maximum stress is at the corner furthest from that axis, and M/Z about the horizontal alone can underestimate by over 50 %.
examTip.mnemonic: **SAG RODS at midspan halve the weak-axis span and quarter its moment** — a few cheap rods transform a purlin design, and omitting them makes purlins sag along the slope.

questions.stem: In a BUILT-UP beam — for example a plate girder, or timber flitches bolted together — the SPACING of the connectors (bolts, rivets or welds) joining the parts is governed by:
options: The bending moment at the section
The total load on the beam
The deflection limit
The shear flow at the interface
questions.solution:
**The SHEAR FLOW at the interface, q = V A ȳ / I** — which the connectors must transmit, so they are spaced closest where the SHEAR is greatest, near the supports.

**Why the connectors are needed at all:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A beam in bending has its parts trying to SLIDE relative to one another** ← | **Longitudinal shear — visible if you bend a stack of loose planks: their ends fan out** ← |
| **For the parts to act as ONE section, that sliding must be prevented** ← | **Which is the connectors' entire job** ← |
| **The force per unit LENGTH they must transmit is the SHEAR FLOW q** ← | **q = V A ȳ / I, where A ȳ is the first moment of the area being connected, about the neutral axis** ← |
| **The spacing follows: s = (capacity of one connector) / q** ← | **Or, for a connector in double shear or a pair, that capacity multiplied accordingly** ← |

> **THE STACK OF PLANKS IS THE IMAGE TO HOLD AND IT MAKES THE WHOLE THING OBVIOUS: bend a stack of loose planks and they slide past one another, each bending about its own axis, and the assembly is weak.**

> **Bolt them together so they cannot slide, and they bend as a single deep member — enormously stiffer, because the depth is now the full stack rather than one plank.**

> **The bolts are what convert several shallow beams into one deep one, and the force they carry is the force that was previously accommodated by sliding.**

**THE SPACING VARIES ALONG THE BEAM, which is the practically important consequence:**

| Location on a simply supported beam with UDL | Shear V | Connector spacing |
|---|---|---|
| **At the SUPPORTS** | **MAXIMUM** ← | **CLOSEST — the connectors are most heavily worked here** ← |
| **At MIDSPAN** | **ZERO** ← | **Widest — theoretically infinite** ← |

> **THIS IS THE EXACT OPPOSITE OF WHERE INTUITION PUTS THE DEMAND, and it is why the question matters: the bending moment is greatest at midspan, so it feels as though the connections should be strongest there.**

> **But the connectors do not resist the bending moment — they resist the SHEAR FLOW, which is proportional to the SHEAR FORCE, and the shear is greatest at the supports and zero at midspan.**

> **So a built-up beam has its bolts crowded near the supports and widely spaced in the middle — and a designer who spaces them uniformly on the basis of the maximum moment has put the steel in the wrong place.**

> **In practice a maximum spacing is also specified regardless of the calculation, to keep the parts in contact, prevent local buckling of the outer plate and exclude moisture from between the plies.**

**The same formula in its other applications, which are worth connecting:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **CONNECTOR spacing in a built-up beam** | **This question** ← |
| **The SHEAR STRESS distribution in a solid section** ← | **τ = V A ȳ / (I b) — the same expression divided by the width b** ← |
| **The WELD size at a plate girder's flange-to-web junction** ← | **The weld must carry the shear flow between flange and web** ← |
| **The check on a composite steel-concrete beam's SHEAR STUDS** ← | **Exactly the same calculation, with the studs transmitting the flow between the steel beam and the concrete slab** ← |

> **THE COMPOSITE BEAM CASE IN THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT MODERN APPLICATION AND IT IS THE SAME IDEA APPLIED ACROSS TWO MATERIALS: a steel beam and a concrete slab acting together are far stronger and stiffer than the two acting separately.**

> **What makes them act together is the SHEAR CONNECTORS — headed studs welded to the beam's top flange and cast into the slab — and their number and spacing are determined by exactly the shear flow calculation above.**

> **Omit them and you have a slab resting on a beam: two independent members, with perhaps 40 per cent of the composite capacity.**

> **Which makes the studs the single most consequential detail in composite construction, and a good illustration of how a small connector's job is to create a structural action rather than merely to hold parts in place.**

Q = V A ȳ / I, which the connectors must transmit.

examTip.trick: **q = V A ȳ / I, and spacing s = (connector capacity)/q.** The connectors resist the SHEAR FLOW, not the bending moment.
examTip.trap: **Closest at the SUPPORTS, widest at midspan** — the opposite of where the moment is greatest. Uniform spacing based on the maximum moment puts the steel in the wrong place.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bend a stack of loose planks and they fan out** — the connectors stop the sliding and convert several shallow beams into one deep one. Same calculation sizes composite SHEAR STUDS.

questions.stem: In the METHOD OF SECTIONS applied to a plane truss, the maximum number of unknown member forces that can be determined from a single cut is:
options: Three, because three independent equations of equilibrium are available for the isolated portion
Two
Four
Any number, provided moments are taken about several points
questions.solution:
**THREE** — because three independent equations of equilibrium are available for the isolated portion.

**Why three:**

| Equation | Note |
|---|---|
| **ΣF_x = 0** | ← |
| **ΣF_y = 0** | ← |
| **ΣM = 0 about any point** ← | **One moment equation only — taking moments about a second point gives no NEW information for a plane body** ← |
| **Total: THREE independent equations, hence three unknowns** ← | ← |

> **OPTION (D) IS THE MISCONCEPTION WORTH ADDRESSING BECAUSE IT SEEMS PLAUSIBLE: taking moments about a second point does produce another equation, and it is not INDEPENDENT.**

> **For a rigid body in a plane, any moment equation about a second point can be derived algebraically from the first moment equation and the two force equations.**

> **So it adds no information — writing it down and solving gives an identity, not a new result.**

> **A plane body has exactly three degrees of freedom (two translations and one rotation), so exactly three equations are available. No arrangement of the algebra creates a fourth.**

**How the method is used efficiently:**

| Technique | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cut through the member whose force is WANTED** ← | **The method's whole advantage: it gives one specific member directly, without working through the truss joint by joint** ← |
| **Take MOMENTS about the point where the other two unknowns INTERSECT** ← | **Which eliminates both of them and gives the wanted force in ONE equation** ← |
| **For two PARALLEL unknowns, resolve PERPENDICULAR to them** ← | **Which eliminates both** ← |
| **Choose the SIMPLER of the two portions to work with** ← | **Fewer forces to consider — usually the one with fewer applied loads** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE TECHNIQUE THAT MAKES THE METHOD POWERFUL AND IT IS THE SAME IDEA MET IN THE SHEET PILE PROBLEM: choose the moment centre so that the unknowns you do not want pass through it and vanish.**

> **Three unknowns and one well-chosen equation gives one answer immediately — which is far quicker than solving three simultaneous equations, and far quicker still than the method of joints working inward from a support.**

> **For a member in the middle of a long truss, the method of joints requires every joint from the support inward to be solved first. The method of sections gets it in one line.**

**When the cut must be made carefully:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The cut may pass through more than three members** ← | **PROVIDED all but three of them are already known, or all but three can be eliminated by a suitable moment centre** ← |
| **The cut must SEPARATE the truss completely into two parts** ← | **A cut that does not divide the structure leaves an indeterminate free body** ← |
| **It may be a curved or stepped cut** | **It need not be a straight line — only a complete separation** ← |
| **Combining with the method of JOINTS is normal practice** ← | **Sections to reach the member of interest, joints to finish off the local members** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS A USEFUL EXTENSION THAT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED: a cut through four members is perfectly usable if one of those four has already been found — from a zero-force rule, from symmetry, or from a previous calculation.**

> **So the three-member limit is really a limit on UNKNOWNS, not on members cut, and identifying the zero-force members first (as noted earlier) frequently makes an otherwise impossible cut workable.**

> **THE LAST ROW DESCRIBES REAL PRACTICE AND IS WORTH STATING: the two methods are not alternatives to choose between but tools to combine.**

> **Sections are used to jump straight to the heavily loaded chord members that govern the design, and joints are used where several small members meet and all of them are wanted.**

> **An examination question asking for one specific member's force is almost always a sections problem, and one asking for all the forces in a small truss is a joints problem.**

examTip.trick: **Three: ΣF_x, ΣF_y and ONE moment equation.** A second moment equation is not independent — it follows algebraically from the first three.
examTip.trap: **Take moments about the point where the two UNWANTED unknowns intersect** — both vanish and the wanted force falls out in one line. For parallel unknowns, resolve perpendicular to them.
examTip.mnemonic: **The limit is on UNKNOWNS, not members cut** — a four-member cut works if one force is already known, which is why finding the zero-force members first pays.

questions.stem: A TWO-HINGED arch is statically INDETERMINATE to the first degree, and its horizontal thrust is found by:
options: Taking moments about the crown
Assuming the thrust equals that of an equivalent three-hinged arch
A compatibility condition
Resolving forces horizontally at a support
questions.solution:
**By a COMPATIBILITY condition** — that the horizontal displacement between the two hinges is ZERO — evaluated by strain energy or the unit load method.

**Why statics alone is not enough:**

| Arch | Unknowns | Equations | Degree |
|---|---|---|---|
| **THREE-HINGED** | **4 reaction components** ← | **3 equilibrium + 1 condition (zero moment at the crown hinge)** ← | **DETERMINATE** ← |
| **TWO-HINGED** | **4 reaction components** ← | **3 equilibrium only — there is NO crown hinge** ← | **Indeterminate to the FIRST degree** ← |
| **FIXED arch** | **6 reaction components** | **3 equilibrium** | **Indeterminate to the THIRD degree** ← |

> **OPTION (A) IS PRECISELY WHAT CANNOT BE DONE AND THAT IS THE POINT: taking moments about the crown works for a THREE-hinged arch because the crown hinge guarantees the moment there is zero.**

> **A two-hinged arch has no crown hinge, so the moment at the crown is an unknown rather than a known zero — and the equation is unavailable.**

> **One extra equation must therefore come from somewhere other than statics, and the only remaining source is the arch's DEFORMATION.**

**The compatibility approach:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Release the redundant — treat the horizontal thrust H as the unknown** ← | **Imagine one support free to slide horizontally** ← |
| **Under the loads alone, that support would move outward by some amount δ_L** ← | ← |
| **The thrust H, acting inward, would move it back by H δ_H** ← | ← |
| **But the real support DOES NOT MOVE, so the two must cancel** ← | **δ_L + H δ_H = 0, which gives H** ← |
| **Evaluated by strain energy: ∂U/∂H = 0** ← | **Castigliano's theorem — the strain energy is a MINIMUM with respect to the redundant** ← |
| **For a rib of constant EI: H = ∫(M₀ y ds/EI) ÷ ∫(y² ds/EI)** ← | **With M₀ the moment of an equivalent simply supported beam** ← |

> **THE STRAIN ENERGY FORM IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ELEGANT STATEMENT AND IT GENERALISES: for any statically indeterminate structure, the redundant forces take the values that MINIMISE the total strain energy.**

> **That is the theorem of least work, and it is the underlying principle of every force-method analysis — the structure distributes its internal forces in whatever way stores the least energy, subject to equilibrium.**

**How the two arches compare in behaviour, which is the practically useful part:**

| Aspect | THREE-HINGED | TWO-HINGED |
|---|---|---|
| **Analysis** | **Statics alone — simple** ← | **Requires a compatibility calculation** ← |
| **Sensitivity to TEMPERATURE change** | **NONE — it simply moves** ← | **Significant — the restrained expansion changes H** ← |
| **Sensitivity to SUPPORT SPREAD** | **NONE** ← | **Significant — a spread of even a few millimetres relieves the thrust and alters the moments** ← |
| **Sensitivity to RIB SHORTENING** | **None** | **Present — the axial compression shortens the rib and reduces H** ← |
| **Material efficiency** | **Less — the crown hinge is a point of zero moment, so the rib is unnecessarily deep elsewhere** ← | **MORE — the moments are lower and better distributed** ← |
| **The hinges themselves** | **Three to build and maintain** | **Two** ← |

> **THE TEMPERATURE AND SPREAD SENSITIVITY IN THE MIDDLE ROWS IS THE RECURRING PRICE OF INDETERMINACY, and it is the same trade met with the Gerber beam and the support settlement question: the two-hinged arch is lighter and more efficient, and it pays for that by developing forces from imposed deformations that the three-hinged arch ignores entirely.**

> **THE RIB SHORTENING EFFECT IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS PECULIAR TO ARCHES: the arch rib is in compression along its whole length, so it SHORTENS axially under load.**

> **A shortened rib spans slightly further between its abutments, which relieves the horizontal thrust — so the actual thrust is a little LESS than a calculation ignoring axial deformation predicts.**

> **The effect is small in a slender masonry or steel arch and appreciable in a thick concrete one, and it acts in the same direction as a support spread — which is why both are commonly allowed for together as a reduction in H.**

examTip.trick: **No crown hinge means no fourth equation from statics** — so the horizontal displacement between the hinges being ZERO supplies it. H = ∫(M₀y ds/EI) ÷ ∫(y² ds/EI).
examTip.trap: **Option (a) works only for a THREE-hinged arch**, where the crown hinge guarantees zero moment there. In a two-hinged arch the crown moment is itself unknown.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two-hinged is more efficient and pays for it in sensitivity** — to temperature, support spread and RIB SHORTENING (the compressed rib shortens, spans further, and relieves H).

questions.stem: In the CONJUGATE BEAM method, a FIXED end of the real beam is replaced, in the conjugate beam, by:
options: A fixed end
A free end
A simple support
An internal hinge
questions.solution:
**A FREE end.**

**The support conversions, and the reasoning behind each:**

| Real beam | Conjugate beam | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED end** — zero slope, zero deflection ← | **FREE end** — zero shear, zero moment ← | **Both quantities are zero at a fixed end, and only a free end has zero shear AND zero moment** ← |
| **FREE end** — slope and deflection both non-zero ← | **FIXED end** ← | **The exact reverse** ← |
| **SIMPLE support (end)** — zero deflection, non-zero slope ← | **SIMPLE support** ← | **Zero moment, non-zero shear — unchanged** ← |
| **INTERNAL support of a continuous beam** — zero deflection, slope CONTINUOUS ← | **INTERNAL HINGE** ← | **Zero moment, shear continuous** ← |
| **INTERNAL HINGE** — deflection continuous, slope DISCONTINUOUS ← | **INTERNAL SUPPORT** ← | **The reverse** ← |

> **THE WHOLE TABLE FOLLOWS FROM ONE ANALOGY, and once it is seen the conversions need not be memorised:**

| Real beam quantity | Corresponds to, in the conjugate beam |
|---|---|
| **SLOPE θ** | **SHEAR force** ← |
| **DEFLECTION y** | **BENDING MOMENT** ← |
| **The M/EI diagram** | **The applied LOAD** ← |

> **So a support in the conjugate beam must permit or prevent shear and moment exactly as the real support permits or prevents slope and deflection.**

> **A fixed end prevents BOTH slope and deflection, so its conjugate must have zero shear and zero moment — and the only support with both is a FREE end.**

> **A free end permits both slope and deflection, so its conjugate must be able to develop shear and moment — a FIXED end.**

> **The conversions are therefore derivable in a few seconds from the analogy, which is far more reliable than recalling a table.**

**Why the method works, which is worth understanding rather than accepting:**

| Real beam | Conjugate beam |
|---|---|
| **d²y/dx² = M/EI** ← | **d²M/dx² = −w** ← |
| **The two equations have the SAME FORM** ← | **With y ↔ M and M/EI ↔ w** ← |
| **So loading a beam with the M/EI diagram makes its bending moment equal to the real beam's DEFLECTION** ← | **And its shear equal to the real beam's SLOPE** ← |

> **THE METHOD IS THEREFORE NOT A TRICK BUT A MATHEMATICAL IDENTITY: the differential equation governing deflection is the same as the one governing bending moment, so a problem in deflection can be converted into a problem in statics — which is much easier.**

> **Instead of integrating twice and finding two constants from the boundary conditions, one computes reactions and bending moments in an ordinary beam.**

> **The boundary conditions are handled automatically by the conjugate supports, which is the method's real advantage over direct integration and the reason the conversions matter so much.**

**Its advantages and where it excels:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **The boundary conditions are built into the SUPPORTS** ← | **No constants of integration to determine — the commonest source of error in the double integration method** ← |
| **It handles VARYING EI naturally** ← | **The M/EI diagram simply changes shape — a stepped or tapered beam is no harder** ← |
| **It gives the deflection at any point, and the slope, directly** | ← |
| **It suits CANTILEVERS and OVERHANGING beams particularly well** ← | **Where moment-area requires a known tangent and the conjugate method does not** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CONJUGATE BEAM METHOD'S ADVANTAGE OVER THE MOMENT-AREA METHOD, and it is worth noting because the two are otherwise very similar: moment-area gives DEVIATIONS from a tangent, and is useful only where a tangent's position is known.**

> **The conjugate beam method gives the deflection DIRECTLY, at any point, with no need to find a reference tangent first.**

> **For an unsymmetrically loaded simply supported beam — where moment-area needs an extra step to locate a tangent — the conjugate beam handles it in one pass, and that is when it is the method to reach for.**

examTip.trick: **Fixed ↔ FREE; simple end stays simple; internal support ↔ internal HINGE.** A fixed end has zero slope AND deflection, so its conjugate needs zero shear AND moment — a free end.
examTip.trap: **Derive the conversions from the analogy: slope ↔ SHEAR, deflection ↔ MOMENT, M/EI ↔ LOAD.** Far more reliable than recalling a table.
examTip.mnemonic: **It is an identity, not a trick** — d²y/dx² = M/EI has the same form as d²M/dx² = −w. And unlike moment-area, it gives deflection DIRECTLY with no reference tangent needed.

questions.stem: The rotational STIFFNESS of a prismatic beam member at one end, for the purpose of computing distribution factors, is:
options: EI/L in both cases
2EI/L for a far end fixed and EI/L for a far end hinged
4EI/L when the far end is fixed, and 3EI/L when the far end is hinged
The same regardless of the far end's condition
questions.solution:
**4EI/L when the far end is FIXED, and 3EI/L when the far end is HINGED** — so a member with a hinged far end is only three quarters as stiff.

**What the stiffness means:**

| Definition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The MOMENT required at one end to produce a UNIT ROTATION there** ← | **With the far end held as stated** ← |
| **Far end FIXED: k = 4EI/L** ← | **And a CARRY-OVER moment of 2EI/L appears at the far end — half the applied moment** ← |
| **Far end HINGED: k = 3EI/L** ← | **And NO carry-over, since a hinge cannot sustain a moment** ← |

> **THE RATIO 3/4 IS THE PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT NUMBER AND THE REASON IS PHYSICAL: a member whose far end is FIXED is restrained at both ends, so rotating one end forces the whole member to bend in a double curvature and it resists strongly.**

> **A member whose far end is FREE TO ROTATE offers less resistance — the far end simply turns rather than developing a restraining moment — so less moment is needed for the same rotation at the near end.**

**Where the 3/4 factor is used, which is the point of knowing it:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **MOMENT DISTRIBUTION distribution factors** ← | **DF = k / Σk at a joint, so using the wrong k misdistributes the moments** ← |
| **A member framing into a SIMPLE SUPPORT at its far end** ← | **Its stiffness is 3EI/L, not 4EI/L** ← |
| **The MODIFIED stiffness saves an entire iteration cycle** ← | **Because a hinged far end need not be carried over to and released repeatedly** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE COMPUTATIONAL ADVANTAGE AND IT IS WHY THE MODIFIED STIFFNESS IS WORTH USING RATHER THAN JUST KNOWING: in moment distribution, an end simply supported must be released after every carry-over, because it cannot hold a moment.**

> **Using 4EI/L for such a member means carrying a moment over to it and then releasing it, cycle after cycle — a great deal of arithmetic that cancels out.**

> **Using 3EI/L accounts for the release ONCE, in the stiffness itself, and the far end is then treated as needing no further attention.**

> **For a continuous beam with simply supported ends, that single substitution can halve the work.**

**The related quantities in moment distribution, gathered:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Stiffness, far end FIXED** | **4EI/L** ← |
| **Stiffness, far end HINGED** | **3EI/L** ← |
| **CARRY-OVER factor, far end fixed** | **+1/2 — half the balancing moment is carried to the far end** ← |
| **Carry-over factor, far end hinged** | **ZERO** ← |
| **DISTRIBUTION factor at a joint** | **DF = k_member / Σk_all members at that joint; the DFs at a joint SUM TO 1** ← |
| **At a FIXED support** | **DF = 0 — a fixed support absorbs everything and distributes nothing** ← |
| **RELATIVE stiffness** | **Only ratios matter, so the common E can be dropped and I/L used** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL SIMPLIFICATION THAT MAKES HAND CALCULATION QUICK: since distribution factors are RATIOS of stiffnesses at a joint, any factor common to all the members cancels.**

> **With the same material throughout, E cancels, and the relative stiffness is simply I/L — or 3I/4L for a member with a hinged far end.**

> **THE FIXED SUPPORT'S ZERO DISTRIBUTION FACTOR IN THE SIXTH ROW IS WORTH STATING EXPLICITLY BECAUSE IT IS FREQUENTLY MISHANDLED: a fixed support is infinitely stiff compared with any member framing into it, so it takes the whole of any moment carried over to it and passes none back.**

> **In the distribution table, that means the fixed end is never balanced — the carry-over simply accumulates there, and its final value is the fixed-end moment of the completed analysis.**

> **A joint at a fixed support therefore appears in the table only as a receiver of carry-overs, which is what makes the calculation terminate.**

examTip.trick: **4EI/L far end FIXED, 3EI/L far end HINGED** — a ratio of 3/4. Carry-over is +1/2 for a fixed far end and ZERO for a hinged one.
examTip.trap: **Using 4EI/L for a simply supported far end means carrying over and releasing every cycle** — arithmetic that cancels. The modified 3EI/L accounts for the release once.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only RATIOS matter, so drop E and use I/L (or 3I/4L).** And a FIXED support has DF = 0 — it receives carry-overs and never distributes, which is what makes the table terminate.

questions.stem: In the lateral load resisting system of a building, the floor slab acting as a DIAPHRAGM serves to:
options: Collect the inertia force generated at each floor level and distribute it to the vertical resisting elements
Carry the gravity load of the floor to the beams
Provide fire separation between storeys
Reduce the building's natural period
questions.solution:
**To COLLECT the inertia force generated at each floor level and DISTRIBUTE it to the vertical resisting elements** in proportion to their stiffness.

**Why a diaphragm is essential:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The earthquake force is an INERTIA force, generated by the MASS** ← | **And most of a building's mass is in its FLOORS** ← |
| **The force therefore appears distributed across each floor's area** ← | **Not conveniently at the shear walls** ← |
| **It must be carried HORIZONTALLY to the vertical elements that can take it down to the foundation** ← | **Which is the diaphragm's job** ← |
| **The slab acts as a deep horizontal BEAM spanning between the vertical elements** ← | **Loaded in its own plane** ← |

> **THE FLOOR IS THEREFORE DOING TWO STRUCTURALLY UNRELATED JOBS AT ONCE, and only one of them is usually designed for: it carries GRAVITY load in bending out of its plane, and it carries SEISMIC force in shear and bending WITHIN its plane.**

> **Option (b) is the first of those, and it is what every slab calculation addresses.**

> **The in-plane action is normally satisfied by inspection — a 125 mm reinforced slab is an extremely stiff and strong horizontal beam — which is why it is easy to forget that the action exists at all.**

**Where the diaphragm assumption FAILS, which is the important part:**

| Case | Note |
|---|---|
| **Large OPENINGS — stair and lift wells, atria, service shafts** ← | **They interrupt the diaphragm; the remaining strips must carry the force around the opening, and they may be too narrow** ← |
| **A long, narrow plan** ← | **The diaphragm's own in-plane deflection becomes significant, so it is FLEXIBLE rather than rigid, and the distribution is no longer by stiffness alone** ← |
| **PRECAST floor units without a structural TOPPING or adequate connection** ← | **They act as separate planks, not as a diaphragm — a serious and common defect** ← |
| **Timber or CGI roofs, and jack-arch or timber-joist floors** ← | **Essentially NO diaphragm action — which is why an eaves band and roof-level tie are so important in masonry buildings** ← |
| **Re-entrant corners — L, T and H shaped plans** | **Stress concentrates at the corner of the notch** ← |

> **THE PRECAST CASE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL DETAILING ISSUE IN MODERN CONSTRUCTION, and it is worth stating firmly: a floor of hollow-core or precast planks simply laid side by side is not a diaphragm.**

> **It is a row of independent beams that can slide and separate along their joints.**

> **What makes it a diaphragm is a reinforced structural TOPPING cast over it, or grouted joints with reinforcement in them, tied into a perimeter tie beam — and the connection to the shear walls and frames must be explicitly detailed to transfer the shear.**

> **Precast floors have separated from their supports and collapsed in earthquakes for exactly this reason, and the omission is invisible once the floor finish is on.**

**THE FLEXIBLE-VERSUS-RIGID DISTINCTION IN THE SECOND ROW GOVERNS THE ANALYSIS and is worth knowing:**

| Diaphragm | Force distribution to the vertical elements |
|---|---|
| **RIGID (a normal RC slab of reasonable proportions)** ← | **In proportion to the elements' STIFFNESS — the stiff walls take most of it** ← |
| **FLEXIBLE (timber, CGI, unconnected precast, very long plan)** ← | **In proportion to the TRIBUTARY AREA — each element takes the force from the floor area near it, regardless of its stiffness** ← |

> **THE TWO ASSUMPTIONS GIVE COMPLETELY DIFFERENT ANSWERS, and the difference is not a refinement: with a rigid diaphragm a stiff shear wall attracts force from the whole floor, and with a flexible one it attracts only what is immediately adjacent to it.**

> **A building analysed as rigid but built with a flexible diaphragm has its walls under-loaded in the model and its frames over-loaded in reality — and the redistribution is not conservative.**

> **Codes therefore define the boundary between the two by comparing the diaphragm's in-plane deflection with the storey drift, and a slab is treated as rigid only if its own deflection is small by comparison.**

The frames, shear walls or cores — in proportion to their stiffness.

examTip.trick: **It collects the floor's inertia force and delivers it in-plane to the walls and frames.** Option (b) is the slab's gravity action — a separate job in a different plane.
examTip.trap: **Precast planks without a structural topping or grouted reinforced joints are NOT a diaphragm** — they are independent beams that can slide apart. Invisible once the finish is on.
examTip.mnemonic: **RIGID diaphragm → force distributed by STIFFNESS; FLEXIBLE → by TRIBUTARY AREA.** The two give completely different answers, and assuming rigid when it is flexible is not conservative.

questions.stem: TORSIONAL IRREGULARITY in a building arises when:
options: The building is taller than it is wide
The floor slab is not square
The columns are of unequal size
The centre of mass and the centre of rigidity do not coincide
questions.solution:
**When the CENTRE OF MASS and the CENTRE OF RIGIDITY do not coincide** — so the inertia force acts at an eccentricity and twists the building in plan.

**The two centres:**

| Centre | Definition | Determined by |
|---|---|---|
| **CENTRE OF MASS (centre of gravity)** ← | **Where the floor's inertia force effectively ACTS** ← | **The distribution of MASS — slabs, walls, finishes, imposed load** ← |
| **CENTRE OF RIGIDITY (centre of stiffness)** ← | **Where the resultant of the vertical elements' RESISTANCE acts** ← | **The position and STIFFNESS of the columns, shear walls and cores** ← |

> **THE ECCENTRICITY BETWEEN THEM IS A LEVER ARM, AND THE PRODUCT IS A TORQUE ON THE WHOLE FLOOR: the force pushes at one point and the resistance pushes back at another, so the building rotates about a vertical axis as well as translating.**

> **That rotation ADDS displacement at the corners furthest from the centre of rigidity — and those elements then carry far more than the translational analysis predicted.**

**Why torsion is so damaging:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The elements FURTHEST from the centre of rigidity get the largest additional displacement** ← | **And displacement demand is what fails a member in an earthquake** ← |
| **A corner column may see two or three times the drift of the building's average** ← | **While the design assumed the average** ← |
| **The overloaded elements are usually the ones on the FLEXIBLE side** ← | **Which are the least able to take it** ← |
| **Failure of one corner element shifts the centre of rigidity FURTHER, increasing the eccentricity** ← | **A progressive, self-worsening mechanism** ← |
| **Torsional response is difficult to detail for** | **Corner columns are biaxially loaded and their confinement is hardest to achieve** ← |

> **THE FEEDBACK IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WHAT MAKES TORSIONAL FAILURE SO OFTEN CATASTROPHIC RATHER THAN PARTIAL: losing a stiff element on one side moves the centre of rigidity away from it, which increases the eccentricity, which increases the torsion, which overloads the next element.**

> **The building unwinds progressively, and corner-first collapses in earthquakes are frequently this mechanism rather than a simple overload.**

**The commonest causes, which are almost all architectural rather than structural:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **A lift core or stair core placed at ONE END or ONE CORNER of the plan** ← | **The single most common cause — a core is very stiff and it pulls the centre of rigidity strongly toward itself** ← |
| **Shear walls on two adjacent sides only** ← | **An L arrangement, which puts the centre of rigidity at the corner** ← |
| **Infill walls on three sides with a glazed shopfront on the fourth** ← | **Very common in commercial buildings, and the infill is usually not modelled at all** ← |
| **Unsymmetrical plan shapes — L, T, U, H** | ← |
| **Heavy masses placed off-centre** | **A water tank, a plant room, an archive floor** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS WORTH DWELLING ON BECAUSE THE ARRANGEMENT IS SO ATTRACTIVE ARCHITECTURALLY: putting the lift and stair core at one end of the plan frees the whole floor for open space, and it is what a great many buildings do.**

> **Structurally it is close to the worst possible arrangement — an extremely stiff element at one extremity, with flexible frames elsewhere, so the centre of rigidity sits almost at the core and the centre of mass near the plan's middle.**

> **The remedy is either to place cores SYMMETRICALLY — two smaller cores at opposite ends, or one central core — or to add shear walls on the far side to balance the stiffness.**

> **This is a decision made at the architectural planning stage, and by the time the structural engineer is appointed it is frequently settled — which is why early structural input into the plan layout is worth more than any subsequent analysis.**

**How codes deal with it:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **The eccentricity is computed, and an ACCIDENTAL eccentricity added** ← | **Commonly 5 per cent of the plan dimension, to cover uncertainty in mass and stiffness** ← |
| **The design eccentricity is amplified — commonly 1.5 times the computed value plus the accidental** ← | **Recognising the dynamic amplification of torsion** ← |
| **Torsional irregularity is DEFINED by comparing corner drifts** ← | **If the maximum storey drift at one end exceeds 1.2 times the average, the building is torsionally irregular** ← |
| **Where it is irregular, a full three-dimensional DYNAMIC analysis is required** ← | **The equivalent static method is not permitted** ← |

> **THE ACCIDENTAL ECCENTRICITY IN THE FIRST ROW IS REQUIRED EVEN FOR A PERFECTLY SYMMETRICAL BUILDING, and the reason is honest: the real mass distribution is never what the drawing shows.**

> **Partitions get moved, storage accumulates on one side, the actual stiffnesses differ from the calculated ones, and the ground motion has a rotational component of its own.**

> **So a nominal 5 per cent eccentricity is imposed regardless — an admission that symmetry on paper is not symmetry in the building.**

The seismic force acts at an ECCENTRICITY and twists the building in plan.

examTip.trick: **Centre of MASS (where the force acts) offset from centre of RIGIDITY (where the resistance acts) gives a lever arm and a plan torque.**
examTip.trap: **The failure is self-worsening** — losing a stiff element moves the centre of rigidity further away, increasing the eccentricity and overloading the next. Hence corner-first collapses.
examTip.mnemonic: **A lift core at ONE END is the commonest cause and the most attractive plan** — put cores symmetrically or balance with walls opposite. And 5 % ACCIDENTAL eccentricity applies even to a symmetric building.

questions.stem: The principal danger in COLD WEATHER concreting is that:
options: The concrete sets too rapidly to be placed
Strength gain is greatly slowed
The water-cement ratio increases
The cement becomes chemically inert and never hydrates
questions.solution:
**Strength gain is greatly SLOWED, and if the fresh concrete FREEZES before gaining sufficient strength the expanding ice permanently disrupts it.**

**The two distinct problems:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **SLOW strength gain** ← | **Hydration is a chemical reaction, and its rate roughly HALVES for every 10 °C fall — so concrete at 5 °C gains strength at perhaps a third of the rate at 20 °C** ← |
| **FREEZING of the fresh concrete** ← | **Water expands about 9 per cent on freezing, and in a paste with no strength yet that expansion tears the structure apart PERMANENTLY** ← |

> **THE SECOND IS THE SERIOUS ONE AND IT IS IRREVERSIBLE, which is the point of the question: slow strength gain is an inconvenience — the concrete catches up eventually if kept above freezing.**

> **Concrete that has FROZEN before it developed strength has been physically disrupted, and it never recovers. Warming it afterwards does not repair it; the damage is done and the member must be removed.**

> **Option (d) is wrong but points at something real: hydration essentially STOPS below about 0 °C, and does not resume as though nothing had happened if freezing occurred.**

**The critical strength threshold:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Concrete becomes resistant to freezing damage once it reaches about 5 MPa** ← | **By then enough of the mix water is chemically combined, and the paste has strength to resist the ice pressure** ← |
| **So the object is to keep it above freezing UNTIL that strength is reached** ← | **A few days at moderate temperature, longer in the cold** ← |
| **Beyond that, slow gain is merely a programme problem** ← | ← |

> **THE 5 MPa FIGURE IS THE ONE TO REMEMBER BECAUSE IT DEFINES WHAT THE PROTECTION MUST ACHIEVE: the concrete does not need protecting for its whole curing period, only until it has passed that threshold.**

> **That converts an indefinite requirement into a manageable one of a few days, and it is why cold weather protection is intensive and short rather than prolonged.**

**The measures:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **HEAT the mixing WATER — the most effective single step** ← | **Water has by far the highest specific heat of the constituents, so heating it warms the mix most efficiently. Not above about 60-70 °C, or it flash-sets on contact with the cement** ← |
| **Heat the AGGREGATE, particularly the fine aggregate** | **And never place concrete containing frozen aggregate or ice lumps** ← |
| **INSULATE the formwork and cover the surfaces** ← | **Insulating blankets, straw, or insulated forms — retaining the heat of hydration, which is substantial** ← |
| **Use RAPID HARDENING cement, or an ACCELERATOR** ← | **To pass the 5 MPa threshold sooner — but NEVER calcium chloride in reinforced work** ← |
| **A richer mix, or a lower water-cement ratio** | **Less free water to freeze, and faster strength gain** ← |
| **Enclose and heat the working area** | **For critical work; the most expensive option** ← |
| **Leave the FORMWORK ON LONGER** ← | **It insulates, and the concrete has gained strength more slowly — so the striking times must be extended, not merely met** ← |

> **THE INSULATION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST EFFICIENT MEASURE AFTER HEATING THE WATER AND IT IS OFTEN UNDERESTIMATED: the hydration reaction is EXOTHERMIC, so the concrete generates its own heat.**

> **In a reasonably thick member, insulating the surfaces retains that heat and the concrete keeps itself well above the ambient temperature for several days — sometimes 20 °C or more above it.**

> **The problem is not usually a lack of heat but its LOSS, so retaining it is cheaper and more effective than supplying more.**

> **Thin members are the difficult case: a 100 mm slab has little mass to generate heat and a large surface to lose it through, so it needs far more protection than a large column of the same concrete.**

> **THE STRIKING TIME POINT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG IN PRACTICE, and it connects directly to the formwork question: the code's minimum striking periods assume normal weather.**

> **In cold weather the concrete has not reached the assumed strength at the tabulated age, so striking on schedule strikes a weaker member — and the correct approach is to strike on MATURITY or on measured cube strength rather than on the calendar.**

examTip.trick: **Hydration roughly halves per 10 °C fall, and freezing before strength develops disrupts the concrete PERMANENTLY** — warming it later does not repair it.
examTip.trap: **The threshold is about 5 MPa** — protect until then, not for the whole curing period. That turns an indefinite requirement into a few days.
examTip.mnemonic: **Heat the WATER (highest specific heat, but under 60-70 °C) and INSULATE to keep the hydration heat in** — the problem is heat LOSS, not supply. Thin members are the hard case.

questions.stem: As per IS 456, the requirements of MINIMUM GRADE of concrete, MINIMUM CEMENT CONTENT and MAXIMUM water-cement ratio are specified according to the:
options: Magnitude of the applied load
Height of the structure
Exposure condition of the member
Type of cement used
questions.solution:
**According to the EXPOSURE CONDITION** — mild, moderate, severe, very severe or extreme — because these requirements exist for DURABILITY rather than for strength.

**The exposure classes and their requirements for REINFORCED concrete:**

| Exposure | Description | Minimum grade | Max w/c | Min cement (kg/m³) | Nominal cover |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **MILD** | **Protected against weather; interior** ← | **M20** | **0.55** | **300** | **20 mm** ← |
| **MODERATE** | **Sheltered from severe rain; buried; permanently under water** ← | **M25** | **0.50** | **300** | **30 mm** ← |
| **SEVERE** | **Alternate wetting and drying; sea water spray; severe rain** ← | **M30** | **0.45** | **320** | **45 mm** ← |
| **VERY SEVERE** | **Sea water; aggressive subsoil; corrosive fumes** ← | **M35** | **0.45** | **340** | **50 mm** ← |
| **EXTREME** | **Tidal zone; direct contact with aggressive chemicals** ← | **M40** | **0.40** | **360** | **75 mm** ← |

> **THE KEY INSIGHT IS THAT THESE ARE DURABILITY REQUIREMENTS, NOT STRENGTH ONES, and it has a consequence that surprises people:**

> **A lightly loaded slab in a tidal zone must be M40, even though M20 would carry its load ten times over.**

> **The grade is not being specified because the concrete needs the strength — it is being specified because a high-grade, low water-cement-ratio concrete is DENSE and IMPERMEABLE, and impermeability is what keeps chlorides, carbon dioxide and sulphates away from the reinforcement.**

> **So in an aggressive exposure the DURABILITY requirement governs, and the structural calculation becomes irrelevant to the choice of grade.**

**Why the three requirements act together:**

| Requirement | What it controls |
|---|---|
| **Maximum WATER-CEMENT RATIO** ← | **PERMEABILITY, above all — a low w/c gives a dense paste with few connected capillaries. This is the most important of the three** ← |
| **Minimum CEMENT content** ← | **Ensures enough paste to fill the aggregate voids and to provide ALKALINITY (the reserve of calcium hydroxide that keeps the steel passive)** ← |
| **Minimum GRADE** | **A verifiable, testable proxy for the above two — since w/c cannot be measured on hardened concrete** ← |
| **Nominal COVER** ← | **The physical thickness of the barrier the aggressive agents must penetrate** ← |
| **And a MAXIMUM cement content of 450 kg/m³** ← | **Too much cement means excessive heat of hydration and shrinkage — so more is not simply better** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW EXPLAINS WHY A GRADE IS SPECIFIED AT ALL WHEN THE REAL CONCERN IS THE WATER-CEMENT RATIO: the w/c of hardened concrete cannot be measured, but its strength can.**

> **Since strength is closely related to w/c for a given cement, specifying a minimum grade is a way of enforcing a maximum w/c through a test that can actually be performed on the finished work.**

> **It is an indirect requirement standing in for a direct one, and that is worth understanding because it explains why the two are always specified together — the grade to be tested, the w/c to be controlled at the plant.**

> **THE MAXIMUM CEMENT LIMIT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT MATTERS: adding cement beyond about 450 kg/m³ increases the heat of hydration, the autogenous and drying shrinkage, and the risk of thermal and shrinkage cracking.**

> **Cracks are a durability defect in themselves — a direct path for water and chlorides to the steel — so an over-rich mix can be LESS durable than a correctly proportioned one, despite having more cement.**

> **The cover and the crack width matter more than the cement content beyond a point, which is why durability is specified as a package rather than by maximising any single parameter.**

**And the practical failure that all of this exists to prevent:**

> **Reinforcement corrosion is by far the commonest cause of premature deterioration in concrete structures worldwide — ahead of overload, ahead of settlement, ahead of every structural cause combined.**

> **It is a durability failure, not a strength failure, and it is entirely governed by the parameters in the table above and by the workmanship in achieving them.**

> **Which makes cover, compaction and curing the three site operations with the greatest influence on how long a structure lasts — and all three are unglamorous, easy to skimp and impossible to verify once the concrete has hardened.**

examTip.trick: **Mild M20, moderate M25, severe M30, very severe M35, extreme M40** — with w/c falling from 0.55 to 0.40 and cover rising from 20 to 75 mm.
examTip.trap: **These are DURABILITY requirements** — a lightly loaded slab in a tidal zone still needs M40. The grade is a testable proxy for the water-cement ratio, which cannot be measured on hardened concrete.
examTip.mnemonic: **There is also a MAXIMUM cement content (450 kg/m³)** — more cement means more heat and shrinkage, and cracks are themselves a durability defect. Cover, compaction and curing decide how long it lasts.

questions.stem: In the shear design of a reinforced concrete beam, if the nominal shear stress τ_v is LESS than the design shear strength of the concrete τ_c, then:
options: No shear reinforcement of any kind is required
Only minimum shear reinforcement need be provided
The section must be redesigned
The beam will fail in shear
questions.solution:
**Only MINIMUM shear reinforcement need be provided** — the code requires stirrups throughout every beam regardless of the calculation.

**The three cases in shear design:**

| Condition | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **τ_v < τ_c** ← | **MINIMUM shear reinforcement — A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)** ← |
| **τ_c < τ_v < τ_c,max** ← | **DESIGNED shear reinforcement to carry the excess (τ_v − τ_c) b d** ← |
| **τ_v > τ_c,max** ← | **The SECTION IS INADEQUATE — it must be enlarged or the concrete grade raised. No amount of stirrups will do** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE WORTH NOTING ALONGSIDE THE ANSWER, because it is where shear differs from bending: there is an absolute upper limit τ_c,max beyond which shear reinforcement cannot help.**

> **The reason is that beyond that stress the concrete itself crushes in the diagonal compression struts of the truss action, and stirrups do nothing about a compression failure.**

> **In bending, adding steel always adds capacity (subject to the ductility limit). In shear, there is a ceiling set by the concrete, and the only remedies are a bigger section or stronger concrete.**

**Why MINIMUM stirrups are required even when the calculation says none are needed:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Shear failure is BRITTLE and SUDDEN, with little warning** ← | **Unlike flexural failure — so a margin against an unexpected shear is worth having** ← |
| **They restrain DIAGONAL cracking and limit its width** ← | **Improving durability as well as strength** ← |
| **They provide ductility and confinement to the compression zone** ← | ← |
| **They hold the longitudinal bars in position during concreting** ← | **A practical necessity — without stirrups the cage cannot be assembled at all** ← |
| **They resist unforeseen effects — torsion, settlement, shrinkage restraint, accidental loads** ← | ← |
| **τ_c itself is an empirical value with real scatter** | **A minimum provision covers the low tail** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE FUNDAMENTAL JUSTIFICATION AND IT IS THE SAME REASONING AS THE UNDER-REINFORCED REQUIREMENT: a shear failure gives no warning.**

> **A beam failing in flexure sags visibly and cracks widely first. A beam failing in shear develops a diagonal crack and collapses, often without a prior deflection that anyone would notice.**

> **Given that, spending a small amount on stirrups everywhere to guard against a failure mode with no warning is obviously worthwhile — and it is why the minimum provision is mandatory rather than advisory.**

**What τ_c depends on, which is worth knowing:**

| Factor | Effect on τ_c |
|---|---|
| **Concrete GRADE** | **Higher grade, higher τ_c — but only weakly, as roughly the sixth root** ← |
| **The PERCENTAGE of tension steel** ← | **More tension steel INCREASES τ_c — which surprises people** ← |
| **Axial COMPRESSION** | **Increases it — hence the enhancement for columns** ← |
| **Member DEPTH** | **Deeper members have LOWER shear strength per unit area — the size effect** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE ONE AND IT HAS A GOOD PHYSICAL EXPLANATION: more tension steel means the flexural cracks are narrower and the neutral axis is deeper.**

> **Narrower cracks transmit more shear across themselves by AGGREGATE INTERLOCK, and a deeper neutral axis leaves a larger uncracked compression zone to carry shear directly.**

> **So the tension steel, provided for bending, incidentally improves the shear capacity — which is why τ_c is tabulated against the steel percentage rather than against the concrete grade alone.**

> **THE SIZE EFFECT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE REASON DEEP BEAMS AND LARGE MEMBERS NEED PROPORTIONATELY MORE SHEAR REINFORCEMENT: aggregate interlock depends on the crack width relative to the aggregate size, and in a deep member the cracks are wider for the same strain.**

> **The interlock is therefore less effective, the shear strength per unit area falls, and scaling up a successfully tested small beam is not safe — a real and well-documented pitfall in the design of large structures.**

As the code requires stirrups throughout every beam regardless of the calculation.

examTip.trick: **τ_v < τ_c → MINIMUM stirrups (not none). τ_c < τ_v < τ_c,max → designed stirrups. τ_v > τ_c,max → the SECTION is inadequate.**
examTip.trap: **Above τ_c,max no quantity of stirrups helps** — the concrete crushes in diagonal compression. Unlike bending, shear has a ceiling set by the concrete.
examTip.mnemonic: **More TENSION steel raises τ_c** — narrower cracks give better aggregate interlock and a deeper compression zone. And DEEPER members have lower shear strength per unit area (size effect).

questions.stem: In the design of a reinforced concrete beam subjected to TORSION together with bending and shear, IS 456 adopts the approach of:
options: Ignoring the torsion if it is less than the bending moment
Providing closed stirrups only, with no change to the longitudinal steel
Designing separately for torsion and adding the results
Converting the torsion into an equivalent shear and an equivalent bending moment
questions.solution:
**Converting the torsion into an EQUIVALENT SHEAR and an EQUIVALENT BENDING MOMENT**, and designing the section for those combined values.

**The equivalent quantities:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **EQUIVALENT SHEAR** | **V_e = V + 1.6 T/b, with b the breadth of the section** ← |
| **EQUIVALENT BENDING MOMENT** | **M_e = M + M_t, where M_t = T (1 + D/b) / 1.7** ← |
| **The section is then designed for V_e and M_e** | **Using the ordinary shear and flexure procedures** ← |
| **If M_t exceeds M, longitudinal steel is required on the FLEXURAL COMPRESSION face too** ← | **Because the torsion can reverse the sense of the moment there** ← |

> **THE APPROACH IS DELIBERATELY EMPIRICAL AND ITS VIRTUE IS PRACTICALITY: torsion in reinforced concrete is genuinely complicated — a space truss of diagonal concrete struts and closed reinforcement loops — and a rigorous treatment is laborious.**

> **The equivalent-shear-and-moment method converts a torsion problem into the two problems the designer already knows how to solve, at the cost of some conservatism.**

> **That is a reasonable trade for a member in which torsion is secondary, which describes most beams that carry any.**

**The reinforcement that torsion demands, which is its distinctive requirement:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **CLOSED stirrups, fully anchored** ← | **Torsion produces a circulating shear flow around the section's perimeter, so the reinforcement must form a CLOSED LOOP. An open U-stirrup is useless in torsion** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL bars in EVERY CORNER of the section** ← | **The diagonal compression struts push outward at the corners, and a corner bar is needed to anchor each stirrup and resist the spalling** ← |
| **Bars distributed around the whole perimeter for a deep section** | **Not only at the top and bottom** ← |
| **Closer stirrup spacing than for shear alone** | ← |

> **THE CLOSED STIRRUP IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT DETAILING CONSEQUENCE AND IT IS WHERE TORSION DESIGN GOES WRONG IN PRACTICE: a beam reinforced with open U-shaped stirrups, adequate for shear, has essentially NO torsional capacity.**

> **Torsion is resisted by a closed circuit of tension around the perimeter, balanced by diagonal compression in the concrete.**

> **Break the circuit — by leaving the top of the stirrup open, or by lapping it inadequately — and there is nothing to carry the tension, so the concrete cracks spirally and the member fails.**

> **The laps of a torsion stirrup must therefore be full tension laps or the stirrup must be welded closed, and hooking it 135° into the core is not merely good seismic practice but a structural necessity here.**

**The distinction between EQUILIBRIUM and COMPATIBILITY torsion, which decides how seriously to treat it:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **EQUILIBRIUM torsion** ← | **The torsion is required for the structure to STAND — there is no alternative load path. It MUST be designed for in full** ← |
| **COMPATIBILITY torsion** ← | **The torsion arises only because the members are connected and must rotate together. If the member cracks and softens torsionally, the torsion REDISTRIBUTES away** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION IS PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT AND IS OFTEN THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A REASONABLE DESIGN AND AN ABSURD ONE:**

> **A cantilevered canopy framing into the side of a spandrel beam imposes EQUILIBRIUM torsion — nothing else holds the canopy up, so the beam must carry the torsion or the canopy falls.**

> **A secondary beam framing into a main beam at an interior connection imposes COMPATIBILITY torsion — the main beam twists only because the secondary beam's end wants to rotate. If the main beam cracks and becomes torsionally flexible, the secondary beam's end simply rotates more and the torsion largely disappears.**

> **Codes therefore permit compatibility torsion to be reduced or, with adequate detailing, neglected — while equilibrium torsion must be carried in full with no reduction whatever.**

> **Identifying which kind is present is the first step in any torsion problem, and getting it wrong in the unsafe direction means designing a canopy's supporting beam on the assumption that the torsion will go away, which it cannot.**

examTip.trick: **V_e = V + 1.6T/b and M_e = M + T(1 + D/b)/1.7**, then design for those by the ordinary procedures.
examTip.trap: **Torsion needs CLOSED stirrups** — an open U-stirrup adequate for shear has essentially NO torsional capacity, because torsion is a closed circuit of perimeter tension. Plus a bar in every corner.
examTip.mnemonic: **EQUILIBRIUM torsion must be carried in full (a canopy has no other load path); COMPATIBILITY torsion redistributes away when the member cracks.** Identify which before designing.

questions.stem: In the design of a reinforced concrete LIQUID RETAINING structure such as a water tank, the permissible stress in the steel is kept LOW — commonly 115 to 150 MPa rather than the usual design values — in order to:
options: Limit the crack width
Reduce the quantity of steel required
Allow the use of mild steel only
Simplify the calculation
questions.solution:
**To limit the CRACK WIDTH** — a crack acceptable in an ordinary member would leak and would admit water to the reinforcement.

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Crack width is roughly PROPORTIONAL to the steel stress** ← | **The steel must stretch for the crack to open, so limiting the stress limits the strain and hence the crack** ← |
| **An ordinary member tolerates cracks of 0.3 mm** ← | **Which are structurally harmless and barely visible** ← |
| **A liquid retaining structure permits only 0.1 to 0.2 mm** ← | **Above which it leaks, and the leakage path carries water to the steel** ← |
| **So the steel stress is capped far below its strength** ← | **Making the section serviceability-governed rather than strength-governed** ← |
| **The consequence is MORE steel and a THICKER section than strength alone requires** ← | ← |

> **THE DESIGN IS THEREFORE CONTROLLED BY CRACKING RATHER THAN BY STRENGTH, and that inverts the usual relationship: in an ordinary beam, strength governs and serviceability is checked afterwards.**

> **In a water tank, the crack width requirement determines the reinforcement, and the resulting section has strength far in excess of what it needs.**

> **Option (b) is therefore exactly backwards — the low permissible stress requires MORE steel, not less.**

**Why leakage matters beyond the loss of water:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Loss of the stored liquid** | **The obvious one, and often the least important** ← |
| **Water reaching the REINFORCEMENT causes corrosion** ← | **And the corrosion products expand, widening the crack, admitting more water — a self-accelerating process** ← |
| **Leakage through a wall causes staining, and in a sewage tank a health hazard** ← | ← |
| **Leakage from a tank on a building causes damage below** | ← |
| **AUTOGENOUS HEALING can seal very fine cracks** ← | **Cracks below about 0.1 mm often seal themselves as calcium carbonate deposits in them — which is precisely why the limit is set there** ← |

> **THE AUTOGENOUS HEALING IN THE LAST ROW IS THE PHYSICAL BASIS OF THE 0.1 mm LIMIT AND IT IS A GENUINELY USEFUL PHENOMENON: water seeping through a very fine crack dissolves calcium hydroxide from the concrete, which reacts with carbon dioxide and precipitates calcium carbonate in the crack.**

> **Over days or weeks the crack blocks itself, and the leakage stops.**

> **A crack wide enough that the flow prevents deposition does not heal, and it will leak indefinitely.**

> **So the limit is not arbitrary — it is set at the width below which the structure repairs itself, which is why a new tank often weeps slightly on first filling and then stops.**

> **That is also why a tank is filled slowly and left full for a period before the water-tightness test is judged, rather than being condemned on the first day.**

**The other provisions specific to liquid retaining structures:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **A minimum concrete grade of M30, with low water-cement ratio** ← | **Density and impermeability** ← |
| **Increased COVER, commonly 40 to 45 mm on the liquid face** ← | ← |
| **Minimum reinforcement of 0.24 to 0.35 per cent in each direction, in each face** ← | **To control SHRINKAGE and THERMAL cracking, which occur whether or not the tank is loaded** ← |
| **Careful attention to CONSTRUCTION JOINTS with water bars** ← | **Joints are where tanks leak, far more often than the body of the concrete** ← |
| **Movement joints in long walls** | **To accommodate shrinkage and thermal movement without cracking** ← |
| **A water-tightness TEST before handover** | ← |

> **THE JOINTS IN THE FOURTH ROW ARE WHERE TANKS ACTUALLY LEAK, and it is worth stating plainly because the design effort usually goes elsewhere: a properly proportioned wall of dense concrete with limited crack widths does not leak through its body.**

> **It leaks at construction joints, at pipe penetrations, at the wall-to-base junction, and around water bars that were displaced or damaged during concreting.**

> **So the detailing and the workmanship at those locations determine whether the tank holds water, and the crack width calculation — while necessary — addresses the part of the problem least likely to fail.**

> **THE MINIMUM REINFORCEMENT IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE CRACK CONTROL AND IT IS INDEPENDENT OF LOAD: a long wall restrained at its base shrinks and cannot contract freely, so it cracks — with no water in the tank at all.**

> **Enough distributed steel in both faces ensures those restraint cracks are numerous and FINE rather than few and wide, which is the whole strategy of crack control: you cannot prevent cracking, so you distribute it.**

A crack that would be acceptable in an ordinary member would allow LEAKAGE and would admit water to the reinforcement.

examTip.trick: **Crack width is roughly proportional to steel STRESS** — so capping the stress at 115-150 MPa caps the crack at 0.1-0.2 mm instead of the usual 0.3 mm.
examTip.trap: **It requires MORE steel, not less** — the design becomes serviceability-governed, with strength far in excess of need. Option (b) is backwards.
examTip.mnemonic: **The 0.1 mm limit is where AUTOGENOUS HEALING works** — calcium carbonate seals the crack, which is why a new tank weeps and then stops. But tanks actually leak at JOINTS, not through the wall.

questions.stem: The END BLOCK (anchorage zone) of a POST-TENSIONED member requires special reinforcement because the concentrated anchorage force produces:
options: Only compressive stresses, which the concrete carries easily
Excessive deflection at the end of the member
Bursting (transverse tensile) stresses as the concentrated force spreads out over the full section
A reduction in the prestressing force
questions.solution:
**BURSTING (transverse tensile) stresses**, as the concentrated force spreads out over the full section — and these would split the concrete if not reinforced.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The prestressing force is applied over a SMALL anchorage area** ← | **Perhaps a few thousand square millimetres, carrying a force of several thousand kilonewtons** ← |
| **It must spread out to act uniformly over the WHOLE cross-section** ← | **Which it does over a length roughly equal to the member's depth** ← |
| **The stress trajectories DIVERGE as they spread** ← | **And diverging compression trajectories generate TRANSVERSE TENSION, exactly as a wedge splits timber** ← |
| **That transverse tension is the BURSTING force** ← | **Peaking at some distance behind the anchorage, not at the face** ← |
| **Concrete has little tensile strength, so it must be reinforced** ← | **Closely spaced closed links, spirals or a mesh grid** ← |

> **THE WEDGE ANALOGY IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE CLEAREST WAY TO SEE IT: driving a wedge into a log splits it, and the wedge itself is in pure compression.**

> **The splitting force is transverse, generated by the compression having to spread sideways.**

> **An anchorage is a wedge of compression driven into the end of a beam, and the beam splits for exactly the same reason — which is why option (a) is wrong even though the applied force is entirely compressive.**

**THE ST VENANT PRINCIPLE, which defines the extent of the problem:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **The disturbance from a concentrated load dies out within a distance roughly EQUAL TO the member's depth** ← | **Beyond that, the stress is uniform and ordinary beam theory applies** ← |
| **So the anchorage zone extends about ONE DEPTH from the end face** ← | **And it is that length which needs the special reinforcement** ← |
| **Within it, the stress distribution is genuinely two- or three-dimensional** ← | **Simple bending theory does NOT apply there** ← |

> **THAT IS WHY THE END BLOCK IS TREATED AS A SEPARATE DESIGN PROBLEM RATHER THAN AS PART OF THE BEAM: within one depth of the end, the beam is not behaving as a beam at all.**

> **It is a block of concrete with a concentrated load on it, and it is analysed by strut-and-tie models, by Guyon's or Magnel's methods, or by finite elements — not by M/Z.**

**The reinforcement provided:**

| Detail | Note |
|---|---|
