| **CLOSED links or SPIRALS immediately behind the anchorage** ← | **Confining the highly stressed concrete under the bearing plate** ← |
| **A grid or mesh in two directions, distributed over the anchorage zone** ← | **Resisting the bursting tension, placed where the tension peaks** ← |
| **SPALLING reinforcement near the end FACE** ← | **A separate tension arising at the face itself, between and around the anchorages** ← |
| **Reinforcement designed for the force at the JACKING (transfer) stage** ← | **Which is the most severe condition — the prestress is at its maximum and the concrete at its youngest** ← |

> **THE TIMING IN THE LAST ROW IS THE CRITICAL DESIGN CASE AND IT IS EASILY OVERLOOKED: the anchorage zone is worst loaded at TRANSFER, the moment the tendon is stressed.**

> **At that instant the prestress is at its highest — no losses have yet occurred — and the concrete is at its youngest and weakest, since transfer is done as early as the strength permits in order to free the casting bed or the formwork.**

> **So maximum force meets minimum strength, and the anchorage zone must be designed for that combination rather than for the service condition.**

> **Failures in anchorage zones consequently occur DURING stressing, on site, with the jack still attached — which is why the area is cleared during tensioning and why nobody stands behind a jack.**

> **A tendon or anchorage failing under jacking releases an enormous quantity of stored energy along the tendon's axis, and it has killed people. The exclusion zone during stressing is not a formality.**

Which would split the concrete.

examTip.trick: **Diverging compression trajectories generate TRANSVERSE TENSION** — a wedge splits a log while itself being in pure compression. Hence closed links, spirals and a mesh grid.
examTip.trap: **The zone extends about ONE DEPTH from the end (St Venant), and within it beam theory does not apply** — it is a strut-and-tie or Guyon problem, not M/Z.
examTip.mnemonic: **The critical case is TRANSFER — maximum prestress meets youngest concrete.** Anchorage failures happen during jacking, which is why the area behind a jack is cleared.

questions.stem: LATERAL TORSIONAL BUCKLING of a steel I-beam in bending is:
options: Local buckling of the web under shear
A failure in which the compression flange buckles sideways and the section twists
Yielding of the tension flange
Crushing of the beam at its supports
questions.solution:
**A failure in which the COMPRESSION FLANGE buckles sideways and the section TWISTS**, so the beam fails at a moment well below its full plastic capacity.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **In bending, one flange is in COMPRESSION** ← | **And a compressed plate wants to buckle** ← |
| **The compression flange is restrained VERTICALLY by the web but is FREE to move SIDEWAYS** ← | ← |
| **It therefore buckles laterally, like a column** ← | **Its weak axis being the vertical one through the web** ← |
| **But it is attached to the web and the tension flange, which resist the sideways movement** ← | **So the section cannot translate purely — it must also TWIST** ← |
| **Hence the combined mode: lateral displacement PLUS torsion** ← | **Which is why it is named for both** ← |

> **THE TENSION FLANGE IS WHAT MAKES IT A TORSIONAL MODE RATHER THAN A SIMPLE COLUMN BUCKLING, and that is the insight worth holding: the compression flange wants to move sideways and the tension flange, being in tension, resists moving.**

> **The section therefore rotates about a longitudinal axis nearer the tension flange, and the beam deflects sideways while twisting — a distinctive and unmistakable failure shape.**

> **Option (a) is WEB buckling, a different local mode addressed by stiffeners.**

**What governs the resistance:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **The UNRESTRAINED LENGTH between lateral supports** ← | **The single most important variable — capacity falls steeply as it increases** ← |
| **The section's TORSIONAL stiffness** | **An OPEN section like an I has very little, which is why I-beams are susceptible and box sections are not** ← |
| **The section's LATERAL (minor axis) stiffness** | **A wide flange helps greatly** ← |
| **The shape of the BENDING MOMENT diagram** ← | **A uniform moment over the whole length is the worst case; a moment varying from a peak to zero is far less severe** ← |
| **The position of the load relative to the shear centre** ← | **A load applied at the TOP flange is DESTABILISING; one applied at the bottom flange is stabilising** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DESIGNER'S PRINCIPAL LEVER AND IT IS WHERE THE SOLUTION LIES: lateral torsional buckling is a SLENDERNESS problem, and providing lateral restraint shortens the effective length.**

> **Halving the unrestrained length can more than double the moment capacity, at the cost of a few small restraint members — which is a far better bargain than increasing the beam size.**

> **THE LOAD POSITION IN THE LAST ROW IS A SUBTLE EFFECT WITH A CLEAR PHYSICAL EXPLANATION: a load sitting ON the top flange moves sideways WITH the flange as it buckles, and its line of action then has a lever arm about the twisting section — so it drives the buckling further.**

> **A load hanging from the BOTTOM flange swings like a pendulum and tends to pull the section back upright.**

> **The same beam therefore has a lower capacity when a load is placed on top of it than when the load hangs beneath it, which is a genuine difference recognised in the codes.**

**How lateral restraint is provided in practice:**

| Restraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **A concrete slab CAST ON or connected to the compression flange** ← | **Full restraint along the length — which is why a composite beam has no lateral torsional buckling problem in service** ← |
| **Secondary beams or purlins framing into the beam** ← | **Restraint at discrete points, provided the connection can transmit the restraint force** ← |
| **Bracing between adjacent beams** | ← |
| **The tension flange restrained plus torsional restraint at points** | **Since restraining the tension flange alone does not prevent the mode** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW EXPLAINS A COMMONLY MISUNDERSTOOD POINT ABOUT CONSTRUCTION SEQUENCE, and it is important: a steel beam supporting a concrete slab is fully restrained ONCE THE SLAB HAS HARDENED and is connected to it.**

> **DURING CONSTRUCTION, carrying the wet concrete and the formwork, it has no such restraint — the wet slab provides none.**

> **So the beam's critical condition for lateral torsional buckling is the CONSTRUCTION stage, with the full weight of wet concrete and no lateral support except at the ends and at any temporary bracing.**

> **Designing such a beam for its service condition alone and neglecting the construction case is a real error, and it has caused collapses during concreting — which is why temporary bracing of steel beams before a pour is a designed requirement rather than the contractor's option.**

examTip.trick: **The compression flange buckles sideways and the tension flange resists, so the section TWISTS as well as translating.** Option (a) is web buckling, a separate local mode.
examTip.trap: **Capacity depends most on the UNRESTRAINED LENGTH** — halving it can more than double the moment capacity for the cost of a few restraint members. Far cheaper than a bigger beam.
examTip.mnemonic: **A load ON the top flange is destabilising; hung from the bottom flange it is stabilising.** And the critical case is CONSTRUCTION — wet concrete gives no restraint, which has caused collapses during pours.

questions.stem: CONFINED MASONRY construction differs from an ordinary reinforced concrete frame with masonry infill in that, in confined masonry:
options: No concrete is used anywhere in the building
The masonry walls are built first and the reinforced concrete tie-columns and tie-beams are cast afterwards against them
The masonry is purely decorative
The walls are built without any mortar
questions.solution:
**The masonry walls are built FIRST and the concrete tie-columns and tie-beams are cast AFTERWARDS against them** — so the two are bonded together and the masonry remains the primary load-carrying element.

**The two systems compared:**

| Aspect | RC FRAME with infill | CONFINED masonry |
|---|---|---|
| **Construction SEQUENCE** | **The FRAME is built first; the masonry is filled in afterwards** ← | **The MASONRY is built first; the tie-columns are cast against it** ← |
| **Which element carries the load?** | **The FRAME — the infill is nominally non-structural** ← | **The MASONRY carries gravity and lateral load; the ties CONFINE it** ← |
| **Bond between the two** | **POOR — a cold interface, often with a deliberate gap** ← | **STRONG — the concrete is cast against the toothed masonry and keys into it** ← |
| **Member sizes** | **Columns and beams sized as a frame — substantial** ← | **Tie-columns are SMALL, typically 150 × 150 mm with 4 bars** ← |
| **Reinforcement** | **Heavy, with designed laps and confinement** | **Light and nominal** ← |
| **Analysis** | **Frame analysis** | **Largely EMPIRICAL, by prescriptive rules** ← |

> **THE SEQUENCE IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE WHOLE DISTINCTION AND IT IS WHAT PRODUCES THE PERFORMANCE DIFFERENCE: because the tie-columns are cast against masonry already built, the concrete flows into the toothed indentations left in the brickwork and the two become monolithic.**

> **In an infilled frame, the masonry is built into a completed opening, and the interface between the two is a construction joint with little or no bond.**

> **Under earthquake shaking, the infill panel in a frame separates from the frame, and once separated it behaves as a loose panel that can fall out of the frame — often outward, into the street.**

> **A confined masonry wall cannot separate, because it is bonded to its confining elements on all four sides. It cracks, and the cracks are held closed by the confinement.**

**Why confined masonry performs so well in earthquakes:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The tie-elements CONFINE the masonry, holding it together after it cracks** ← | **Which preserves its gravity load capacity and prevents disintegration** ← |
| **They provide a continuous LOAD PATH from roof to foundation** ← | **All four sides of every panel are tied** ← |
| **The wall's own in-plane strength and stiffness are used** ← | **Rather than being ignored as "non-structural"** ← |
| **Out-of-plane collapse is prevented** ← | **The panel is held on all four edges — the failure that kills people in unreinforced masonry** ← |
| **It is BUILDABLE by ordinary masons with ordinary materials** ← | **The most important practical advantage in a country like Nepal** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE DECISIVE ARGUMENT FOR NEPAL AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: confined masonry uses the same bricks, the same mortar and the same masons as ordinary construction, with a modest addition of small concrete elements and light reinforcement.**

> **An RC frame requires accurate formwork, correctly bent and lapped reinforcement, properly detailed beam-column joints, and concrete of controlled quality — all of which are frequently not achieved in small buildings built without engineering supervision.**

> **A badly built RC frame is far more dangerous than a well-built confined masonry house, because the frame carries everything and its joints are the hardest part to get right.**

> **Confined masonry is more forgiving: the walls do the work, and the ties need only be continuous and reasonably placed.**

**The rules that make it work, which are prescriptive rather than calculated:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Tie-columns at every WALL INTERSECTION and at every free end and opening jamb** ← | **Spacing not more than about 4 m, or 1.5 times the wall height** ← |
| **Tie-beams at every floor and roof level, CONTINUOUS around the building** ← | **The same continuity requirement as a seismic band** ← |
| **The masonry must be TOOTHED, or dowels provided, at the tie-column interface** ← | **This is the detail that creates the bond, and the whole system depends on it** ← |
| **Walls in BOTH directions, reasonably symmetrical in plan** ← | **A wall density requirement, typically expressed as a percentage of floor area** ← |
| **Openings limited in size and kept away from wall ends** | ← |

> **THE TOOTHING IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE SINGLE DETAIL THAT DISTINGUISHES CONFINED MASONRY FROM AN INFILLED FRAME ON SITE, and it is the one most often omitted by a mason who has not been shown why it matters.**

> **Leaving the brickwork with a straight vertical edge and casting the column against it produces a smooth cold joint — which is an infilled frame built in the wrong order, with all the weaknesses of both systems and the advantages of neither.**

> **Toothing every second or third course, so that bricks project into the column's space, is what makes the two act together — and it costs nothing but the mason's understanding.**

The two are bonded and the masonry is the primary load-carrying element.

examTip.trick: **Masonry FIRST, tie-columns cast against it afterwards — so they bond, and the masonry is the load-carrying element.** In an infilled frame the sequence and the roles are reversed.
examTip.trap: **Infill panels SEPARATE from a frame and can fall out; confined panels cannot** — they are bonded on all four sides, so they crack but stay together.
examTip.mnemonic: **TOOTHING the brickwork is the detail the whole system depends on** — a straight vertical edge gives a cold joint, which is an infilled frame built in the wrong order, with the advantages of neither.

questions.stem: In estimating the total per capita water demand of a town, the component that is usually the LARGEST is:
options: Domestic demand
Fire demand
Institutional and public demand
Industrial demand in every case
questions.solution:
**DOMESTIC demand** — typically 135 litres per capita per day, and about half of the total in an ordinary town.

**The components of total demand:**

| Component | Typical allowance (lpcd) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **DOMESTIC** | **135** ← | **Drinking, cooking, bathing, washing, flushing — the largest single component** ← |
| **INDUSTRIAL** | **20 to 25 for an ordinary town** ← | **But it DOMINATES in an industrial city, and may exceed all other components combined** ← |
| **INSTITUTIONAL and COMMERCIAL** | **20** | **Schools, hospitals, offices, hotels, markets** ← |
| **PUBLIC USE** | **10** ← | **Street washing, parks and gardens, public fountains, sewer flushing** ← |
| **FIRE demand** | **About 1 lpcd when averaged over the year** ← | **Tiny as an average, and enormous as an INSTANTANEOUS rate** ← |
| **LOSSES and WASTE (non-revenue water)** | **15 per cent of the total, or more** ← | **In practice often 30 to 40 per cent — see the NRW figures** ← |
| **TOTAL** | **About 200 to 270 lpcd** ← | ← |

> **THE INDUSTRIAL ROW IS WHY OPTION (D) IS QUALIFIED AND WRONG AS STATED: industrial demand is modest in an ordinary town and can be the dominant component in a city with a large industrial base.**

> **A single large industry — a paper mill, a brewery, a textile plant, a thermal power station — can use more water than the whole residential population.**

> **So industrial demand must be assessed from the actual and planned industries rather than taken from a per capita table, and it is the component with the greatest uncertainty in a growing town.**

**THE FIRE DEMAND IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE ENTRY AND IT IS ROUTINELY MISUNDERSTOOD:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **As an ANNUAL AVERAGE it is negligible — about 1 lpcd** ← | **Fires are rare, and each uses water for a few hours only** ← |
| **As an INSTANTANEOUS demand it is very large** ← | **A single hydrant may draw 10 to 30 litres per second for hours** ← |
| **So it does NOT affect the source or the treatment plant's capacity** ← | **The annual volume is trivial** ← |
| **But it GOVERNS the distribution main sizes and the service reservoir's storage** ← | **Which must deliver that rate at an adequate pressure, at any point in the network, on top of the peak domestic demand** ← |

> **THAT SPLIT IS THE KEY TO USING FIRE DEMAND CORRECTLY: it is a RATE requirement and not a VOLUME requirement, so it sizes the pipes and the storage and not the source.**

> **A designer who adds a per capita fire allowance to the total and sizes the treatment plant on it has oversized the plant; one who omits fire flow from the network analysis has undersized the mains.**

> **The empirical formulae — Kuichling's, Freeman's, the Buston formula — all give a fire flow RATE as a function of population, and they are used in the network analysis rather than in the demand total.**

**And the LOSSES row deserves the closing note, because it is the largest avoidable item:**

> **A 15 per cent allowance for losses is the design assumption; 30 to 40 per cent is the common reality in South Asian systems.**

> **So a town whose real losses are 35 per cent is abstracting, treating and pumping roughly a quarter more water than the design allowed for, and its source and plant are correspondingly overloaded from the day they open.**

> **Reducing losses is therefore not merely a revenue measure but a capacity measure — the cheapest new source available to almost any existing system is the water it is already losing, as noted under non-revenue water.**

Drinking, cooking, bathing, washing and sanitation — typically 135 litres per capita per day and about half of the total.

examTip.trick: **Domestic 135, industrial 20-25, institutional 20, public 10, fire ~1, losses 15 % — total about 200-270 lpcd.** Domestic is roughly half.
examTip.trap: **FIRE demand is a RATE requirement, not a VOLUME one** — negligible as an annual average, so it sizes the MAINS and STORAGE but not the source or treatment plant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Industrial demand can exceed everything else combined in an industrial city** — assess it from the actual industries, never from a per capita table. And real LOSSES are often double the 15 % assumed.

questions.stem: In a water supply system, the MAXIMUM DAILY demand is conventionally taken as about 1.8 times the average daily demand, and the MAXIMUM HOURLY demand as about 1.5 times the maximum daily rate. These two factors are used respectively to size:
options: The service reservoir and the source
Both are used for the distribution mains only
Neither — they are used only for revenue estimation
The source, treatment plant and pumping to the reservoir (maximum daily) and the distribution mains (maximum hourly)
questions.solution:
**The maximum DAILY rate sizes the source, treatment plant and the pumping into the service reservoir; the maximum HOURLY rate sizes the DISTRIBUTION MAINS.**

**Why the two components are sized on different rates:**

| Element | Sized on | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **SOURCE, intake, treatment plant, transmission main, pumping to storage** ← | **MAXIMUM DAILY demand** ← | **The SERVICE RESERVOIR absorbs the hourly variation, so these elements need only keep up with the day's total** ← |
| **SERVICE RESERVOIR** | **The BALANCING volume required** | **Computed from the difference between the steady inflow and the varying outflow** ← |
| **DISTRIBUTION mains and the network** ← | **MAXIMUM HOURLY demand** ← | **They must deliver the peak instantaneous rate, since there is no storage downstream of them** ← |
| **And a separate check on maximum daily PLUS FIRE flow** | **Which may govern** ← |

> **THE SERVICE RESERVOIR IS THE DEVICE THAT MAKES THE DISTINCTION POSSIBLE, AND THAT IS THE POINT OF THE QUESTION: it stands between the two parts of the system and decouples them.**

> **Upstream of it, everything can run at a steady rate all day, because the reservoir stores the surplus during the quiet hours and releases it at the peak.**

> **Downstream of it, the mains must handle whatever the consumers draw at the moment they draw it.**

> **Without the reservoir, the treatment plant and the transmission main would have to be sized for the maximum HOURLY rate — some 2.7 times the average instead of 1.8 — which would make them half again as large for no benefit.**

> **So the reservoir pays for itself by reducing the size of every element upstream of it, which is the strongest argument for providing one even where the head does not require it.**

**The peak factors, gathered:**

| Factor | Typical value | Relative to |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum DAILY demand** | **1.8 × average daily** ← | **The seasonal and day-to-day variation** ← |
| **Maximum HOURLY demand** | **1.5 × maximum daily, so 2.7 × average** ← | **The variation through the day** ← |
| **Combined peak factor** | **About 2.7** ← | **The average** ← |
| **For a SMALL population the peaks are SHARPER** ← | **Up to 3 or 4 times the average** ← | **Fewer consumers means less statistical smoothing** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL REFINEMENT AND IT FOLLOWS FROM THE SAME DIVERSITY ARGUMENT MET IN POWER SYSTEMS: in a large city, some households are drawing water at every hour, so the aggregate demand curve is relatively smooth.**

> **In a village of thirty houses, nearly everyone draws water in the same two hours of the morning, and the peak is very much sharper relative to the average.**

> **So a rural scheme needs a proportionately larger peak factor and relatively more storage than an urban one, and applying an urban factor to a village supply gives mains that run dry at the morning peak.**

> **The IS code accordingly grades the peak factor by population served, and it is one of those provisions whose reason is worth knowing because it prevents the figure being applied blindly.**

**The shape of a typical daily demand curve, which underlies all of it:**

| Period | Demand |
|---|---|
| **Early morning, 5 to 9 a.m.** | **The MORNING PEAK — the highest of the day, as the town washes, cooks and fills** ← |
| **Midday** | **Moderate** |
| **Evening, 5 to 8 p.m.** | **A SECOND peak, usually lower than the morning's** ← |
| **Late night, 1 to 4 a.m.** | **The MINIMUM — often only 20 to 30 per cent of the average** ← |

> **THE NIGHT MINIMUM IN THE LAST ROW HAS A USE BEYOND DESIGN AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: the MINIMUM NIGHT FLOW is the standard measure of LEAKAGE in a distribution zone.**

> **At 3 a.m. legitimate consumption is nearly zero, so whatever is still flowing into the zone is very largely leaking out of it.**

> **Measuring the minimum night flow into a district metered area therefore gives a direct estimate of that district's leakage, without any need to find the individual leaks — which is why district metering and night-flow monitoring are the foundation of every serious leakage reduction programme.**

examTip.trick: **Maximum DAILY (1.8 × average) sizes the source, plant and transmission; maximum HOURLY (2.7 × average) sizes the DISTRIBUTION mains.** The service reservoir separates the two.
examTip.trap: **Without a service reservoir the plant would need sizing on the HOURLY peak** — half again as large. The reservoir pays for itself by shrinking everything upstream of it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Small populations peak more sharply (3-4×)** — less statistical smoothing, so village schemes need bigger factors. And the MINIMUM NIGHT FLOW is the standard leakage measurement.

questions.stem: For lifting water from a deep tube well, the type of pump almost always used is a:
options: Submersible (or vertical turbine) pump
Horizontal centrifugal pump at ground level
Reciprocating pump
Jet pump
questions.solution:
**A SUBMERSIBLE (or vertical turbine) pump**, with the impellers below the water level so there is no suction lift at all.

**Why a surface pump cannot serve a deep well:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A pump does not "suck" water up — ATMOSPHERIC pressure pushes it** ← | **So the theoretical maximum suction lift is the atmospheric head, 10.3 m at sea level** ← |
| **In practice the limit is about 6 to 7 m** ← | **After allowing for friction, velocity head, the vapour pressure and the required NPSH** ← |
| **And LESS at altitude — about 5 m in Kathmandu** ← | **The same altitude limitation as the siphon and the turbine setting** ← |
| **A tube well's water level may be 30, 50 or 100 m down** ← | **Far beyond any suction lift** ← |
| **So the pump must be placed BELOW the water and PUSH** ← | ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE IS THAT THERE IS NO LIMIT TO HOW HIGH A PUMP CAN PUSH WATER AND A STRICT LIMIT TO HOW FAR IT CAN PULL IT, and that single asymmetry determines the whole arrangement:**

> **Pushing is limited only by the pump's power and the pipe's pressure rating, both of which can be increased.**

> **Pulling is limited by atmospheric pressure, which cannot be increased at all.**

> **So any lift beyond a few metres must be achieved by putting the pump at the bottom, and that is why every deep well pump — submersible or vertical turbine — has its impellers underwater.**

**The two deep-well arrangements:**

| Type | Motor position | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **SUBMERSIBLE** | **The MOTOR is submerged too, directly coupled beneath or above the pump** ← | **Simple, no long shaft, quiet, no pump house needed — the standard choice today** ← |
| **VERTICAL TURBINE (deep well turbine)** | **The motor is at the SURFACE, driving the submerged impellers through a long vertical SHAFT** ← | **The motor is accessible and easily maintained; but the long shaft needs bearings, alignment and lubrication** ← |

> **THE SUBMERSIBLE HAS LARGELY DISPLACED THE VERTICAL TURBINE FOR ORDINARY WELLS, and the reason is the shaft: a 60 m vertical shaft with bearings every few metres, requiring alignment and lubrication, is a maintenance liability that a sealed submersible motor avoids entirely.**

> **The vertical turbine survives where the motor must be accessible, where the water is hot or chemically aggressive, or where the well is crooked — since a long rigid shaft cannot follow a bend, but neither can it be installed in one, which limits the argument.**

**The pump types and their proper applications:**

| Pump | Suits |
|---|---|
| **CENTRIFUGAL (horizontal, surface)** ← | **The workhorse — moderate to high discharge at moderate head, with a suction lift within a few metres, or fed under positive pressure** ← |
| **SUBMERSIBLE / vertical turbine** | **Deep wells and sumps — this question** ← |
| **RECIPROCATING (positive displacement)** ← | **SMALL discharge at VERY HIGH head; and hand pumps for village wells — it is self-priming and delivers against any head, but pulsating and slow** ← |
| **JET pump (ejector)** ← | **Shallow to moderate wells; no moving parts underground, but very INEFFICIENT — 20 to 30 per cent** ← |
| **AIR LIFT pump** | **Sandy or corrosive water, and well development — crude and inefficient, but nothing to damage** ← |
| **Screw and progressive cavity pumps** | **Viscous liquids and sludges** ← |

> **THE HAND PUMP IN THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH ITS EMPHASIS FOR RURAL NEPAL AND SOUTH ASIA: a reciprocating pump is SELF-PRIMING and delivers against whatever head is required, which is exactly what a village well needs.**

> **But its cylinder must still be within suction reach of the surface unless it is a DEEP-WELL hand pump, in which case the cylinder is lowered into the water and the rod extended — the India Mark III arrangement, which is precisely the same solution as the submersible's: put the pumping element below the water.**

> **The engineering principle is identical whether the power is electrical or a person's arm, and it is the one principle to carry from this whole subject: water is pushed, never pulled, beyond about six metres.**

The impellers placed BELOW the water level so that there is no suction lift at all.

examTip.trick: **Impellers BELOW the water, so there is no suction lift.** A surface pump is limited to about 6-7 m of lift (5 m at Kathmandu's altitude) by atmospheric pressure.
examTip.trap: **A pump does not suck — atmosphere PUSHES.** So pushing is limited only by power and pipe rating; pulling is capped at the atmospheric head, which cannot be increased.
examTip.mnemonic: **A deep-well HAND pump does the same thing** — cylinder lowered into the water, rod extended. Electrical or human, the principle is identical: water is pushed, never pulled beyond six metres.

questions.stem: A REFLUX (non-return or check) VALVE is provided on the delivery side of a pump principally to:
options: Regulate the discharge to the required value
Release air accumulated at the pump's casing
Prevent reverse flow when the pump stops
Reduce the pressure downstream of the pump
questions.solution:
**To prevent REVERSE FLOW when the pump stops** — protecting the pump from reverse rotation and the system from the water hammer of a returning column.

**What happens without one:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The water in the rising main FLOWS BACK through the pump** ← | **Driven by the static head it was pumped against** ← |
| **The pump and motor are driven BACKWARDS** ← | **Which can damage the bearings, unscrew the impeller, and destroy the motor if it restarts against reverse rotation** ← |
| **The DELIVERY main and the sump are emptied** ← | **So the pump loses its prime and the main must be refilled on every restart** ← |
| **And the returning column, when arrested, generates severe WATER HAMMER** ← | **Which is the most damaging consequence** ← |

> **THE WATER HAMMER IN THE LAST ROW IS THE REASON THE VALVE MATTERS STRUCTURALLY AND NOT MERELY OPERATIONALLY, and it is worth following the sequence:**

> **When the pump stops, the water in the rising main decelerates, reverses, and accelerates back down the pipe.**

> **When it reaches the check valve — or the pump — it is stopped abruptly, and a large moving mass stopped abruptly generates a pressure surge exactly as a closing valve does.**

> **The surge can exceed the pump's normal delivery pressure and burst the main, and it recurs on every shutdown.**

> **So the check valve is not merely a convenience; it is part of the pipeline's pressure protection.**

**The paradox of the check valve, which is worth understanding:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A check valve prevents the reverse flow, and its own SLAM generates a surge** ← | **The faster it closes on the reversing flow, the sharper the surge** ← |
| **So the valve solves one problem and creates a smaller version of it** ← | ← |
| **A SLOW-CLOSING or dashpot-damped check valve reduces the slam** ← | **At the cost of allowing a little reverse flow** ← |
| **The severity depends on the pipeline's length and profile** ← | **A long rising main with a high point is the worst case** ← |

> **VALVE SLAM IS A REAL AND COMMON SOURCE OF PIPELINE DAMAGE, and it is the reason a swing check valve on a long rising main is often replaced by a slow-closing or a nozzle-type check valve, or supplemented by a surge vessel.**

> **The trade is the same one met with the turbine governor: fast closure protects one thing and endangers another, and the resolution is a controlled rather than an instantaneous closure.**

**The valves in a pumping installation and what each does:**

| Valve | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **FOOT valve** | **A check valve at the bottom of the suction pipe, holding the prime** ← |
| **SLUICE (gate) valve on the SUCTION side** | **Isolation for maintenance — normally fully open** ← |
| **REFLUX (check) valve on the DELIVERY side** ← | **This question — and it goes BETWEEN the pump and the delivery sluice valve** ← |
| **SLUICE valve on the delivery side, beyond the check valve** ← | **Isolation, and it allows the check valve to be serviced without draining the main** ← |
| **AIR valve at high points** | **Admitting and releasing air** ← |
| **PRESSURE RELIEF valve, or a surge vessel** | **Limiting the surge pressure** ← |
| **SCOUR valve at low points** | **Draining and flushing the main** ← |

> **THE ORDER IN ROWS THREE AND FOUR IS A DETAIL WORTH GETTING RIGHT AND IT IS OFTEN GOT WRONG: the check valve goes immediately after the pump, and the isolating sluice valve goes AFTER the check valve.**

> **With that arrangement, closing the sluice valve isolates both the pump and the check valve from the main, so either can be dismantled without draining a kilometre of pipeline.**

> **Put the sluice valve first and the check valve cannot be serviced without emptying the main — which means it never gets serviced, and a check valve that has silently failed open provides no protection at all while appearing to be present.**

> **That is the characteristic failure of check valves: they fail in a way that is invisible until the pump stops and the main drains back, and the only defence is periodic testing.**

examTip.trick: **It stops the delivery main draining back through the pump** — preventing reverse rotation, loss of prime, and the water hammer of an arrested returning column.
examTip.trap: **The valve's own SLAM generates a surge** — it solves one problem and creates a smaller version of it. Long rising mains need slow-closing or damped check valves.
examTip.mnemonic: **Order: pump → CHECK valve → SLUICE valve.** That way closing the sluice isolates both for servicing without draining the main. Reversed, the check valve never gets serviced.

questions.stem: In modern disinfection practice, the effectiveness of a disinfectant is expressed by the CT value, which is:
options: The chlorine dose divided by the water temperature
The product of the disinfectant concentration and the contact time
The total chlorine consumed per day
The ratio of combined to free chlorine
questions.solution:
**The product of the disinfectant CONCENTRATION and the CONTACT TIME** — because a given degree of inactivation can be achieved by a high dose for a short time or a low dose for a long time.

**The concept:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **CT = concentration (mg/L) × time (minutes)** ← | **Units of mg·min/L** ← |
| **A specified LOG INACTIVATION of a given organism requires a specified CT** ← | **For example 3-log (99.9 per cent) removal of Giardia** ← |
| **The trade is therefore explicit** ← | **Double the concentration and halve the time, or vice versa** ← |
| **It replaces the older approach of specifying a residual and a nominal contact period** ← | **Which said nothing about whether the combination was actually sufficient** ← |

> **THE VALUE OF THE CT CONCEPT IS THAT IT MAKES THE DESIGN QUANTITATIVE RATHER THAN PRESCRIPTIVE, and that is a real advance: the older rule — "maintain 0.2 mg/L residual after 30 minutes contact" — is a recipe with no stated objective.**

> **CT states the objective (a required log inactivation of a named organism) and lets the designer meet it by whatever combination of dose and contact time the plant allows.**

> **A plant with a large contact tank can use a small dose; one with little contact volume must use a larger dose. Both are acceptable if the CT is achieved.**

**The CT required varies enormously by ORGANISM, which is the most important practical point:**

| Organism | Relative resistance to free chlorine |
|---|---|
| **BACTERIA — E. coli, cholera, typhoid** | **Very LOW resistance — killed almost instantly by a small residual** ← |
| **VIRUSES** | **Moderate** ← |
| **GIARDIA cysts** | **HIGH — requiring a CT hundreds of times greater than bacteria** ← |
| **CRYPTOSPORIDIUM oocysts** ← | **EXTREMELY high — effectively NOT achievable with chlorine at any practical CT** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE FACT THAT CHANGED DISINFECTION PRACTICE, and it connects to the UV question: Cryptosporidium's CT requirement for chlorine is so large that no realistic plant can deliver it.**

> **Chlorine is therefore simply not a barrier against Cryptosporidium, and the barriers that are — FILTRATION, UV and ozone — must be relied on instead.**

> **This is why the CT framework matters: it makes the inadequacy explicit and quantitative, where the older residual-based rule concealed it entirely. A plant meeting its chlorine residual could be, and was, passing Cryptosporidium unhindered.**

**What affects the CT achieved, and why the T is the difficult part:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **pH** ← | **Lower pH means more HOCl and a much better CT — the same point as breakpoint chlorination** ← |
| **TEMPERATURE** ← | **Cold water needs a HIGHER CT — roughly doubling for each 10 °C fall, so winter is the design condition** ← |
| **TURBIDITY** | **Particles shield organisms, so the water must be clarified first** ← |
| **The effective contact time T** ← | **NOT the tank's theoretical detention time, but the T₁₀ — the time within which only 10 per cent of the water has passed through** ← |

> **THE T₁₀ IN THE LAST ROW IS THE SUBTLETY THAT MAKES CT ANALYSIS HONEST, and it is worth understanding: a contact tank does not deliver its nominal detention time to every parcel of water.**

> **Short-circuiting means some water passes through in a fraction of the nominal time, and that water is the water that matters — it is the least disinfected.**

> **So the effective contact time is taken as T₁₀, established by a TRACER TEST, and for a poorly baffled tank T₁₀ may be only 30 per cent of the theoretical detention time.**

> **Baffling a contact tank properly can therefore treble its effective CT without changing its volume or its dose at all — which makes baffles one of the cheapest disinfection improvements available, and one of the most commonly missing.**

> **The design lesson is the same one met with settling basins and flocculators: the hydraulics of the tank determine what the process achieves, and a tank's volume is not its performance.**

examTip.trick: **CT = concentration × contact time, in mg·min/L** — a stated log inactivation needs a stated CT, achievable by a high dose briefly or a low dose for longer.
examTip.trap: **CRYPTOSPORIDIUM's chlorine CT is unachievable in practice** — so chlorine is no barrier against it, and filtration, UV or ozone must be. The old residual rule hid this entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Use T₁₀, not the nominal detention time** — the fastest 10 % of the water is the least disinfected. Proper BAFFLING can treble the effective CT with no extra volume or dose.

questions.stem: Among the pressure-driven membrane processes used in water treatment, the one capable of removing DISSOLVED SALTS — and therefore used for desalination — is:
options: Microfiltration
Ultrafiltration
Nanofiltration, which removes all dissolved salts completely
Reverse osmosis, whose membrane rejects dissolved ions and requires the highest operating pressure of the four
questions.solution:
**REVERSE OSMOSIS** — its membrane rejects dissolved ions, and it requires the highest operating pressure of the four.

**The membrane processes in order of decreasing pore size:**

| Process | Removes | Typical pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **MICROFILTRATION (MF)** | **Suspended solids, PROTOZOA (Giardia, Cryptosporidium), most BACTERIA — pore about 0.1 µm** ← | **0.1 to 2 bar** ← |
| **ULTRAFILTRATION (UF)** | **All of the above plus VIRUSES and large organic molecules — about 0.01 µm** ← | **1 to 5 bar** ← |
| **NANOFILTRATION (NF)** ← | **Plus HARDNESS ions (divalent — calcium, magnesium, sulphate) and colour, while passing much of the monovalent salt — the "softening membrane"** ← | **5 to 20 bar** ← |
| **REVERSE OSMOSIS (RO)** ← | **Essentially ALL dissolved ions, including sodium chloride — non-porous, working by solution-diffusion** ← | **15 to 80 bar, and higher for seawater** ← |

> **OPTION (C) IS THE WELL-MADE DISTRACTOR AND ITS ERROR IS THE WORD "COMPLETELY": nanofiltration removes DIVALENT ions well and monovalent ions only partially.**

> **That selectivity is its whole purpose — it softens the water and removes colour and organics while leaving much of the salinity, at a fraction of RO's energy cost.**

> **For a hard, coloured but not saline source, nanofiltration is the right choice and RO would be wasteful; for a brackish or seawater source, only RO will do.**

**THE MF/UF DISTINCTION IN THE FIRST TWO ROWS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST FOR ORDINARY WATER SUPPLY, and it connects to the disinfection discussion:**

> **Ultrafiltration provides an ABSOLUTE physical barrier to bacteria, protozoa AND viruses — organisms are simply too large to pass, regardless of dose, contact time, pH or temperature.**

> **That makes it fundamentally different from chemical disinfection, which is a rate process that can be defeated by cold water, high pH, turbidity or short-circuiting.**

> **A membrane either has an intact pore structure or it does not, and its integrity can be tested directly by a pressure decay test.**

> **This is why UF has displaced conventional clarification and filtration in many new plants: it removes Cryptosporidium reliably, which the conventional train achieves only with careful operation, and its performance does not depend on the operator's skill from day to day.**

**The practical difficulties, which are the reason membranes are not universal:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **FOULING — the dominant operating problem** ← | **Particles, organics, biofilm and mineral scale accumulate on the membrane, raising the pressure needed and cutting the output** ← |
| **PRE-TREATMENT is essential** ← | **Coagulation, filtration or cartridge filters before the membrane — an RO plant fed raw water fouls within days** ← |
| **Chemical CLEANING at intervals** | **Acid and alkali cycles, which consume membrane life** ← |
| **ENERGY, for RO especially** | **3 to 6 kWh per cubic metre for seawater RO — the dominant cost** ← |
| **CONCENTRATE (brine) disposal** ← | **A stream of 20 to 50 per cent of the feed, containing all the rejected salts — and its disposal is often the hardest permitting problem** ← |
| **Membrane replacement every 3 to 7 years** | **A recurring capital cost** ← |

> **THE BRINE DISPOSAL IN THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ISSUE THAT MOST OFTEN LIMITS AN RO SCHEME AND IT IS ROUTINELY UNDERESTIMATED AT THE PLANNING STAGE: reverse osmosis does not destroy the salts, it CONCENTRATES them.**

> **A plant recovering 60 per cent of its feed as product water discharges the remaining 40 per cent carrying all of the original salt — so the brine is roughly two and a half times as saline as the feed.**

> **Discharging that to a river, a lake or the ground destroys the receiving environment; discharging it to the sea requires a diffuser and dilution; and evaporating it requires land and produces a solid waste.**

> **For an inland brackish-water RO plant, brine disposal is frequently the binding constraint on whether the scheme can proceed at all — and it is a good general reminder that a treatment process which SEPARATES a contaminant has not removed it from the world, only concentrated it into a smaller stream that must still be dealt with.**

examTip.trick: **MF (0.1 µm, protozoa/bacteria) → UF (0.01 µm, plus viruses) → NF (divalent ions, softening) → RO (all dissolved ions, highest pressure).**
examTip.trap: **Nanofiltration removes DIVALENT ions well and monovalent only partially** — that selectivity is its purpose. Option (c)'s "completely" is the error.
examTip.mnemonic: **A membrane is an ABSOLUTE barrier; chemical disinfection is a rate process** — unaffected by pH, temperature or short-circuiting. But RO CONCENTRATES the salt: brine disposal often decides the scheme.

questions.stem: In a SEWAGE PUMPING STATION, the volume of the WET WELL between the pump start and stop levels is fixed so as to:
options: Limit the number of pump starts per hour
Store a full day's sewage flow
Provide primary settlement of the sewage
Allow the grit to settle out completely
questions.solution:
**To limit the NUMBER OF PUMP STARTS per hour**, while keeping the detention short enough that the sewage does not turn septic.

**The two competing requirements:**

| Requirement | Wants the volume to be |
|---|---|
| **Limit the starts per hour — frequent starting overheats the motor and wears the starter and the bearings** ← | **LARGE, so each cycle is longer** ← |
| **Limit the DETENTION time — sewage held too long goes SEPTIC, producing hydrogen sulphide, odour and corrosion** ← | **SMALL, so the contents are turned over quickly** ← |
| **Typical limits** | **6 to 10 starts per hour maximum; detention not more than about 10 to 30 minutes at average flow** ← |

> **THE TWO PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS AND THE VOLUME IS THE COMPROMISE, which is the point of the question — and it is the same structure of problem as the sewer's velocity limits or the governor's closing time.**

> **A wet well sized only to reduce starts becomes a small septic tank, and the hydrogen sulphide it generates corrodes the station, the rising main and everything downstream — the crown corrosion mechanism met earlier.**

> **A wet well sized only to minimise detention makes the pumps cycle every few minutes, and motors fail from repeated starting long before they wear out from running.**

**How the conflict is eased in practice:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **MULTIPLE pumps, brought in as the level rises (duty and assist)** ← | **Each pump starts less often, and the station matches the varying inflow better** ← |
| **VARIABLE SPEED drives** ← | **The pump runs CONTINUOUSLY at a rate matching the inflow, so there are no starts at all and the detention is minimal — the modern answer** ← |
| **Alternating the duty pump automatically** | **So wear is shared and each pump is proven to work** ← |
| **A benched, self-cleansing wet well floor** ← | **So solids do not accumulate in corners and go septic even if the water is turned over** ← |
| **Ventilation and, where needed, odour control** | ← |

> **THE VARIABLE SPEED DRIVE IN THE SECOND ROW DISSOLVES THE CONFLICT RATHER THAN COMPROMISING BETWEEN ITS HORNS, and that is why it has become standard for new stations: a pump whose speed follows the inflow neither starts and stops nor holds sewage.**

> **It also reduces the energy consumption substantially, because the pump is not repeatedly accelerating a stationary column of water in the rising main, and it eliminates the surge on each start and stop.**

> **The cost is the drive itself and the electronics to control it, which is now modest — and the recurring theme is worth noting: where two requirements genuinely conflict, look for the device that separates them rather than the volume that splits the difference.**

**WET WELL versus DRY WELL, which is the other design decision:**

| Arrangement | Note |
|---|---|
| **WET WELL only (submersible pumps)** ← | **The pumps sit IN the sewage; no separate chamber, so the station is compact and cheap. Maintenance means lifting the pump out** ← |
| **WET WELL plus DRY WELL** ← | **The pumps sit in a dry chamber beside the wet well, with suction pipes through the wall — accessible, dry and pleasant to maintain, and much more expensive** ← |
| **Which is used** | **Submersibles dominate for small and medium stations; dry wells for large and important ones** ← |

> **THE DRY WELL'S ADVANTAGE IS ENTIRELY ABOUT MAINTENANCE AND SAFETY, and it is a real one: a dry well lets a fitter work on a pump standing on a dry floor in a lit, ventilated room, rather than hauling a fouled pump out of a wet well by chain hoist.**

> **Its disadvantages are cost, footprint and a serious hazard of its own — a dry well is a CONFINED SPACE below ground adjacent to sewage, so it can accumulate hydrogen sulphide and must be treated with the full confined-space entry procedure.**

> **The submersible arrangement avoids that by having no space for anyone to enter, which is why it is preferred for unmanned stations despite the awkwardness of lifting a pump for repair — the safest confined space is the one that does not exist.**

Frequent starting overheats and wears the motor, while keeping the detention short enough that the sewage does not turn SEPTIC.

examTip.trick: **Large volume → fewer starts; small volume → shorter detention.** Limits: 6-10 starts per hour, detention under about 10-30 minutes before the sewage goes septic.
examTip.trap: **An oversized wet well is a small septic tank** — the H₂S it generates corrodes the station and the rising main. Undersized, the motors fail from repeated starting.
examTip.mnemonic: **A VARIABLE SPEED drive dissolves the conflict** — the pump matches the inflow, so no starts and no detention. And the safest confined space is the one that does not exist: hence submersibles.

questions.stem: In house drainage, the TWO-PIPE system differs from the ONE-PIPE system in that the two-pipe system:
options: Uses two separate drains to the public sewer
Requires no traps on the appliances
Keeps the soil appliances (WCs) and the waste appliances (basins
Carries rainwater in a second pipe alongside the sewage
questions.solution:
**It keeps SOIL appliances (WCs) and WASTE appliances (basins, baths, sinks) on SEPARATE stacks**, each with its own ventilating pipe.

**The systems compared:**

| System | Arrangement | Pipes |
|---|---|---|
| **TWO-PIPE** ← | **Separate SOIL stack and WASTE stack, each separately ventilated** ← | **FOUR pipes: soil, soil vent, waste, waste vent** ← |
| **ONE-PIPE** | **Soil and waste appliances discharge into a SINGLE stack, with a separate ventilating pipe** ← | **TWO pipes: one discharge stack and one vent** ← |
| **SINGLE-STACK** ← | **ONE stack only, with NO separate vent — the stack itself is ventilated through its open top** ← | **ONE pipe — the modern standard** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION FROM FOUR PIPES TO ONE IS THE HISTORY OF THE SUBJECT AND IT REFLECTS AN IMPROVED UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN A RELAXATION OF STANDARDS:**

> **The two-pipe system dates from a period when it was believed that "sewer gas" from WCs must be kept entirely separate from waste water, and that waste appliances should discharge over an open trapped gully in the open air.**

> **The single-stack system rests on the recognition that what actually matters is preventing the trap seals from being siphoned or blown, and that this can be achieved by sizing the stack generously and limiting the branch lengths and gradients — without any separate vent pipe at all.**

> **Fewer pipes means less cost, less builder's work, fewer joints to leak and a simpler installation, so the change was a genuine improvement once the mechanism was understood.**

**What the SINGLE-STACK system requires in order to work:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **A generously sized stack — 100 mm minimum for a WC** ← | **So an AIR CORE survives and the stack never runs full — the point made earlier** ← |
| **Branch lengths and gradients LIMITED** ← | **A long, steeply sloping branch lets the discharge run full and siphon its own trap** ← |
| **The stack carried up FULL BORE and open above roof level** ← | **This is the ventilation** ← |
| **A large-radius bend at the FOOT of the stack** ← | **To limit the back pressure where the falling water is turned horizontal** ← |
| **The lowest branch connection kept a minimum distance ABOVE the stack's foot** ← | **Because the back pressure is greatest there — otherwise the ground floor WC's seal is blown** ← |
| **No branch connection opposite another** | **To avoid cross-flow between branches** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MOST OFTEN VIOLATED REQUIREMENT AND IT PRODUCES A CHARACTERISTIC AND UNPLEASANT DEFECT: the water falling down a tall stack compresses the air at the bottom where it turns to run horizontally.**

> **A branch connected too close to that point receives that back pressure, and the trap seal is BLOWN — foul air and water are pushed up through the appliance into the room.**

> **The remedy is geometric: keep the lowest connection a specified distance above the bend, or connect the lowest appliance directly to the drain rather than to the stack.**

> **This is the failure that produces the complaint of a ground-floor WC bubbling or gurgling when an upper-floor WC is flushed — an unmistakable symptom, and one that is expensive to correct after construction because it requires re-routing a buried connection.**

**Where each system is still appropriate:**

| System | Suits |
|---|---|
| **SINGLE-STACK** | **Most domestic and low-rise buildings — the standard** ← |
| **ONE-PIPE, with a vent** | **Tall buildings, and where branch runs are long or appliance groups are large** ← |
| **TWO-PIPE** | **Rarely specified for new work; encountered in older buildings, and it must be understood for alterations** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL REASON TO KNOW THE TWO-PIPE SYSTEM AT ALL: it is not specified for new work, and a great deal of existing building stock has it.**

> **Altering such a building — adding a bathroom, converting a house into flats — means connecting into a system whose logic differs from current practice, and the commonest mistake is to connect a new WC into an existing WASTE stack.**

> **A waste stack is typically only 50 to 75 mm and was never intended to carry solids, so it blocks — and the alteration produces a chronic problem that is blamed on the drainage rather than on the connection.**

Baths, sinks) on SEPARATE stacks, each with its own ventilating pipe.

examTip.trick: **Two-pipe: separate SOIL and WASTE stacks, each vented — four pipes. One-pipe: combined stack plus a vent — two. SINGLE-STACK: one pipe, self-ventilating — the modern standard.**
examTip.trap: **The single-stack system needs a generous stack (100 mm) so an AIR CORE survives, plus limited branch lengths and gradients.** It is not a relaxation but a better-understood design.
examTip.mnemonic: **A ground-floor WC that gurgles when an upper one flushes is BACK PRESSURE at the stack foot** — the lowest branch was connected too close to the bend. Expensive to fix after construction.

questions.stem: The UASB (Upflow Anaerobic Sludge Blanket) reactor treats sewage by:
options: Aerating the sewage intensively while recirculating settled sludge
Passing the sewage upward through a blanket of granular anaerobic sludge, which degrades the organic matter and produces biogas
Trickling the sewage over a bed of stones colonised by aerobic organisms
Storing the sewage in shallow ponds for several weeks
questions.solution:
**By passing the sewage UPWARD through a blanket of granular ANAEROBIC sludge**, which degrades the organic matter and produces biogas — with no aeration, and hence very low energy consumption.

**How it works:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sewage enters at the BOTTOM and flows upward** ← | **Through a dense blanket of anaerobic sludge that has GRANULATED into dense, settleable pellets** ← |
| **The granules are heavy enough to remain in the reactor** ← | **So a very high concentration of active biomass is retained without any recycle pump** ← |
| **The organic matter is converted to METHANE and carbon dioxide** ← | **Rather than to more biomass, as in an aerobic process** ← |
| **A GAS-SOLIDS separator at the top collects the biogas and returns the solids** ← | **The characteristic inverted-cone arrangement** ← |
| **Treated effluent leaves over weirs at the top** | ← |

> **THE GRANULATION IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE PHENOMENON ON WHICH THE WHOLE PROCESS DEPENDS, and it is what distinguishes UASB from earlier anaerobic reactors: under the right conditions the anaerobic organisms aggregate into dense granules a few millimetres across rather than remaining as dispersed flocs.**

> **Granules settle rapidly, so they stay in the reactor against the upflow, and the biomass concentration reaches levels no suspended-growth system could hold.**

> **That high biomass allows a short hydraulic retention time — 6 to 10 hours — with a very long SOLIDS retention time, which is exactly what a slow-growing anaerobic culture needs.**

> **If granulation fails and the sludge remains flocculent, it washes out and the reactor does not work — which is why start-up and seeding are the critical phase of a UASB plant's life.**

**Its advantages, which are considerable for South Asia:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **NO AERATION, so very low energy consumption** ← | **Aeration is 50 to 70 per cent of an activated sludge plant's energy bill; UASB eliminates it** ← |
| **Produces BIOGAS, which can generate power or be used directly** ← | **A net energy PRODUCER rather than consumer** ← |
| **Very LOW SLUDGE production** ← | **Anaerobic organisms convert most of the carbon to methane rather than to cell mass — perhaps a fifth of the sludge of an aerobic plant** ← |
| **Simple, with few moving parts** | **No blowers, no returned sludge pumps, no mechanical aerators** ← |
| **Compact — a small footprint compared with ponds** | ← |
| **Suits WARM climates** ← | **Anaerobic digestion needs 20 °C or above to work well, which the Terai and much of South Asia provides year-round** ← |

> **THE TEMPERATURE REQUIREMENT IN THE LAST ROW IS WHAT MAKES UASB APPROPRIATE HERE AND UNSUITABLE IN COLD CLIMATES, and it is the reason the technology spread through India, Brazil and Colombia rather than through northern Europe.**

> **Sewage at 25 to 30 °C digests readily; at 12 °C the reaction is so slow that the reactor must be enormous or heated, and heating sewage is out of the question.**

> **In Nepal that gives a clear geographical division: UASB is well suited to the Terai and the lower valleys, and questionable at altitude where the sewage is cold for much of the year.**

**Its limitations, which must be stated honestly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The effluent does NOT meet discharge standards alone** ← | **BOD removal is 70 to 85 per cent, so a POST-TREATMENT stage is essential — usually a polishing pond or a trickling filter** ← |
| **It removes almost no NITROGEN or PHOSPHORUS** ← | **Anaerobic processes do not nitrify, so the ammonia passes through** ← |
| **The effluent contains dissolved SULPHIDE and is odorous** ← | **Requiring aeration or a polishing stage before discharge** ← |
| **Pathogen removal is limited** | **Disinfection is still needed for restricted uses** ← |
| **A long, difficult START-UP — months to establish granulation** ← | **And it can be lost by a toxic shock or a hydraulic overload** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE POINT MOST OFTEN MISREPRESENTED WHEN UASB IS PROPOSED, and it must be understood at the planning stage: a UASB reactor is not a complete sewage treatment plant.**

> **It is an extremely efficient FIRST STAGE that removes most of the organic load at almost no energy cost, and it must be followed by a polishing stage to meet any normal discharge standard.**

> **A UASB built without its post-treatment — which has happened, when the budget ran out after the reactor — discharges a partially treated, odorous, ammonia-rich effluent, and the scheme is judged a failure though the reactor is working exactly as designed.**

> **The combination UASB plus polishing pond is the proven arrangement, and it is the combination rather than the reactor that should be compared with activated sludge.**

No aeration and hence very low energy use.

examTip.trick: **Upflow through a GRANULAR anaerobic sludge blanket, producing biogas with no aeration.** Option (c) is a trickling filter, (d) waste stabilisation ponds.
examTip.trap: **GRANULATION is what makes it work** — dense pellets stay in against the upflow, giving a huge biomass at a 6-10 hour retention. Flocculent sludge washes out and the reactor fails.
examTip.mnemonic: **It is a FIRST STAGE, not a plant** — 70-85 % BOD removal, no nitrogen removal, sulphidic effluent. UASB PLUS a polishing pond is what should be compared with activated sludge. And it needs 20 °C+.

questions.stem: An ENVIRONMENTAL AUDIT of a completed project differs from the Environmental Impact Assessment carried out before it in that the audit:
options: Is a preliminary screening to decide whether an EIA is needed
Predicts the impacts that the project will cause
Replaces the need for a monitoring programme
Examines the project as built AND operating
questions.solution:
**It examines the project AS BUILT AND OPERATING** — comparing the actual impacts with those predicted, and checking whether the committed mitigation measures were implemented and are working.

**The two compared:**

| Aspect | EIA | ENVIRONMENTAL AUDIT |
|---|---|---|
| **Timing** | **BEFORE the project — at the approval stage** ← | **AFTER construction, and periodically during operation** ← |
| **Nature** | **PREDICTIVE — what is expected to happen** ← (option b) | **RETROSPECTIVE — what actually happened** ← |
| **Basis** | **Modelling, judgement and baseline surveys** | **MEASUREMENT and inspection of the real thing** ← |
| **Purpose** | **To inform the decision and set conditions** | **To verify COMPLIANCE and to LEARN** ← |
| **Output** | **A report with an EMP** | **Findings, non-compliances and corrective actions** ← |

> **THE PAIRING IS ESSENTIAL AND ONE WITHOUT THE OTHER IS OF LIMITED VALUE, which is the point worth taking: an EIA makes predictions and commitments, and without an audit nobody ever checks whether either was sound.**

> **A prediction that is never tested cannot be improved, and a commitment that is never verified need not be kept.**

**What an audit examines:**

| Item | Note |
|---|---|
| **COMPLIANCE with the conditions of approval and with the law** ← | **The most basic function — were the license conditions met?** ← |
| **Whether the EMP's mitigation measures were actually IMPLEMENTED** ← | **The measures listed in the report, and whether they exist on the ground** ← |
| **Whether those measures are WORKING** ← | **Implementation is not the same as effectiveness — a silt trap built and never cleaned is implemented and useless** ← |
| **How the ACTUAL impacts compare with the PREDICTED ones** ← | **The learning function, and the one most often omitted** ← |
| **Whether impacts arose that were NOT predicted at all** ← | **The most valuable finding of any audit** ← |
| **The adequacy of the monitoring itself** | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE WHERE THE REAL VALUE LIES AND THEY ARE THE PARTS ROUTINELY SKIPPED IN FAVOUR OF A COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST:**

> **Comparing actual against predicted impacts is the ONLY mechanism by which environmental assessment practice can improve.**

> **Without it, the same models and the same assumptions are used indefinitely, whether or not they have ever been right — and the accumulated evidence is that predictions in EIAs are frequently wrong, in both directions.**

> **The UNPREDICTED impacts in the fifth row are more valuable still, because they reveal what the assessment method missed entirely — and the spring drying up above a hydropower tunnel, or the dengue arising from household water storage, are exactly the kind of impact that appears in an audit and not in an EIA.**

**Why audits are so seldom done properly:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Nobody is obliged to fund a comparison with the prediction** ← | **Compliance is a legal requirement; learning is nobody's duty** ← |
| **The BASELINE data needed for comparison were often never collected properly** ← | **Without a baseline, no comparison is possible — which is why baseline monitoring matters so much** ← |
| **The consultants who made the predictions are rarely the ones audited** ← | **So there is no professional feedback loop** ← |
| **Adverse findings are unwelcome to the proponent paying for the audit** ← | **Hence the argument for INDEPENDENT or regulator-commissioned audits** ← |
| **The staff who made the commitments have moved on** | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE PRACTICAL KILLER AND IT CONNECTS BACK TO A POINT MADE ABOUT TUNNELS AND SPRINGS: an audit can only compare with a baseline that exists.**

> **If the pre-project spring flows, water quality, noise levels and fish populations were never measured, then no amount of post-project monitoring can establish what the project changed.**

> **Baseline data collection produces nothing visible, costs money at the least convenient moment, and is the first item cut — and cutting it forecloses the possibility of ever knowing the project's real effect.**

> **That is the strongest argument for insisting on it: not that it improves the EIA's predictions, but that without it the project's actual impact becomes permanently unknowable, and every subsequent dispute is settled by assertion rather than by evidence.**

examTip.trick: **EIA is PREDICTIVE and before; the audit is RETROSPECTIVE and after** — verifying compliance, checking the EMP was implemented AND is working, and comparing actual with predicted impacts.
examTip.trap: **Implementation is not effectiveness** — a silt trap built and never cleaned is implemented and useless. And UNPREDICTED impacts are an audit's most valuable finding.
examTip.mnemonic: **An audit can only compare against a BASELINE that exists** — and baseline data is the first item cut. Without it the project's real effect is permanently unknowable, and disputes are settled by assertion.

questions.stem: In irrigation practice, the BASE PERIOD of a crop differs from its CROP PERIOD in that the base period is:
options: The period from sowing to the first watering
Always exactly equal to the crop period
The period from the first watering to the last watering
The period during which the field lies fallow
questions.solution:
**The period from the FIRST watering to the LAST watering** — slightly shorter than the crop period, which runs from sowing to harvest.

**The two periods:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **CROP PERIOD** | **From SOWING to HARVESTING — the crop's full life in the field** ← |
| **BASE PERIOD** ← | **From the FIRST watering to the LAST watering** ← |
| **The difference** | **The base period is a few days SHORTER, because no water is applied in the last days before harvest** ← |

> **THE TWO ARE SO NEARLY EQUAL THAT THEY ARE ROUTINELY TREATED AS INTERCHANGEABLE IN CALCULATIONS, and that is normally acceptable — the difference is a few days in a hundred, well within the accuracy of any duty or delta estimate.**

> **The distinction is nevertheless real and worth knowing, because the base period is the one that belongs in the irrigation formulae: it is the period over which water is actually being SUPPLIED, and the duty and delta relations are statements about the supply.**

> **Using the crop period where the base period is meant slightly OVERSTATES the duration and therefore slightly understates the required discharge — an error in the unsafe direction, though a small one.**

**Where the base period enters the calculations:**

| Relation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Δ = 8.64 B / D** ← | **Delta in metres, B the BASE PERIOD in days, D the duty in hectares per cumec** ← |
| **The constant 8.64** | **= 86,400 seconds per day ÷ 10,000 m² per hectare, so a cumec for a day over a hectare gives 8.64 m depth** ← |
| **Duty D = 8.64 B / Δ** | **The same relation rearranged** ← |
| **The DISCHARGE required = area ÷ duty** | ← |

> **THE ORIGIN OF THE 8.64 IN THE SECOND ROW IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT MAKES THE FORMULA RECOVERABLE RATHER THAN MEMORISED: one cumec flowing for one day delivers 86,400 cubic metres.**

> **Spread over one hectare (10,000 m²), that is a depth of 8.64 metres.**

> **So the constant is a pure unit conversion, and anyone who forgets the formula can rebuild it from that observation in a few seconds — which is far more reliable than recalling whether the 8.64 goes on top or underneath.**

**The base periods and deltas of the common crops, for reference:**

| Crop | Base period (days) | Delta (mm) |
|---|---|---|
| **RICE (paddy)** | **120** ← | **1,000 to 1,250 — much the largest** ← |
| **WHEAT** | **120** | **375 to 400** ← |
| **SUGARCANE** | **320 to 360** ← | **800 to 900 — a long-duration crop** ← |
| **COTTON** | **200** | **About 500** |
| **MAIZE** | **100** | **About 250** |
| **Gram, barley** | **120** | **250 to 300** |

> **THE SUGARCANE ROW IS THE ONE THAT COMPLICATES CANAL OPERATION AND IS WORTH NOTING: sugarcane occupies the field for nearly the whole year, so it draws water in BOTH the kharif and the rabi seasons and through the hot weather between them.**

> **A command with a large area under sugarcane therefore has no slack season in which the canal can be closed for maintenance — and canal closure for desilting and repair is essential.**

> **Managing that conflict is a real operational problem: the closure period must be fitted around the cropping pattern, and a command that has shifted heavily toward perennial crops may have no adequate window at all.**

> **This is one reason the CROPPING PATTERN is a matter for the irrigation authority and not only for the cultivators — the canal's maintenance regime depends on it.**

examTip.trick: **Base period = first watering to last; crop period = sowing to harvest.** The base period is a few days shorter and is the one that belongs in the formulae.
examTip.trap: **Δ = 8.64 B/D uses the BASE period** — using the crop period slightly understates the discharge required. The two are usually treated as equal, which is acceptable but not exact.
examTip.mnemonic: **8.64 is pure unit conversion: 1 cumec for 1 day = 86,400 m³, over 1 hectare = 8.64 m depth.** Rebuild the formula from that rather than memorising where the constant goes.

questions.stem: CROP ROTATION is practised in an irrigated command principally because it:
options: Reduces the total quantity of water needed to zero in alternate years
Allows the same crop to be grown continuously with higher yields
Eliminates the need for any fertiliser
Restores soil fertility and structure, breaks pest and disease cycles, and
questions.solution:
**It restores soil fertility and structure, breaks pest and disease cycles, and evens out the demand on both the soil and the water supply.**

**The benefits, and the mechanism of each:**

| Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Restores NITROGEN** ← | **A LEGUME in the rotation — gram, lentil, groundnut, berseem — fixes atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule bacteria, enriching the soil for the following cereal** ← |
| **Draws on DIFFERENT nutrients and different soil depths** ← | **A deep-rooted crop reaches nutrients and moisture a shallow-rooted one cannot, so neither depletes one layer repeatedly** ← |
| **Breaks PEST and DISEASE cycles** ← | **A pest specific to one crop starves when a different crop follows; continuous monoculture allows it to build up indefinitely** ← |
| **Controls WEEDS** | **Different crops suppress different weeds, and the cultivation for each disturbs a different weed cycle** ← |
| **Improves soil STRUCTURE** | **Deep roots open the soil; a green manure or fodder crop adds organic matter** ← |
| **Evens the WATER demand** ← | **Alternating a high-delta crop such as paddy with a low-delta one such as gram spreads the load on the canal** ← |

> **THE LEGUME IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST VALUABLE ELEMENT OF ANY ROTATION AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING WHY IT IS FREE: legumes host Rhizobium bacteria in their root nodules, and those bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form the plant can use.**

> **When the legume is harvested and its roots and residues left in the soil, that fixed nitrogen becomes available to the next crop.**

> **A legume in the rotation can supply 40 to 60 kg of nitrogen per hectare — a substantial fraction of a cereal's requirement — obtained from the air at no cost and with no energy input.**

> **Industrial nitrogen fertiliser, by contrast, is made by the Haber process and is one of the most energy-intensive commodities in agriculture. So a rotation that includes a legume is displacing an expensive, energy-costly input with a free one.**

**THE WATER DEMAND POINT IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS TO THE IRRIGATION ENGINEER AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED IN AGRONOMIC DISCUSSIONS:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The canal's capacity is fixed by the PEAK demand** ← | **So a cropping pattern with a sharp peak requires a larger canal than one with a flat demand** ← |
| **A command entirely under PADDY in kharif has an enormous simultaneous peak** ← | **Every field wants water at once** ← |
| **A varied pattern staggers the sowing and the kor waterings** ← | **Flattening the peak, so the same canal serves more land** ← |
| **The irrigation authority therefore has a direct interest in the cropping pattern** ← | **And commonly prescribes a permitted pattern as a condition of supply** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW EXPLAINS A FEATURE OF CANAL ADMINISTRATION THAT OTHERWISE SEEMS INTRUSIVE: many systems specify what may be grown, and how much of each, as a condition of receiving water.**

> **The justification is that the canal was designed for an assumed cropping pattern, and a shift toward high-delta crops — sugarcane and paddy in particular — increases the demand beyond what the canal can deliver.**

> **The tail-enders then receive nothing, so one group of cultivators' choice of crop deprives another group entirely.**

> **Prescribing the pattern is therefore a way of allocating a fixed resource rather than an interference for its own sake — though it is naturally resented, and it is enforceable only where the authority has real control over the outlets.**

**And the OVERLAP with the crop-period question, which completes the picture:**

> **A rotation must also fit the SEASONS: kharif, rabi and the zaid period between, with the sowing and harvesting dates of each crop determining what can follow it.**

> **A long-duration crop such as sugarcane occupies the land for a whole year and excludes any rotation at all during that time, which is why sugarcane-dominated commands suffer both the water-demand problem and the soil-depletion problem together.**

> **The classic rotations of the region — paddy followed by wheat followed by a legume, or cotton followed by wheat followed by fallow — are worked out to satisfy the seasons, the soil and the water supply simultaneously, and they represent a great deal of accumulated agronomic knowledge rather than mere custom.**

By alternating deep and shallow rooted and high and low water-demand crops — evens out the demand on the soil and on the water supply.

examTip.trick: **Restores fertility (legumes fix nitrogen), breaks pest cycles, varies rooting depth, and flattens the water demand.**
examTip.trap: **A legume supplies 40-60 kg N/ha from the AIR at no cost** — displacing the most energy-intensive input in agriculture. That is the rotation's single largest benefit.
examTip.mnemonic: **The canal is sized on the PEAK, so a varied pattern lets the same canal serve more land** — which is why irrigation authorities prescribe cropping patterns. Sugarcane excludes rotation and peaks the demand at once.

questions.stem: The SARDA TYPE canal fall is characterised by:
options: A gently sloping glacis on which a hydraulic jump forms
An ogee-shaped crest following the lower nappe profile
A raised crest with a vertical (or nearly vertical) drop into a cistern below
A series of small stepped drops
questions.solution:
**A RAISED CREST with a vertical drop into a cistern below** — the crest being trapezoidal for larger discharges and rectangular for smaller ones.

**The types of canal fall, in the order they were developed:**

| Fall | Character |
|---|---|
| **OGEE fall** ← | **The crest shaped to the lower nappe profile, giving a smooth transition — an early type; it caused SCOUR downstream because the energy was not dissipated** ← |
| **RAPID fall** | **A long sloping glacis of masonry, with the water running down it — used for small drops** ← |
| **STEPPED fall** | **A series of small drops in steps — energy dissipated at each** ← (option d) |
| **TRAPEZOIDAL NOTCH fall** ← | **Notches in a wall, proportioned so the fall is also a METERING device and maintains the upstream depth** ← |
| **SARDA type fall** ← | **A RAISED crest with a vertical drop into a cistern — this question; developed on the Sarda Canal in India** ← |
| **VERTICAL DROP (Sarda) with a cistern** | **The cistern's water cushion dissipates the energy by impact** ← |
| **GLACIS fall (straight or parabolic)** ← | **The MODERN type — energy dissipated by a HYDRAULIC JUMP on the glacis** ← (option a) |
| **Baffle (Inglis) fall** | **A glacis with a baffle wall to stabilise the jump** ← |

> **THE DEVELOPMENT FROM THE OGEE TO THE GLACIS FALL IS THE SAME PROGRESSION AS FOR WEIRS, AND FOR THE SAME REASON: the early types passed the water smoothly and left its energy intact to scour the channel below.**

> **The later types dissipate the energy deliberately — by impact into a cistern, or by a hydraulic jump on a glacis — and the glacis type prevailed because the jump's position and length can be CALCULATED.**

**The Sarda fall's distinctive features:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The crest is RAISED above the upstream bed** ← | **Which is what makes it also a check on the upstream water level** ← |
| **A TRAPEZOIDAL crest for discharges above about 14 cumec, RECTANGULAR below** ← | **The shape affects the discharge coefficient and the flow's stability** ← |
| **A CISTERN below, depressed beneath the downstream bed** ← | **Providing a water cushion to absorb the falling nappe's impact** ← |
| **The cistern's depth and length are given by empirical formulae** ← | **Based on the drop and the discharge per metre** ← |
| **Sheet piles or cut-offs at both ends of the floor** | **For seepage and scour** ← |

> **THE RAISED CREST IN THE FIRST ROW GIVES THE SARDA FALL A SECOND FUNCTION THAT IS OFTEN THE REAL REASON FOR CHOOSING IT: it maintains the upstream water level.**

> **A canal fall is placed where the ground drops faster than the canal's designed gradient, and if the fall does nothing to hold the upstream level, the canal above it draws down and the outlets in that reach lose their command.**

> **A raised crest acts as a weir, holding the upstream depth at the designed full supply level regardless of the discharge — so the outlets upstream continue to work.**

> **That is why falls are so often combined with other functions: a fall may incorporate a bridge, a regulator, a metering device, or all three.**

**WHY FALLS ARE NEEDED AT ALL, which is the underlying point:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The GROUND slope is usually steeper than the canal's designed bed slope** ← | **A canal needs perhaps 1 in 5,000; the country may fall at 1 in 1,000** ← |
| **If the canal followed the ground, its velocity would be erosive** ← | **Exceeding the permissible non-scouring velocity** ← |
| **So the canal is given its own gentle slope, and the accumulated difference is taken up in DROPS** ← | **Each drop concentrating the surplus fall at one structure** ← |
| **The alternative — a steeper canal — would require LINING throughout** ← | **Which is far more expensive than a few falls** ← |

> **THE ECONOMIC COMPARISON IN THE LAST ROW IS THE DESIGN DECISION: a canal can either follow the ground steeply and be lined to withstand the velocity, or run at a gentle gradient and shed the surplus height at intervals through falls.**

> **For most alluvial canals the second is far cheaper, because a fall is a single compact structure while lining is a cost per metre over the whole length.**

> **The falls also provide convenient sites for bridges, regulators and gauging, and the energy they dissipate can even be used — small canal-fall hydropower installations exist, generating from the surplus head that would otherwise be destroyed.**

examTip.trick: **Sarda: RAISED crest, vertical drop into a cistern — trapezoidal crest above about 14 cumec, rectangular below.** Option (a) is the glacis fall, (b) the ogee.
