examTip.trap: **The RAISED crest also holds the upstream water level** — without it the reach above draws down and its outlets lose command. Falls are usually combined with other functions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Falls exist because the GROUND is steeper than the canal** — the choice is a gentle canal with falls, or a steep lined canal. Falls win, being compact structures against a cost per metre.

questions.stem: The progressive loss of an unlined canal's discharge capacity over years of operation is caused principally by:
options: Silt deposition reducing the section
An increase in the canal's bed slope
A reduction in the water's viscosity
Compaction of the canal banks
questions.solution:
**SILT DEPOSITION reducing the section, together with WEED growth increasing the roughness** — both reducing the velocity and hence the discharge.

**The two mechanisms and their effects:**

| Mechanism | Effect on the discharge |
|---|---|
| **SILT deposition** ← | **Reduces the cross-sectional AREA directly, and raises the bed so the depth available is less** ← |
| **WEED and vegetation growth** ← | **Raises Manning's n substantially — from about 0.020 for a clean earth canal to 0.035 or more when weed-choked** ← |
| **Since Q = (1/n) A R^(2/3) S^(1/2)** | **Both A and 1/n fall, so the discharge falls twice over** ← |
| **The combined loss can exceed 50 per cent** ← | **A canal that has not been maintained for several seasons may carry less than half its design discharge** ← |

> **THE WEED EFFECT IN THE SECOND ROW IS LARGER THAN MOST PEOPLE EXPECT AND IT IS WORTH QUANTIFYING: raising n from 0.020 to 0.035 reduces the discharge by 43 per cent for an unchanged section.**

> **Weeds also trap silt, so the two mechanisms reinforce one another: vegetation slows the flow, the slowed flow deposits more silt, and the silt provides a better rooting medium for more vegetation.**

> **The process is therefore self-accelerating, and a canal that is falling behind on maintenance deteriorates faster each year.**

**The maintenance activities and their timing:**

| Activity | Note |
|---|---|
| **DESILTING — removal of the deposited silt** ← | **By manual labour, dragline or excavator; the spoil placed where it does not block drainage** ← |
| **WEED clearance from the bed and banks** ← | **Manual cutting, mechanical, or biological control** ← |
| **Repair of the banks, breaches and rodent burrows** ← | **Rodent and crab burrows through a canal bank are a common cause of breaches** ← |
| **Repair and lubrication of the gates and regulators** | ← |
| **Repair of the lining, where lined** | ← |
| **All of it done during the CANAL CLOSURE** ← | **The annual period when the canal is dry — which must be fitted around the cropping pattern** ← |

> **THE CANAL CLOSURE IN THE LAST ROW IS THE OPERATIONAL CONSTRAINT THAT GOVERNS EVERYTHING ELSE, and it connects to the cropping pattern point: maintenance can only be done when the canal is EMPTY.**

> **The closure must therefore be scheduled in a period when no crop critically needs water, and its length is limited by that window.**

> **A command with perennial crops has almost no window, so its canal accumulates silt and weed year after year — and the loss of capacity then hurts the very perennial crops that prevented the closure.**

> **That is a genuine and unresolved tension in canal management, and it is one reason the shift toward sugarcane in a command is not merely an agronomic matter.**

**THE RODENT BURROW IN THE THIRD ROW DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT CAUSES SO MANY BREACHES:**

> **Rats, crabs and other burrowing animals tunnel through the canal's embankment above the water line during the closure, when the bank is dry and easy to dig.**

> **When the canal is refilled, water finds the burrow, flows through it, and the flow rapidly enlarges the hole by erosion — the same piping mechanism as in an earth dam.**

> **A breach develops within hours and floods the land below, and the canal is out of service until it is repaired.**

> **Which is why bank inspection and burrow filling are a standard pre-filling activity after every closure, and why the first filling after a closure is done SLOWLY and under observation.**

**And the argument this makes for LINING, which is the wider point:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A lined canal accumulates far less silt, because its higher velocity carries the load through** ← | ← |
| **It grows no weeds at all** ← | **There is no rooting medium** ← |
| **Its roughness stays constant over its life** ← | **So its discharge does not decline** ← |
| **And it cannot be burrowed through** | ← |
| **So the maintenance saving is a major part of lining's economic case** ← | **Alongside the water saved, the land saved and the extended command noted earlier** ← |

> **The maintenance saving is the item most often omitted from the economic comparison, and over a canal's life it can rival the value of the water conserved — which is why the case for lining almost always looks stronger when the whole life is considered than when only the capital cost and the seepage saving are compared.**

Both of which reduce the velocity and hence the discharge.

Together with WEED and vegetation growth increasing the roughness.

examTip.trick: **Silt reduces AREA and weed raises ROUGHNESS** — and Q depends on both, so the discharge falls twice over. Combined losses can exceed 50 %.
examTip.trap: **The two reinforce each other** — weeds slow the flow, the slowed flow deposits silt, and the silt roots more weeds. Deterioration accelerates each year without maintenance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maintenance needs a CANAL CLOSURE, which perennial crops prevent** — and the resulting capacity loss then hurts those same crops. And fill slowly after a closure: rodent burrows breach banks.

questions.stem: The GUIDE BANKS provided at a barrage or a major bridge across an alluvial river are given a curved head at the upstream end, known as the MOLE HEAD, in order to:
options: Provide a road access to the structure
Reduce the quantity of earthwork required
Trap the sediment carried by the river
Guide the flow smoothly into the waterway without a sharp change of direction
questions.solution:
**To guide the flow smoothly into the waterway without a sharp change of direction, and to keep the deep SCOUR that forms at the nose away from the straight shank of the bank.**

**The geometry of a guide bank:**

| Element | Typical proportion |
|---|---|
| **LENGTH of the upstream shank** | **1.0 to 1.5 times the waterway's length — commonly 1.25 L** ← |
| **Length of the DOWNSTREAM shank** | **About 0.2 to 0.4 times the waterway's length** ← |
| **The upstream MOLE HEAD** | **A curved head, swept away from the structure, of radius about 0.4 to 0.5 times the waterway** ← |
| **The downstream curved tail** | **A shorter curve, radius about 0.3 to 0.4 of the upstream head's** ← |
| **Side slopes** | **2:1 to 3:1, pitched with stone** ← |
| **A LAUNCHING APRON at the toe** ← | **Loose stone, which slides down the scour hole's face as it forms** ← |

> **THE MOLE HEAD'S CURVATURE PERFORMS TWO DISTINCT FUNCTIONS AND BOTH ARE WORTH SEEING:**

> **HYDRAULICALLY, it turns the approaching flow gradually into the waterway. A blunt or square end would cause the flow to separate, forming eddies and an intense local scour.**

> **STRUCTURALLY, it locates the deepest scour at the NOSE — away from the long straight shank.**

> **That second function is the more important: scour will occur somewhere, and the curved head ensures it occurs at a compact, heavily protected point rather than along a great length of embankment.**

> **The nose is therefore built with the deepest foundation and the most launching apron, and the shank needs proportionately less — which concentrates the expenditure where the attack is.**

**The scour depths, which govern the protection:**

| Location | Scour depth |
|---|---|
| **Normal scour in a straight reach, by Lacey** | **R = 0.47 (Q/f)^(1/3)** ← |
| **At the NOSE of a guide bank** | **2.0 to 2.5 R — the deepest anywhere on the works** ← |
| **Along the straight SHANK** | **1.25 to 1.5 R** ← |
| **At the downstream tail** | **1.5 R** ← |

> **THE FACTOR OF 2 TO 2.5 AT THE NOSE IS THE FIGURE THAT DECIDES THE FOUNDATION AND THE APRON QUANTITY, and underestimating it is the classic cause of guide bank failure.**

> **On a river whose normal scour is 6 m below the flood level, the nose must be protected to 12 to 15 m — and the launching apron must contain enough stone to pave the whole face of a hole that deep when it forms.**

> **The apron's stone quantity is computed for exactly that: the volume needed to cover the anticipated scour slope at the required thickness, laid out horizontally so that it launches into place as the hole develops.**

**What guide banks are FOR, which is the underlying purpose:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **CONFINE a braided or meandering river to the waterway provided** ← | **A Himalayan river in the Terai may wander over a belt kilometres wide; the structure spans only a few hundred metres** ← |
| **Ensure the flow approaches the structure CENTRALLY and AXIALLY** ← | **Rather than obliquely, which would attack one abutment and shoal the other** ← |
| **Protect the approach embankments from being outflanked** ← | **The failure in which the river cuts around the end of the works and leaves the bridge standing in a dry channel** ← |
| **Prevent the river changing course away from the structure** | ← |

> **THE OUTFLANKING FAILURE IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE THAT DESTROYS BRIDGES ON ALLUVIAL RIVERS AND IT IS SPECTACULAR WHEN IT HAPPENS: the river does not overload the bridge, it goes ROUND it.**

> **It erodes the approach embankment at the end of the guide bank, cuts a new channel across the floodplain, and abandons the waterway entirely — leaving an intact bridge spanning dry ground while the river flows through a field beside it.**

> **This has happened repeatedly in the Terai and across the Indo-Gangetic plain, and the guide bank's length is chosen specifically to make it improbable: the upstream shank must extend far enough that the river cannot develop a meander loop tight enough to attack behind it.**

> **That is why the length is specified as a multiple of the WATERWAY rather than as an absolute figure — it must be proportionate to the size of the river being confined.**

examTip.trick: **The curved head guides the flow in smoothly AND locates the deepest scour at the nose, away from the shank** — concentrating the protection where the attack is.
examTip.trap: **Scour at the NOSE is 2.0-2.5 times the normal Lacey value** — twice as deep as along the shank. Underestimating it is the classic cause of guide bank failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **The failure to fear is OUTFLANKING — the river goes ROUND the bridge**, cutting a new channel and leaving it spanning dry ground. Hence a shank of 1.0-1.5 times the waterway.

questions.stem: MARGINAL BUNDS (afflux bunds) constructed upstream of a diversion headworks are provided to:
options: Retain the water for the canal
Protect the land and settlements upstream from being submerged by the afflux
Guide the river's flow into the waterway
Provide a road along the river bank
questions.solution:
**To PROTECT the land and settlements upstream from submergence by the AFFLUX** — the rise in flood level that the weir or barrage itself causes.

**The problem they solve:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A weir or barrage OBSTRUCTS the river's flood flow** ← | ← |
| **The upstream water level therefore RISES above what it would naturally be** ← | **That rise is the AFFLUX** ← |
| **The raised level extends UPSTREAM as a backwater curve, dying away gradually** ← | **The M1 profile — and on a flat river it extends for kilometres** ← |
| **Land that never flooded before is now submerged during floods** ← | **Along both banks, for the whole length of the backwater** ← |
| **MARGINAL BUNDS are earth embankments along both banks, confining that raised water** ← | **Protecting the land behind them** ← |

> **THE AFFLUX IS A COST THAT THE STRUCTURE IMPOSES ON THIRD PARTIES, and the marginal bunds are how it is dealt with — which makes them a genuine part of the project rather than an optional extra.**

> **The alternative is to acquire and abandon the land that will be submerged, which on a flat alluvial plain may be a very large area indeed.**

**Their design features:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **They extend UPSTREAM until the afflux dies away to nothing** ← | **Which can be several kilometres on a flat river — so they are long and their length is the principal cost** ← |
| **Their TOP LEVEL follows the AFFLUXED flood profile, plus freeboard** ← | **So they are highest at the barrage and taper upstream as the afflux diminishes** ← |
| **They tie into HIGH GROUND at their upstream ends** ← | **Or the water simply flows around them** ← |
| **The river face is PITCHED against wave and current attack** | ← |
| **DRAINAGE of the country behind them must be provided** ← | **With sluices or pumps, since the bund now blocks the natural drainage to the river** ← |

> **THE DRAINAGE PROBLEM IN THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN UNDERESTIMATED AND IT IS A SERIOUS ONE: a marginal bund protects the land from the river and simultaneously prevents that land draining INTO the river.**

> **Local rainfall and irrigation drainage now accumulate behind the bund with nowhere to go.**

> **So a bund built to prevent flooding can cause waterlogging — the very problem discussed under drainage — unless drainage sluices are provided through it, and those sluices can only discharge when the river is LOWER than the water behind them.**

> **During a flood, when the drainage is most needed, the river is high and the sluices must be closed. Water then ponds behind the bund until the flood recedes.**

> **Where that ponding is unacceptable, PUMPED drainage is required — a permanent operating cost created by a flood protection work, and one that is regularly omitted from the project's economics.**

**THE AFFLUX BUND'S TERMINATION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE DETAIL THAT DECIDES WHETHER IT WORKS:**

> **A bund that stops short of high ground leaves an open flank, and the water flows round its end into the land it was built to protect.**

> **Worse, the flow round the end concentrates and erodes, so the bund is progressively outflanked — the same failure mode as a guide bank being outflanked, on a larger scale.**

> **The upstream end must therefore be tied into ground above the afflux flood level, and the tie must be long enough that the water cannot work its way behind it.**

> **Determining where that point lies requires the backwater profile to be computed properly, which is why the M1 profile calculation is a practical necessity at a headworks and not an academic exercise.**

**And the design decision that the afflux drives:**

| Choice | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **A HIGH weir crest with a small waterway** | **LARGE afflux, long and high marginal bunds, much land affected — cheap structure, expensive consequences** ← |
| **A LOW crest with gates (a barrage) and an adequate waterway** ← | **SMALL afflux, short bunds, little land affected — expensive structure, cheap consequences** ← |

> **THE COMPARISON IS THE ONE MADE EARLIER BETWEEN A WEIR AND A BARRAGE, SEEN FROM THE AFFLUX SIDE — and it shows why the two must be compared on their TOTAL cost including the bunds and the land, rather than on the structure alone.**

> **A weir that is cheaper than a barrage by a wide margin can be dearer once its marginal bunds, its land acquisition, its drainage sluices and its pumping are added — which is exactly the sort of comparison that project appraisal exists to make, and exactly the sort that gets truncated when the structure is designed before the consequences are assessed.**

The rise in flood level caused by the weir or barrage itself.

examTip.trick: **They confine the AFFLUX — the rise in flood level the structure itself causes** — protecting upstream land along the whole backwater length. Option (c) is the guide bank.
examTip.trap: **A bund that protects land from the river also stops that land DRAINING into it** — so drainage sluices are essential, and they cannot discharge during a flood. Pumping may be needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tie the upstream end into HIGH GROUND above the affluxed level** — or the water goes round the end and outflanks it. Which is why the M1 backwater profile must actually be computed.

questions.stem: In the classification of a Himalayan river's reaches from its source to the sea, the BOULDER stage is the reach in which:
options: The river flows through a rocky gorge with the bed in rock and negligible sediment deposition
The bed consists of fine sand and silt and the river meanders freely across a wide floodplain
The river carries and deposits boulders, shingle and gravel, typically where it emerges from the hills onto the plain and its slope falls abruptly
The river divides into distributaries approaching the sea
questions.solution:
**The reach in which the river carries and DEPOSITS boulders, shingle and gravel** — typically where it emerges from the hills onto the plain and its slope falls abruptly.

**The four stages of a river, from source to sea:**

| Stage | Character | Bed material |
|---|---|---|
| **ROCKY (mountainous) stage** ← | **A steep, confined gorge cut in rock; high velocity; little or no deposition** ← (option a) | **ROCK, with occasional boulders** ← |
| **BOULDER stage** ← | **Where the river leaves the hills; the slope falls sharply and the coarse load is dropped; braided channels and alluvial FANS** ← | **BOULDERS, shingle, gravel** ← |
| **TROUGH (alluvial) stage** | **A well-defined channel meandering across its own alluvium; moderate slope** ← | **SAND and gravel** ← |
| **DELTAIC stage** ← | **The river divides into DISTRIBUTARIES approaching the sea; very flat; heavy silt deposition** ← (option d) | **SILT and clay** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION IS ONE OF DECREASING SLOPE AND DECREASING GRAIN SIZE, and the two are directly linked: a river can carry only what its velocity permits, and its velocity falls as its slope flattens.**

> **So each reach deposits the coarsest fraction it can no longer carry and passes the finer material on — which is why the bed material grades systematically from rock to boulders to sand to silt along the river's length.**

**Why the BOULDER stage is the most difficult for engineering, which is the practical point:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **Violent AGGRADATION — the bed rises rapidly** ← | **This is where the slope breaks, so the coarse load is dumped here** ← |
| **The channel BRAIDS and shifts unpredictably** ← | **A structure built on one channel may find the river in another next monsoon** ← |
| **Enormous BOULDERS are moved during floods** ← | **Which destroy intakes, weirs, piers and protection works by impact** ← |
| **Very high sediment concentrations** | **Which is the settling basin problem for hydropower** ← |
| **Deep and unpredictable SCOUR** | ← |

> **THIS IS THE REACH IN WHICH MOST OF NEPAL'S HEADWORKS ARE BUILT, and it explains a great deal of what has been discussed elsewhere: the Tyrolean intake, the gravel trap, the settling basin, the launching apron and the braided-river migration risk all belong to the boulder stage.**

> **A river in its trough or deltaic stage presents quite different problems — mainly meandering, bank erosion and silting — and the structures that suit one reach are inappropriate in the other.**

> **Which is why importing a design from the Indo-Gangetic plain into a Chure-front river, or vice versa, produces works that fail for reasons the designer did not anticipate.**

**THE ALLUVIAL FAN IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE CHARACTERISTIC LANDFORM AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING ON THE GROUND:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **A cone of coarse sediment spread where the river leaves its confining valley** ← | **Steepest at the apex, flattening outward** ← |
| **The channel migrates ACROSS the fan over time** ← | **Depositing, raising its own bed, and then switching to a lower course — the same perched-river mechanism as an embanked aggrading river** ← |
| **Highly permeable, so much of the flow goes UNDERGROUND** ← | **A river can disappear into its own fan in the dry season and reappear downstream** ← |
| **Excellent GROUNDWATER recharge, and hence good aquifers below** ← | **Which is why the Bhabar zone at the foot of the Chure is a major recharge area for the Terai's aquifers** ← |

> **THE DISAPPEARING FLOW IN THE THIRD ROW HAS DIRECT CONSEQUENCES FOR IRRIGATION AND WATER SUPPLY IN THE BHABAR ZONE: a river with abundant flow at the hill front may have no surface flow at all a few kilometres downstream in the dry season, because it has sunk into the gravel.**

> **So a surface intake sited on the fan may be dry when it is most needed, while a well a short distance away yields well.**

> **And the RECHARGE in the fourth row is the corresponding benefit: the water has not been lost, it has entered the aquifer, and it can be recovered by pumping further down — which is the conjunctive use argument arising naturally from the river's own geomorphology.**

examTip.trick: **Rocky → BOULDER → trough → deltaic**, with slope and grain size both decreasing. Option (a) is the rocky stage, (d) the deltaic.
examTip.trap: **The boulder stage is where the slope BREAKS**, so the coarse load is dumped — violent aggradation, braiding, and boulders that destroy structures. Most Nepali headworks sit here.
examTip.mnemonic: **A river can vanish into its own alluvial FAN in the dry season and reappear downstream** — a surface intake there may be dry while a nearby well yields well. That is the Bhabar recharge zone.

questions.stem: A CROSS REGULATOR is provided in a main canal DOWNSTREAM of an off-taking distributary principally so that:
options: The water level upstream of it can be raised when the main canal is running below full supply
The main canal's discharge can be measured
Silt can be excluded from the distributary
The main canal can be drained for maintenance
questions.solution:
**So that the water level upstream of it can be RAISED when the main canal is running below full supply** — allowing the distributary's head regulator to receive its designed supply.

**The problem it solves:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **A distributary's head regulator needs a certain UPSTREAM LEVEL to pass its designed discharge** ← | **The working head across it, as discussed for the canal head regulator** ← |
| **When the main canal runs at FULL supply, that level exists naturally** ← | ← |
| **When the main canal runs at PART supply — as it must at times of low river flow — its depth is less** ← | **And the distributary's regulator can no longer command its supply** ← |
| **A CROSS REGULATOR downstream of the offtake, partly closed, RAISES the level locally** ← | **Restoring the head across the distributary's regulator** ← |

> **THE CROSS REGULATOR IS THEREFORE A LEVEL CONTROL DEVICE AND NOT A DISCHARGE CONTROL, which is the distinction to hold: it does not decide how much water goes down the main canal, it decides what DEPTH the canal runs at upstream of it.**

> **By throttling the main canal it backs the water up, and that raised level is what the distributary draws from.**

> **The two regulators work as a pair — the head regulator admits the distributary's share, and the cross regulator provides the head for it to do so.**

**The functions of a cross regulator, gathered:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **RAISE the upstream water level for the offtakes** ← | **The principal function — this question** ← |
| **Enable ROTATIONAL operation of the distributaries** ← | **By raising the level in one reach, a group of distributaries can be run at full supply while others are closed — which is how a system with insufficient water delivers a usable supply to some rather than an inadequate one to all** ← |
| **Help to control the SILT drawn into the offtakes** | **By influencing the velocity and the level in the reach** ← |
| **Allow the canal downstream to be closed for maintenance while the upstream reach continues to serve its offtakes** ← | ← |
| **Often combined with a ROAD BRIDGE and a metering device** | ← |

> **THE ROTATIONAL OPERATION IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT OPERATIONAL USE AND IT DESERVES EXPLAINING, because it is how a canal system copes with a shortage:**

> **When the available water is less than the full demand, there are two ways to distribute it.**

> **Either every distributary runs at part supply — in which case each runs below its self-cleansing velocity, silts up, and the tail-enders of every distributary get nothing.**

> **Or the distributaries are run in ROTATION: a group runs at FULL supply for a period while the others are closed, then the next group takes its turn.**

> **The second is far better: each channel runs at its design velocity when it runs at all, it does not silt, and its whole command including the tail receives water during its turn.**

> **The cross regulators are what make that possible, by allowing the level in each reach to be maintained at full supply regardless of how much is passing down the main canal — and the system of turns is the WARABANDI or rotational water supply that governs most canal systems in the region.**

**And the distinction from the other regulating structures:**

| Structure | Function |
|---|---|
| **CANAL HEAD REGULATOR** | **At the offtake FROM the river — regulates the whole canal's supply and excludes silt** ← |
| **DISTRIBUTARY HEAD REGULATOR** ← | **At the offtake of a distributary from the main canal — regulates the DISTRIBUTARY's supply** ← |
| **CROSS REGULATOR** ← | **ACROSS the main canal, downstream of the offtake — raises the main canal's LEVEL** ← |
| **CANAL ESCAPE** | **Sheds surplus water out of the canal** ← |
| **CANAL FALL** | **Takes up surplus bed height** ← |

> **THE PAIRING OF THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS IS THE ARRANGEMENT TO PICTURE: at every significant offtake there are TWO gated structures — one across the distributary's mouth and one across the main canal just below it.**

> **Together they let the operator set the distributary's discharge and the main canal's level independently, which is exactly the control a rotational system requires.**

> **Seeing them as a pair rather than as two separate structures is the key to understanding canal regulation, and it is why they are almost always built as a single combined work with a common road bridge over both.**

The distributary's head regulator still receives its designed supply.

examTip.trick: **It raises the main canal's LEVEL upstream of itself**, restoring the head across the distributary's head regulator when the canal runs at part supply. A level control, not a discharge control.
examTip.trap: **The head regulator and the cross regulator work as a PAIR** — one sets the distributary's discharge, the other provides the level for it. Usually built as one combined structure.
examTip.mnemonic: **They make ROTATIONAL supply possible** — running a group of distributaries at FULL supply in turns, rather than all at part supply where every channel silts and every tail gets nothing.

questions.stem: BIO-DRAINAGE, as a means of controlling a rising water table in an irrigated command, works by:
options: Planting shallow-rooted grasses to intercept rainfall before it infiltrates
Planting fast-growing, high transpiration trees
Growing crops that require no irrigation at all
Applying biological agents to increase the soil's permeability
questions.solution:
**Planting fast-growing, high-TRANSPIRATION trees** — eucalyptus and similar species — whose roots draw water from the saturated zone and release it to the atmosphere, lowering the water table with no pipes and no pumps.

**How it works:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **A mature fast-growing tree transpires a very large quantity of water** ← | **Tens to hundreds of litres a day in a warm climate** ← |
| **Its roots reach into the CAPILLARY FRINGE and the saturated zone** ← | **Drawing water directly from the water table** ← |
| **A plantation therefore acts as a distributed, solar-powered PUMP** ← | **Removing water continuously and discharging it to the atmosphere** ← |
| **Trees are planted in strips or blocks along canals, drains and field boundaries** ← | **So they occupy little cultivable land** ← |
| **The water table falls in the vicinity** | **The effect extending some tens of metres from the planting** ← |

> **THE DESCRIPTION IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE TO CARRY: bio-drainage is a pump powered by the sun, requiring no fuel, no maintenance and no operator, and improving in capacity as the trees grow.**

> **That is a genuinely attractive proposition set against a piped drainage system with its capital cost, or a tube well with its permanent energy bill.**

**Its advantages:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **NO capital works, no pipes, no pumps, no energy** ← | **A fraction of the cost of a subsurface drainage system** ← |
| **NO effluent to dispose of** ← | **Which is the great advantage — conventional drainage produces a saline effluent that must be discharged somewhere, and bio-drainage produces none, since only water leaves and the salts stay behind** ← |
| **It improves with time as the trees mature** | **The reverse of every mechanical system** ← |
| **Produces TIMBER, fuelwood and fodder** ← | **A return rather than a cost** ← |
| **Sequesters carbon, provides shade and shelter, and stabilises banks** | ← |
| **Simple to establish and understand** | ← |

> **THE ABSENCE OF AN EFFLUENT IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST VALUABLE PROPERTY AND IT SOLVES THE HARDEST PROBLEM IN CONVENTIONAL DRAINAGE: a tile drainage system removes saline water from the land, and that water must then go somewhere.**

> **In an inland command with no adequate outfall, there may be nowhere to put it — the same problem noted with the outfall requirement, and with reverse osmosis brine.**

> **Bio-drainage removes the WATER and leaves the SALT in the soil, so there is no effluent at all.**

**Which is also its FUNDAMENTAL LIMITATION, and it must be stated plainly:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The SALTS ARE NOT REMOVED — they are LEFT BEHIND and CONCENTRATED** ← | **Transpiration removes pure water; every dissolved salt stays in the root zone** ← |
| **So salinity in the planted strip INCREASES over time** ← | **Progressively, and eventually the trees themselves cannot tolerate it** ← |
| **It controls WATERLOGGING but NOT SALINITY** ← | **Which is the crucial distinction, since the two problems usually occur together** ← |
| **The trees compete with crops for water and light near the boundary** | ← |
| **Eucalyptus in particular is criticised for lowering the water table too far and for its effect on other vegetation** ← | **A genuine controversy, and a reason for using it deliberately rather than indiscriminately** ← |

> **THE FIRST THREE ROWS TOGETHER DEFINE EXACTLY WHERE BIO-DRAINAGE IS APPROPRIATE, and getting this right is the whole of its correct application:**

> **It is suitable where the problem is WATERLOGGING from excess fresh water — canal seepage in a command with good quality water — because there the salt load is small and the concentration builds slowly.**

> **It is NOT a solution where the problem is SALINITY, because it makes the salinity worse: removing water and leaving salt is precisely the process that creates a saline soil.**

> **So bio-drainage and leaching are OPPOSITE interventions — leaching washes salt down and out, and bio-drainage draws water up and concentrates salt — and applying the wrong one accelerates the problem it was meant to solve.**

> **The correct role of bio-drainage is therefore as a COMPLEMENT to conventional drainage rather than a substitute for it: bio-drainage strips along canals to intercept the seepage and control the water table, with conventional drainage where salt must actually be exported.**

Such as eucalyptus — whose roots draw water from the saturated zone and release it to the atmosphere, lowering the water table without pipes or pumps.

examTip.trick: **High-transpiration trees act as a distributed solar-powered pump** — no pipes, no energy, no operator, and it improves as they grow.
examTip.trap: **The SALTS are left behind and CONCENTRATED** — transpiration removes pure water. So it controls WATERLOGGING but makes SALINITY worse, which is the opposite of leaching.
examTip.mnemonic: **Its best property is no EFFLUENT** — the hardest problem in conventional drainage, where there may be no outfall. Use it as a COMPLEMENT where salt must still be exported.

questions.stem: The ENVELOPE (or filter) material placed around a buried perforated subsurface drain in agricultural land is required in order to:
options: Increase the pipe's structural strength against the soil load
Insulate the pipe against frost
Chemically neutralise salts in the drainage water
Prevent the surrounding soil's fine particles from entering and silting up the pipe
questions.solution:
**To prevent the soil's FINE PARTICLES entering and silting up the pipe, while letting water enter freely** — and incidentally to improve the flow into the drain by increasing its effective diameter.

**The two functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **FILTRATION — retain the soil, pass the water** ← | **The primary function; without it the pipe fills with silt and the system fails** ← |
| **HYDRAULIC — increase the drain's EFFECTIVE diameter** ← | **A permeable envelope acts as part of the drain, so water converges into a larger cylinder and the entry resistance falls** ← |
| **BEDDING — support the pipe and distribute the load** | **A secondary benefit** ← |

> **THE FILTER CRITERIA ARE THE SAME TWO CONDITIONS MET IN EVERY OTHER APPLICATION, and this is their fifth appearance in the subject:**

| Criterion | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **RETENTION** | **The envelope must be FINE enough that the soil cannot wash through it** ← |
| **PERMEABILITY** | **And COARSE enough that water passes freely without building up a pressure** ← |

> **THE TWO PULL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, exactly as they do behind a retaining wall, in an earth dam's chimney drain, beneath a revetment and under a pavement sub-base.**

> **Recognising it as ONE recurring problem rather than five separate specifications is worth doing: whenever water flows from a finer material into a coarser one, an intermediate grading is required, and its design is always this same pair of conditions.**

**The envelope materials:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **GRAVEL and coarse sand, graded** ← | **The traditional envelope — effective, and the volume of material needed makes it expensive and awkward to place** ← |
| **GEOTEXTILE, wrapped around the pipe** ← | **Now the commonest — light, quick, consistent and cheap; but it can CLOG with fines or iron ochre, and once clogged it cannot be cleaned** ← |
| **Organic materials — coir, straw, sawdust, coconut fibre** ← | **Traditional and cheap; they DECAY over some years and must eventually be replaced** ← |
| **No envelope at all** | **Acceptable only in stable, coarse, non-dispersive soils** ← |

> **THE GEOTEXTILE'S CLOGGING RISK IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE PRINCIPAL LONG-TERM CONCERN AND IT IS INVISIBLE: a wrapped pipe whose geotextile has blinded with fines or with iron ochre stops draining, and there is no way to tell from the surface except that the land waterlogs again.**

> **IRON OCHRE is a particular problem in soils with dissolved ferrous iron: as the water enters the aerated drain, the iron oxidises and precipitates as a gelatinous ochre that blocks the fabric and the perforations.**

> **It is not preventable by better filtration, since the blocking material forms IN the drain rather than arriving with the soil — so where ochre is expected, the design response is to keep the drain permanently SUBMERGED (excluding oxygen), or to use large-diameter pipes that can be jetted clean.**

> **That is a good illustration of why the site's water chemistry must be established before a drainage system is designed: a system perfectly designed against silt can fail entirely from a chemical process the filter cannot address.**

**And the layout of a subsurface drainage system, to place the envelope in context:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **LATERAL drains — perforated pipes, at 1.0 to 2.0 m depth and 15 to 60 m spacing** ← | **The spacing from Hooghoudt's or a similar equation, depending on the permeability and the depth to the impermeable layer** ← |
| **COLLECTOR drains — larger, unperforated, gathering the laterals** ← | ← |
| **A MAIN drain, and an OUTFALL to a natural watercourse or a sump** ← | **The item without which none of it works** ← |
| **MANHOLES and inspection points at junctions** ← | **So the system can be inspected and jetted — and their omission means a blockage can never be located** ← |
| **Surface water inlets, where needed** | ← |

> **THE INSPECTION PROVISION IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ONE ROUTINELY OMITTED TO SAVE COST, and it has the same consequence as everywhere else in buried drainage: a system that cannot be inspected cannot be maintained.**

> **A blocked lateral among forty identical buried laterals is undiscoverable without access points, and the field simply waterlogs in patches with no way to identify which drain has failed.**

> **Manholes at the collector junctions, and a record drawing showing where every lateral runs, are what make the difference between a drainage system that lasts thirty years and one that quietly stops working in five — which returns to the as-built drawing point made earlier, in a different setting.**

And to improve the flow into the drain by increasing its effective diameter.

Allowing water to enter freely.

examTip.trick: **Retain the soil, pass the water — and increase the drain's effective diameter.** The same two filter criteria met behind walls, in dam cores, under revetments and beneath pavements.
examTip.trap: **IRON OCHRE forms INSIDE the drain and no filter can stop it** — where it is expected, keep the drain submerged to exclude oxygen, or use pipes large enough to jet clean.
examTip.mnemonic: **A system that cannot be INSPECTED cannot be maintained** — one blocked lateral among forty is undiscoverable without manholes and a record drawing. The as-built point again.

questions.stem: The FIRST hydropower plant built in Nepal was:
options: The PHARPING (Chandrajyoti) plant near Kathmandu, of 500 kW, commissioned in 1911
The Sundarijal plant, of 900 kW, commissioned in 1936
The Panauti plant, of 2,400 kW, commissioned in 1965
The Trishuli plant, of 21 MW, commissioned in 1967
questions.solution:
**The PHARPING plant (Chandrajyoti) near Kathmandu, of 500 kW, commissioned in 1911.**

**The early landmarks of hydropower in Nepal:**

| Year | Plant | Capacity |
|---|---|---|
| **1911 (1968 BS)** ← | **PHARPING (Chandrajyoti), near Kathmandu — the FIRST** ← | **500 kW** ← |
| **1936** | **Sundarijal** ← (option b) | **900 kW** |
| **1965** | **Panauti** ← (option c) | **2,400 kW** |
| **1967-71** | **Trishuli** ← (option d) | **21 MW** |
| **1982** | **Kulekhani I — Nepal's only STORAGE plant** ← | **60 MW** |
| **1985** | **Devighat** | **14.1 MW** |
| **1995** | **Marsyangdi** | **69 MW** |
| **2002** | **Kali Gandaki A — the largest for many years** ← | **144 MW** |

> **THE 1911 DATE IS WORTH APPRECIATING FOR ITS CONTEXT RATHER THAN AS A DATE TO MEMORISE: Pharping was among the earliest hydropower plants in the whole of South Asia, built only a little after the first plants in India and long before electrification was general anywhere in the region.**

> **It was built to light the Rana palaces rather than to serve the public, which is why a very early start produced no early general electrification — a distinction between technical capability and public provision that recurs throughout the sector's history.**

> **The Pharping powerhouse still stands and is preserved as a museum, with its original machinery.**

**KULEKHANI IN THE FIFTH ROW DESERVES ITS EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS STILL UNIQUE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is Nepal's ONLY storage (reservoir) hydropower plant** ← | **Every other plant is run-of-river or peaking run-of-river** ← |
| **Which means Nepal's system has almost NO dry-season storage** ← | **So generation collapses in the dry months when the rivers fall, while demand does not** ← |
| **That is the single defining weakness of the system** ← | **And the reason storage projects dominate the planning discussion** ← |
| **Its reservoir has also lost capacity to SEDIMENTATION** ← | **Severely, after the 1993 flood in particular — the reservoir sedimentation problem in its most concrete Nepali form** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN WHY NEPAL IMPORTS POWER IN THE DRY SEASON DESPITE ITS ENORMOUS POTENTIAL, and it is worth being precise about the mechanism.**

> **A run-of-river plant generates what the river gives it. In the monsoon the rivers are high and the plants run at full capacity, producing a surplus. In the dry season the same rivers may fall to a tenth of their monsoon flow, and the same plants produce a tenth of the energy.**

> **Demand, meanwhile, is roughly constant through the year and actually PEAKS in the dry winter evenings.**

> **So the system has surplus when it does not need it and shortage when it does — and no amount of additional run-of-river capacity fixes that, because every new run-of-river plant has the same seasonal shape.**

> **Only STORAGE, which holds monsoon water for dry-season use, changes the shape — which is why the argument for storage projects is a structural one and not merely a matter of adding megawatts.**

**The potential figures, for completeness:**

| Figure | Value |
|---|---|
| **THEORETICAL (gross) potential** | **About 83,000 MW** ← |
| **TECHNICALLY feasible** | **About 45,000 MW** ← |
| **ECONOMICALLY feasible** ← | **About 42,000 MW — the figure most often quoted** ← |
| **Installed to date** | **A small fraction of it** ← |

> **The gap between the last two rows is the whole subject of hydropower development in Nepal, and it is a matter of finance, transmission, access and institutional capacity far more than of engineering feasibility.**

examTip.trick: **Pharping (Chandrajyoti), 500 kW, 1911** — among the earliest in South Asia. Then Sundarijal 1936, Panauti 1965, Trishuli 1967.
examTip.trap: **Kulekhani (60 MW, 1982) is still Nepal's ONLY storage plant** — everything else is run-of-river, which is why the system has a dry-season deficit despite the monsoon surplus.
examTip.mnemonic: **Run-of-river plants all have the SAME seasonal shape**, so adding more of them never fixes the dry-season shortage. Only storage changes the shape.

questions.stem: Private hydropower projects in Nepal are developed under the BOOT arrangement, which means that the developer:
options: Borrows the plant from the Government, operates it, and returns it
Buys the plant from the Government outright and owns it permanently
Builds the plant on behalf of the Government and hands it over immediately on completion
Builds, owns and operates the plant for the period of the generation license, and then transfers it to the Government
questions.solution:
**BUILDS, OWNS and OPERATES the plant for the period of the generation license, and then TRANSFERS it to the Government.**

**The letters:**

| Letter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **B — BUILD** ← | **The developer finances, designs and constructs the project at its own risk** ← |
| **O — OWN** ← | **The developer owns the asset during the license period** ← |
| **O — OPERATE** ← | **And operates it, selling the energy under a POWER PURCHASE AGREEMENT** ← |
| **T — TRANSFER** ← | **At the end of the license period the plant is TRANSFERRED to the Government, in working order and normally without payment** ← |

> **THE TRANSFER IN THE LAST ROW IS WHAT MAKES THE ARRANGEMENT ATTRACTIVE TO THE STATE, and it is worth stating what it means in practice: the Government obtains a working hydropower plant, built with private capital and private risk, at the end of the term for nothing.**

> **The developer, in exchange, has the exclusive right to sell the energy for that term at a tariff agreed in advance.**

> **So the state converts a capital problem into a tariff problem — it does not have to raise the money, but it does commit to buying the output at an agreed price for decades.**

**The structure of the arrangement in Nepal:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURVEY license** ← | **Granted first, for the study period — permitting investigation but not construction** ← |
| **GENERATION license** ← | **Granted for the construction and operation period, after which the transfer falls due** ← |
| **POWER PURCHASE AGREEMENT (PPA)** ← | **With the utility, fixing the tariff, the take-or-pay terms and the dry-season and wet-season rates separately** ← |
| **The DRY and WET season tariffs differ substantially** ← | **Dry-season energy is worth far more, for the seasonality reason** ← |
| **Royalty payable to the Government** ← | **On capacity and on energy, at rates that step up after the early years of operation** ← |
| **A share of the energy to the local community, and local shareholding** ← | **Benefit-sharing provisions** ← |

> **THE SEPARATE SEASONAL TARIFFS IN THE FOURTH ROW ARE A DIRECT AND SENSIBLE RESPONSE TO THE SYSTEM'S CHARACTER, and they are the mechanism by which the tariff structure tries to correct the run-of-river problem.**

> **Since dry-season energy is scarce and monsoon energy is in surplus, paying the same price for both would give a developer no reason to build anything but the cheapest run-of-river scheme.**

> **A higher dry-season rate makes a peaking or storage project — which delivers when the system needs it — commercially viable, and it prices the surplus monsoon energy at what it is actually worth.**

> **This is a good example of a TARIFF being used as an instrument of planning rather than merely as a payment: the price signal is what determines which projects private capital chooses to build, so getting the seasonal differential right matters as much as any engineering decision.**

**Other forms of the same family, for the distinction:**

| Form | Difference |
|---|---|
| **BOT — Build, Operate, Transfer** | **The developer does not OWN during the term, only operates** ← |
| **BOO — Build, Own, Operate** | **NO transfer at all — the asset stays private** ← |
| **BOOT / BOOST** ← | **Own and operate, then transfer — this question** ← |
| **EPC (turnkey)** ← | **The contractor builds and hands over on completion — no operation, no ownership** ← (option c) |
| **DBFO — Design, Build, Finance, Operate** | **Common in roads** ← |

> **OPTION (c) IS THE EPC MODEL IN THE FOURTH ROW AND IT IS A DIFFERENT THING ENTIRELY: an EPC contractor is paid to build, takes no revenue risk, and walks away on completion.**

> **A BOOT developer takes the revenue risk for decades — which is why a BOOT arrangement transfers a great deal more risk to the private party, and why it demands a much higher return to be worth undertaking.**

> **Understanding that difference is central to project financing: the choice of model is essentially a choice about WHO carries which risk, and the cost of the project to the public follows from that allocation rather than from the construction cost alone.**

examTip.trick: **Build, Own, Operate, Transfer** — the developer owns and runs it for the license term, then hands it to the Government in working order, normally free.
examTip.trap: **BOT has no OWN, BOO has no TRANSFER, and EPC (option c) is neither** — the EPC contractor hands over on completion and takes no revenue risk at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dry-season and wet-season tariffs differ deliberately** — equal prices would make only the cheapest run-of-river scheme worth building. The tariff is a planning instrument.

questions.stem: The UTILISATION FACTOR of a power plant is defined as the ratio of:
options: The average load to the peak load over a given period
The maximum demand on the plant to its rated installed capacity
The energy actually generated to the energy that could be generated at rated capacity throughout the period
The sum of the individual maximum demands to the maximum demand on the system
questions.solution:
**The MAXIMUM DEMAND on the plant to its RATED INSTALLED CAPACITY.**

**The family of factors, set out together — because they are all ratios of similar-sounding quantities and are constantly confused:**

| Factor | Definition |
|---|---|
| **LOAD FACTOR** ← | **AVERAGE load ÷ PEAK load, over the period** ← (option a) |
| **CAPACITY (plant capacity) FACTOR** ← | **Energy ACTUALLY generated ÷ energy possible at RATED capacity for the whole period** ← (option c) |
| **UTILISATION FACTOR** ← | **MAXIMUM DEMAND ÷ RATED INSTALLED CAPACITY — this question** ← |
| **PLANT USE FACTOR** ← | **Energy generated ÷ (rated capacity × hours the plant was ACTUALLY IN OPERATION)** ← |
| **DIVERSITY FACTOR** ← | **Sum of the individual maximum demands ÷ the maximum demand on the system** ← (option d) |
| **DEMAND FACTOR** | **Maximum demand ÷ total connected load** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE THE PAIR MOST WORTH SEPARATING CAREFULLY, and the distinction is between CAPACITY and TIME:**

> **The UTILISATION factor asks how much of the installed capacity is ever CALLED UPON — it compares two powers.**

> **The PLANT USE factor asks how fully the plant was loaded during the hours it was RUNNING — it excludes the idle hours from the denominator, which the capacity factor includes.**

> **So a plant that runs at full load for three months and is shut down for nine has a plant use factor near 1.0 and a capacity factor near 0.25 — and quoting one where the other is meant misrepresents the plant entirely.**

**Why the utilisation factor matters, which is the practical point:**

| Value | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Utilisation factor near 1.0** ← | **The plant's full capacity is being called on — the installation is well matched to the demand** ← |
| **Utilisation factor much less than 1.0** ← | **Capacity has been installed that is never used — capital spent for nothing** ← |
| **Utilisation factor greater than 1.0** ← | **The plant is being OVERLOADED beyond its rating — possible briefly, but it shortens the machine's life** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE DIAGNOSIS THE FACTOR EXISTS TO MAKE, and it identifies a specific and expensive kind of planning error: capacity installed in excess of anything the system will ever ask for.**

> **A hydropower plant sized on an optimistic load forecast, or on a design discharge the river seldom delivers, carries turbines and generators that were paid for and are never fully loaded.**

> **The remedy is not obvious after the fact — the machinery cannot be un-bought — which is why the installed capacity decision is made with such care at the planning stage, and why the flow duration curve and the load forecast are studied together rather than separately.**

**The relation between the load factor and the capacity factor, which is often examined:**

> **CAPACITY FACTOR = LOAD FACTOR × UTILISATION FACTOR.**

> **Which follows directly from the definitions: (average ÷ rated) = (average ÷ peak) × (peak ÷ rated).**

> **And it gives the useful corollary that the CAPACITY FACTOR EQUALS THE LOAD FACTOR when the utilisation factor is unity — that is, when the maximum demand exactly equals the installed capacity, so the plant is neither over-built nor overloaded.**

> **Deriving the relation from the definitions rather than memorising it is the reliable approach here, because all six factors are ratios of the same four quantities — average load, peak load, rated capacity and hours — and any of them can be reconstructed in a moment by writing down which two are being compared.**

examTip.trick: **Utilisation factor = maximum DEMAND ÷ rated CAPACITY** — a ratio of two powers. Option (a) is the load factor, (c) the capacity factor, (d) the diversity factor.
examTip.trap: **Plant USE factor excludes the idle hours; capacity factor includes them.** A plant running full for 3 months of 12 has a use factor near 1.0 and a capacity factor near 0.25.
examTip.mnemonic: **Capacity factor = load factor × utilisation factor**, straight from the definitions. So capacity factor equals load factor only when maximum demand equals installed capacity.

questions.stem: A SIPHON SPILLWAY is distinguished from other spillway types by the fact that it:
options: Discharges over a free crest whose profile follows the lower nappe
Carries the flow down a steep open chute to a stilling basin below
Primes itself once the reservoir rises slightly above the crest
Discharges through a vertical shaft into a horizontal tunnel
questions.solution:
**It PRIMES ITSELF once the reservoir rises slightly above the crest**, and thereafter discharges at full capacity under the whole available head, stopping abruptly when the level falls again.

**The spillway types, for the distinction:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **OGEE (overflow)** ← | **A free crest shaped to the lower nappe profile — the commonest, used on gravity dams** ← (option a) |
| **CHUTE (trough)** ← | **An open channel carrying the flow down a slope, often clear of the dam** ← (option b) |
| **SIDE CHANNEL** | **The crest alongside a channel that runs parallel to it** ← |
| **SHAFT (morning glory)** ← | **A circular crest leading to a vertical shaft and a horizontal tunnel** ← (option d) |
| **SIPHON** ← | **A closed conduit that primes and runs full — this question** ← |
| **DUCKBILL / labyrinth** | **A crest lengthened in plan to increase capacity for a given width** ← |

**How the siphon works, step by step:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **The reservoir is BELOW the crest** | **No flow; the siphon is dry** ← |
| **The level rises just ABOVE the crest** | **Water begins to trickle over, as an ordinary weir** ← |
| **The falling water ENTRAINS and expels the air from the barrel** ← | **The deprimer air vent being above the water level, air is drawn out and not replaced** ← |
| **The barrel fills — the siphon PRIMES** ← | **And now runs FULL, under the entire head from reservoir level to outlet** ← |
| **Discharge jumps ABRUPTLY to full capacity** ← | **Far greater than a free weir of the same crest length, because the head is the whole drop, not the depth over the crest** ← |
| **The level falls to the DEPRIMER vent** ← | **Air re-enters, the siphon breaks, and the flow stops abruptly** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS CONTAIN THE WHOLE ADVANTAGE OF THE TYPE, and it is worth seeing why the discharge is so large.**

> **An ordinary weir's discharge depends on the DEPTH OF WATER OVER ITS CREST — a small quantity, since the reservoir is only allowed to rise a little.**

> **A primed siphon's discharge depends on the FULL HEAD from the reservoir surface down to the outlet, which may be tens of metres.**

> **So a siphon of modest size passes what would need a very much longer free crest — which is exactly what is wanted where the dam is narrow, or where the reservoir level must be held within very tight limits.**

**Its advantages and its serious drawbacks:**

| Advantages | Drawbacks |
|---|---|
| **Very LARGE discharge for a small structure** ← | **The abrupt ON-OFF action sends a sudden surge down the river — a hazard below** ← |
| **AUTOMATIC — no gates, no operator, no power** ← | **HUNTING: it can prime and deprime repeatedly, cycling and causing vibration** ← |
| **Holds the reservoir level within a very NARROW range** ← | **Easily BLOCKED by floating debris or ice, and then it does not work at all** ← |
| **Useful where the crest length available is limited** | **Cavitation risk in the barrel at high heads** ← |
| **No moving parts to fail** | **Cannot pass a large flood if several siphons fail to prime together** ← |

> **THE BLOCKAGE RISK IN THE THIRD DRAWBACK IS THE REASON SIPHONS ARE NOT USED AS A DAM'S PRINCIPAL SPILLWAY, and the logic is the same as with any automatic device that has no manual override.**

> **A spillway's whole purpose is to work during the worst flood the dam will ever see — and the worst flood is precisely the occasion on which the river carries the most floating trees, debris and rubbish.**

> **A device that can be disabled by a log is therefore unsuited to that duty, however elegant its action.**

> **So siphons are used as AUXILIARY or emergency spillways alongside a conventional one, or on small structures such as canal escapes and small barrages where the consequence of failure is limited — and the main spillway is an ogee or a gated arrangement whose behaviour under debris is predictable.**

examTip.trick: **It primes itself and then runs FULL under the whole head** — so it passes far more than a free weir of the same crest length, and stops abruptly when the deprimer vent admits air.
examTip.trap: **Never a dam's PRINCIPAL spillway** — the worst flood carries the most debris, and a log can disable it. Use it as an auxiliary, or on small structures.
examTip.mnemonic: **A weir's discharge depends on the depth OVER the crest; a primed siphon's on the FULL drop to the outlet.** That is where the extra capacity comes from.

questions.stem: DRAWDOWN FLUSHING as a means of managing sedimentation in a storage reservoir consists of:
options: Lowering the reservoir so that the river re-establishes a free-flowing channel through its own deposits and scours them out through low-level outlets
Dredging the deposited sediment mechanically and disposing of it on land
Passing the incoming sediment-laden flood through the reservoir without allowing it to settle, while the reservoir remains full
Injecting compressed air at the reservoir bed to keep the sediment in suspension
questions.solution:
**LOWERING the reservoir so that the river re-establishes a free-flowing channel through its own deposits and scours them out through low-level outlets.**

**The methods of reservoir sediment management, which fall into three families:**

| Family | Methods |
|---|---|
| **REDUCE the inflowing sediment** ← | **Catchment conservation, afforestation, check dams, gully control, sediment-trapping upstream** ← |
| **ROUTE the sediment THROUGH** ← | **SLUICING (drawing the reservoir down during the flood so the turbid water passes through), and DENSITY CURRENT VENTING (drawing off the turbid underflow through a low outlet while the reservoir stays full)** ← (option c) |
| **REMOVE what has deposited** ← | **DRAWDOWN FLUSHING (this question), DREDGING (option b), hydrosuction, and mechanical excavation in the dry** ← |

> **THE THREE FAMILIES ARE IN DESCENDING ORDER OF DESIRABILITY AND THAT ORDER IS WORTH HOLDING, because it reflects how much the intervention costs per tonne of sediment dealt with.**

> **Keeping sediment OUT of the reservoir is best but slow and only partly achievable, since a Himalayan catchment produces sediment by natural erosion regardless of land management.**

> **Passing it THROUGH is next best, because it costs only some water and some generation.**

> **Taking it OUT after it has settled is by far the most expensive, which is why flushing and dredging are last resorts rather than first choices.**

**How drawdown flushing works, and what it requires:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **LOW-LEVEL OUTLETS of adequate size, at or near the original riverbed** ← | **Without these, flushing is IMPOSSIBLE — and they must be designed in from the start** ← |
| **The reservoir drawn down far enough for RIVERINE flow to be re-established** ← | **The impoundment must be effectively emptied, not merely lowered** ← |
| **Sufficient inflow during the flushing period** ← | **The river's own discharge does the scouring, so flushing is done in the monsoon** ← |
| **A narrow, steep reservoir helps greatly** ← | **A wide flat reservoir flushes only a narrow channel and leaves the flanks untouched** ← |
| **Acceptance of the DOWNSTREAM impact** ← | **The flushed water is extremely turbid and kills aquatic life for a distance below** ← |
| **Acceptance of the LOST generation and lost storage during the operation** | **The plant is off and the reservoir empty while it proceeds** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE DECISION THAT CANNOT BE REVISITED AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT SENTENCE IN THIS ANSWER: a dam built without low-level outlets can NEVER be flushed.**

> **The outlets must be provided at construction, at the level of the original riverbed, and sized to pass enough water to scour.**

> **They are expensive, they complicate the dam, and they serve no purpose for decades — so there is a permanent temptation to omit or undersize them.**

> **A dam so built will silt up progressively and the storage will be lost permanently, because by the time the problem is evident there is no way to reach the bottom of the reservoir.**

> **This is why sediment management must be designed at the outset rather than addressed when the deposits appear — an instance of the general principle that a facility's whole-life operation has to be provided for while it is still on the drawing board.**

**THE FOURTH ROW EXPLAINS WHY FLUSHING SUCCEEDS ON SOME RESERVOIRS AND NOT OTHERS:**

| Reservoir shape | Flushing effectiveness |
|---|---|
| **NARROW and STEEP, in a gorge** ← | **GOOD — the flushing channel occupies most of the width, so most deposits are removed** ← |
| **WIDE and FLAT** ← | **POOR — the river cuts one narrow channel and the deposits on either side remain** ← |
| **Long, with a large dead storage** | **Poor — the deposits far from the outlet are not reached** ← |

> **The Himalayan situation is therefore mixed: the gorge sites that suit dam construction also flush well, which is fortunate, but the sediment loads are so enormous that flushing must be frequent and the water cost is correspondingly high.**

> **Kulekhani's experience is the local illustration — a reservoir that lost a substantial part of its capacity to a single extreme event, in a country whose only storage plant it was, and remains the standing argument for taking sediment seriously in every Nepali storage proposal.**

examTip.trick: **Empty the reservoir so the river scours its own deposits out through low-level outlets.** Option (c) is sluicing — routing sediment through, not removing deposits.
examTip.trap: **No low-level outlets means flushing is IMPOSSIBLE, for ever** — they must be built in at the start, at original bed level, though they serve no purpose for decades.
examTip.mnemonic: **Reduce inflow, then route through, then remove deposits** — in descending order of desirability, because that is the order of cost per tonne. Narrow steep reservoirs flush well; wide flat ones do not.

questions.stem: A settling basin is 3 m deep and the flow-through velocity along it is 0.30 m/s. If the design particle has a fall (settling) velocity of 0.02 m/s, the MINIMUM theoretical length of the basin is:
options: 9 m
questions.solution:
**45 m.**

**The principle — the ideal settling basin condition:**

> **A particle entering at the WATER SURFACE at the basin's inlet must reach the FLOOR before it is carried out at the outlet.**

> **So the time it takes to FALL through the full depth must be no more than the time it takes to TRAVEL the full length.**

| Time | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Time to FALL the depth h at settling velocity w** | **t_fall = h / w** ← |
| **Time to TRAVEL the length L at through-velocity V** | **t_travel = L / V** ← |
| **The condition** | **t_travel ≥ t_fall** ← |
| **Giving** | **L / V ≥ h / w, so L ≥ V h / w** ← |

**The calculation:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Depth h** | **3 m** |
| **Through-velocity V** | **0.30 m/s** |
| **Settling velocity w** | **0.02 m/s** |
| **L = V h / w** | **= 0.30 × 3 / 0.02** ← |
| **= 0.9 / 0.02** | **= 45 m** ← |

> **The answer is therefore 45 m as the theoretical minimum.**

**THE RELATION L = V h / w REWARDS A MOMENT'S THOUGHT BECAUSE ITS STRUCTURE IS INFORMATIVE:**

| Observation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **L is proportional to V** ← | **HALVING the through-velocity halves the length needed — which is why settling basins are made WIDE and the velocity kept low, typically 0.2 to 0.4 m/s** ← |
| **L is proportional to h** ← | **A SHALLOWER basin needs less length for the same duty** ← |
| **L is inversely proportional to w** ← | **And w falls with the SQUARE of the particle diameter by Stokes' law, so halving the design particle size QUADRUPLES the settling length** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS A RESULT THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND IS WORTH DWELLING ON: a shallower basin settles just as well.**

> **The reason is that a particle in a shallow basin has less distance to fall, so it reaches the floor sooner even though its fall velocity is the same.**

> **Rearranging the relation makes it plainer still: the condition can be written as w ≥ V h / L = Q / (surface area), since Q = V × h × B and the surface area is L × B.**

> **So the basin's performance depends only on its PLAN AREA and not on its depth at all — the SURFACE LOADING RATE, which is exactly the same quantity that governs a sedimentation tank in water treatment.**

> **Depth is then chosen for other reasons: sediment storage between flushes, and keeping the flow tranquil.**

**The practical corrections to the theoretical length:**

| Correction | Effect |
|---|---|
| **TURBULENCE keeps particles in suspension longer than the ideal theory allows** ← | **Requiring the length to be increased, commonly by 20 to 50 per cent** ← |
| **INLET and OUTLET transitions must be long and gradual** ← | **Or the flow separates and short-circuits, and much of the basin does no work** ← |
| **The basin floor is SLOPED toward the flushing outlet** ← | **Adding to the length** ← |
| **A trap efficiency of 100 per cent is neither expected nor economic** ← | **90 to 95 per cent for the design particle is the usual target** ← |

> **THE SHORT-CIRCUITING RISK IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMMONEST REASON A BASIN OF CORRECT COMPUTED LENGTH PERFORMS BADLY: if the flow enters as a jet and hugs one side or the floor, the effective length is a fraction of the constructed length and the rest of the tank is a dead zone.**

> **A well-designed inlet spreads the flow across the full width slowly — with a diverging transition of gentle angle, sometimes with baffles or a distribution wall — and this detail deserves as much attention as the length calculation itself.**

> **A basin 45 m long with a bad inlet may perform like one 20 m long with a good one, and no amount of extra length compensates for flow that never uses it.**

examTip.trick: **L = V·h/w** — the particle must fall the depth in the time it takes to travel the length. 0.30 × 3 / 0.02 = **45 m**.
examTip.trap: **Rearranged, the condition is w ≥ Q/(plan area) — so performance depends on PLAN AREA, not depth.** A shallower basin settles just as well; depth is for sediment storage.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stokes gives w proportional to d², so halving the design particle QUADRUPLES the length.** And add 20-50 % for turbulence, plus a gradual inlet, or the flow short-circuits and the length is wasted.

questions.stem: The LIMITING (design) particle size that the settling basin of a hydropower plant is required to remove becomes SMALLER as the plant's head becomes GREATER, because:
options: The discharge is smaller at high heads, so a finer particle can be afforded
High-head plants use longer settling basins in any case
Abrasive wear of the turbine rises steeply with the water's velocity, and the velocity at the runner is set by the head
The water becomes less dense at high heads
questions.solution:
**ABRASIVE WEAR rises steeply with the water's velocity, and the velocity at the runner is set by the head** — so a high-head machine is damaged by particles that a low-head machine tolerates.

**The mechanism:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The water's velocity at the runner follows from the head** ← | **V ≈ √(2gH), so a 400 m head gives about 88 m/s at a Pelton jet and a 20 m head about 20 m/s** ← |
| **A sediment particle strikes the metal at that velocity** ← | **And each impact removes a minute quantity of material** ← |
| **The rate of abrasive wear rises with a HIGH POWER of the velocity** ← | **Commonly taken as the CUBE, and sometimes higher — so tripling the velocity increases the wear roughly TWENTY-SEVENFOLD** ← |
| **So the same water that merely polishes a low-head Kaplan runner destroys a high-head Pelton bucket** ← | **The sediment is identical; the velocity is not** ← |
| **The settling basin must therefore be far more demanding at high heads** ← | **Removing finer particles, which means a much larger and costlier basin** ← |

> **THE CUBE LAW IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE WHOLE ANSWER AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING HOW SEVERE IT IS: wear is not a little worse at high head, it is worse by an order of magnitude or more.**

> **That single fact explains the entire design difference between a high-head and a low-head plant's headworks — the settling basin, the flushing arrangement and the turbine material selection all follow from it.**

**The design particle sizes in practice:**

| Plant type | Head | Design particle to be removed |
|---|---|---|
| **PELTON, high head** ← | **Above about 250 m** | **0.1 to 0.2 mm — the most demanding** ← |
| **FRANCIS, medium head** ← | **50 to 250 m** | **About 0.2 to 0.3 mm** ← |
| **KAPLAN / propeller, low head** ← | **Below about 50 m** | **0.5 mm or coarser — often only a gravel trap is needed** ← |

> **THE PELTON ROW IS THE UNCOMFORTABLE ONE FOR NEPALI SCHEMES, AND IT IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT ABOUT WHY, because it is where the country's geography and its engineering collide.**

> **Nepal's rivers offer very high heads, which favour Pelton and high-head Francis machines.**

> **The same rivers, draining a young and rapidly eroding mountain range, carry among the highest sediment concentrations in the world — and much of that sediment is QUARTZ, which is harder than the steel of a turbine runner.**

> **So the country's best hydropower resource comes with the worst possible sediment problem attached, and the two are geologically linked: the uplift that creates the head creates the erosion.**

> **That is why the settling basin is frequently the largest single structure in a Nepali run-of-river scheme, and why it can absorb a substantial share of the civil cost.**

**The responses available to the designer, in order of preference:**

| Response | Note |
|---|---|
| **A properly sized SETTLING BASIN** ← | **The primary defence — remove the particles before they reach the machine** ← |
| **HARD COATINGS on the runner — tungsten carbide, ceramic** ← | **Greatly extending the life of the wearing surfaces** ← |
| **HARDER runner materials, and replaceable wearing parts** ← | **Pelton buckets and Francis guide vanes designed to be renewed** ← |
| **Shutting down during the WORST of the monsoon** ← | **Deliberately foregoing generation while the sediment concentration is extreme — sometimes the cheapest option overall** ← |
| **Accepting the wear and overhauling frequently** | **Which costs generation as well as money** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A GENUINELY COUNTER-INTUITIVE OPERATING DECISION AND IT IS MADE IN PRACTICE: a plant may be shut down at the very time the river is highest and generation would be greatest.**

> **The arithmetic is that a few days of extreme sediment concentration can do more damage than months of ordinary operation, and the repair cost plus the outage for the overhaul exceeds the value of the energy foregone.**

> **Making that judgment requires actual measurement of the sediment concentration rather than an assumption — which is why continuous turbidity monitoring at the intake is a worthwhile investment on a high-head Himalayan plant, and why the sediment record from the feasibility studies matters as much as the flow record.**

examTip.trick: **Wear rises with roughly the CUBE of the velocity, and velocity is about √(2gH)** — so a high-head machine is destroyed by particles a low-head machine merely polishes.
examTip.trap: **Pelton 0.1-0.2 mm, Francis 0.2-0.3 mm, Kaplan 0.5 mm or coarser.** The finer the target, the larger the basin, which is why it can be the biggest structure on a Nepali scheme.
examTip.mnemonic: **The uplift that creates the head creates the erosion** — Nepal's best heads come with the worst sediment, and much of it is quartz, harder than the runner steel.

questions.stem: For an UNLINED or lightly lined PRESSURE TUNNEL, the minimum ROCK COVER is governed by the requirement that:
options: The tunnel must be deep enough for the excavated rock to be self-supporting
The weight of the overlying rock, measured perpendicular to the ground surface, must exceed the internal water pressure by a factor of safety
The rock cover must exceed three times the tunnel diameter in all cases
The temperature of the rock must remain constant along the tunnel
questions.solution:
**The WEIGHT of the overlying rock, measured PERPENDICULAR to the ground surface, must exceed the internal water pressure with a factor of safety** — otherwise the water hydraulically jacks the rock apart and escapes.

**The mechanism of failure:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The tunnel carries water at high internal pressure** ← | **Up to the full static head of the scheme above it** ← |
| **That pressure acts OUTWARD on the rock, in every direction** ← | **Not merely downward or upward** ← |
| **If it exceeds the confining stress from the rock's own weight, it OPENS the joints** ← | **Water enters the joint, and the pressure then acts over a larger area, opening it further** ← |
| **The process runs away — HYDRAULIC JACKING** ← | **The rock mass is progressively split and the water escapes to the surface or to a valley side** ← |
| **The consequence can be catastrophic** ← | **Loss of the water, a landslide on the hillside above, and a tunnel that cannot be repressurised** ← |

> **THE RUNAWAY CHARACTER IN THE FOURTH ROW IS WHAT MAKES THIS A LIMIT STATE RATHER THAN A SERVICEABILITY MATTER: the failure is not a gradual leak that can be grouted, it is a progressive splitting that gets worse as it proceeds.**

> **Once the water has found a path to daylight, the tunnel cannot be operated at pressure at all, and the remedy is a full steel lining of the affected reach — enormously expensive and requiring a long outage.**

**The criterion, in its usual form:**

| Form | Expression |
|---|---|
| **The basic requirement** | **γ_rock × h × cos α ≥ F × γ_water × H** ← |
| **Where** | **h is the rock cover, α the surface slope, H the internal head, F a factor of safety of about 1.3 to 1.5** ← |
| **Rearranged, roughly** ← | **h ≥ F × H × (γ_water / γ_rock) / cos α, which comes to about H/2 for typical rock on flat ground** ← |
| **The Norwegian rule of thumb** ← | **The cover must be about HALF the static head, increased where the surface slopes** ← |

> **THE ROUGH RESULT IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE TO CARRY, AND ITS ORIGIN IS SIMPLE: rock weighs roughly 2.6 times as much as water, so with a factor of safety of about 1.3 the required cover comes out at about half the head.**

> **A tunnel with 200 m of static head therefore needs roughly 100 m of rock above it — and being able to reconstruct that from the densities means the criterion never has to be looked up.**

**THE cos α TERM IS THE PART MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG AND IT MATTERS MOST WHERE IT IS EASIEST TO MISS:**

| Situation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **On FLAT ground, cos α = 1 and the vertical cover is the whole story** ← | **The simple case, and the one people picture** ← |
| **On a STEEP hillside, the cover must be measured PERPENDICULAR to the slope** ← | **Which is much less than the vertical depth below the surface directly overhead** ← |
| **The critical direction is toward the VALLEY SIDE, not upward** ← | **Because that is where the rock is thinnest** ← |
| **A tunnel with ample vertical cover can still fail sideways into a gorge** ← | **The classic error, and it has caused real failures** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL TRAP AND IT ARISES CONSTANTLY IN HIMALAYAN SCHEMES, where tunnels run along the flank of a deep valley.**

> **A designer who checks only the vertical depth to the surface concludes there is plenty of cover, while the shortest distance from the tunnel to daylight — horizontally out toward the gorge — may be a small fraction of it.**

> **The water does not care which direction is up; it will escape by whichever path offers the least resistance.**

> **So the check must be made on the MINIMUM distance to any free surface in any direction, and it is best done graphically on cross-sections taken along the tunnel — which is why the tunnel alignment on a steep valley flank is set back from the slope rather than following the shortest line.**

**And what to do where the cover is inadequate:**

| Response | Note |
|---|---|
| **STEEL LINING of the reach, anchored and backfilled with concrete** ← | **The reliable answer, and the reason the lower end of a pressure shaft is always steel-lined** ← |
| **Realign the tunnel deeper into the hillside** ← | **Cheaper if caught at the design stage** ← |
| **Consolidation GROUTING of the rock mass** | **Helps, but is not a substitute for cover** ← |
| **Reduce the internal pressure by relocating the surge tank or forebay** | **A planning-stage remedy only** ← |

> **The first row explains a feature of every high-head scheme that would otherwise look inconsistent: the headrace tunnel may be unlined or shotcreted, while the pressure shaft and the final reach to the powerhouse are lined in steel — because it is precisely there that the internal head is greatest and the rock cover, near the valley floor, is least.**

examTip.trick: **The overlying rock's weight must exceed the internal water pressure.** Rock is about 2.6 times water, so with F about 1.3 the cover works out at roughly HALF the head.
examTip.trap: **Measure the cover PERPENDICULAR to the slope, toward the VALLEY SIDE** — not vertically. A tunnel with ample vertical cover can still jack sideways into a gorge.
examTip.mnemonic: **Jacking runs away** — the water opens a joint, then acts over more area, and opens it further. Which is why the pressure shaft's lower reach is always steel-lined.

questions.stem: A DIFFERENTIAL (Johnson) surge tank differs from a simple surge tank in that it contains:
options: An internal riser of small diameter connected to the outer tank through ports
Two separate tanks placed at different points along the tunnel
A tank whose diameter increases with height
A closed tank with a cushion of compressed air above the water surface
questions.solution:
**An internal RISER of small diameter connected to the outer tank through ports** — so the riser's level changes rapidly to supply the accelerating head, while the outer tank stores the surplus water and the oscillation is damped faster.

**The types of surge tank:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE (cylindrical)** ← | **A plain shaft open to the atmosphere — the reference case; large amplitude, slow damping** ← |
| **RESTRICTED ORIFICE (throttled)** ← | **A restriction at the junction with the tunnel, which dissipates energy and damps the surge — at the cost of a higher pressure rise in the tunnel** ← |
| **DIFFERENTIAL (Johnson)** ← | **An internal riser plus an outer tank — this question; combines fast response with storage** ← |
