| **EXPANSION CHAMBER type** ← | **A shaft with enlarged chambers at the upper and lower extremes, to limit the surge amplitude economically** ← |
| **AIR CUSHION (closed) surge chamber** ← | **A sealed chamber with compressed air above the water — used where no shaft to the surface is practicable** ← (option d) |
| **CONICAL / tapering** | **Cross-section varying with height** ← (option c) |

> **THE PROGRESSION FROM THE FIRST TO THE THIRD ROW IS A RESPONSE TO A CONFLICT INHERENT IN THE SIMPLE TANK, and identifying that conflict is the key to the whole subject.**

**What the conflict is:**

| Requirement | Implies |
|---|---|
| **To supply the ACCELERATING head quickly when the load increases, the level must change FAST** ← | **Which wants a SMALL cross-section** ← |
| **To absorb the surplus water when the load is rejected without an excessive rise, it must STORE a lot** ← | **Which wants a LARGE cross-section** ← |
| **A simple tank must choose one compromise diameter for both duties** ← | **And is therefore too sluggish for one or too small for the other** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENTIAL TANK RESOLVES THAT CONFLICT BY PROVIDING BOTH CROSS-SECTIONS AT ONCE, and the arrangement is elegant:**

| Element | Duty |
|---|---|
| **The narrow inner RISER, connected directly to the tunnel** ← | **Its level rises and falls RAPIDLY, immediately generating the retarding or accelerating head the tunnel needs** ← |
| **The large outer TANK, connected only through small PORTS** ← | **It fills and empties SLOWLY, providing the storage volume** ← |
| **On load rejection** ← | **The riser level shoots up at once, decelerating the tunnel flow promptly, and the surplus then spills over the riser's top into the outer tank** ← |
| **On load acceptance** ← | **The riser level falls at once, accelerating the tunnel flow, and the outer tank feeds it through the ports** ← |
| **Net effect** ← | **A faster response AND a smaller surge amplitude than a simple tank of the same total volume — the oscillation dies away in fewer cycles** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE WHERE THE BENEFIT ACTUALLY ARISES AND THEY REPAY A CAREFUL READING: the useful trick is that the riser gives the TUNNEL its signal immediately, while the storage is dealt with at leisure.**

> **In a simple tank those two things happen in the same vessel at the same rate, so a tank big enough to store is slow to signal, and the tunnel keeps accelerating for longer before it feels the change.**

> **Separating the functions means neither compromises the other, which is why a differential tank can be materially smaller in total volume than a simple tank giving the same performance.**

**Why any of this matters, which is the underlying purpose:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A surge tank's function is to protect the TUNNEL from water hammer and to supply or absorb water during load changes** ← | **The pressure wave is reflected at the tank and does not travel up the tunnel** ← |
| **It converts the sudden pressure wave into a slow MASS OSCILLATION of the water column** ← | **Which the tunnel can withstand** ← |
| **It also improves the plant's SPEED REGULATION** ← | **Because the governor can open the turbine faster when there is a nearby reservoir of water to draw on** ← |
| **The damping matters as much as the amplitude** ← | **An undamped oscillation of many cycles interferes with the governor and can make the plant unstable on isolated operation** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE REASON DAMPING IS WORTH PAYING FOR AND IT IS EASILY OVERLOOKED: an oscillation that merely persists, even at a modest amplitude, feeds back into the governor.**

> **The governor sees the head varying, adjusts the gate, and the adjustment excites the oscillation further — the classic instability of a hydropower plant with an under-damped conveyance system, and the reason a plant may be perfectly stable on a stiff grid and unstable when islanded.**

> **A restricted orifice or a differential tank addresses that directly by dissipating the oscillation's energy, and the choice between them turns on whether the extra pressure rise the throttle causes in the tunnel can be accommodated.**

Damping the oscillation faster.

examTip.trick: **A narrow inner riser for FAST response plus a large outer tank for STORAGE**, joined by ports. Option (d) is the air-cushion chamber, (c) the conical tank.
examTip.trap: **The simple tank's conflict: fast response wants a SMALL section, storage wants a LARGE one.** A differential tank supplies both, so it can be smaller in total volume for the same performance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Damping matters as much as amplitude** — a persistent oscillation feeds back into the governor and can destabilise the plant when islanded, even at modest amplitude.

questions.stem: A Pelton turbine works under a net head of 250 m at 500 rpm. Taking the coefficient of velocity of the nozzle as 0.98 and the speed ratio as 0.46, the runner's pitch diameter is about:
questions.solution:
**About 1.21 m.**

**The three steps:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **1. The JET velocity** | **V = C_v √(2gH) = 0.98 × √(2 × 9.81 × 250)** ← |
| **The square root** | **√4905 = 70.04 m/s, so V = 0.98 × 70.04 = 68.64 m/s** ← |
| **2. The BUCKET (peripheral) velocity** | **u = φ V = 0.46 × 68.64 = 31.57 m/s** ← |
| **3. The DIAMETER from u = πDN/60** | **D = 60u / (πN) = 60 × 31.57 / (π × 500)** ← |
| **Evaluating** | **= 1894.4 / 1570.8 = 1.206 m, about 1.21 m** ← |

> **So the pitch diameter is about 1.21 m.**

**THE SPEED RATIO OF 0.46 IS THE ONE FIGURE IN THIS CALCULATION THAT LOOKS ARBITRARY, AND IT IS NOT — IT IS VERY NEARLY A THEORETICAL RESULT:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **The power a jet delivers to a moving bucket is maximum when u = V/2** ← | **A standard result from the impulse momentum analysis** ← |
| **So the ideal speed ratio is EXACTLY 0.5** ← | **On the ideal analysis, with no losses** ← |
| **In practice 0.44 to 0.48 is used, commonly 0.46** ← | **Slightly below the ideal, to allow for windage, bearing friction and the fact that the bucket does not deflect the jet through a full 180 degrees** ← |
| **The power curve is FLAT near its maximum** ← | **So the small departure from 0.5 costs almost nothing in efficiency** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE REASON THE PRACTICAL VALUE CAN DEPART FROM THE THEORETICAL ONE SO CASUALLY, and it is a general lesson about optimisation: near a maximum, the function is flat.**

> **Running at 0.46 instead of 0.50 changes the power by a fraction of a per cent, because the efficiency curve is a parabola with its vertex at 0.5 — so the designer is free to choose the speed ratio on other grounds, such as obtaining a convenient synchronous speed.**

**And that freedom is exactly what makes the design work, which is worth spelling out:**

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **The generator's speed is NOT free — it must be a SYNCHRONOUS speed** ← | **N = 120f/p, so at 50 Hz only 3000, 1500, 1000, 750, 600, 500, 375 rpm and so on are available** ← |
| **The head is fixed by the site** ← | **So the jet velocity is fixed** ← |
| **The diameter therefore follows from the chosen speed** ← | **As in this calculation** ← |
| **And the JET RATIO m = D/d must come out sensible** ← | **Normally 10 to 14 for a Pelton wheel; below about 9 the buckets interfere and above about 16 the wheel is needlessly large** ← |

> **THE JET RATIO IN THE LAST ROW IS THE CHECK THAT CLOSES THE PRELIMINARY DESIGN, and it is what decides how many jets the machine needs.**

> **If the discharge is large, a single jet of the diameter required would give a jet ratio below the acceptable range — the jet too big for the wheel.**

> **The remedy is to split the flow between SEVERAL jets: two, four or six nozzles round the same wheel, each carrying a fraction of the discharge, so each jet is small enough to give an acceptable ratio.**

> **A multi-jet Pelton is therefore not a refinement but a necessity at higher discharges, and the number of jets is determined by this geometric constraint rather than chosen for convenience.**

**The other quantities in a Pelton preliminary design, for completeness:**

| Quantity | Usual value |
|---|---|
| **Number of BUCKETS** | **Z ≈ 15 + D/(2d) = 15 + m/2 — about 20 to 22 for a jet ratio of 12** ← |
| **Bucket WIDTH** | **About 3 to 4 times the jet diameter** ← |
| **Bucket DEPTH** | **About 0.8 to 1.2 times the jet diameter** ← |
| **Deflection angle of the jet** | **160 to 170 degrees — not 180, or the outgoing water would strike the following bucket** ← |
| **Specific speed range** | **8 to 30 for a single jet, rising with the number of jets** ← |

> **The deflection angle in the fourth row is a good instance of theory yielding to practicality: the momentum analysis says 180 degrees extracts the most work, and the geometry of a wheel says that the water leaving one bucket would then hit the next.**

> **The 165 degrees actually used sacrifices about one per cent of the theoretical work to send the discharge clear of the runner — and that trade, like the speed ratio, is affordable precisely because the loss near the optimum is second-order.**

examTip.trick: **V = C_v√(2gH), then u = φV, then D = 60u/(πN).** 68.64, then 31.57, then **1.21 m**. Three steps, in that order.
examTip.trap: **The speed ratio 0.46 is not arbitrary** — maximum power is at u = V/2 exactly, and 0.44-0.48 is used for windage and the sub-180° deflection. The curve is flat there, so it costs nothing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the jet ratio m = D/d: 10 to 14.** If a single jet would give less, split the flow between several nozzles, which is why multi-jet Peltons exist at all.

questions.stem: The FIRST highway constructed in Nepal was the:
options: Araniko Highway, from Kathmandu to Kodari
Prithvi Highway, from Kathmandu to Pokhara
TRIBHUVAN highway (Tribhuvan Rajpath)
Mahendra Highway, running east to west across the Terai
questions.solution:
**The TRIBHUVAN HIGHWAY (Tribhuvan Rajpath), from Kathmandu through Naubise and Hetauda to Birgunj, opened in 1956.**

**The principal highways of Nepal, in the order they were built:**

| Highway | Route | Opened |
|---|---|---|
| **TRIBHUVAN (Rajpath)** ← | **Kathmandu — Naubise — Hetauda — Birgunj; about 200 km** ← | **1956, with Indian assistance — the FIRST** ← |
| **ARANIKO (Kodari)** ← | **Kathmandu — Bhaktapur — Barabise — Kodari, to the Tibetan border** ← (option a) | **1967, with Chinese assistance** ← |
| **PRITHVI** ← | **Kathmandu — Naubise — Mugling — Pokhara** ← (option b) | **1973, with Chinese assistance** ← |
| **MAHENDRA (East-West)** ← | **Mechi to Mahakali across the Terai; about 1,028 km — the LONGEST** ← (option d) | **Built in stages from the 1960s** ← |
| **SIDDHARTHA** | **Sunauli — Butwal — Pokhara** | **1968-72** |
| **B P Koirala (Banepa-Bardibas)** | **A shorter Kathmandu-Terai route** | **2015** |

> **THE 1956 DATE IS WORTH SETTING BESIDE THE 1911 DATE FOR PHARPING, and the contrast is instructive: Nepal had hydroelectric power for forty-five years before it had a single highway.**

> **Before the Rajpath, Kathmandu was reached on foot or by porter over the hills, with a ropeway carrying freight from Hetauda — so the valley's first motor cars had been carried in on poles.**

> **The Rajpath therefore marks the beginning of the country's road era rather than merely one road among several, and Nepal's road network is consequently very young: essentially all of it postdates 1956.**

**Why the ROUTE of the Rajpath is itself a lesson in alignment:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **It crosses the Mahabharat range at a summit above 2,400 m** ← | **Rising from about 300 m at Hetauda and descending again to Kathmandu at 1,300 m** ← |
| **Extremely tortuous, with hundreds of hairpin bends** ← | **The classic hill-road alignment problem, solved by developing length rather than gradient** ← |
| **It follows a RIDGE for much of its length** ← | **Ridge alignments are drier, more stable and less exposed to landslides than valley routes, though they demand more climbing** ← |
| **The Prithvi and later routes chose VALLEY alignments instead** ← | **Shorter and flatter, but far more exposed to landslides and to river erosion** ← |
| **Which is why the Rajpath, though slow, remains the more reliable route in the monsoon** ← | **A trade-off still argued about** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS SET OUT THE CENTRAL CHOICE IN HILL ROAD LOCATION AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY, because it recurs on every project in the hills.**

> **A RIDGE alignment is dry, geologically stable, needs few cross-drainage structures and is not threatened by the river — but it must climb to the ridge and descend again, so it is long, steep and slow.**

> **A VALLEY alignment follows the river at a gentle gradient and is much shorter — but it sits in the zone of active erosion, requires many bridges, and is cut by every landslide and every flood.**

> **Nepal's experience since 1956 has largely vindicated the ridge routes for reliability and the valley routes for economy, and the country has both — which is fortunate, because a network with alternative routes of different character is more robust than one built entirely to a single philosophy.**

> **That redundancy argument is a real planning consideration and not merely a consolation: when the Prithvi Highway closes for a landslide, traffic can still reach Kathmandu by the Rajpath or the B P Highway, and a network without such alternatives isolates the capital entirely.**

examTip.trick: **Tribhuvan Rajpath, Kathmandu-Birgunj, 1956** — the first. Then Araniko 1967, Siddhartha 1968-72, Prithvi 1973. Mahendra (East-West) is the longest at about 1,028 km.
examTip.trap: **Nepal had hydropower from 1911 but no highway until 1956** — the whole road network postdates the Rajpath, which is why it is so young.
examTip.mnemonic: **RIDGE alignments are dry, stable and slow; VALLEY alignments short, flat and landslide-prone.** The Rajpath is a ridge route, the Prithvi a valley one — and having both makes the network robust.

questions.stem: For carrying BULK commodities over LONG distances, the modes of transport ranked from the CHEAPEST to the dearest per tonne-kilometre are:
options: Inland waterways, then railway, then road, then air
Road, then railway, then inland waterways, then air
Air, then road, then railway, then inland waterways
Railway, then road, then air, then inland waterways
questions.solution:
**INLAND WATERWAYS, then RAILWAY, then ROAD, then AIR** — road transport being dearer per tonne-kilometre but unmatched for door-to-door flexibility.

**The modes compared:**

| Mode | Cost per tonne-km | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **INLAND WATERWAY / shipping** ← | **LOWEST** ← | **Very slow, very large loads, needs navigable water at both ends** ← |
| **RAILWAY** ← | **Low** ← | **Efficient for bulk over long hauls; needs a terminal at each end, and transhipment to road for delivery** ← |
| **ROAD** ← | **Moderate to high** ← | **DOOR TO DOOR with no transhipment — its decisive advantage** ← |
| **AIR** ← | **HIGHEST by a wide margin** ← | **Only for high-value, urgent or perishable goods, or where no surface access exists** ← |
| **PIPELINE** ← | **Very low for what it can carry** ← | **Only fluids, and only between fixed points** ← |
| **ROPEWAY / cableway** | **Low over difficult terrain** | **Fixed route, limited capacity, but crosses ground no road can** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE REASON ROAD TRANSPORT DOMINATES DESPITE NOT BEING THE CHEAPEST, and the point is easy to state and often missed: the cost per tonne-kilometre is not the cost of the journey.**

> **A rail consignment must be carted to the railhead, loaded, hauled, unloaded and carted again to its destination — and the two road legs plus two handlings can exceed the rail haul's own cost on a short journey.**

> **Road transport does the whole journey in one vehicle with one loading, so it wins on TOTAL cost for anything but long-distance bulk.**

> **The break-even distance below which road is cheaper overall is therefore considerable — commonly several hundred kilometres — and it lengthens as handling costs rise.**

**WHY THIS MATTERS PARTICULARLY IN NEPAL, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL POINT:**

| Circumstance | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Nepal is LANDLOCKED** ← | **All overseas trade passes through an Indian port and then overland — so transport cost is a permanent burden on every import and export** ← |
| **There are NO navigable inland waterways of consequence** ← | **The cheapest mode is simply unavailable** ← |
| **The railway network is minimal** ← | **A short line at Janakpur, and the new Jayanagar-Kurtha and Raxaul-Birgunj links — nothing that serves the hills** ← |
| **AIR is essential rather than a luxury in the mountains** ← | **Many districts have no road at all, so an airstrip is the only access, and freight costs are extraordinary** ← |
| **ROPEWAYS have a real place in Nepal** ← | **The Hetauda-Kathmandu ropeway carried the valley's freight for decades, and small gravity ropeways serve remote settlements still** ← |
| **Which leaves ROAD carrying essentially everything** ← | **On a network that is young, steep, and closed by landslides each monsoon** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS DESERVE MORE ATTENTION THAN THEY USUALLY RECEIVE, because they represent modes that are marginal elsewhere and central here.**

> **In a country of deep valleys and high ridges, a ropeway or a cable crossing can deliver goods over ground where a road would cost a hundred times as much per tonne delivered and would be closed half the year.**

> **Gravity ropeways, which need no power at all because the descending loaded carrier lifts the ascending empty one, are in use for carrying produce down from hill farms — and they are a genuinely appropriate technology rather than a curiosity.**

> **The engineering lesson is that the ranking of modes by cost per tonne-kilometre is a general statement about flat, well-connected countries, and the correct choice on any particular route depends on the terrain, the distance, the volume and the value of what is being moved.**

> **A mode that is uneconomic in general may be the only sensible answer in a particular valley — which is why transport planning is a matter of examining each corridor rather than applying a national preference.**

Road transport being dearer per tonne-km but unmatched for door-to-door flexibility.

examTip.trick: **Waterway < rail < road < air**, cheapest to dearest per tonne-km. Pipeline is very cheap for fluids between fixed points.
examTip.trap: **Cost per tonne-km is not the cost of the JOURNEY** — rail needs two road legs and two handlings, so road wins on total cost below a break-even of some hundreds of km.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepal is landlocked with no waterways and almost no rail, so road carries everything** — and ropeways, marginal elsewhere, are genuinely appropriate in deep valleys.

questions.stem: A SUMMIT (crest) vertical curve on a highway is set out as a simple PARABOLA rather than as a circular arc because the parabola:
options: Gives a longer curve for the same grades, and hence a greater sight distance
Is the only shape on which a vehicle experiences no centrifugal force
Reduces the earthwork required at the summit
Gives a rate of change of grade that is constant along the curve, and its offsets from the tangent are simple to compute
questions.solution:
**It gives a rate of change of grade that is CONSTANT along the curve, and its offsets from the tangent are simple to compute** — while for the flat grades used on roads it is very nearly identical to a circular arc in any case.

**The reasons, in order of weight:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The rate of change of grade is CONSTANT** ← | **Which gives the smoothest possible transition from one grade to the other, and a constant vertical acceleration** ← |
| **The OFFSETS are simple** ← | **The offset from the tangent varies as the SQUARE of the distance, so levels along the curve are computed in one line of arithmetic** ← |
| **It is EASY to set out in the field** ← | **Levels at regular chainages, computed from the tangent** ← |
| **For flat grades the difference from a circular arc is NEGLIGIBLE** ← | **Road grades are a few per cent, so the two curves are almost coincident — the choice is one of convenience, not of behaviour** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE POINT THAT MAKES THE WHOLE MATTER UNDRAMATIC AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT: the parabola is not chosen because a circular arc would perform badly.**

> **At the gradients used on highways — say 2 to 6 per cent — a parabola and a circular arc of the same length differ by millimetres.**

> **The parabola is chosen because the ARITHMETIC is easier, and that mattered a great deal when curves were computed by hand.**

> **It is a good example of a design convention adopted for computational convenience that has been retained because it works perfectly well and everyone is used to it.**

**The geometry, for use:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **The deviation angle** | **N = n₁ − n₂, the algebraic difference of the grades** ← |
| **The offset at distance x from the tangent point** | **y = N x² / (2L), for a curve of length L** ← |
| **The offset at the MID-POINT (the greatest)** | **y_mid = N L / 8** ← |
| **The highest point's position** | **At x = n₁ L / N from the first tangent point** ← |

> **THE SIGN CONVENTION IN THE FIRST ROW IS WHERE MOST ERRORS ARISE AND IT IS WORTH FIXING FIRMLY: upgrades are POSITIVE and downgrades NEGATIVE, and N is their ALGEBRAIC difference.**

> **So a +3 per cent grade meeting a −2 per cent grade gives N = 3 − (−2) = 5 per cent, not 1 per cent.**

> **A SUMMIT curve has N positive; a VALLEY (sag) curve has N negative.**

> **Getting that wrong produces a curve of the wrong sign and a design that is nonsense, and it is the single commonest slip in vertical alignment work.**

**And the LENGTH of the curve, which is the design decision the parabola merely accommodates:**

| Governing criterion | Note |
|---|---|
| **SUMMIT curve: SIGHT DISTANCE** ← | **The curve must be long enough that a driver can see the required stopping (or overtaking) distance over the crest — this alone governs** ← |
| **Not comfort** ← | **Because on a summit the centrifugal force acts UPWARD, relieving the vehicle's weight, so it is felt as a slight lightness rather than as discomfort** ← |
| **VALLEY curve: HEADLIGHT sight distance and COMFORT both** ← | **On a sag, the centrifugal force adds to the weight and is felt, and the headlight beam limits the visibility at night** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW EXPLAINS WHY THE TWO KINDS OF VERTICAL CURVE ARE DESIGNED BY DIFFERENT CRITERIA, and the asymmetry is worth understanding rather than memorising.**

> **Over a crest, the vehicle's path curves downward, so the centrifugal effect acts away from the road and the occupants feel LIGHTER — mildly pleasant, and never a controlling consideration.**

> **In a sag, the path curves upward, the centrifugal effect presses the vehicle into the road, and the occupants feel HEAVIER — which becomes uncomfortable, and is limited to about 0.6 m/s² of vertical acceleration.**

> **By day a sag curve poses no sight distance problem at all, since the driver can see right across it; by night the headlights illuminate only a limited distance ahead because the beam runs off the rising road.**

> **So the summit curve is a daylight geometry problem and the sag curve a night-time and comfort problem — the same structure, designed for entirely different reasons.**

examTip.trick: **Constant rate of change of grade and offsets varying as x²** — chosen for computational convenience, since at road gradients a parabola and a circular arc differ by millimetres.
examTip.trap: **N = n₁ − n₂ ALGEBRAICALLY** — a +3 % meeting a −2 % gives N = 5 %, not 1 %. Positive N is a summit, negative a sag. The commonest slip in vertical alignment.
examTip.mnemonic: **Summit = sight distance only** (the centrifugal force lifts, so comfort never governs). **Sag = headlight distance AND comfort** (the force presses down and is felt).

questions.stem: The DUCTILITY test on a paving bitumen measures:
options: The depth in tenths of a millimetre to which a standard needle penetrates the sample
The distance in centimetres to which a standard briquette of the bitumen can be stretched before the thread breaks, at 27 °C and a pull of 50 mm per minute
The temperature at which the bitumen becomes soft enough for a steel ball to sink through it
The loss in mass of the sample when heated in a thin film at 163 °C
questions.solution:
**The DISTANCE IN CENTIMETRES to which a standard briquette of the bitumen can be stretched before the thread breaks** — at 27 °C and a pull of 50 mm per minute.

**The test:**

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| **The sample is cast in a standard BRIQUETTE mould** ← | **A dumbbell shape with a minimum cross-section of 1 cm²** ← |
| **Conditioned and tested in a water bath at 27 °C** ← | **The standard test temperature** ← |
| **Pulled apart at 50 mm per minute** ← | **The two clips separating at a constant rate** ← |
| **The distance at which the thread SNAPS is the ductility, in cm** ← | **The result, read directly off the machine's scale** ← |
| **Specified minima of about 40 to 75 cm, depending on the grade** ← | **VG-30, for example, requires at least 40 cm** ← |

> **WHAT THE TEST IS ACTUALLY FOR IS WORTH STATING, BECAUSE THE MEASURED QUANTITY LOOKS ARTIFICIAL: a bitumen that stretches a long way before breaking has the capacity to deform without cracking.**

> **A pavement's binder must accommodate the repeated flexing of the layer under traffic and the thermal movement of the surface through the day and the seasons.**

> **A brittle binder cracks instead of stretching, and the cracks then admit water — which is the beginning of most pavement failures.**

> **So the ductility figure is a proxy for the binder's ability to hold the mixture together under strain, and a low ductility is a warning of a pavement that will crack early.**

**The tests on bitumen, gathered — since they are constantly confused with one another:**

| Test | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **PENETRATION** ← | **Depth in tenths of a mm to which a standard needle sinks in 5 s under 100 g at 25 °C — a measure of CONSISTENCY** ← (option a) |
| **SOFTENING POINT (ring and ball)** ← | **The temperature at which a steel ball sinks through the sample in a brass ring** ← (option c) |
| **DUCTILITY** ← | **Stretch in cm before the thread breaks — this question** ← |
| **VISCOSITY (absolute, at 60 °C)** ← | **The basis of the VG grading system — VG-30 means 3,000 poise at 60 °C** ← |
| **THIN FILM OVEN / loss on heating** ← | **The change after ageing in a thin film at 163 °C — a durability test** ← (option d) |
| **FLASH and FIRE point** | **The temperature at which vapours ignite — a safety limit for handling** ← |
| **SPECIFIC GRAVITY** | **Usually 0.97 to 1.02, needed for volumetric calculations in mix design** ← |
| **SOLUBILITY in trichloroethylene** | **Purity — should exceed 99 per cent** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW MARKS THE MOST IMPORTANT CHANGE IN BITUMEN SPECIFICATION IN RECENT DECADES AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING WHY IT HAPPENED: grading has moved from PENETRATION to VISCOSITY.**

> **The penetration test is made at 25 °C, which is nothing like the temperature at which a pavement actually works — a road surface in the Terai reaches 60 °C and more.**

> **Two bitumens of identical penetration at 25 °C can behave quite differently at 60 °C, so a penetration grade does not reliably predict performance in service.**

> **Viscosity grading measures the binder at 60 °C, close to the maximum pavement temperature, and therefore discriminates between binders on the property that matters — which is why IS 73 was revised to the VG system and why the VG designation is now the one quoted in specifications.**

> **The penetration test remains in use as a quick consistency check and appears in older documents, so both systems must be recognised — but a specification written today calls for VG-30 or VG-40, not for 60/70 or 80/100 penetration grade.**

examTip.trick: **Stretch in CENTIMETRES before the thread breaks**, at 27 °C and 50 mm/min. Option (a) is penetration, (c) softening point, (d) the thin film oven test.
examTip.trap: **Ductility is a proxy for crack resistance** — a brittle binder cracks rather than stretching, and the cracks admit water. That is how most pavement failures begin.
examTip.mnemonic: **Penetration is measured at 25 °C, viscosity at 60 °C** — and a pavement works at 60 °C, which is exactly why grading moved from penetration to the VG system.

questions.stem: In the design of a bituminous concrete mix, the AIR VOIDS (Va) in the compacted specimen are required to lie in a narrow band of about 3 to 5 per cent because:
options: Air voids have no effect on performance, and the band is a purely conventional requirement
A higher voids content always improves the mix's stability
Too few voids leave no room for the binder to expand in hot weather
Voids are needed to allow water to drain freely through the surfacing
questions.solution:
**TOO FEW voids leave no room for the binder to expand in hot weather, so the mix bleeds and ruts; too many admit air and water, so the binder oxidises and the mix ravels and strips.**

**The two failure directions:**

| Voids too LOW (below about 3 %) | Voids too HIGH (above about 5 %) |
|---|---|
| **The binder fills the voids completely** ← | **The mix is permeable to air and water** ← |
| **On a hot day the bitumen EXPANDS with nowhere to go** ← | **The binder OXIDISES and hardens — it ages rapidly** ← |
| **It is squeezed to the surface — BLEEDING and a slippery, fatty surface** ← | **Water reaches the aggregate-binder bond and STRIPPING follows** ← |
| **The mix loses internal friction and RUTS under wheel loads** ← | **The mix RAVELS — aggregate is progressively dislodged** ← |
| **A plastic, unstable mix** ← | **A brittle, disintegrating mix** ← |

> **THE NARROW BAND EXISTS BECAUSE THE TWO FAILURE MODES APPROACH FROM OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, and that is the whole answer: there is no safe side to err on.**

> **Almost every other quantity in engineering has a conservative direction — more steel, thicker concrete, deeper foundations.**

> **Air voids do not: a mix with 2 per cent voids fails by rutting and bleeding, and one with 7 per cent fails by ravelling and stripping.**

> **The designer must land inside the band, which is why mix design is a matter of trial mixes at several binder contents rather than a calculation.**

**The volumetric quantities in a bituminous mix, which must be distinguished:**

| Quantity | Meaning | Typical requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Va — AIR VOIDS** ← | **The voids filled with AIR, as a percentage of the total volume** ← | **3 to 5 %** ← |
| **VMA — VOIDS IN THE MINERAL AGGREGATE** ← | **The total void space BETWEEN the aggregate particles — air plus binder** ← | **A minimum depending on the nominal maximum aggregate size, commonly 12 to 15 %** ← |
| **VFB — VOIDS FILLED WITH BITUMEN** ← | **The percentage of the VMA that the binder occupies** ← | **65 to 75 %** ← |
| **The relation between them** | **VFB = (VMA − Va) / VMA × 100** ← | ← |

> **THE VMA MINIMUM IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE REQUIREMENT MOST OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD, AND ITS PURPOSE IS SPECIFIC: it guarantees that there is ENOUGH ROOM for an adequate film of binder.**

> **A very densely graded aggregate can have such small voids between its particles that the correct air voids content is achieved with hardly any bitumen at all.**

> **The mix then satisfies the air voids requirement while having a binder film so thin that it oxidises through in a few years and the pavement fails by ravelling.**

> **So the VMA minimum is a durability requirement rather than a strength one, and it constrains the AGGREGATE GRADING rather than the binder content: a grading that cannot achieve the minimum VMA must be changed, not compensated for with more bitumen.**

> **This is the reason a mix cannot be designed on air voids alone, and the reason the gradation and the binder content have to be settled together.**

**And the practical consequence for CONSTRUCTION, which is where the design is won or lost:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **The design voids are achieved in the laboratory at a specified compactive effort** ← | **75 blows per face in the Marshall method for heavy traffic** ← |
| **The field compaction must reach the same density** ← | **Usually specified as a percentage of the laboratory or the job-mix density** ← |
| **UNDER-compaction in the field leaves the voids TOO HIGH** ← | **So a correctly designed mix ravels and strips because it was rolled too little or too cold** ← |
| **Which is why rolling temperature and the number of passes are specified and checked** ← | **A mix design is only as good as the compaction that realises it** ← |

> **The third row is the commonest cause of premature failure in bituminous surfacing, and it is a construction failure rather than a design one: the mix leaving the plant may be exactly right, and the pavement still fails because the voids in the laid layer are 8 per cent instead of 4.**

> **Field density testing by core cutting is therefore not a formality but the check that the designed mix actually exists in the road — and where it is omitted, the design's careful voids band means very little.**

examTip.trick: **Too low: the binder expands, bleeds and the mix ruts. Too high: air and water get in, the binder oxidises, and it ravels and strips.** No safe side to err on.
examTip.trap: **VMA is a DURABILITY requirement constraining the GRADING** — a too-dense aggregate meets the air voids with too little bitumen, giving a film that oxidises through in years.
examTip.mnemonic: **VFB = (VMA − Va)/VMA × 100.** And under-compaction in the field ruins a correct mix — 8 % voids in the road instead of 4 % is a construction failure, not a design one.

questions.stem: At a signalised intersection the total lost time per cycle is 12 seconds and the sum of the critical flow ratios (Y) is 0.60. By Webster's formula, the OPTIMUM cycle length is:
questions.solution:
**57.5 seconds.**

**Webster's formula:**

| Element | Expression |
|---|---|
| **The optimum cycle length** | **C₀ = (1.5 L + 5) / (1 − Y)** ← |
| **L** | **The total LOST TIME per cycle, in seconds** ← |
| **Y** | **The sum of the CRITICAL flow ratios (q/s) for the phases** ← |

**The calculation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Numerator** | **1.5 × 12 + 5 = 18 + 5 = 23** ← |
| **Denominator** | **1 − 0.60 = 0.40** ← |
| **C₀** | **= 23 / 0.40 = 57.5 s** ← |

> **So the optimum cycle length is 57.5 seconds, which would be rounded up to 60 s in practice.**

**WHAT 'OPTIMUM' MEANS HERE IS WORTH BEING PRECISE ABOUT, because the word is doing specific work:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The cycle is optimum in the sense of MINIMISING the total DELAY to all vehicles** ← | **Not maximising capacity, and not minimising the delay to any one movement** ← |
| **The delay curve is FLAT near the optimum** ← | **So any cycle from about 0.75 C₀ to 1.5 C₀ gives nearly the same total delay** ← |
| **Which gives the designer latitude to round to a convenient value** ← | **And to satisfy the minimum green requirements for pedestrians** ← |

> **THE FLATNESS IN THE SECOND ROW IS THE SAME KIND OF OBSERVATION MADE ABOUT THE PELTON SPEED RATIO, and it has the same practical value: precision in the answer is not needed, because the penalty for departing from it is small.**

> **Computing C₀ as 57.5 s and adopting 60 s costs almost nothing in delay, and 60 s divides conveniently into phases.**

> **What DOES matter is not straying far outside the range: a cycle much too short wastes a large fraction of the time on lost time, and one much too long leaves vehicles waiting through a long red for no benefit.**

**The structure of the formula, which shows what drives the answer:**

| Observation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **As Y approaches 1.0, the denominator approaches ZERO and C₀ approaches INFINITY** ← | **Meaning the intersection is at capacity and NO cycle length will serve it — the signal cannot help** ← |
| **A larger LOST TIME lengthens the cycle** ← | **Which is why the number of PHASES matters so much: each phase adds its own lost time** ← |
| **A four-phase signal has roughly twice the lost time of a two-phase one** ← | **And therefore a much longer cycle and much more delay** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL DIAGNOSTIC THE FORMULA OFFERS AND IT SHOULD BE READ AS A WARNING RATHER THAN AS A CALCULATION: if Y comes out near or above 1.0, the arithmetic is telling you that the intersection is oversaturated.**

> **No signal timing can then clear the demand, because the sum of the flows exceeds what the approaches can discharge even with all the green time allocated.**

> **The remedy is geometric or strategic — more lanes, a flyover, a restriction on turning movements, or diverting traffic elsewhere — and persisting with signal optimisation at that point is wasted effort.**

> **THE PHASE COUNT IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE DESIGN LEVER MOST OFTEN PULLED IN THE WRONG DIRECTION: adding a phase feels safer, because it separates conflicting movements.**

> **But each phase costs its own lost time — the intergreen and the start-up delay — and four phases can consume 20 seconds or more of every cycle in which no vehicle moves usefully.**

> **So a signal designer economises on phases, combining movements wherever it is safe to do so, and accepts an extra phase only where the conflict genuinely warrants it.**

> **That is a real trade between safety and capacity, and it is settled by judgment about the specific movements rather than by the formula, which only tells you what the phasing decision will cost.**

examTip.trap: **If Y approaches 1.0 the formula blows up** — that is the intersection telling you it is oversaturated and no timing will serve it. The remedy is geometric, not signal timing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Every extra PHASE adds its own lost time**, so a four-phase signal needs a much longer cycle. Economise on phases. And the delay curve is flat near C₀, so rounding costs nothing.

questions.stem: In a parking study, the PARKING LOAD is obtained as:
options: The number of vehicles parked at the time of the peak accumulation
The sum over all parked vehicles of the time each remained parked, expressed in VEHICLE-HOURS
The total number of vehicles that used the parking facility during the survey period
The ratio of the vehicles parked to the number of spaces available
questions.solution:
**The SUM over all parked vehicles of the TIME each remained parked, expressed in VEHICLE-HOURS.**

**The quantities a parking survey produces, which must be kept apart:**

| Quantity | Definition |
|---|---|
| **PARKING ACCUMULATION** ← | **The NUMBER of vehicles parked at a given instant — plotted against time of day** ← (option a is its peak) |
| **PARKING LOAD** ← | **The AREA under the accumulation curve — vehicle-hours; equivalently Σ (vehicles × duration)** ← |
| **PARKING VOLUME (turnover count)** ← | **The total NUMBER of vehicles that used the facility over the period** ← (option c) |
| **AVERAGE PARKING DURATION** ← | **= Parking load ÷ Parking volume — hours per vehicle** ← |
| **PARKING TURNOVER** ← | **= Parking volume ÷ number of spaces — vehicles per space per period** ← |
| **PARKING INDEX (occupancy)** ← | **= (Vehicles parked ÷ spaces available) × 100, as a percentage** ← (option d, as a ratio) |

> **THE SECOND AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER GIVE THE MOST USEFUL RESULT A PARKING SURVEY YIELDS, and the relation between them is worth holding: the load divided by the volume is the average duration.**

> **So a facility with a load of 400 vehicle-hours used by 200 vehicles has an average duration of 2 hours — and that single number tells you what KIND of parking demand you are dealing with.**

**Why the DURATION matters more than the count, which is the substance of parking planning:**

| Duration profile | Character and remedy |
|---|---|
| **SHORT durations, high turnover** ← | **Shoppers and visitors — each space serves many vehicles a day, so a few spaces meet a large demand** ← |
| **LONG durations, low turnover** ← | **Commuters and employees — each space serves ONE vehicle all day, so the same demand needs many times as many spaces** ← |
| **A mixture, with long-stay vehicles occupying the prime spaces** ← | **The commonest and worst case: all-day parkers take the kerbside spaces that shoppers need** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PROBLEM THAT PARKING POLICY EXISTS TO SOLVE, and it explains why parking is managed by TIME LIMITS and PRICING rather than simply by providing more spaces.**

> **A kerbside space in a commercial street can serve perhaps eight shoppers in a day if each stays half an hour, or one employee if he arrives at nine and leaves at five.**

> **So converting long-stay parking to short-stay multiplies the effective capacity eightfold without building anything — which is an enormous return for an administrative measure.**

> **That is achieved by time limits, by progressive charging that rises steeply with duration, and by providing cheaper long-stay parking away from the frontage where the commuters can go.**

> **Understanding this is what separates parking ENGINEERING from merely counting cars: the survey's purpose is to find out how long people stay, because that is the variable policy can actually change.**

**The survey methods, for completeness:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **IN-OUT survey** ← | **Count the initial occupancy, then the vehicles entering and leaving in each interval — gives accumulation and load but not individual durations** ← |
| **LICENSE PLATE method** ← | **Record the plates of all parked vehicles at fixed intervals — gives the duration of each vehicle, and hence everything else** ← |
| **Fixed period sampling** | **Occupancy counts at intervals, the simplest and least informative** ← |

> **The license plate method in the second row is much the most informative, because it is the only one that yields the DURATION DISTRIBUTION rather than an average — and the distribution is what matters, since it is the tail of long-stay vehicles that causes the problem rather than the mean.**

> **A facility with an average duration of two hours may consist entirely of two-hour parkers, or half of half-hour shoppers and half of all-day commuters, and those two situations call for completely different remedies from the same average.**

examTip.trick: **Parking load = vehicle-HOURS**, the area under the accumulation curve. Option (a) is peak accumulation, (c) parking volume, (d) the parking index.
examTip.trap: **Load ÷ volume = average duration** — and duration matters more than count. One all-day commuter occupies a space that could serve eight half-hour shoppers.
examTip.mnemonic: **Time limits and pricing multiply effective capacity without building anything.** And use the LICENSE PLATE method — only it gives the duration distribution, and the long-stay tail is the problem.

questions.stem: The RADIUS OF RELATIVE STIFFNESS (l) used in Westergaard's analysis of rigid pavements is:
options: The radius of the loaded area, expressed in terms of the slab thickness
A dimensionless ratio of the slab's modulus to the subgrade's modulus
The minimum radius of a horizontal curve on which a concrete pavement may be laid
A length, equal to the fourth root of E h³ / [12 k (1 − μ²)], which measures the stiffness of the slab relative to that of the subgrade and so governs the distance over which a wheel load is spread
questions.solution:
**A LENGTH**, equal to the fourth root of E h³ / [12 k (1 − μ²)], which measures the stiffness of the slab relative to that of the subgrade and so governs the distance over which a wheel load is spread.

**The expression:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **l** | **The radius of relative stiffness, in cm or m — a LENGTH, not a ratio** ← |
| **E** | **The modulus of elasticity of the concrete** ← |
| **h** | **The slab THICKNESS** ← |
| **k** | **The modulus of subgrade reaction, from the plate load test** ← |
| **μ** | **Poisson's ratio for the concrete, about 0.15** ← |
| **The form** | **l = [E h³ / (12 k (1 − μ²))]^(1/4)** ← |

> **THE PHYSICAL MEANING IS WORTH GETTING CLEAR, BECAUSE THE NAME IS OPAQUE AND THE FORMULA LOOKS FORBIDDING: l tells you how far from a wheel load the slab still carries appreciable stress.**

> **The numerator E h³ / 12 is the slab's FLEXURAL RIGIDITY — its resistance to bending.**

> **The denominator k is the subgrade's stiffness — its resistance to being pushed down.**

> **A stiff slab on a soft subgrade has a LARGE l: it bridges over the soft ground and distributes the load widely.**

> **A thin slab on a stiff subgrade has a SMALL l: the load is carried locally, almost directly down.**

**Why it appears in the analysis at all:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A rigid pavement is analysed as a SLAB ON AN ELASTIC FOUNDATION** ← | **The subgrade represented as a bed of independent springs of stiffness k — the Winkler model** ← |
| **The governing differential equation's solution contains the length l naturally** ← | **It is the characteristic length of the problem, exactly as it is for a beam on an elastic foundation** ← |
| **Every one of Westergaard's stress formulae uses l** ← | **Interior, edge and corner loading all express the stress in terms of the ratio of the load radius a to l** ← |
| **And the corner stress formula uses (a√2 / l)** ← | **So the corner's severity depends on how the load size compares with the relative stiffness** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHY l IS NOT AN ARBITRARY DEFINITION BUT AN INEVITABLE ONE: when the equation for a slab resting on springs is solved, this combination of E, h, k and μ appears as the length by which every distance in the problem is naturally measured.**

> **It is the same phenomenon as the characteristic length in a beam on an elastic foundation, or the skin depth in an electromagnetic problem: the physics itself supplies the yardstick.**

> **So the correct way to read a Westergaard formula is that distances only matter RELATIVE to l — and a slab is 'large' or 'small' according to how many multiples of l across it is, not according to its dimensions in metres.**

**THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES ARE MORE INTERESTING THAN THE FORMULA:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A STIFFER SUBGRADE (higher k) REDUCES l** ← | **Concentrating the load and, counter-intuitively, sometimes INCREASING the slab's bending stress at the corner** ← |
| **So improving the subgrade does not always reduce the slab's stress** ← | **The load is spread less widely, and the corner condition can worsen** ← |
| **It does, however, reduce DEFLECTION and improve the pavement's durability** ← | **Which is why subgrade improvement is worthwhile for other reasons** ← |
| **Slab thickness enters as h³ inside a fourth root, so as h^(3/4)** ← | **A weak dependence, so l changes only slowly with thickness** ← |

> **THE FIRST TWO ROWS CONTAIN A GENUINELY COUNTER-INTUITIVE RESULT, and it is one of the most instructive things in pavement analysis: making the ground stronger can make the slab work harder.**

> **The reason is that a slab on soft ground behaves like a raft, deflecting over a wide area and sharing the load among a large expanse of subgrade.**

> **On stiff ground it cannot deflect, so the load is resisted locally and the bending is concentrated near the wheel.**

> **The practical resolution is that rigid pavements want a UNIFORM subgrade of moderate stiffness rather than the stiffest possible one — uniformity mattering far more than magnitude, because differential support is what cracks slabs.**

> **This is why a rigid pavement is laid on a well-prepared sub-base of consistent quality rather than on the strongest material available, and why a patch of unusually stiff ground beneath a slab is a defect rather than a bonus.**

examTip.trick: **l = [Eh³/(12k(1 − μ²))]^(1/4) — a LENGTH**, measuring how far from the wheel the slab still carries stress. Stiff slab on soft ground gives a large l.
examTip.trap: **A stiffer subgrade REDUCES l and can INCREASE the corner bending stress** — the slab can no longer spread the load like a raft. Stronger ground is not always better for the slab.
examTip.mnemonic: **Uniformity beats magnitude** — differential support cracks slabs, so a rigid pavement wants a consistent sub-base, and a stiff patch under one slab is a defect.

questions.stem: CONTRACTION (transverse) joints are provided in a cement concrete pavement at intervals of about 4.5 m in order to:
options: Provide a weakened plane at which the inevitable shrinkage and thermal contraction cracking occurs in a straight
Allow the slab to expand freely in hot weather without any restraint
Permit the pavement to be laid in convenient daily lengths
Transfer the wheel load from one slab to the next
questions.solution:
**To provide a WEAKENED PLANE at which the inevitable shrinkage and thermal contraction cracking occurs in a straight, controlled line that can be sealed** — rather than as random cracks across the slab.

**The reasoning, which is a general principle of concrete construction:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Concrete SHRINKS as it cures, and CONTRACTS as it cools** ← | **Both unavoidable** ← |
| **A long slab is restrained by FRICTION against the sub-base** ← | **So the contraction cannot occur freely** ← |
| **Tensile stress therefore develops, and concrete is weak in tension** ← | **It WILL crack — the only question is where** ← |
| **A contraction joint decides WHERE** ← | **By cutting a groove that reduces the section, so the crack forms there and nowhere else** ← |
| **The crack is then STRAIGHT, at a known location, and SEALABLE** ← | **Instead of a ragged random crack that admits water and spalls** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE THE WHOLE IDEA AND THEY DESERVE STATING BALDLY: the joint does not PREVENT cracking, it LOCATES it.**

> **This distinction is the source of most confusion about joints in concrete, and it applies equally to a pavement, a floor slab, a retaining wall and a water tank.**

> **Concrete of any appreciable length will crack from shrinkage. A designer who provides no joints has not avoided the cracks — he has merely declined to choose their position, and the concrete will choose worse.**

**The groove and the crack beneath it:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The groove is cut to about ONE QUARTER of the slab depth** ← | **Enough to weaken the section decisively, not enough to weaken the slab structurally** ← |
| **It is SAW-CUT within hours of placing, or formed with an insert** ← | **Timing is critical — too early and the concrete ravels, too late and it has already cracked elsewhere** ← |
| **The crack propagates DOWN from the groove through the remaining depth** ← | **Giving an interlocking, irregular crack face below the neat sawn groove** ← |
| **The groove is then SEALED with a flexible sealant** ← | **To exclude water and incompressible grit** ← |
| **DOWEL BARS across the joint transfer the load** ← | **Which is option (d) — the dowel's function, not the joint's purpose** ← |

> **THE TIMING IN THE SECOND ROW IS ONE OF THE FEW GENUINELY UNFORGIVING WINDOWS IN CONCRETE CONSTRUCTION, and getting it wrong cannot be corrected.**

> **Cut too soon and the aggregate is not yet bonded, so the saw tears a ragged edge that spalls under traffic for the rest of the pavement's life.**

> **Cut too late and the slab has already cracked where it chose to — and the joint, cut afterwards, is then a useless groove beside a random crack.**

> **The window is a matter of hours and it depends on the temperature, so the sawing crew must work through the night behind a day's paving.**

**The three kinds of joint, distinguished — because they are constantly muddled:**

| Joint | Purpose | Load transfer |
|---|---|---|
| **CONTRACTION (transverse), about 4.5 m apart** ← | **Locate the shrinkage crack — this question** ← | **DOWEL bars, which slide** ← |
| **EXPANSION, at long intervals or at structures** ← | **Allow room for EXPANSION — a full gap through the slab with a filler** ← (option b) | **Dowels, one end greased** ← |
| **LONGITUDINAL, between lanes** ← | **Control cracking along the pavement and allow slight differential movement** ← | **TIE bars, which are bonded and do NOT slide** ← |

> **THE DOWEL AND TIE BAR DISTINCTION IN THE LAST COLUMN IS THE ONE THAT REPAYS PRECISION: a DOWEL is smooth and greased or sleeved at one end, because it must transfer shear while permitting the slabs to move apart along its axis.**

> **A TIE BAR is deformed and fully bonded at both ends, because it is intended to HOLD the lanes together and prevent them separating — it transfers no significant load and is not meant to slide.**

> **So the two look similar in a drawing and do opposite things: one permits movement while carrying load, the other prevents movement and carries little.**

> **Placing a deformed bar where a dowel belongs locks the joint, the slab cannot contract, and it cracks somewhere else — which returns to the opening point, that the concrete will crack regardless and the only real choice is whether the engineer or the concrete decides where.**

examTip.trick: **The joint does not PREVENT cracking, it LOCATES it** — a groove a quarter of the depth gives a straight, sealable crack instead of a random one.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is the DOWEL's function, not the joint's purpose**, and (b) is the expansion joint. Contraction, expansion and longitudinal joints do three different things.
examTip.mnemonic: **Saw within hours: too early ravels, too late and the slab has already cracked elsewhere.** And dowels SLIDE (smooth) while tie bars BOND (deformed) — opposite duties, similar drawings.

questions.stem: In the construction of a bituminous concrete layer, the ROLLING must be completed before the mat cools below about 90 °C because:
options: Below that temperature the bitumen begins to burn off and the mix loses binder
Rolling a cool mat causes the aggregate to crush under the roller
The mix stiffens as it cools, so further rolling achieves no additional density
The roller's tyres pick up the mix once it has cooled
questions.solution:
**The mix STIFFENS as it cools, so further rolling achieves no additional density** — leaving the layer with excessive air voids and hence prone to ravelling and stripping.

**The temperature regime of a bituminous concrete layer:**

| Operation | Temperature |
|---|---|
| **MIXING at the plant** ← | **150 to 165 °C, depending on the binder grade** ← |
| **Arrival at site and LAYING** ← | **Not below about 130 °C** ← |
| **BREAKDOWN (initial) rolling** ← | **Immediately, at the highest temperature the mat will bear without shoving — around 130 to 140 °C** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE rolling** ← | **The main densifying pass, while the mat is still well above 100 °C** ← |
| **FINISH rolling** ← | **To remove roller marks — completed before about 90 °C** ← |
| **BELOW about 90 °C** ← | **Rolling accomplishes nothing further; the density is whatever it is** ← |
| **Opening to traffic** | **When the mat has cooled to ambient, or nearly so** ← |

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE HARD DEADLINE OF BITUMINOUS PAVING AND IT IS ABSOLUTE: once the mat is cold, the achieved density is final and cannot be improved by any amount of further rolling.**

> **The bitumen at 140 °C is a fluid that lets the aggregate particles slide past one another into a denser packing.**

> **At 90 °C it is stiff, and the aggregate skeleton has locked; the roller simply rides over the surface.**

> **So the compaction of a bituminous layer is a race against cooling, and everything about the operation is organised around it.**

**Which is why the following all matter so much:**

| Consideration | Reason |
|---|---|
| **The HAUL DISTANCE from the plant, and insulated, sheeted trucks** ← | **A long haul on a cold day can deliver the mix below the laying temperature, and it must then be rejected** ← |
| **Enough ROLLERS on site, immediately behind the paver** ← | **The compaction must be finished within the window, so the roller capacity must match the paver's output** ← |
| **Not paving in cold, wet or windy weather** ← | **A thin mat on a cold base in a wind loses its heat in minutes** ← |
| **THIN layers cool faster than thick ones** ← | **So a thin wearing course has a much shorter rolling window than a thick binder course** ← |
| **Continuous paving without stoppages** ← | **Every stoppage leaves a transverse joint and a length of mat cooling while nothing happens** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN THE SEASONAL RESTRICTION ON BITUMINOUS WORK, and in Nepal that restriction is severe.**

> **Bituminous surfacing cannot be laid in the monsoon, because the base must be dry and the rain cools the mat.**

> **It cannot be laid in the winter at altitude, because the ambient temperature is too low to allow the rolling window.**

> **That leaves a limited working season, which is one reason road contracts in the hills slip so often — and why a programme that assumes year-round paving is unrealistic from the start.**

> **A planner who does not build the weather window into the schedule has written a programme that cannot be achieved regardless of the contractor's diligence.**

**The rolling sequence and its purposes:**

| Roller | Duty |
|---|---|
| **BREAKDOWN — a steel-wheeled tandem, or a vibratory roller** ← | **Achieves most of the density, immediately behind the paver** ← |
| **INTERMEDIATE — a PNEUMATIC-TYRED roller** ← | **Kneads the mix, sealing the surface and improving the aggregate interlock** ← |
| **FINISH — a static steel-wheeled roller** ← | **Removes the marks left by the earlier passes; adds little density** ← |
| **Rolling proceeds from the LOWER edge toward the crown** ← | **So the mat is pushed against already-compacted material rather than being shoved outward** ← |
| **The wheels are kept damp, not wet** ← | **Just enough water to stop the mix sticking; too much cools the mat** ← |

> **The fourth row is a detail that is easy to get wrong on a superelevated or cambered surface and it matters: rolling downhill on the cross-slope shoves the unsupported mat sideways and the layer loses its shape.**

> **Starting at the low edge means each pass is supported by the compacted material beside it, so the mat is confined and densifies instead of moving — the same confinement principle that governs compaction of an embankment against an existing slope.**

examTip.trick: **The mix stiffens as it cools, so cold rolling adds no density** — the layer is left with high voids, and then ravels and strips. Compaction is a race against cooling.
examTip.trap: **Mix at 150-165 °C, lay above 130 °C, finish rolling before 90 °C.** Thin layers cool fastest, so a wearing course has the shortest window.
examTip.mnemonic: **Breakdown (steel) → intermediate (pneumatic, kneads) → finish (steel, marks only)**, rolling from the LOW edge toward the crown so the mat is confined and does not shove sideways.

questions.stem: In a TRUE ISOMETRIC drawing, lengths measured along the isometric axes are related to the object's actual dimensions by the ISOMETRIC SCALE, whose ratio is:
options: 1.000 — the axes are drawn to true length
0.816 — approximately, being the ratio √2 : √3
0.707 — the ratio 1 : √2
1.225 — the axes are drawn longer than true length
questions.solution:
**0.816 — approximately, being the ratio √2 : √3.**

**Where the figure comes from:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **In isometric projection the object is turned so that all THREE axes make equal angles with the plane of projection** ← | **Which is what makes the projection 'iso-metric' — equal measure on all three** ← |
| **Each axis is therefore INCLINED to the plane, and its projection is FORESHORTENED** ← | **A line inclined to a plane projects shorter than it is** ← |
| **The geometry gives a foreshortening ratio of cos(35°16') = √2/√3** ← | **= 0.8165** ← |
| **So a 100 mm edge projects as 81.65 mm on a true isometric drawing** ← | ← |

> **THE PRACTICAL POINT, HOWEVER, IS THAT THIS SCALE IS ALMOST NEVER USED, and knowing why matters more than knowing the number:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ISOMETRIC PROJECTION (true)** ← | **Drawn with the 0.816 isometric scale — a geometrically correct projection** ← |
| **ISOMETRIC DRAWING (or isometric VIEW)** ← | **Drawn with TRUE lengths along the axes — geometrically 22.5 per cent oversized, but far easier to draw** ← |
| **The difference between the two** ← | **Only one of overall SIZE — the shape, the angles and the proportions are IDENTICAL** ← |
| **So the isometric DRAWING is used almost universally** ← | **Since nothing is lost but absolute size, and pictorial views are not scaled off in any case** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE WHOLE JUSTIFICATION AND IT IS A SOUND ONE: because the foreshortening is IDENTICAL on all three axes, ignoring it enlarges the whole figure uniformly and distorts nothing.**

> **A pictorial view exists to convey the shape of an object to someone reading the drawing, not to be measured — the orthographic views carry the dimensions.**

> **So the small nuisance of an isometric scale buys nothing, and drawing to true lengths along the axes is standard practice.**

> **The distinction survives in the terminology and in examinations, and it is worth being able to state: an isometric PROJECTION uses the isometric scale, an isometric DRAWING does not.**

**The axonometric family, for the distinction:**

| Type | Axis angles | Foreshortening |
|---|---|---|
| **ISOMETRIC** ← | **All three equal — 120° apart, drawn at 30° to the horizontal** ← | **EQUAL on all three axes (0.816)** ← |
| **DIMETRIC** | **Two axes equally inclined, the third different** ← | **Two ratios equal, one different** ← |
| **TRIMETRIC** | **All three different** ← | **Three different ratios — the most realistic and the most laborious** ← |
| **OBLIQUE (cavalier / cabinet)** ← | **One face drawn TRUE, in its own plane, with the third axis at an angle** ← | **Cavalier: no foreshortening. Cabinet: the receding axis halved** ← |
| **PERSPECTIVE** ← | **Not axonometric at all — parallel lines CONVERGE to vanishing points** ← | **Varies with distance, as the eye sees it** ← |

> **THE OBLIQUE ROW IS THE ONE MOST USEFUL TO A CIVIL ENGINEER IN PRACTICE, and its advantage is specific: one face is drawn TRUE, in its actual shape.**

> **So an object with an important circular or intricate face — a pipe fitting, a manhole cover, a column with a complex profile — is best drawn obliquely with that face parallel to the paper, where its circles remain circles and can be drawn with a compass.**

> **In an isometric view every circle becomes an ELLIPSE, which is why isometric drawings of pipework are so tedious and why the four-centre approximation for isometric circles is taught at all.**

> **Choosing the pictorial method to suit the object, rather than defaulting to isometric, is a small piece of judgment that saves a great deal of drawing time.**

examTip.trick: **0.816, being √2/√3 = cos 35°16'** — the foreshortening of an axis equally inclined to the projection plane. A 100 mm edge projects as 81.65 mm.
examTip.trap: **Isometric PROJECTION uses the scale; isometric DRAWING uses true lengths** and is 22.5 % oversized. Since the foreshortening is equal on all three axes, nothing is distorted — only the size.
examTip.mnemonic: **In isometric every circle becomes an ELLIPSE** — so for an object with one important circular face, use an OBLIQUE view with that face true, and draw the circles with a compass.

questions.stem: A LINE DIAGRAM of a structure or a system is:
options: A drawing showing only the outline of the structure, with all internal detail omitted
A drawing in which every line is of the same thickness throughout
A detailed drawing showing the reinforcement in each member
A schematic representation in which members, pipes or components are shown as single lines along their centre lines
questions.solution:
**A SCHEMATIC representation in which members, pipes or components are shown as SINGLE LINES along their centre lines** — connections and relationships shown, but sizes and shapes not drawn to scale.

**What it is and what it is for:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Members are reduced to SINGLE LINES along their centre lines** ← | **A beam 400 mm deep and a beam 200 mm deep look identical** ← |
| **The purpose is to show the ARRANGEMENT and CONNECTIVITY** ← | **What connects to what, and in what order** ← |
| **Sizes are NOT to scale, though the layout usually is approximately** ← | **The diagram is topological rather than dimensional** ← |
| **It is used for ANALYSIS and for COMMUNICATION of the concept** ← | **A structural frame's line diagram is what the analysis is performed on** ← |
| **Node and member NUMBERS, and support conditions, are marked on it** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHERE THE LINE DIAGRAM DOES ITS MOST IMPORTANT WORK, AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY IT IS INDISPENSABLE: structural analysis is performed on the line diagram, not on the detailed drawing.**

> **A frame is analysed as an assembly of one-dimensional members meeting at points, with the members' properties represented by their length, area and moment of inertia.**

> **The line diagram IS that idealisation, drawn.**

> **So preparing the line diagram is the act of deciding what the structure will be assumed to be — where the supports are, which joints are rigid and which are pinned, and what the effective spans are.**

> **Those decisions govern the answer entirely, and they are made on the line diagram before any calculation begins.**

**Where line diagrams are used across civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **STRUCTURAL frames and trusses** ← | **For analysis, as above** ← |
| **WATER SUPPLY and drainage networks** ← | **Pipes as single lines, with nodes, valves, tanks and pumps as symbols — the hydraulic network on which the analysis is run** ← |
| **ELECTRICAL single-line diagrams** ← | **Generators, transformers, busbars and feeders, showing the system's topology** ← |
| **PROCESS flow diagrams for a treatment plant** ← | **Units in sequence with the flow paths between them** ← |
| **Project NETWORK diagrams** ← | **Activities and their dependencies — the same idea applied to a schedule rather than a structure** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS AN OBSERVATION WORTH MAKING BECAUSE IT UNIFIES TWO PARTS OF THIS SUBJECT THAT USUALLY SIT APART: a CPM network is a line diagram of a project.**

> **It shows what depends on what, with activities as lines or nodes and the dependencies as connections, and it is deliberately NOT to scale — an activity of 30 days and one of 2 days are drawn the same length.**

> **The same abstraction that makes a structural line diagram analysable makes a network analysable: strip away everything but the connectivity, and the underlying logic becomes visible and computable.**

> **A bar chart, by contrast, IS to scale in time, which is precisely why it shows durations well and dependencies badly — the trade-off between the two representations, and the reason a planner uses both.**

**What it is NOT, to close off the other options:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| **(a) Outline only, detail omitted** ← | **That is an OUTLINE or key plan — still drawn to scale and to shape** ← |
| **(b) Uniform line thickness** ← | **The opposite of drawing practice, which uses line thickness to distinguish visible edges, hidden edges, centre lines and dimensions** ← |
| **(c) Reinforcement detail** ← | **That is a BAR BENDING or reinforcement detail drawing — the most dimensionally detailed drawing of all** ← |

> **Option (b) is worth a moment's attention because it inverts a real convention: line THICKNESS carries meaning in an engineering drawing, and a drawing in which every line is the same weight is difficult to read for exactly that reason.**

> **Continuous thick lines for visible edges, thin for dimensions and hatching, dashed for hidden edges, and long-dash-dot for centre lines — the reader interprets the drawing partly by line character before reading a single label, which is why the conventions are worth respecting even in a hurried sketch.**

Connections and relationships shown but sizes and shapes NOT drawn to scale.

examTip.trick: **Members as single lines along their centre lines — connectivity shown, sizes not to scale.** Option (a) is an outline plan, (c) a reinforcement detail.
examTip.trap: **Structural analysis is performed on the LINE DIAGRAM, not the detailed drawing** — so preparing it is the act of deciding what the structure is assumed to be. Those decisions govern the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **A CPM network is a line diagram of a project** — connectivity, deliberately not to scale. A bar chart is the reverse: to scale in time, so good on duration and bad on dependency.

questions.stem: A piece of construction plant costing Rs 8,00,000 is depreciated at 20 per cent per annum by the DECLINING BALANCE (written-down value) method. Its book value at the end of the THIRD year is:
questions.solution:
**Rs 4,09,600.**

**The method:**

> **In the declining balance method a FIXED PERCENTAGE is written off the REMAINING book value each year — not off the original cost.**

> **So the book value after n years is BV = C (1 − r)ⁿ.**

**The calculation, year by year:**

| Year | Depreciation for the year | Book value at year end |
|---|---|---|
| **Start** | ← | **Rs 8,00,000** |
| **1** | **20 % of 8,00,000 = 1,60,000** ← | **Rs 6,40,000** ← |
| **2** | **20 % of 6,40,000 = 1,28,000** ← | **Rs 5,12,000** ← |
| **3** | **20 % of 5,12,000 = 1,02,400** ← | **Rs 4,09,600** ← |

**Or directly:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **BV = C (1 − r)ⁿ** | **= 8,00,000 × (0.80)³** ← |
| **(0.80)³** | **= 0.512** ← |
| **BV** | **= 8,00,000 × 0.512 = Rs 4,09,600** ← |

> **So the book value at the end of the third year is Rs 4,09,600.**

**THE DISTRACTORS ARE ALL THE RESULTS OF SPECIFIC ERRORS AND EACH IS WORTH RECOGNISING:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **Rs 3,20,000** ← | **STRAIGHT LINE depreciation: 20 % of the ORIGINAL cost each year, so 3 × 1,60,000 = 4,80,000 written off, leaving 3,20,000 — the commonest error** ← |
| **Rs 5,12,000** ← | **The value after TWO years, not three — an off-by-one in the exponent** ← |
| **Rs 4,80,000** ← | **The total depreciation under the straight line method, mistaken for the book value** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE ERROR TO GUARD AGAINST, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE QUESTION: straight line takes the percentage of the ORIGINAL cost, declining balance takes it of the CURRENT book value.**

> **The two give very different results, and they never converge — the declining balance method never reaches zero, however many years pass, which is one of its characteristic features.**

**The depreciation methods compared:**

| Method | Pattern | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **STRAIGHT LINE** ← | **Equal amount each year: (C − S)/n** ← | **Simplest; assumes uniform loss of value** ← |
| **DECLINING BALANCE (WDV)** ← | **A fixed percentage of the reducing balance — HEAVY early, light later** ← | **This question; never reaches zero** ← |
| **SUM OF THE YEARS' DIGITS** ← | **Also accelerated, but reaches the salvage value exactly** ← | **A compromise between the two above** ← |
| **SINKING FUND** ← | **Provides for replacement by accumulating a fund with interest** ← | **The only method that considers the TIME VALUE of money** ← |
| **SERVICE OUTPUT (unit of production)** | **Per hour worked or per unit produced** | **The most realistic for plant whose use varies** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW'S ACCELERATED PATTERN IS THE REASON DECLINING BALANCE IS SO WIDELY USED FOR CONSTRUCTION PLANT, AND IT IS AN ARGUMENT WORTH KNOWING: the method matches the way plant actually loses value.**

> **A new excavator loses a large fraction of its market value in its first year and rather little in its tenth — the depreciation curve of the real second-hand market is a decaying one, not a straight line.**

> **It also has a tax advantage, since larger early deductions defer tax, which is worth money by the time value of money.**

> **And it is prudent in a different sense: it writes the asset down quickly, so the accounts do not carry an optimistic book value for equipment that could not be sold for anything like it.**

> **The one thing it does NOT do is reach zero, so a residual value is carried indefinitely and the asset must eventually be written off or sold to clear it from the books.**

examTip.trap: **Rs 3,20,000 is the STRAIGHT LINE answer** — 20 % of the ORIGINAL cost each year. Declining balance takes the percentage of the CURRENT book value. Rs 5,12,000 is the two-year value.
examTip.mnemonic: **Declining balance never reaches zero** — and it is used for plant because the real second-hand market loses value that way: heavy in year one, light in year ten.

questions.stem: In engineering economic analysis, the OPPORTUNITY COST of using a resource in a project is:
options: The cash actually paid for the resource
The cost already incurred on the resource before the decision was taken
The value of the best alternative use that is forgone by committing the resource to this project
The cost of replacing the resource at today's market price
questions.solution:
**The value of the BEST ALTERNATIVE USE that is FORGONE by committing the resource to this project.**

**What the concept requires:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A resource committed here CANNOT be used elsewhere** ← | **Land, capital, plant, skilled staff, management attention** ← |
| **The benefit that the best forgone alternative would have produced is a real cost of this decision** ← | **Even though no money changes hands for it** ← |
| **So it must enter the appraisal, whether or not it appears in any account** ← | ← |
| **It is the BEST forgone alternative, not the sum of all of them** ← | **Since only one alternative could have been chosen in any case** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE POINT THAT MAKES OPPORTUNITY COST DIFFICULT IN PRACTICE, AND IT IS WORTH BEING BLUNT ABOUT: an opportunity cost is invisible in the accounts.**

> **Nothing is paid, no invoice is raised, and no auditor will find it — yet it is as real a cost as the cement, because the organisation is genuinely poorer by the benefit it gave up.**

> **Which is why economic appraisal is not the same activity as accounting, and why a project that looks profitable on a cash basis may be a poor use of resources.**

**Worked examples, which make the idea concrete:**

| Situation | The opportunity cost |
|---|---|
| **A project built on land the organisation ALREADY OWNS** ← | **The land is NOT free — its cost is what it would fetch if sold or let. Treating owned land as costless is the classic error** ← |
| **Capital invested in a project** ← | **The return it would have earned in the next-best investment — which is precisely what the DISCOUNT RATE represents** ← |
| **A firm's own plant used on a job instead of being hired out** ← | **The hire income forgone, not merely the fuel and the operator** ← |
| **The best engineers assigned to project A** ← | **What they would have contributed on project B** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT CONNECTION IN THIS ANSWER, AND IT EXPLAINS SOMETHING THAT OTHERWISE LOOKS ARBITRARY: the discount rate IS an opportunity cost.**

> **Money committed to a project for ten years cannot earn anything else during those ten years, and the return forgone is the cost of tying it up.**

> **Which is why the MARR is set at or above the organisation's cost of capital or its best alternative return — a project that yields less than the alternative destroys value even while showing a profit.**

> **Seeing discounting as the pricing of an opportunity cost, rather than as a financial convention, makes the whole of engineering economics more coherent: NPV asks whether the project beats the alternative use of the same money.**

**And the CONTRAST with sunk cost, which is the natural companion idea:**

| Concept | Rule |
|---|---|
| **OPPORTUNITY cost — a forgone alternative** ← | **MUST be included, though it never appears in the accounts** ← |
| **SUNK cost — already incurred and unrecoverable** ← | **Must be EXCLUDED, though it is fully documented in the accounts** ← (option b) |

> **THE PAIRING IS INSTRUCTIVE BECAUSE THE TWO ARE EXACT OPPOSITES IN BOTH RESPECTS, and stating it plainly is the most useful thing to remember here.**

> **The cost you can prove with a receipt must be ignored; the cost nobody billed you for must be counted.**

> **Both errors are made constantly and both point the same way — toward continuing with a poor project, because the money already spent seems to demand it and the alternative forgone seems to cost nothing.**

> **Recognising that pattern is worth more than either definition on its own: a decision that keeps invoking what has already been spent, and never asks what else the remaining resources could do, is being made on exactly the two quantities that ought to be reversed.**

examTip.trick: **The value of the BEST forgone alternative** — not the cash paid (a), not the sunk cost (b), not the replacement cost (d).
examTip.trap: **Land already owned is NOT free** — its opportunity cost is what it would fetch if sold or let. The classic error in public project appraisal.
examTip.mnemonic: **Opportunity cost: no receipt, must be counted. Sunk cost: full receipt, must be ignored.** Exact opposites — and both errors push toward continuing a poor project.

questions.stem: In a PRECEDENCE (activity-on-node) network, a START-TO-START relationship with a LAG of 5 days between activity A and activity B means that:
options: B can start only after A has finished, and then after a further 5 days
B can start 5 days after A has started — the two then proceeding in parallel
A and B must both start on the same day, and B must last 5 days longer
B must finish 5 days after A finishes
questions.solution:
**B can START 5 days after A has STARTED** — the two then proceeding in parallel.

**The four precedence relationships:**

| Relationship | Meaning | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **FINISH-TO-START (FS)** ← | **B starts after A finishes — the DEFAULT, and the only relationship an arrow diagram can express** ← (option a with lag) | **Strip the formwork, then plaster** ← |
| **START-TO-START (SS)** ← | **B starts a stated time after A starts — this question** ← | **Start trenching, and begin laying pipe 5 days behind the trencher** ← |
| **FINISH-TO-FINISH (FF)** ← | **B finishes a stated time after A finishes** ← (option d) | **Backfilling must finish 2 days after pipe-laying finishes** ← |
| **START-TO-FINISH (SF)** | **B cannot FINISH until a stated time after A STARTS — rare and confusing** ← | **A shift handover; seldom used** ← |

> **THE SS AND FF RELATIONSHIPS TOGETHER ARE WHAT MAKE PRECEDENCE NETWORKS SO MUCH MORE USEFUL THAN ARROW DIAGRAMS FOR CONSTRUCTION, and the reason is worth setting out because it is the practical heart of the matter.**

> **Construction work OVERLAPS. Trenching, pipe-laying, jointing, testing and backfilling all proceed simultaneously along a pipeline, each crew following the one ahead at a interval.**
