> **A finish-to-start network cannot express that at all: it must either show them strictly in sequence, which is absurdly long, or break each activity into many small pieces to fake the overlap, which makes the network unmanageably large.**

> **An SS relationship with a lag expresses the real arrangement in one link — the pipe-layers start five days behind the trencher and follow along.**

> **That is why linear and repetitive work is planned with precedence networks or with the Line of Balance technique rather than with arrow diagrams.**

**A useful pairing, which is how the relationship is normally used in practice:**

| Combination | Effect |
|---|---|
| **SS lag 5 with FF lag 3 between the same pair** ← | **B starts 5 days after A starts, and finishes 3 days after A finishes — so B trails A throughout** ← |
| **This is the standard way to model a FOLLOWING CREW** ← | **It constrains both ends, so B cannot overtake A at either the start or the finish** ← |
| **With only the SS link, B could finish BEFORE A** ← | **Which is physically impossible if B follows A along the same route — the pipe cannot be laid where the trench is not yet dug** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ERROR THIS PAIRING EXISTS TO PREVENT AND IT IS AN EASY ONE TO MAKE: an SS link alone constrains only the beginning.**

> **If B is scheduled with a shorter duration than A, the software will happily show B overtaking A and finishing first, which on a linear job means laying pipe into unexcavated ground.**

> **Adding the FF link closes that gap, and a planner modelling any following operation should provide both.**

> **This is a good illustration of a general truth about scheduling software: it enforces exactly the logic it is given and no more, so a relationship that is physically obvious to the site team must still be stated explicitly or it will be violated.**

**And a caution about LAGS, which is worth carrying:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **A lag is a WAITING TIME, not an activity** ← | **So it consumes no resources and appears on no report** ← |
| **Which makes lags INVISIBLE in most schedule outputs** ← | **A 20-day lag can hide 20 days of programme where nobody looks** ← |
| **A lag that represents real work should be an ACTIVITY instead** ← | **Concrete curing, for instance, is better shown as an activity than as a lag, so it is visible and can be tracked** ← |
| **Excessive lags make a network hard to audit** ← | **And are a common way of concealing float or padding a programme** ← |

> **The second and fourth rows are the practical warning: a network full of long lags is difficult for anyone but its author to understand, and a schedule that cannot be independently checked is of limited value in a contract where it may have to be defended.**

examTip.trick: **B starts 5 days after A STARTS**, then runs in parallel. Option (a) is FS with a lag, (d) is FF.
examTip.trap: **Use SS and FF TOGETHER for a following crew** — an SS link alone lets a shorter B overtake A and finish first, which means laying pipe into an undug trench.
examTip.mnemonic: **SS and FF are why precedence networks beat arrow diagrams on construction** — real work overlaps, and FS alone cannot express a crew following 5 days behind. And lags are invisible on reports.

questions.stem: The WORK BREAKDOWN STRUCTURE (WBS) of a project is:
options: A chart showing the reporting relationships between the members of the project team
A list of the activities in the order in which they will be executed
A schedule showing the planned start and finish date of every activity
A hierarchical decomposition of the project's total scope into progressively smaller deliverables and work packages
questions.solution:
**A HIERARCHICAL decomposition of the project's total scope into progressively smaller DELIVERABLES and work packages** — until each package is small enough to be estimated, assigned and controlled.

**What it is:**

| Level | Example, for a water supply project |
|---|---|
| **Level 1 — the PROJECT** | **Town water supply scheme** ← |
| **Level 2 — major deliverables** ← | **Intake works / Treatment plant / Transmission main / Reservoir / Distribution network** ← |
| **Level 3 — components** ← | **Reservoir: excavation / foundation / walls / roof / pipework / testing** ← |
| **Level 4 — WORK PACKAGES** ← | **Walls: reinforcement fixing / formwork / concreting / curing / water-tightness test** ← |
| **The bottom level is the WORK PACKAGE** ← | **The smallest unit that is separately estimated, assigned to one responsible party, and reported on** ← |

> **THE DECOMPOSITION IS BY DELIVERABLE RATHER THAN BY ACTIVITY, AND THAT DISTINCTION IS THE ONE MOST WORTH GETTING RIGHT: a WBS answers 'WHAT is to be produced', not 'what is to be done' and not 'when'.**

> **The activities follow from the work packages, and the schedule follows from the activities — so the WBS comes FIRST and everything else is built on it.**

> **A project planned without one tends to have a schedule of activities that does not add up to the whole scope, because nobody ever established what the whole scope was.**

**Why it matters, which is more than an organising convenience:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **It DEFINES THE SCOPE completely** ← | **The rule is that the WBS is exhaustive: work not in the WBS is not in the project — the 100 per cent rule** ← |
| **It is the basis of the ESTIMATE** ← | **Costs are built up package by package and summed, which is far more reliable than estimating the whole** ← |
| **It is the basis of RESPONSIBILITY** ← | **Each package has one owner, so nothing falls between two parties** ← |
| **It is the basis of PROGRESS MEASUREMENT and earned value** ← | **A package is complete or it is not, and the earned value is the sum of the completed packages' budgets** ← |
| **It is the basis of the COST CODING system** ← | **Each package carries a code, so actual costs are captured against the same structure as the estimate** ← |
| **And of RISK identification** ← | **Risks are looked for package by package rather than in the abstract** ← |

> **THE 100 PER CENT RULE IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL SINGLE PRINCIPLE IN THIS ANSWER AND IT CUTS BOTH WAYS: the children of any element must together account for exactly 100 per cent of that element — no more and no less.**

> **No more, because work that belongs to another element must not be duplicated here, or it will be estimated and paid for twice.**

> **No less, because anything omitted is invisible: it appears in no estimate, has no owner, is in nobody's programme, and will be discovered on site as an unbudgeted surprise.**

> **Applying that test element by element is a genuine quality check on a WBS and it catches real omissions — commissioning, testing, as-built drawings, training the operators, and the disposal of surplus material being the ones habitually forgotten.**

**THE FIFTH ROW IS THE CONNECTION THAT MAKES A WBS OPERATIONALLY VALUABLE RATHER THAN MERELY TIDY:**

> **If the ESTIMATE, the SCHEDULE and the ACCOUNTS all use the same breakdown and the same codes, then planned cost, planned progress and actual cost can be compared package by package.**

> **That comparison IS earned value analysis, and it is only possible when the three systems share a structure.**

> **Where the estimator, the planner and the accountant each invented their own breakdown — which happens constantly — no meaningful comparison can be made at all, and the project cannot tell whether it is over budget because it has done more work or because the work cost more.**

> **So the WBS's real function is to make the project MEASURABLE, and establishing it before the estimate rather than after is what makes control possible later.**

examTip.trick: **A hierarchical decomposition by DELIVERABLE down to work packages** — it answers WHAT is produced, not what is done (b) or when (c). Option (a) is the organisation chart.
examTip.trap: **The 100 PER CENT RULE: the children must sum to exactly the parent** — no duplication, no omission. Commissioning, testing, as-built drawings and operator training are the habitual omissions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Estimate, schedule and accounts must share the WBS and its codes** — otherwise earned value is impossible and you cannot tell whether you did more work or paid more for it.

questions.stem: The BID SECURITY (earnest money) submitted with a tender is:
options: A deduction from each running bill, retained until the defects liability period expires
A guarantee that the contractor will complete the works to the required quality
A guarantee, forfeited if the bidder withdraws its bid within the validity period or fails to sign the contract after being awarded it
An advance paid by the employer to enable the contractor to mobilise plant and labour
questions.solution:
**A guarantee, forfeited if the bidder WITHDRAWS its bid within the validity period or FAILS to sign the contract after being awarded it** — protecting the employer against frivolous or speculative bidding.

**The securities and deductions in a construction contract, which are constantly confused:**

| Instrument | When | Purpose | Typical amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BID SECURITY (earnest money)** ← | **WITH the tender** ← | **Deters withdrawal and refusal to sign — this question** ← | **1 to 3 per cent of the estimated cost** ← |
| **PERFORMANCE SECURITY (bond)** ← | **On SIGNING the contract** ← | **Secures PERFORMANCE of the works** ← (option b) | **5 to 10 per cent of the contract price** ← |
| **RETENTION MONEY** ← | **Deducted from EACH BILL** ← | **Held against defects until the liability period expires** ← (option a) | **5 to 10 per cent of each bill, up to a ceiling** ← |
| **MOBILISATION ADVANCE** ← | **After signing, ON REQUEST** ← | **Funds the contractor's start-up — recovered from later bills** ← (option d) | **10 to 20 per cent, against a bank guarantee** ← |
| **ADVANCE PAYMENT GUARANTEE** | **With the advance** | **Secures the employer against the advance not being repaid** | **The full advance** ← |

> **THE SEQUENCE IN THE 'WHEN' COLUMN IS THE EASIEST WAY TO KEEP THESE APART, and it is worth reading down it once: bid security comes with the BID, performance security on SIGNING, retention with each BILL, and the advance AFTER signing.**

> **Each instrument covers a different risk at a different stage, and each is released when that risk has passed.**

**What the bid security actually protects against:**

| Risk | Note |
|---|---|
| **A bidder submitting a low bid and then WITHDRAWING when it realises its error** ← | **Which forces the employer to award to the next bidder at a higher price, or to re-tender** ← |
| **A successful bidder REFUSING to sign** ← | **Same consequence, after the employer has already committed to the award** ← |
| **FRIVOLOUS bidding by parties with no serious intention or capacity** ← | **Because a bid costs something to submit, unserious bids are deterred** ← |
| **The security is RELEASED to unsuccessful bidders once the award is made** ← | **And to the successful bidder once the performance security is furnished** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW MATTERS TO A CONTRACTOR'S CASH FLOW MORE THAN IT MIGHT SEEM, and it is a real cost of bidding: a firm tendering for several jobs at once has bid securities locked up on all of them simultaneously.**

> **A contractor bidding on ten projects of Rs 10 crore each has as much as Rs 3 crore tied up in bid securities, none of which is earning anything, and it is released only when each award is decided.**

> **Which is why bid securities are usually furnished as BANK GUARANTEES rather than in cash: the bank charges a commission but the contractor's money is not immobilised.**

> **And why a procurement process that takes an unreasonably long time to make its award imposes a real cost on every bidder — a cost that is eventually recovered in higher prices, so the employer pays for its own delay.**

**THE PERFORMANCE SECURITY AND RETENTION MONEY IN THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS ARE THE PAIR MOST OFTEN MUDDLED, AND THE DISTINCTION IS BOTH IN TIMING AND IN SUBSTANCE:**

| Aspect | Performance security | Retention money |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | **Provided by the contractor, usually as a BANK GUARANTEE** ← | **DEDUCTED from money already earned** ← |
| **Covers** | **Failure to perform the CONTRACT at all — abandonment, insolvency, termination** ← | **DEFECTS in completed work** ← |
| **Released** | **On completion, or on issue of the completion certificate** ← | **Half at completion, half at the end of the DEFECTS LIABILITY period** ← |
| **Effect on the contractor** | **Costs a bank commission** | **Withholds the contractor's own money — a direct cash flow cost** ← |

> **The last row explains why contractors press so hard to substitute a bank guarantee for retention: retention is their own earned money withheld, sometimes for years after completion, whereas a guarantee costs only a commission.**

> **Many contracts now permit that substitution for exactly that reason, and it is a fair arrangement provided the guarantee's validity actually extends to the end of the defects liability period — a detail worth checking, since a guarantee that expires before the liability does secures nothing.**

examTip.trick: **Forfeited if the bidder withdraws or refuses to sign** — 1 to 3 % with the BID. Option (a) is retention, (b) performance security, (d) mobilisation advance.
examTip.trap: **Keep them apart by TIMING: bid security with the BID, performance security on SIGNING, retention with each BILL, advance AFTER signing.** Each covers a different stage's risk.
examTip.mnemonic: **Retention is the contractor's OWN earned money withheld; a performance bond costs only a bank commission** — which is why contractors press to substitute one for the other.

questions.stem: A PRICE ADJUSTMENT (escalation) clause in a long-duration construction contract:
options: Adjusts the payments up or down according to published indices for labour, fuel, cement, steel and other inputs
Allows the contractor to revise its rates at will if its costs increase
Permits the employer to reduce the contract price if the market falls
Fixes the contract price absolutely for the whole duration of the works
questions.solution:
**It ADJUSTS the payments up or down according to published INDICES** for labour, fuel, cement, steel and other inputs — so that the contractor bears the risk of its own productivity but not of general market price movement.

**How the clause works:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **The contract price is broken into COMPONENTS** ← | **Labour, cement, steel, bitumen, fuel, plant and a fixed (non-adjustable) portion** ← |
| **Each component is given a WEIGHTING** ← | **Its share of the contract value, stated in the contract** ← |
| **Each is linked to a PUBLISHED INDEX** ← | **Official price indices or gazetted rates — from a source outside both parties' control** ← |
| **Each interim payment is adjusted by the movement of those indices since the BASE DATE** ← | **Applying the weightings, so the adjustment reflects the actual input mix** ← |
| **A portion — commonly 10 to 15 per cent — is NON-ADJUSTABLE** ← | **Representing overheads and profit, which are not assumed to escalate** ← |
| **The adjustment can be NEGATIVE** ← | **If prices FALL, the employer recovers — the clause runs both ways** ← (which is why option c is only half the truth) |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE FEATURE THAT MAKES THE CLAUSE WORKABLE AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: the adjustment depends on a PUBLISHED index, not on the contractor's actual costs.**

> **That is deliberate, and it has two consequences worth separating.**

> **First, it removes any need to audit the contractor's purchases — nobody has to prove what was paid for the cement, which would be an endless argument.**

> **Second, it leaves the contractor exposed to its OWN performance: a firm that buys badly or works inefficiently bears that loss, since the index does not care what it actually paid.**

> **So the clause transfers only the MARKET risk and leaves the MANAGEMENT risk where it belongs — which is precisely the right allocation, because the contractor controls one and neither party controls the other.**

**Why the clause exists at all, which is the argument for it:**

| Without the clause | With it |
|---|---|
| **The contractor must PRICE the risk of inflation over the contract period** ← | **The contractor prices only the work** ← |
| **It must therefore add a CONTINGENCY, guessing at future prices** ← | **No such contingency is needed** ← |
| **If it guesses HIGH, the employer overpays** ← | **The employer pays actual market movement, no more** ← |
| **If it guesses LOW, the contractor faces loss, cuts corners, claims, or abandons** ← | **A situation that serves nobody, least of all the employer** ← |
| **Only large, well-capitalised firms can bid at all** ← | **Smaller firms can compete, so competition improves** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT AND IT IS OFTEN MISSED IN DISCUSSIONS THAT TREAT THE CLAUSE AS A CONCESSION TO CONTRACTORS: a contractor facing ruin from price rises it cannot recover is a serious problem FOR THE EMPLOYER.**

> **Such a contractor slows down, substitutes inferior materials, pursues every possible claim, disputes every measurement, and may ultimately abandon the site — leaving the employer to re-tender an incomplete works, which is the most expensive outcome available.**

> **So the price adjustment clause protects the employer's interest in a solvent, motivated contractor at least as much as it protects the contractor.**

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE COMPETITION ARGUMENT AND IT MATTERS PARTICULARLY IN A SMALL MARKET: if inflation risk must be absorbed by the bidder, only firms with deep reserves can take it on, and the field of genuine competitors narrows.**

> **A clause that removes that risk allows medium-sized firms to bid on long contracts, which widens competition and lowers prices — a benefit that accrues entirely to the employer.**

**And the practical requirements for the clause to work:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The INDICES must be published, official and available throughout the contract** ← | **An index that is discontinued mid-contract creates an insoluble dispute** ← |
| **The BASE DATE must be clearly fixed** ← | **Usually 28 days before the bid submission deadline** ← |
| **The WEIGHTINGS must reflect the actual work** ← | **A road contract is fuel and bitumen heavy; a building contract cement, steel and labour heavy** ← |
| **The adjustment applies only to work done WITHIN the contract period** ← | **Work delayed by the contractor's own fault does not attract escalation at the later, higher rates** ← |

> **The last row is an important limitation and a fair one: a contractor in culpable delay must not be rewarded with escalation on prices that have risen during the very period of its own delay.**

> **Which is why the entitlement to extension of time is so closely bound up with escalation entitlement, and why the determination of who caused a delay has direct financial consequences well beyond the liquidated damages.**

examTip.trick: **Adjustment by PUBLISHED INDICES, applied to weighted components, both up and down** — with 10-15 % non-adjustable for overheads and profit.
examTip.trap: **The index, not the contractor's actual costs** — so no audit of purchases is needed, and the contractor still bears its own inefficiency. Market risk transfers; management risk does not.
examTip.mnemonic: **A ruined contractor is the employer's problem** — it slows, substitutes, claims and abandons. And no escalation on work delayed by the contractor's own fault.

questions.stem: In occupational health and safety management, the HIERARCHY OF CONTROLS ranks the measures for dealing with a hazard. The correct order, from the MOST effective to the LEAST, is:
options: Personal protective equipment, administrative controls, engineering controls, substitution, elimination
Engineering controls, elimination, substitution, personal protective equipment, administrative controls
Administrative controls, personal protective equipment, engineering controls, substitution, elimination
Elimination, then substitution, then engineering controls, then administrative controls, and personal protective equipment last
questions.solution:
**ELIMINATION, then SUBSTITUTION, then ENGINEERING controls, then ADMINISTRATIVE controls, and PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT last.**

**The hierarchy, with a construction example of each:**

| Rank | Control | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — ELIMINATION** ← | **Remove the hazard entirely** ← | **Prefabricate at ground level so nobody works at height at all** ← |
| **2 — SUBSTITUTION** ← | **Replace it with something less hazardous** ← | **A water-based sealant instead of a solvent-based one** ← |
| **3 — ENGINEERING controls** ← | **Isolate people from the hazard by a physical means** ← | **Edge protection, guard rails, machine guards, local exhaust ventilation, a trench box** ← |
| **4 — ADMINISTRATIVE controls** ← | **Change how people work** ← | **Permits to work, method statements, training, signage, rotating workers to limit exposure** ← |
| **5 — PPE** ← | **Protect the individual at the point of exposure** ← | **Helmet, harness, boots, gloves, respirator, ear defenders** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE BEHIND THE ORDER IS SIMPLE AND WORTH STATING BECAUSE IT EXPLAINS EVERY RANKING IN THE TABLE: the higher measures do not depend on human behaviour, and the lower ones do.**

> **A hazard that has been ELIMINATED cannot hurt anyone, whatever anyone does or forgets.**

> **A guard rail protects everyone who comes near it, including a visitor who was never trained and a worker who is tired at the end of a shift.**

> **A harness protects only the person who is wearing it, wearing it correctly, and clipped on — three conditions that must be satisfied every single time.**

> **So the effectiveness declines as the reliance on individual compliance increases, and that is the whole logic of the hierarchy.**

**WHY PPE IS RANKED LAST DESPITE BEING THE MOST VISIBLE SAFETY MEASURE ON ANY SITE:**

| Weakness of PPE | Note |
|---|---|
| **It protects ONE person, not everyone exposed** ← | ← |
| **It depends on correct selection, fit, use and maintenance** ← | **A harness worn loose, or clipped to an inadequate anchor, protects nobody** ← |
| **It does nothing about the hazard itself** ← | **The fall risk, the dust, the noise all remain exactly as they were** ← |
| **It is uncomfortable, so compliance decays** ← | **Particularly in heat, and particularly for tasks that take a moment** ← |
| **It fails silently** ← | **A defective respirator gives no warning that it has stopped protecting** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST INSIDIOUS PROPERTY AND IT DESERVES ITS PLACE: a failed engineering control is usually obvious — a guard rail is either there or it is not.**

> **A failed PPE control is invisible: the worker is wearing the equipment, everyone can see that he is, and it is not working.**

> **So an inspection regime that checks whether PPE is being WORN is measuring the wrong thing — it should be asking whether the higher controls were considered first.**

> **AND THAT IS THE REAL FAILURE OF SAFETY MANAGEMENT ON MANY SITES: PPE is issued and enforced diligently while elimination, substitution and engineering controls are never seriously examined, because PPE is cheap, quick and visibly demonstrates that something is being done.**

> **A site where everyone wears a harness at a height that could have been avoided by prefabrication has complied with the letter of safety practice and missed its substance.**

**The high-risk activities in construction, for which the hierarchy is most needed:**

| Hazard | Note |
|---|---|
| **FALLS from height** ← | **The largest single cause of construction deaths worldwide** ← |
| **EXCAVATION collapse** ← | **A cubic metre of soil weighs nearly two tonnes; burial to the chest is usually fatal** ← |
| **Struck by moving plant or falling objects** ← | ← |
| **Electricity — overhead lines and temporary supplies** ← | ← |
| **CONFINED spaces — manholes, tanks, sewers, wet wells** ← | **Where the hazard is invisible and the rescuers frequently become the additional casualties** ← |

> **The last row is worth a closing note because it inverts an instinct: in a confined space fatality, a majority of the deaths are often would-be rescuers who entered without breathing apparatus to help a colleague who had collapsed.**

> **The atmosphere that overcame the first person overcomes the second within seconds, and the entire lesson of confined space procedure is that nobody enters to rescue without equipment and a plan — which is a rule that runs directly against every human instinct, and therefore has to be trained and rehearsed rather than merely written down.**

examTip.trick: **Elimination, substitution, engineering, administrative, PPE** — most to least effective. Remember it as removing the hazard, then the exposure, then finally protecting the person.
examTip.trap: **PPE is LAST, despite being the most visible measure** — it protects one person, depends on correct use every time, does nothing about the hazard, and fails silently.
examTip.mnemonic: **The higher controls do not depend on human behaviour; the lower ones do.** A guard rail protects the untrained visitor; a harness protects only whoever clipped on correctly.

questions.stem: The REGISTRATION (license) EXAMINATION conducted by the Nepal Engineering Council for graduate engineers exists in order to:
options: Rank the graduates of different institutions against one another for the purpose of employment
Establish that each applicant possesses the minimum professional competence
Replace the academic degree as the qualification for entry to the profession
Restrict the number of engineers entering practice each year to match the demand for them
questions.solution:
**To establish that each applicant possesses the MINIMUM PROFESSIONAL COMPETENCE, across the whole prescribed syllabus**, required before being licensed to practise and to take responsibility for engineering work.

**The nature of the examination:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is a COMPETENCE examination, not a competitive one** ← | **Every candidate who reaches the standard passes; there is no quota and no ranking** ← |
| **The pass mark is an ABSOLUTE standard** ← | **50 out of 100, and not a proportion of the candidates** ← |
| **It covers the WHOLE breadth of the discipline** ← | **All ten chapters of the syllabus, since a licensed engineer may be called on in any of them** ← |
| **It is in ADDITION to the academic degree, not a substitute for it** ← | **The degree remains the entry qualification; the examination tests retained, integrated competence** ← (which is why option c is wrong) |
| **It is not a device to limit numbers** ← | **A licensing body that failed competent candidates to control supply would be abusing its statutory purpose** ← (option d) |

> **THE FIRST AND SECOND ROWS TOGETHER MARK THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS MOST, AND IT IS WORTH BEING CLEAR ABOUT BECAUSE IT CHANGES HOW THE EXAMINATION SHOULD BE APPROACHED: this is not a competition against the other candidates.**

> **In a competitive examination, a candidate must outperform others, and there is a reason to specialise and to gamble.**

> **In a competence examination, a candidate must reach a fixed standard across the whole syllabus, and the winning strategy is therefore quite different: cover everything to an adequate depth rather than anything to great depth.**

> **A candidate who is excellent in structures and ignorant of transportation fails, while one who is merely sound in all ten chapters passes comfortably — and that follows directly from the breadth requirement in the third row.**

**Why licensing exists at all, which is the underlying justification:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Engineering work affects PUBLIC SAFETY, and the public cannot assess an engineer's competence** ← | **A client cannot check a structural design; the state therefore certifies competence on the public's behalf** ← |
| **The consequences of incompetence are borne by THIRD PARTIES** ← | **The occupants of a building, the users of a bridge — people who never chose the engineer** ← |
| **Failures are often DELAYED and hidden** ← | **A defective design may stand for years and fail in the one earthquake it was meant for** ← |
| **So the market cannot regulate quality by itself** ← | **Which is the standard economic justification for professional licensing** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ARGUMENT THAT DISTINGUISHES ENGINEERING FROM MOST OTHER SERVICES, AND IT IS THE ONE MOST WORTH UNDERSTANDING: a bad meal is apparent at once and a bad haircut within the hour.**

> **A bad structural design is apparent when the earthquake comes, which may be thirty years after the engineer has been paid, retired, or died.**

> **So the ordinary mechanism by which poor service is punished — customers noticing and going elsewhere — does not operate, and something must stand in its place.**

> **A license granted on demonstrated competence before practice begins is that substitute, and it is why the profession is regulated by statute rather than by reputation.**

**What licensing carries with it, which is the responsibility side of the same coin:**

| Obligation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Only a licensed engineer may practise or use the title** ← | **Practising without registration is an offence under the Act** ← |
| **The licensed engineer takes PERSONAL responsibility for the work they sign** ← | **Which is the substance of the license — a signature that means something** ← |
| **They are bound by the code of professional conduct** ← | **With the public's safety as the paramount obligation** ← |
| **And are subject to the Council's DISCIPLINARY jurisdiction** ← | **Including removal from the register — the sanction that gives the code its force** ← |
| **The license must be kept current** ← | **A lapsed registration is not a license to practise** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHERE THE WHOLE STRUCTURE COMES TO REST AND IT IS THE RIGHT NOTE TO END ON: the point of the license is that a licensed engineer's signature on a drawing is a personal undertaking that the work is competent and safe.**

> **The examination establishes that the person signing has the knowledge to make that undertaking meaningfully; the code of conduct establishes what they owe; and the disciplinary power establishes that it is not merely advice.**

> **Each part of the system depends on the others, and the examination is the gate at the beginning of it — which is why it is set across the full breadth of the discipline rather than on a specialism, and why its standard is absolute rather than relative.**

Across the whole prescribed syllabus, that is required before being licensed to practise and to take responsibility for engineering work.

examTip.trick: **Minimum competence across the WHOLE syllabus before being licensed to take responsibility.** Not a ranking (a), not a substitute for the degree (c), not a quota (d).
examTip.trap: **It is a COMPETENCE examination with an absolute pass mark, not a competition** — so cover all ten chapters adequately rather than a few deeply. Excellent in one and ignorant of another still fails.
examTip.mnemonic: **A bad meal is obvious at once; a bad design when the earthquake comes.** That delay is why the market cannot regulate engineering and why a license is required before practice.
